title: Learning Adaptable Dexterous Skills via Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking
authors: Yuxuan Kuang,Jiashun Wang,Yixuan Sun,Yufei Ye,Sungjae Park,Umar Iqbal,Katerina Fragkiadaki,Shubham Tulsiani
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Graphics (cs.GR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract:
Dexterous multi-finger hands hold promise to unlock diverse skills like functional grasps, in-hand reorientation, and dynamic handover that the human-designed world assumes, yet existing learning recipes force a trade-off. Goal-reaching reinforcement learning generalizes to arbitrary object poses but, lacking any human prior, converges to unnatural and unreliable finger strategies; motion tracking reproduces human-like behavior from a single clip but cannot deviate from it. We present AdaDex, a goal-conditioned RL framework that turns a single hand-object trajectory of a few seconds—from mocap data or HOI reconstruction from in-the-wild RGB(D) video—into an adaptable dexterous skill. At the core of AdaDex is Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking: a shared policy is trained on two populations of massively parallel environments: motion tracking environments trained with dense motion tracking objective, which instill the human prior from human motion; and generalization environments with noised initial states and goals and a sparse object-success reward, which force the skill to work far off the reference. From seconds of human motion per skill, the resulting policies can learn diverse adaptable dexterous skills, such as functional grasping, object reposing, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch. Our method outperforms baselines in terms of generalization and functionality, and we demonstrate transfer across simulators and to the real world.

introduction:
Our built environment is designed around the human hand: tools, handles, lids, and switches all presuppose a multi-fingered end-effector.
Many of the skills this design affords, including functional tool use, in-hand reorientation, and dynamic behaviors such as throwing and catching, remain difficult for parallel-jaw grippers, which makes dexterous hands a natural embodiment for general-purpose manipulation.
Despite this promise, learning dexterous skills is challenging.
A multi-fingered hand must act in a high-dimensional continuous action space with 20+ degrees of freedom, and each skill must regulate contact forces, friction, and gravity across many simultaneous and often intermittent contacts under fast dynamics.

Two paradigms currently dominate learning-based dexterous manipulation, and they fail in complementary ways. Consider picking up a hammer lying on a table and striking a nail. Goal-reaching reinforcement learning (Kuang et al., 2026; Kedia et al., 2026) trains a single policy to move an object from any initial pose to any target pose, achieving broad coverage. Given target hammer poses, such a policy can bring the hammer to the nail. However, an object-centric reward specifies only where the object should end up, not how to get it there. Without explicit shaping, the policy could seize the hammer by its head or pinch it mid-shaft. These grasps might satisfy the goal but are not functional for hammering.
Additionally, behaviors that require finger gaiting or regrasping, such as reorienting the hammer in hand from a lying-flat pickup to a striking grip with functional thumb bracing, are rarely discovered at all. As a result, the intricate motion the task demands remain largely out of reach.
Motion tracking (Li et al., 2025; Mandi et al., 2025), in contrast, imitates a hand-object trajectory under dense supervision and thereby inherits the demonstrator’s functional grasp, in-hand regrasp, and swing. The resulting policy, however, is bound to the reference. If the nail sits at a different location or angle, the policy has no mechanism to adapt, and it typically requires the dense reference as input at inference time. In short, tracking supplies the human prior and goal reaching supplies generalization, but neither alone yields a skill that is both human-like and adaptable.

To that end, we present AdaDex, which treats the two paradigms as complements rather than alternatives. At the core of AdaDex is Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking, built on the observation that motion tracking and goal reaching are the same goal-conditioned problem: both ask a policy πθ​(a∣s,g)\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s,g) to bring the object and wrist to a target pose gg, and differ only in where gg comes from and how progress is rewarded. We therefore train one policy across two kinds of massively parallel environments: Tracking Environments (TrackEnv) initialize along a human hand-object reference τ^\hat{\tau}, take goals from τ^\hat{\tau}, and apply a dense tracking reward on object, wrist, fingers, and contacts, teaching the policy how a human grasps, gaits, and releases. Generalization Environments (GenEnv) perturb the initialization with large noise, offset the goal by a random SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) transformation that can be far from any frame of τ^\hat{\tau}, and reward only sparse object success plus wrist guidance, with no finger terms. The two are mutually reinforcing. TrackEnv supplies the prior and the exploration: skills that sparse reward almost never discovers, such as throwing an object and catching it mid-flight, are learned under dense tracking and, because gg is the only channel of task information, become directly addressable by novel goals. GenEnv supplies the generalization: it forces success from off-reference states toward off-reference goals so the skill can be adaptable to new scenarios and does not collapse into replaying one clip, while leaving the finger strategy to the human prior. Neither suffices alone; together they yield a skill that is both functional and adaptable. The recipe needs no discriminator, phase variable, or distillation stage, and the dense reference is not required at test time: at deployment the policy consumes only proprioception, object pose, object shape, and a goal pose, so it can be driven by any goal source, such as VLM Agent planner’s output waypoints.

We evaluate AdaDex on functional grasping of diverse tools and household objects, in-hand reorientation requiring finger gaiting and contact switching, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch. Every skill is learned from a single human motion trajectory of a few seconds. The learned policies preserve the grasp type, in-hand manipulation, and dynamic behaviors from human motion, while generalizing to unseen trajectories and randomized object goals far from the reference, and achieve various downstream tasks with VLM Agents under multiple embodiments. Additionally, we demonstrate that our recipe can be embedded in between real-to-sim and sim-to-real, where a few seconds of human motion from in-the-wild RGB(D) videos is converted into a simulation-ready hand-object reference via our advanced HOI reconstruction pipeline. And then the reference is broadened into an adaptable skill in simulation as described above, and the resulting simulation rollout is transferred to a real arm-hand robotic system with real-time dynamics. In summary, our contributions are:

Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking. A goal-conditioned RL formulation in which dense reference tracking and sparse goal reaching are trained as parallel environment types under a single shared actor, so that the human prior from tracking and the coverage from goal reaching reinforce one another. The formulation requires no dense reference input at inference.

Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking. A goal-conditioned RL formulation in which dense reference tracking and sparse goal reaching are trained as parallel environment types under a single shared actor, so that the human prior from tracking and the coverage from goal reaching reinforce one another. The formulation requires no dense reference input at inference.

Adaptable dexterous skills. Human-like functional grasping, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch, each learned from seconds of human motion and generalized to novel states and goals. The resulting adaptable skills can achieve various downstream tasks under diverse embodiments with VLM Agent planners.

Learning from real-to-sim HOI motions. A reconstruction pipeline that converts a clip of in-the-wild human video into a simulation-ready hand-object reference, outperforming existing HOI reconstruction baselines. This pipeline allows us to learn adaptable dexterous skills from human data and transfer their simulation rollouts across simulators and to the real world.

1. Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking. A goal-conditioned RL formulation in which dense reference tracking and sparse goal reaching are trained as parallel environment types under a single shared actor, so that the human prior from tracking and the coverage from goal reaching reinforce one another. The formulation requires no dense reference input at inference.

2. Adaptable dexterous skills. Human-like functional grasping, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch, each learned from seconds of human motion and generalized to novel states and goals. The resulting adaptable skills can achieve various downstream tasks under diverse embodiments with VLM Agent planners.

3. Learning from real-to-sim HOI motions. A reconstruction pipeline that converts a clip of in-the-wild human video into a simulation-ready hand-object reference, outperforming existing HOI reconstruction baselines. This pipeline allows us to learn adaptable dexterous skills from human data and transfer their simulation rollouts across simulators and to the real world.

title: UniWALM: Unified World Action Language Model for Embodied Robot Control
authors: Rahul Sajnani,Diego Romeres,Mingyuan Zhang,Kai Gao,Carl Qi,Baichuan Huang,Srinath Sridhar,Dylan Randle,Lillian J. Ratliff,Jose Barreiros,Manikantan Nambi,Jeroen Vanbaar
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Motivated by the human ability to integrate experience across language, perception, and action, we introduce UniWALM, a unified world-action-language model that learns video, action, and language in a single shared representation, where each modality is both a conditioning signal and a supervision target.
We ask: can jointly generating language enrich this shared representation, improving manipulation and supporting memory-dependent behavior?
Unlike prior approaches that attach a reasoning or vision-language model to a video-action backbone and run them as distinct stages, UniWALM unifies all three modalities inside a single mixture-of-transformers backbone whose per-modality diffusion heads co-denoise synchronously, decoding subtask and textual memory in the same pass as action with no separate planning stage; the generated language is re-consumed on the next step, closing a language-as-memory loop without an external planner or memory bank.
To keep the action stream reliable under this richer objective, we further introduce Flow Matching with Correction (FMC), a training objective that teaches recovery from perturbed action trajectories at no inference-time cost.
UniWALM consistently improves over same-backbone baselines (e.g., FastWAM [52]) on compositional pick-and-place (MolmoSpaces) and across the memory-dependent subset of RMBench [10], where it reaches 34.5% without any pretrained language or reasoning model and exceeds Mem-0’s keyframe-equipped setup (28.5%) using only a single anchor frame.
On a real-world Find-the-Item task, generating textual memory lifts success from 11.1% to 61.1%, while state-of-the-art VLAs stay at or below chance (≤33.3%\leq 33.3\%).
introduction:
Humans integrate perception, language, and action in an any-to-any manner: regions like the posterior parietal and premotor cortex continuously fuse afferent inputs with efferent motor copies [2], and cognitive representations are inherently shaped by what an agent can do in the world [19, 12]. For embodied agents, language, video, and action are three complementary views of a single interaction; a unified representation should let each one inform the others: language guiding physical prediction, visual dynamics grounding action, and action anchoring predictions in embodied behavior. Multimodal models have operationalized this framing for vision and text [31, 47, 55] but largely omit action and motor control.

The same substrate that integrates these modalities also remembers: the hippocampus, which the brain uses to recall past experience, is also recruited to imagine the future and locate the self in time [17, 53]. We routinely enlist language itself as working memory (counting out loud, repeating a phone number, silently rehearsing a passage while reading to retain it) to track state through long-horizon, memory-dependent tasks. A truly unified representation should therefore not only let modalities inform one another but also let generated language serve as the working memory that threads behavior across step boundaries. Concretely, because language is co-denoised with action in one representation, the generated string serves as a learned, in-loop plan (next subtask) and textual memory (what has been done so far), while an anchor-frame visual memory preserves scene context across occlusion; re-consumed on the next step, these close a memory loop with no external planner, VLM, or retrieval buffer.

Recent robotic foundation models connect video, language, and action, but typically along only a subset of these directions. Vision-language-action models [36, 26] consume language as fixed conditioning but do not generate it. Chain-of-thought VLAs [21, 6, 54, 3, 56] generate intermediate language within a control step, but autoregressively, so action must wait for token decoding, and the generated string is not re-consumed across steps. World-action models (DreamZero [51], FastWAM [52]) co-model video and action but drop language entirely. Memory-augmented systems [42, 35, 10] attach retrieval buffers or an external planner to a pretrained backbone; π0.7\pi_{0.7} [35] supplies language from a high-level semantic policy while a separate world model generates subgoal images that condition a VLA (Fig. 1(f)). On memory-dependent evaluations like RMBench [10]’s M⁡(n)M(n) subset, where decisions require nn task-relevant past observations, policies that condition only on the current frame and prompt collapse.

A natural response is to compose a pretrained vision-language model with a video-action backbone and supply reasoning via auxiliary conditioning or an additional loss (Fig. 1(f)). This family (hybrid planner + VLA systems [35], concurrent compositional WALMs) is more accurately described as WAM + VLM features: it typically uses two vision backbones optimized for different objectives and only loosely coupled, treats language as an external hidden state rather than a generation target, and bolts memory on as a separate retrieval module. UniWALM (Fig. 1(g)) uses a single video backbone jointly optimized for all three modalities, with video, action, and language as first-class diffusion heads co-denoised in one pass; the generated language is re-consumed next step, closing a language-as-memory loop with no external planner, VLM, or memory bank. Where prior world-action models supervise the backbone with frame-level predictive structure (future video), UniWALM adds a task-level predictive stream (future subtask and task state as language), a second, longer-horizon supervision signal that frame prediction alone cannot cheaply express.

In this work we study two questions: (i) does jointly generating language enrich the shared representation of a video-action model and improve manipulation? (Fig. 1(g)) and (ii) can a policy use its own generated language, re-consumed across steps, as working memory on memory-dependent tasks? (Fig. 2)

We introduce UniWALM, a multimodal world-model architecture that takes a step toward any-to-any modeling across language, video, and actions, where each modality serves as both a conditioning signal and a supervision target. Specifically:

World-Action-Language Model (WALM): We introduce WALM, a unified World Action Language Model implemented as a mixture of transformers that takes video, language, and actions as input and generates all three as output. The language stream emits a subtask and textual memory in the same denoising pass as action, and re-consumes them as prompt on the next control step, closing a language-as-memory loop. UniWALM’s language and action experts are trained from scratch on a video-only backbone: no pretrained language or reasoning model is used.

World-Action-Language Model (WALM): We introduce WALM, a unified World Action Language Model implemented as a mixture of transformers that takes video, language, and actions as input and generates all three as output. The language stream emits a subtask and textual memory in the same denoising pass as action, and re-consumes them as prompt on the next control step, closing a language-as-memory loop. UniWALM’s language and action experts are trained from scratch on a video-only backbone: no pretrained language or reasoning model is used.

Flow Matching with Correction (FMC). We introduce FMC to improve the reliability of generated actions. During training, FMC perturbs action trajectories and supervises a corrective velocity that returns the perturbed denoising path toward the clean trajectory. This trains recovery from action-space perturbations without adding model capacity or sampling steps at inference.

Evaluation in simulation and real-world manipulation. UniWALM achieves the highest success on all three MolmoSpaces [24] compositional pick-and-place variants, improving over the same-backbone FastWAM baseline by +14.8% on average (Tab. 1). On RMBench’s memory-dependent M(n) subset, UniWALM reaches 34.5% without pretrained language or reasoning model, improving over same-backbone FastWAM (13.3%) by +21.2 points and above Mem-0’s keyframe-equipped setup (28.5%) using a single anchor frame instead of per-task privileged keyframes (Tab. 3). On a real-world bimanual Find-the-Item task, generating textual memory lifts success from 11.1% (FastWAM, same video backbone, no language) to 61.1%, while state-of-the-art VLAs stay at or below chance (≤33.3%\leq 33.3\%) (Tab. 2).

Together, these results motivate further investigation of any-to-any world modeling as a foundation for generalist embodied agents.

UniWALM’s language and action experts are trained from scratch on a video-only backbone: no pretrained language or reasoning model is used.

2. Flow Matching with Correction (FMC). We introduce FMC to improve the reliability of generated actions. title: Industrial ReMEmbR: Scaling Spatiotemporal Memory to Robot Fleets
authors: Jad Yammine,Malek Wahidi,Abrar Anwar,Yan Chang,Mihir Acharya,Anthony Rizk
abstract: Warehouse robot fleets continuously observe operational conditions, but preserving these observations as reusable semantic memory incurs substantial computation, communication, and storage costs. For example, explaining recurring aisle blockages can require reviewing video from multiple robots across several shifts. We present Industrial ReMEmbR, a shared spatiotemporal memory system that extends NVIDIA ReMEmbR to robot fleets and reduces server-side computation by generating scene descriptions only on demand. On each robot, an NVIDIA Jetson encodes video clips into retrieval embeddings with Cosmos-Embed1, vision tokens with Cosmos3-Edge, and reconstruction latents with the Wan2.2 VAE, without uploading raw camera frames. The encoding models are re-used to detect people in image patches, zeroing them out to support PII abstraction for GDPR-compliant deployments. We split Cosmos3-Edge at its vision–language boundary, placing the vision encoder on the robot and the language decoder on an on-premises server. A Nemotron agent retrieves memories by content, position, and time and queries the decoder using cached vision tokens. This design eliminates caption generation at write time, while cached-token decoding reproduces the unsplit model’s output in all 450 tested decodes. On the NaVQA benchmark, the updated model stack achieves comparable retrieval recall while reducing unparsable answers from 4.5% to 1.9% with an agent half the parameter size. We further demonstrate a live semantic traffic map that classifies aisle conditions directly from retrieval embeddings. Across 914 simulated warehouse frames, this method exceeds the best caption-based alternative by 6.0 percentage points. By decoupling memory encoding from description, Industrial ReMEmbR transforms a fleet’s collective experience into an extensible foundation for spatial and temporal reasoning, including faithful scene reconstruction, context-guided elaboration, and semantic mapping of dynamic warehouse conditions as they unfold.
introduction:
An embodied memory lets a robot recall what it has seen, where, and when, long after the moment has passed. NVIDIA’s ReMEmbR (Anwar et al., 2025), a spatiotemporal memory system designed for long-horizon visual question answering for robot navigation, showed that a single robot can build such a memory from its own camera stream. On a warehouse floor, however, that robot is only one of many. A fleet management system, or fleet manager, continuously tracks dozens of autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) and other integrated devices in a modern warehouse, assigning them orders and planning their routes over VDA5050, the standard interface between mobile robots and fleet management systems. Obstacles outside the tracking system are left to each robot’s intelligent navigation system to recognize and avoid. What a passing robot sees is rarely kept, because continuously uploading and storing raw video from every robot is expensive, so the rich semantic context of each scene never reaches the rest of the fleet.

To illustrate, consider the case of a fleet management system that keeps routing AMRs through an aisle partially blocked by a clutter of untracked obstacles. Each robot independently maneuvers around the clutter, losing time before carrying on with its scheduled tasks. A few days later, a human operator reviewing the daily logs notices that task completion times slipped that day, but has no record of the scene from which to trace its root cause. Neither the fleet manager nor the operator has the semantic context that could have prevented the congestion, by adaptively routing later robots away from the aisle, or its recurrence, by revealing what caused it.

Closing this contextual blind spot requires scaling embodied memory from a single robot to the entire fleet, with every connected robot acting as a live reporter from the warehouse floor that continuously contributes its observations, tagged with location and time, to a shared fleet memory. In the scenario above, the first robot to encounter the clutter would report it on a live semantic map, letting the fleet manager route subsequent robots around the blocked aisle. Days later, the operator could ask the fleet’s shared semantic memory what caused the reroutes and receive an answer grounded in direct visual observation: when and where the clutter appeared, and what it consisted of. The same record can supply the world state of a centralized planner such as RobotFleet (Gupta et al., 2025), which schedules heterogeneous robots from declarative statements about the site and replans when a robot reports a discovery.

To this end, we build on ReMEmbR, which captions each short video clip, stores the caption along with the robot’s time and location and a corresponding caption embedding, and lets an agentic model perform semantic retrieval over the vector database to answer arbitrary questions. Scaling this design from one robot to a fleet breaks three of its assumptions, and each break motivates one principle of our design. First, ReMEmbR generates a caption for every clip as it is written, so its cost grows with every robot added and every hour it operates, and continuously uploading raw video from every robot is costly to begin with. We therefore encode once, compressing each clip on the robot’s own edge compute into compact representations that every later step reuses. Second, ReMEmbR answers occasional questions, whereas the fleet manager also needs a continuously updated view of the site. We therefore interpret continuously, reading that state directly from each memory as it arrives, without generating any text. Third, the questions a memory must answer are not known when it is first encoded. We therefore elaborate on demand, deferring any description of a scene until a question about it arrives. In the blocked aisle example, the clutter is encoded once by the first robot that passes it, flagged on the live map as soon as its memory arrives, and described in detail only when the operator asks about it days later.

We present Industrial ReMEmbR (Fig. 1), a shared memory system built around these three principles. It encodes clips on edge compute across the fleet, continuously aggregates and interprets them on server compute for live semantic mapping, and elaborates on any of them on demand. Each robot’s onboard Jetson edge-compute device runs iw.encode, the edge component for efficient multi-purpose encoding. This deployed service continuously generates video-text embedding vectors for memory retrieval derived from Cosmos-Embed1 (NVIDIA, 2025), vision tokens for optional scene description derived from the detached vision encoder of Cosmos3-Edge (NVIDIA, 2026a), and compressed latent frames for optional scene inspection generated by the Wan2.2 VAE (Team Wan, 2025b; Team Wan, 2025a) encoder. Only the aforementioned multi-purpose scene representations, robot pose and memory timestamp are uploaded into a shared fleet memory, whose vector index is accelerated with NVIDIA cuVS (RAPIDS Team, 2024).

To reduce server-side computation, we generate scene descriptions and answers on demand for memories retrieved by the agent, rather than captioning every encoded clip.
We enable this by splitting Cosmos3-Edge at its vision–language boundary, where its server-side language decoder answers questions from cached vision tokens without accessing or re-encoding the original clips.
We deploy a Nemotron-3-Nano-4B (NVIDIA, 2026b; NVIDIA et al., 2025) agent through an NVIDIA NIM inference microservice to retrieve memories by content, position, and time, and optionally query the decoder with a text prompt and the retrieved vision tokens.
Operators can also reconstruct scenes from stored latent frames for visual inspection.
On NaVQA, Upgraded ReMEmbR, our version of ReMEmbR updated with the NVIDIA models and a video-based index, achieves comparable retrieval recall while reducing unparseable answers from 4.5% to 1.9% with an agent half the parameter size.

We demonstrate the system through a live semantic traffic map that communicates observed aisle conditions to the fleet manager.
We classify each robot’s latest observation by comparing its retrieval embedding with paired text prompts describing occupied and clear aisles.
A map service periodically queries the agent for these classifications and updates predefined semantic zones using robot poses already reported to the fleet manager over VDA5050.
In a simulated warehouse, this approach achieves 71.3% balanced accuracy, exceeding the best caption-based alternative evaluated with the same models by 6.0 percentage points.
We deploy each model as a modular service to support future extensions for station-readiness checks, landmark-based navigation guidance for deployed policy models, and curation of diverse preprocessed training data (Section 7).

Our contributions are:

Video-native agentic memory. We rebuild ReMEmbR on an efficient NVIDIA model stack and move its index key from the caption to the video itself. Retrieval is no longer bottlenecked by what a captioner chose to mention, and a smaller, tool-calling agent returns more reliable structured answers (Section 3).

title: Physical Canvas: A Vision Tactile World Model For Robot Policy Evaluation And Learning
authors: Zebin Xing,Yuhang Zheng,Yupeng Zheng,Yichen Zhang,Zichen Li,Shangqing Zhou,Yujie Zang,Yuchen Liu,Zhongpu Xia,Haoran Li,Qichao Zhang
abstract: Evaluating and post-training robot policies through physical interaction is costly and difficult to scale, motivating action-conditioned world models as interactive simulators. However, visually plausible predictions can misrepresent contact dynamics, providing unreliable feedback for policy evaluation and learning. We introduce PhysCanvas, a state-consistent visuo-tactile world model for contact-rich robot manipulation. PhysCanvas unifies multi-view RGB, tactile images, marker displacement, task state, and actions within a unified vision space. All modalities share a video VAE and pretrained generative backbone, allowing optical touch to reuse visual and temporal priors. Motion images derived through forward kinematics and camera projection provide spatially aligned action conditioning, while an initial RGB anchor and updated reference observations guide sequential generation. Our consistency-aware post-training uses the frozen Scene Reward Model, Modality Reward Model, and State Reward Model to supervise scene preservation, visual–tactile compatibility, and agreement with real task outcomes. The resulting world model supports closed-loop policy rollouts for evaluation and provides imagined interactions and rewards for GRPO policy updates. Across four real-world manipulation tasks, when policies are rolled out in the world model, State Reward Model supervision increases the arithmetic mean of task-wise Pearson correlations between world-model and real-world success rates from 0.6020.602 to 0.8850.885. Policy post-training in the reward-guided world model further increases π0.5\pi_{0.5}’s mean real-world success rate from a 59.1%59.1\% SFT baseline to 70.8%70.8\%. These results demonstrate the value of unified multimodal modeling and consistency-aware post-training for robot policy evaluation and learning. Project page: https://zebinx.github.io/PhysCanvas_HomePage/.
introduction:
Robot world models predict how environments evolve in response to actions, offering low-cost, reproducible interactions for policy evaluation and learning (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Wu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2026). Contact-rich manipulation requires both visual observations of scene dynamics and tactile feedback about contact changes (Yuan et al., 2017; Lambeta et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Guzey et al., 2024). A world model that captures these complementary signals and their associated task outcomes could reduce the need for repeated physical trials.

Recent action-conditioned video models combine pretrained generative priors with action representations to support interactive prediction, policy evaluation, and learning in imagination (Wu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a). Existing visuo-tactile models, however, typically require a dedicated tactile encoder and a custom interface for injecting tactile features into a general backbone (Zheng et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026). Adapting to new tactile data or sensor configurations may therefore require retraining, limiting generality and complicating the pipeline. Meanwhile, token-wise reconstruction supervision emphasizes local fidelity and can miss high-level semantics such as task success. Reliable rollouts thus require visual observations, tactile feedback, and predicted task outcomes to describe the consequences of the same action; inconsistencies can mislead policy optimization (Yang et al., 2026b; Jiang et al., 2026). For example, after an object slips, predicting stable tactile contact or eventual success is semantically inconsistent despite visually plausible frames. The challenge is to build a reusable multimodal model while preserving scene, cross-modal, and task-outcome consistency for policy evaluation and learning.

We investigate two questions: (1) Can a simple, general mechanism encode heterogeneous modalities in a shared space? (2) Can high-level semantics be injected into the world model without additional networks?

To address this challenge, we introduce PhysCanvas, a world model with state consistency for visual and tactile prediction, robot policy evaluation, and learning. PhysCanvas places multiple modalities in a shared generative space and uses consistency supervision during post training to preserve the interaction dynamics and task outcomes induced by actions, providing interactive, coherent observations.

Specifically, PhysCanvas places multiview RGB, tactile images, marker displacement, and task state on a unified canvas predicted by a shared video VAE and generative backbone, allowing optical touch to reuse pretrained visual and temporal priors (Wan Team et al., 2025). Actions are encoded as spatially aligned motion images through forward kinematics and camera projection (Wu et al., 2026), while an initial RGB anchor and updated references guide sequential generation. During post training, the frozen Scene Reward Model, Modality Reward Model, and State Reward Model enforce scene preservation, visual and tactile compatibility, and agreement with real outcomes, including both success and failure. The resulting model supports evaluation in a closed loop and supplies imagined interactions and rewards for GRPO policy updates (Shao et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2026).

We evaluate PhysCanvas on four real-world manipulation tasks: test-tube placement, bottle-cap unscrewing, block relocation, and Rubik’s Cube manipulation (Figure 2). When policies are rolled out in the world model, post-training improves the Pearson correlation between their world-model and real-world success rates on every task, increasing the arithmetic mean of task-wise correlations from 0.6020.602 to 0.8850.885. Each task includes nine evaluation batches spanning ACT, FM, and π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Zhao et al., 2023; Lipman et al., 2023; Black et al., 2025); the batches are evaluated at different times, and each task receives equal weight in the summary. Policy optimization through reward-guided imagined interactions further improves the mean real-world success rate of π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 11.711.7 percentage points over SFT, from 59.1%59.1\% to 70.8%70.8\% across the four tasks. These results demonstrate utility for reliable evaluation and policy improvement.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a unified canvas space that jointly models vision, touch, task state, and actions using a shared video generation framework; (2) consistency-aware post-training that constrains generated interactions through scene, modality, and task-state supervision; and (3) a framework for policy evaluation and learning in imagination, evaluated on real robots.

title: AgenticRoboRL: Bringing Coding-Agent Post-Training to Agentic Robotics
authors: Xinxin Liu,Bingxin Xu,Wenrui Bao,Ming Li,Wentao Bao,Chen Chen,Yuzhang Shang
abstract: Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses to perform complex manipulation tasks. Recent work improves these systems through better harnesses and external memory, but relies on powerful closed-source models as planners and does not improve the planners’ own capabilities. In contrast, coding agents have improved substantially by post-training the model itself. We therefore investigate whether post-training can also improve robot planners. However, applying it across robot harnesses requires accommodating different execution mechanisms, including VLA skill invocation and control-code generation. To this end, we introduce AgenticRoboRL, a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses. The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning. To accommodate different execution mechanisms, harness-specific adapters connect recorded planner interactions with task outcomes, enabling a common RL training pipeline while keeping execution components fixed. On LIBERO-PRO, AgenticRoboRL raises the success rate of a 9B-parameter planner from 18.1% to 71.0% without external memory, approaching the 72.1% achieved by Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory. These results demonstrate post-training as an effective approach for improving robot planners. We will release the framework and trained planner checkpoints.
introduction:
Agentic robotics systems can perform complex manipulation tasks by combining a planner with a robot harness. The planner invokes VLA skills (Zhang et al., 2026c) or generates control code (Liang et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2026), observes the execution results, and decides what to do next over multiple rounds of interaction. Recent work has improved performance by refining robot harnesses and storing experience from task exploration in external memory (Zhang et al., 2026c; Xu et al., 2026b), with coding agents such as Codex and Claude Code (OpenAI, 2025; Anthropic, 2025) serving as planners. However, these approaches primarily leverage existing planner capabilities and strengthen the support available to the planner. We explore a complementary direction: enhancing planners’ own capabilities to improve the performance of agentic robotics systems.

For coding agents, enhancing the model’s own capabilities through post-training, including supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, has proven highly effective (Pan et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026; Cao et al., 2025). These advances raise a natural question: Can the post-training methods used for coding agents also improve the performance of agentic robotics systems?

Applying these methods to robot planners is complicated by the fact that robot harnesses differ in how they carry out a planner’s response. In some harnesses the planner calls learned VLA skills, and a VLA policy executes each call. In others the planner writes control code over perception and control APIs, and a motion controller executes it. Harnesses also differ in what feedback they return to the planner and in how they decide whether the task has succeeded. Training planners across harnesses therefore requires a single pipeline that supports these different execution mechanisms.

To realize such a pipeline, we introduce AgenticRoboRL, a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses (Figure 1). The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL). SFT trains the planner on successful demonstrations, providing a starting point for RL. During RL, we train on recorded planner requests and responses, while harness-specific adapters associate these interactions with episode outcomes. This allows the same RL pipeline to support VLA skill invocation and control-code generation without changing their execution interfaces. In both stages, only the planner is optimized, while the underlying execution components remain fixed (Figure 2).

We evaluate the pipeline across these two execution mechanisms using a 9B planner. With RPent (Zhang et al., 2026c), a harness that invokes VLA skills, SFT improves success on LIBERO-PRO from 18.1% to 65.1%, and RL further raises it to 71.0%, without external memory. The same checkpoint achieves 72.2% on LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025a) without additional training, compared with 19.2% for the original model. With the CaP-X harness (Fu et al., 2026), post-training improves success from 2.7% to 28.5%. These results establish post-training as an effective approach for improving agentic robotics systems.

Our contributions are threefold:

To our knowledge, AgenticRoboRL is the first general post-training framework to agentic robotics systems.

AgenticRoboRL first fine-tunes the planner on successful demonstrations and then refines it with RL, updating only the planner while keeping execution components fixed. Lightweight harness-specific adapters link each recorded planner call to its episode outcome, so the harnesses do not need a shared low-level action representation.

Strong empirical results and an open release. With AgenticRoboRL, a 9B planner improves from 18.1% to 71.0% on LIBERO-PRO without external memory. This nearly matches Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory (72.1%) (Zhang et al., 2026c). With the CaP-X harness, it improves from 2.7% to 28.5%. We will release the AgenticRoboRL framework and trained planner checkpoints.

2. AgenticRoboRL first fine-tunes the planner on successful demonstrations and then refines it with RL, updating only the planner while keeping execution components fixed. Lightweight harness-specific adapters link each recorded planner call to its episode outcome, so the harnesses do not need a shared low-level action representation.

3. Strong empirical results and an open release. With AgenticRoboRL, a 9B planner improves from 18.1% to 71.0% on LIBERO-PRO without external memory. This nearly matches Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory (72.1%) (Zhang et al., 2026c). With the CaP-X harness, it improves from 2.7% to 28.5%. title: SceneRig: An Agentic System for Simulation-Ready 3D Scene Reconstruction from Single Images
authors: Rundong Luo,Yunong Liu,Di Cao,Matthew Tancik,Shyamal Buch,Colton Stearns,Wenqi Xian
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026 Agentic Robotics Workshop. Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Simulation is a powerful tool for robotics, but building diverse, simulation-ready scenes at scale remains difficult. Reconstructing scenes from single images is a promising alternative, but visual similarity alone is insufficient: objects must also be recovered, accurately placed, and physically grounded. Existing methods that rely on post-hoc physics settling often misplace objects, producing scenes that look correct but behave poorly under manipulation.
We present SceneRig, an agentic system that turns a single image into an editable, simulation-ready scene. SceneRig combines geometric, visual, and physical tools to reconstruct a faithful 3D scene. An agent then performs edit-and-validate loops inside a physics simulator to achieve physical stability.
Across diverse inputs, SceneRig improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement while keeping the reconstructed scenes physically stable. Furthermore, SceneRig is effective for downstream robotics: its scenes predict real-robot policy outcomes more accurately than the baseline method and more reliably support replay of recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation.
introduction:
Evaluating the quality and robustness of action policies remains a fundamental bottleneck in robotics.
While physical execution is the gold standard, on-robot evaluations are notoriously difficult to scale: they demand expensive hardware, human supervision, and repeated trials across tasks and conditions [li2024simpler].
Consequently, simulation is a powerful alternative that enables large-scale policy evaluation [yang2026robolab].
However, scaling these environments remains difficult, as constructing realistic scenes requires substantial manual effort [jain2025polaris].

Recent advances in agentic reconstruction and 3D generation have made real-to-sim scene reconstruction a promising route to scaling simulation environments [viga2026, chen2026sam3d, simfoundry2026].
In fact, real-to-sim digital twins go beyond mere scaling: they capture the objects and arrangements of physical workspaces and let anyone turn a single photo into a simulation environment for policy evaluation.
Yet, despite recent progress in real-to-sim, balancing high-quality 3D reconstruction with faithful, robot-ready simulation physics remains challenging [ma2026rest3d, chen2026agentic].
Even when a reconstruction is physically settled, objects can move away from their observed positions, producing a stable scene that no longer matches the robot’s workspace.
To bridge this gap, we propose SceneRig, an agentic system for simulation-ready 3D scene reconstruction from a single image.
SceneRig addresses this problem by coupling image-guided pose refinement with physical validation for faithful trajectory replay and policy evaluation.

Making this coupling effective requires the agent to inspect the effects of physical simulation and use that feedback to guide further corrections.
Even GPT-6 Astra struggles to achieve accurate, physically stable object placement through VIGA or a general-purpose coding agent when the reconstructed scenes are evaluated after physical settling (Table 4).
SceneRig’s core contribution is therefore a harness that connects the agent’s visual reasoning with geometric and physical tools for accurate, stable scene reconstruction. The agent uses the updated scene and feedback from the edit to decide what to investigate or correct next.

More concretely, SceneRig uses a flexible, modular harness with four stages.
First, SceneRig builds a relational scene graph, identifying objects and their support relationships.
Next, scene object creation uses 2D and 3D vision
models to estimate metric geometry and reconstruct object meshes. We then assign physical properties and initialize object placement through geometric alignment and support-ordered settling.
Third, specialized agents construct the surrounding geometry, materials, and lighting, with
strict rule-based verification gates for geometry and visual verification of all three.
Finally, and most importantly, SceneRig executes a physical edit-and-validate loop.
The agent selects which object to adjust and whether to change its position, scale, or orientation; geometric and physical tools search for an adjustment and test its effects in simulation.
Although the current implementation leverages specific state-of-the-art models, SceneRig is designed to incorporate future foundation models.

We evaluate SceneRig on diverse images, spanning synthetic renderings, real robot workspaces, AI-generated images, and in-the-wild smartphone captures.
We demonstrate that SceneRig improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D object placement over existing methods, with all evaluated scenes passing physical stability checks (Tables 1, 2).
Beyond geometric reconstruction, we show that SceneRig yields robot-ready environments (Figure 1), supporting both real-to-sim policy evaluation and open-loop trajectory replay.
In summary, our contributions are:

We introduce SceneRig, an agentic system that reconstructs simulation-ready digital twins from a single image, prioritizing physical grounding in addition to visual similarity.

We build a modular harness that equips agents with geometric and physical tools.
Through iterative edit-and-validate loops, SceneRig directly incorporates physics into pose refinement.

SceneRig improves reconstruction quality and robotics performance over single-image real-to-sim systems. Compared with the baseline, it increases open-loop trajectory replay success from 36% to 80% and episode-level agreement with real-world policy result from 54% to 69%.

1. We introduce SceneRig, an agentic system that reconstructs simulation-ready digital twins from a single image, prioritizing physical grounding in addition to visual similarity.

2. We build a modular harness that equips agents with geometric and physical tools.
Through iterative edit-and-validate loops, SceneRig directly incorporates physics into pose refinement.

3. SceneRig improves reconstruction quality and robotics performance over single-image real-to-sim systems. Compared with the baseline, it increases open-loop trajectory replay success from 36% to 80% and episode-level agreement with real-world policy result from 54% to 69%.

title: MAPLE: Mondrian-Anchored Prior for Learning-free Indoor Exploration
authors: Kelvin Aladum,Nisar Ahmed
abstract: Robots exploring unknown indoor environments must decide where to move while much of the environment remains unseen. Predicting the occupancy of unseen space beyond the current sensor range can improve these decisions, but recent approaches commonly rely on learned models that require offline training and repeated inference during exploration. We introduce the Mondrian-Anchored Prior for Learning-free Indoor Exploration (MAPLE), a training-free predictive approach that adapts the Mondrian process into an online generative prior conditioned on observed geometric cues in the current partial map. MAPLE generates multiple plausible map hypotheses and evaluates visibility separately within each to estimate frontier gain, preserving differences in predicted visibility across hypotheses. Across KTH floor-plans and real-SLAM environments at multiple sensor ranges, MAPLE consistently improves over non-predictive exploration and remains competitive with learned predictive approaches. Its lightweight procedural construction enables predictive exploration with limited computational resources. Experimental results further show that more accurate map prediction does not necessarily produce better exploration, highlighting the importance of how predictions are represented and used in exploration decisions.
introduction:
Autonomous exploration is a key capability for robots operating in unknown or dangerous environments, with applications in search and rescue, emergency response, and infrastructure inspection [1, 2]. In these settings, robots must repeatedly decide where to move while much of the environment remains unseen. Frontier-based exploration makes this decision by identifying frontiers at the boundary between observed free space and unknown space [3]. Connected frontier regions are represented by frontier candidates that serve as possible exploration goals, and selecting among them directly affects exploration efficiency.

Classical frontier methods select frontiers using measures such as travel cost, expected coverage, or information gain [3, 4, 5, 6]. These measures are typically computed from the current partial occupancy map, so they provide little information about occupancy beyond the sensor range, even though that occupancy can strongly affect how much new space a frontier will reveal. Predictive exploration addresses this limitation by estimating the occupancy of unseen space before frontier selection [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13].
Most recent predictive approaches rely on learned models [8, 10, 11]. These methods can produce useful occupancy predictions but require offline training and repeated inference during exploration. Their computational demands can be restrictive for robots with limited compute and power, and performance may degrade when the operating environment differs from the training data. This tradeoff is particularly relevant at short sensor ranges, where frontier selection depends more heavily on occupancy beyond the current sensor range [14]. These considerations motivate a lightweight alternative that can generate predictions directly from the partial map during exploration.

We introduce the Mondrian-Anchored Prior for Learning-free Indoor Exploration (MAPLE), a training-free predictive approach for two-dimensional occupancy-grid exploration. MAPLE builds on the Mondrian process [15], which recursively partitions a rectangular region using axis-aligned cuts, and guides this process using geometric cues from the current partial map. Repeated sampling produces multiple plausible map completions of the unseen space, each treated as a map hypothesis.
Different map hypotheses can imply different visibility from the same frontier candidate. MAPLE therefore evaluates each hypothesis separately and averages the resulting coverage gains before accounting for travel cost. Fig. 1 illustrates how differing predicted walls can change visibility for the same candidate.

We evaluate MAPLE on ten KTH floor plans and ten real-SLAM maps at sensor ranges of 5, 10, and 20 m. The experiments examine end-to-end exploration, map-prediction quality, frontier-decision quality, and computational cost. Controlled ablations also test the effects of the map-prediction method, gain estimator, conditioning on observed geometry, and the number of hypotheses.

Our contributions are as follows:

We introduce MAPLE, a lightweight training-free generative prior that adapts the Mondrian process to generate multiple plausible map hypotheses from geometric cues in the current partial map.

We formulate a hypothesis-wise frontier-gain estimator that evaluates visibility separately within each map hypothesis before averaging the resulting gains.

We provide a controlled comparison of learned, training-free, and non-predictive exploration under shared sensing, frontier candidates, and travel cost, separating prediction, decision, exploration, and computational performance.

2. We formulate a hypothesis-wise frontier-gain estimator that evaluates visibility separately within each map hypothesis before averaging the resulting gains.

3. We provide a controlled comparison of learned, training-free, and non-predictive exploration under shared sensing, frontier candidates, and travel cost, separating prediction, decision, exploration, and computational performance.

title: VLM-Guided Contact Retargeting and Generative Partner Modeling for Humanoid-Human Interaction
authors: Yuto Shibata,Kotaro Amaya,Kashu Yamazaki,Lalit Jayanti,Yoshimitsu Aoki,Mariko Isogawa,Katerina Fragkiadaki
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Humanoid–human interaction requires robots to operate under severe partial observability: during close physical contact, the human partner is occluded, truncated, or outside the robot’s field of view, causing pose estimation to fail and often necessitating external tracking or privileged human state. At the same time, heavy mutual occlusions introduce errors into the human–human motion-capture data used for learning. We present REACT, a framework for learning deployable humanoid–human interaction policies from human–human demonstrations. REACT treats semantic contact structure as the key supervisory signal connecting demonstration processing, interaction learning, and onboard control. First, a VLM-guided contact modeling and retargeting pipeline identifies semantically meaningful contacts and transfers them onto humanoid–human geometry while preserving interaction structure. Using these annotations, privileged interaction policies learn physically grounded behaviors through interaction-aware contact rewards and are then distilled into deployable egocentric depth policies trained entirely from onboard sensing using photorealistic human depth rendering. To address severe partial observability, we introduce generative partner-state modeling objectives that predict partner motion from occluded egocentric views. We evaluate REACT in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid across five contact-rich interactions. Semantic contact modeling substantially improves preservation of demonstrated interactions, while generative partner-state modeling improves contact recall on four of five interactions, most under heavy occlusion. On real hardware, REACT performs all five interactions using onboard sensing alone.
introduction:
Humanoid hardware and learning-based control have advanced rapidly in recent years, bringing the deployment of humanoid robots in homes, workplaces, and care settings increasingly within reach. Realizing this vision, however, requires robots capable of sustained, reactive physical interaction with humans using only onboard sensing. Unlike existing humanoid controllers, which primarily focus on isolated motion tracking or interaction with static scenes and objects [14, 21, 3], humanoid–human interaction (HHI) requires continuous perception, prediction, and physical coordination with a human partner whose motion evolves under independent intent and frequent contact.

A central challenge in HHI is that close-contact interaction fundamentally operates under severe partial observability. During interaction, the human partner is frequently self-occluded, truncated, or partially outside the robot’s field of view, causing off-the-shelf human pose-estimation systems to fail precisely when accurate perception matters most. As a result, many existing approaches rely on external tracking systems, motion-capture instrumentation, or privileged access to human state during deployment, limiting robustness and real-world deployability. The problem begins even earlier in the learning pipeline: heavy mutual occlusions also corrupt the underlying human–human motion-capture data itself, introducing reconstruction artifacts and inconsistent contact geometry that propagate through downstream retargeting [2, 46] and policy-learning pipelines.

We argue that deployable humanoid–human interaction fundamentally requires recovering the interaction state from incomplete observations, and that semantic contact structure provides the key supervisory signal connecting noisy demonstrations, physics-based learning, and onboard control. While motion trajectories may vary substantially across embodiments, interactions are often defined by a much more stable structure: who touches whom, where, and when. We therefore propose to represent interactions through semantic contacts and train policies to infer latent partner state under severe partial observability.

To this end, we introduce REACT (Reactive Egocentric Agent for Contact-rich Humanoid-Human InTeraction), a framework for learning deployable humanoid–human interaction policies from large-scale human–human motion-capture data (Figure 1). REACT first runs a VLM-guided semantic contact pipeline that retargets the demonstrated interaction contacts onto humanoid–human geometry while preserving interaction structure across the embodiment gap. These semantic contacts then supervise a privileged interaction teacher through interaction-aware contact rewards, anchoring the policy in physics. The teacher is distilled into an egocentric depth student trained entirely on onboard sensing via photorealistic in-simulator SMPL-X rendering of dynamic human partners. To address severe partial observability, the student is further trained with a generative partner-state prediction objective that infers past, present, and future partner motion from egocentric observations.

We evaluate REACT on a large corpus of close-contact human–human interactions in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Our experiments show that semantic contact modeling substantially improves preservation of demonstrated interaction structure compared to existing retargeting approaches, and its contact annotations improve downstream interaction learning. We further show that generative partner-state prediction improves contact recall on four of five interactions, most where the partner is hardest to see, enabling depth-based policies to recover most of the contact recall of privileged interaction teachers (75%75\% at a 3030\,cm tolerance). On real hardware, REACT successfully executes diverse contact-rich interactions, including high-fives, hugs, handshakes, link-arms, and pats on the back, using onboard sensing alone.

In summary, our contributions are
(1) A semantic contact modeling and retargeting framework that transfers human–human demonstrations to humanoid–human interactions while preserving interaction structure across embodiments,
(2) An interaction-learning framework that uses semantic contacts as supervision for physics-based humanoid–human behavior learning,
(3) Generative partner-state prediction objectives that enable latent interaction-state inference under severe partial observability from egocentric observations, and
(4) extensive simulation ablations and real-world deployment on a Unitree G1 across diverse contact-rich humanoid–human interactions.

title: Fast Motion Retargeting Pipeline for Scalable Humanoid Robot Learning
authors: Daniel Marew,Sangjun Park,Nisal Perera,Donghyun Kim
abstract: While large-scale human motion capture datasets provide a rich source of demonstrations for humanoid robot learning, retargeting the diverse motions to different humanoid robots remains a nontrivial challenge. Existing kinodynamic trajectory optimization pipelines are computationally expensive and often require manual adjustments per motion. We present FRDV (Fast Retargeting with Dynamics Validation), a scalable framework consisting of rapid constrained kinematic retargeting and an additional dynamics validation pipeline. Its kinematic stage integrates a custom Sequential Quadratic Programming solver, Real-Time Iteration, and parallel chunk-based processing, achieving up to 9,156 frames per second — approximately up to 𝟏𝟑𝟔×\mathbf{136\times} faster than GMR and ProtoMotions — while robot-specific constraints are incorporated into the optimization to reduce common retargeting artifacts, such as ground penetration and self-collision. For motions requiring additional verification, a contact implicit iLQR controller is utilized to test the retargeted reference under full rigid body dynamics. This dynamics-based validation identifies dynamically infeasible motions and refines contact-related artifacts such as foot floating and foot skating. We evaluate retargeting quality by training motion tracking reinforcement learning policies using several state-of-the-art pipelines and comparing their tracking fidelity and success rates. Furthermore, sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated on a Unitree G1 humanoid. Videos and code are available at: https://daroslab.github.io/frdv/.
introduction:
Large-scale human motion capture (MoCap) datasets are increasingly used to train humanoid robots to reproduce diverse locomotion, manipulation, and whole-body behaviors [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Datasets such as AMASS [6], LAFAN1 [7], OMOMO [8], and BONES-SEED [9] collectively contain hundreds of thousands of human motion sequences. However, these motions are hard to directly use for humanoid learning due to differences in morphology, joint structure, and hardware limitations. A common approach is to adapt human motion data to the morphology and kinematic constraints of a target robot through motion retargeting [10, 11, 12].

Despite its widespread use, existing retargeting pipelines face two major challenges when applied to large-scale datasets. The first is computational efficiency. For example, our runtime evaluation shows that existing retargeting methods, such as ProtoMotions [13], require more than 40 hours to process the AMASS dataset (see Table II), which contains approximately 11,000 motion sequences spanning over 40 hours of motion data from more than 300 subjects [6]. The second challenge is retargeting quality. Differences in body proportions, joint limits, and kinematic structures between humans and humanoid robots can introduce artifacts such as foot sliding, ground penetration, and self-collisions. These artifacts can reduce the robustness of downstream reinforcement learning (RL)-based motion-tracking policies and, for challenging motions, may even prevent successful policy learning [12].

To address these challenges, we introduce FRDV (Fast Retargeting with Dynamics Validation), which combines high-speed kinematic retargeting with optional dynamics validation. Its kinematic stage uses a specialized Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) solver, Real-Time Iteration (RTI), and chunk-based parallelism, achieving up to 9,156 FPS—approximately 136×136\times and 191×191\times the throughput of ProtoMotions [14] and GMR [12], respectively—while enforcing robot-specific constraints to reduce ground penetration and self-collision. For motions requiring further verification, contact-implicit iLQR [15] tracks the resulting references under MuJoCo dynamics and actuator limits to assess trackability and refine residual contact artifacts before RL training.

We evaluate downstream trackability beyond kinematic similarity by training motion-tracking RL policies on LAFAN1 references generated by FRDV, GMR [12], and ProtoMotions [14] and comparing tracking fidelity and success rates across diverse motion categories. We also evaluate sim-to-real transfer by deploying the trained policy on Unitree G1 to execute FRDV-retargeted motions. In summary, the main contributions of this work are:

A fast motion retargeting pipeline based on a custom SQP solver, RTI, and parallel chunk-based processing, achieving up to 9,156 frames per second on average while enforcing robot-specific constraints to prevent self-collision and ground penetration.

A contact-implicit iLQR stage for dynamics validation and refinement under full rigid-body dynamics and actuator bounds.

A comprehensive evaluation using motion-tracking reinforcement learning, including comparisons with existing retargeting pipelines and a zero-shot hardware demonstration on the Unitree G1 humanoid robot.

title: MARE: An Open-Source Lunar Rover Simulator with Shadow Ground Truth for Perception and Autonomy
authors: Raúl Castilla-Arquillo,Miguel Olivares-Mendez
comment: . Code:this https URL. Video:this https URL
abstract: Lunar surface exploration increasingly relies on autonomous rovers that must perceive and traverse unstructured terrain under extreme illumination conditions. Near the lunar poles, low sun elevations produce long, high-contrast shadows that challenge stereo vision, terrain segmentation, and localization. Developing perception and navigation algorithms for these conditions requires large amounts of sensor data with accurate ground truth, which field campaigns and analog facilities can only provide at high cost and with limited variety. This paper presents MARE (Modular Autonomy and Rendering Environment), an open-source simulation suite for lunar rover perception and autonomy built on Unreal Engine 5 and ROS 2. MARE consists of three integrated components. Terrain Studio generates cratered and rocky lunar Digital Elevation Maps (DEMs) to build simulation scenes. A dedicated Unreal Engine project hosts two physics-based rovers with plugins for stereo, lidar, event, and Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) cameras, streaming time-stamped sensor data and pixel-accurate ground truth. Lastly, a Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC) stack provides web-based mission control. Validation shows a mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.79 between predicted and rendered shadows at low sun elevations, and stereo depth analysis verifies decreased pixel coverage in shadowed regions relative to sunlit terrain.
introduction:
Planetary rovers depend on their Guidance, Navigation, and Control system to traverse complex terrain autonomously, since communication delays limit direct human control. On the Moon, extreme illumination conditions complicate this task: near the poles, the sun remains only a few degrees above the horizon, casting long, high-contrast shadows that continuously alter the terrain’s appearance over time [1, 2]. Developing and validating perception and navigation algorithms for these environments requires large volumes of sensor data paired with accurate ground truth, including object labels, shadow masks, depth maps, and the rover pose.

While field campaigns at analog sites and laboratories produce realistic datasets, they are costly and provide little control over terrain geometry and illumination. Simulation bridges this gap by generating labeled data within strictly controlled, repeatable environments. Building on the success of terrestrial game-engine simulators like CARLA [3] and AirSim [4], recent work has adapted high-fidelity rendering for planetary contexts. Allan et al. [5] developed a Gazebo simulator utilizing physically based rendering and fractal terrain for polar rovers. OmniLRS [6] leverages NVIDIA Isaac Sim to offer ray-traced lunar rendering, terrain deformation, and mission integration. Similarly, Space Robotics Bench [7] applies procedural generation and domain randomization in parallel environments for zero-shot sim-to-real learning. Other notable platforms include LunarSim [8], which pairs Unity’s visuals with ROS 2 for computer vision evaluation, and MarsSim [9], which links multiscale Martian landscapes with a Gazebo wheel-soil terramechanics plugin.

Despite these advances, planetary simulation tools remain fragmented. A recent survey [10] noted that only eight of fifteen reviewed simulators are publicly available, limiting reproducibility in the community. Current systems typically isolate specific domains like rendering, policy learning, or vehicle dynamics, rather than providing a unified pipeline from terrain creation to closed-loop autonomy with pixel-accurate labeling. Bridging this gap requires complete stack consistency: the same terrain model used to build the scene must also generate the ground truth and serve as the rover’s planning map, ensuring labels, maps, and sensors all operate within the same world.

Within this ground truth, shadows and wheel tracks deserve particular attention. Because the Moon lacks an atmosphere, shadowed regions remain almost completely dark; a shadow can conceal a rock or crater, eliminate the surface texture needed for stereo matching, or be mistaken for an obstacle. Consequently, rock and crater detection depends strongly on illumination [11]. At low sun elevations, the rover’s own shadow also extends far ahead of or behind the vehicle, occupying a large portion of the navigation camera images. Because this shadow moves with the rover, it undermines the static-scene assumption of visual odometry and compromises terrain segmentation. Similarly, the wheel tracks the rover leaves alter the appearance of the traversed surface. Perception algorithms operating under these conditions must therefore be trained and evaluated with labels that distinguish sunlit from shadowed terrain, the rover’s self-shadow from static terrain shadows, and wheel tracks from the undisturbed surface, which existing planetary simulators rarely provide.

These illumination extremes also motivate sensing modalities beyond conventional cameras and lidar. Emerging sensors, such as event cameras and Single-Photon Avalanche Diode cameras, are of growing interest for lunar perception under low- and high-contrast lighting [2]. However, they remain largely absent from existing planetary simulators: none of the surveyed platforms supports event cameras, and only one provides limited Single-Photon Avalanche Diode support [10].

To address these gaps, we present MARE (Modular Autonomy and Rendering Environment), an open-source simulation suite for lunar rover perception and autonomy built on Unreal Engine 5 and ROS 2. Figure 1 shows its end-to-end pipeline. Terrain Studio generates procedural or real lunar terrain with craters and rock fields and builds the scene in Unreal Engine. Two physics-based rovers carry reusable sensor plugins, including stereo, lidar, event, and Single-Photon Avalanche Diode cameras, synchronized by a shared simulation clock. A ground-truth module produces pixel-accurate object and shadow masks for craters, crater rims, rocks, wheel tracks, and the rover’s own shadow. Finally, a containerized Guidance, Navigation, and Control stack drives the rover autonomously, supervised from a web-based mission control. We validate the suite in two ways: by comparing shadows predicted from the terrain model with those rendered by the engine on three terrains, and by evaluating stereo depth separately on sunlit and shadowed terrain using the ground-truth masks. The source code is publicly available on GitHub11

title: GPT-6-Astra Understands Touch and Outperform Vision--Tactile--Language--Action Models
authors: Ziyong Wang,Yupei Lin,Runxuan Huang,Liang Lin,Dongyu Zhang,Guangrun Wang
abstract:
General-purpose multimodal models have shown promise as direct robot action policies, yet whether they grasp the physics underlying real-world interactions and can apply that understanding to guide action remains underexplored. We investigate this question using contact-rich manipulation as a representative testbed, examining tactile understanding as a concrete instance of this broader capability.
Contact-rich manipulation requires interpreting tactile feedback and adjusting actions after obstruction. Existing learned tactile policies acquire these capabilities through specialized pretraining and per-task optimization, with substantial data and training costs. We present GPT-as-Tactile-Policy, which summarizes expert demonstrations into task guidance and tactile references for contact assessment and corrective action. GPT-6-Astra combines this context with multimodal observations and interaction history to generate control commands and adjust actions through contact feedback. Without additional robotics-specific pretraining or per-task policy fine-tuning, our method achieves 93.8% mean success across five UniVTAC tasks. Overall performance is comparable to state-of-the-art policies, with higher success on selected tasks. On Insert Hole, tactile feedback improves success from 31% to 99%. Execution analysis further demonstrates contact-guided probing and correction, supporting manipulation progress through explicit expert experience and online feedback.
introduction:
The role of general-purpose large models in robotics is expanding
from task planning and skill selection (Brohan et al., 2023)
and control program generation (Liang et al., 2023)
to direct action decisions. Recent evaluations of GPT-6-Astra
show that a general-purpose multimodal model can generate
numerical robot actions from observations, task instructions,
and execution history, using feedback to determine subsequent
behavior (Team et al., 2026a).
These studies progressively connect general knowledge to robot action,
raising a fundamental question: do general-purpose multimodal models
grasp the physics underlying real-world interactions, and can they
apply that understanding to guide their actions? Exploring this
question requires examining how models reason the physical
consequences of their actions and use interaction feedback to adjust
subsequent behavior
(Huang et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023).

Tactile understanding provides a representative test case for a model’s grasp of physics, because interpreting tactile feedback involves making sense of physical phenomena such as contact, deformation, and constrained motion. We therefore choose contact-rich tasks such as insertion and alignment as our experimental setting (Huang et al., 2025; Bi et al., 2026). Even after identifying a target and reaching the contact location, a robot can be obstructed by local pose errors and hidden geometric constraints (Huang et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2025). External vision provides scene layout and visible object motion, but offers limited access to deformation and motion constraints at the contact interface (Chen et al., 2026; Higuera et al., 2026). In this setting, tactile feedback allows us to examine whether models can connect the observed physical effects to their own actions and use that understanding to guide subsequent control.

Existing research has developed learned policies that integrate
touch into contact-rich manipulation. Representative approaches
include ACT with the UniVTAC encoder (Chen et al., 2026),
the tactile-predictive 𝒩0\mathcal{N}_{0}-VTLA
(Team et al., 2026c), and the tactile-native world-action model
𝒩0\mathcal{N}_{0}-TWAM (Team et al., 2026b). These approaches
acquire contact representations and manipulation capabilities
through representation learning, pretraining, and downstream
policy optimization. Their use of expert experience therefore
involves training dedicated representations or updating policy
parameters for downstream tasks. This motivates exploring an
alternative: making expert manipulation experience directly
available to a general-purpose model as task guidance,
without an additional task-specific policy training stage.

To investigate this question without additional specialized pretraining
or per-task policy fine-tuning, we introduce GPT-as-Tactile-Policy,
which summarizes expert manipulation experience into task guidance
that a general-purpose model can use directly. As shown in Fig. 1A, the model
combines this experience with current visual and tactile observations
and interaction history to directly generate robot actions, revising
subsequent attempts based on contact changes. Expert experience provides
principles for probing and correction, while real-time tactile feedback
helps the model determine how to apply them to the current interaction.
This process requires no policy parameter updates;
Tab. 1 compares its training
requirements with those of existing methods.

Fig. 1B and Fig. 2 illustrate how tactile feedback changes the policy’s response to obstruction. Without tactile feedback, the policy repeatedly presses downward, retracts, and retries, but its orientation and lateral adjustments remain limited, leaving insertion incomplete. With tactile feedback, the policy actively explores alternative insertion directions and progressively adjusts the tube orientation and lateral position until insertion succeeds. This contrast illustrates how tactile feedback helps identify ineffective attempts, guide local correction, and restore manipulation progress. Across five contact-rich UniVTAC tasks, our method achieves overall performance comparable to extensively pretrained state-of-the-art methods and higher success rates on selected tasks, without additional robotics-specific pretraining or per-task policy fine-tuning, as shown in Fig. 1C. Our main contributions are:

Direct visuo-tactile control.
We introduce GPT-as-Tactile-Policy, enabling a fixed-parameter
general-purpose multimodal model to translate tactile feedback into
effective action adjustments. By relating contact changes to preceding
motions, the model revises its approach and pose to improve alignment
and make progress after obstruction.

Direct visuo-tactile control.
We introduce GPT-as-Tactile-Policy, enabling a fixed-parameter
general-purpose multimodal model to translate tactile feedback into
effective action adjustments. By relating contact changes to preceding
motions, the model revises its approach and pose to improve alignment
and make progress after obstruction.

Experience-guided tactile reasoning.
We summarize expert manipulation experience into fixed task guidance
covering contact cues, probing, and corrective strategies. Together
with representative tactile references, this guidance helps the model
apply prior experience to current interactions.

SOTA-level performance without policy fine-tuning.
Across five UniVTAC tasks, evaluated over 100 seeds per task
following the benchmark protocol, our method achieves overall
performance comparable to extensively pretrained state-of-the-art
methods and higher success rates on selected tasks, without additional
robotics-specific pretraining or per-task policy fine-tuning.
Execution analyses further demonstrate how the model uses tactile
feedback to select probing directions, correct its pose, and make
progress after obstruction.
