title: Physical AI for Intralogistics: Benchmarking the NVIDIA Sim-to-Real Ecosystem for Cosmos-Enhanced COMPASS Navigation on Industrial Mobile Robots
authors: Charbel Abi Hana(1),Rayan Zaitouni(1),Kameel Amareen(1),Mohamad Mostafa(1),Hasan Sayour(1),Wei Liu(2),Yan Chang(2),Mihir Acharya(2),Anthony Rizk(1) ((1) Idealworks, (2) NVIDIA)
abstract:
Classical robot navigation stacks are reliable but often require re-engineering
for each new robot type and site. Learning-based navigation shifts this effort
from hand-tuned parameters to data generation and training, where a policy
adapts to each new embodiment or facility by fine-tuning in simulation. Whether policies
adapted this way stay reliable on real industrial robots has seen little
systematic testing. We study this for NVIDIA’s
X-Mobility and COMPASS workflow for training learned navigation policies on
Idealworks robots. In simulation, we
extend the COMPASS benchmark with two embodiments, the differential-drive iw.hub
and an omnidirectional Humanoid Mobile Platform (HMP), and with a digital twin of the Idealworks R&D
center. For the real world, we fine-tune X-Mobility on data from this digital
twin, with and without sim-to-real variants generated by NVIDIA Cosmos, train
COMPASS on top of it from scratch in the digital twin, deploy the resulting policies on the iw.hub’s onboard Jetson AGX
Xavier, and benchmark them in the Idealworks R&D center against COMPASS trained only on
NVIDIA’s environments and the existing Idealworks navigation stack on task success, efficiency,
safety, smoothness and onboard compute. Running every static scenario both in a
digital-twin replica and in the real facility measures the sim-to-real gap and
how far Cosmos-augmented data closes it.
Training in the digital twin with Cosmos sim-to-real augmentation raises
the real-world success rate of learned navigation from 65.3% to 91.7% across
four scenarios and nearly halves its weighted travel time compared with
simulation-only training, bringing it within 8.3 points of the production
navigation stack, fully onboard; with an integrated global planner, it also
reaches far, occluded goals in every trial.
introduction:
Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) have become a core component of modern
intralogistics, moving material between storage, production and shipping areas
without fixed infrastructure. Their navigation is typically built as a modular
pipeline: the robot localizes itself in a prior map, a global planner computes a
route to the goal, and a local planner follows that route while avoiding
obstacles, as in the widely used ROS 2 navigation stack
Nav2 (Macenski et al., 2020). The local planners of such stacks are
hand-designed, for example the dynamic window approach (Fox et al., 1997) or
timed elastic bands (Rösmann et al., 2017), and operate on costmaps built from
lidar and depth sensors.

These stacks are mature and dependable in the conditions they were engineered
for, but they are expensive to extend. Their behavior emerges from many
interacting parameters, such as cost weights, inflation radii, velocity and
acceleration limits and recovery behaviors, which must be re-tuned for every new
robot geometry, drive configuration and facility layout. Their perception is
largely geometric: an obstacle is an occupied cell, with no notion of what it
is or how it will move, which limits their behavior around people, other
vehicles and semi-structured clutter. As fleets grow to more robot types and
more sites, this per-robot and per-site engineering becomes a dominant cost of
deployment.

Physical AI, the application of learned models to systems that perceive and act
in the physical world, offers a different path: rather than being engineered, a
navigation policy is learned from data and improves as more data becomes
available. Several developments now make this practical. GPU-accelerated
simulation such as Isaac Lab (Mittal et al., 2023) trains policies across
thousands of parallel environments, which makes
interaction data cheap. World models learn compact, predictive representations
of the environment from which behavior can be
learned (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018). Navigation foundation
models trained on data from many robots, such as GNM, ViNT and
NoMaD (Shah et al., 2023a; Shah et al., 2023b; Sridhar et al., 2024), show that a single
policy can drive different embodiments, in line with the cross-embodiment
results of large-scale robot learning (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024). Training in simulation, however, raises its own
challenge: a policy that performs well in simulation can fail on a real robot,
because rendered images, physics and sensor noise never match reality exactly.
This sim-to-real gap is the main obstacle to deploying simulation-trained
policies (Zhao et al., 2020). A classical answer is domain randomization,
which varies textures, lighting and other simulation parameters during training
so that the real world appears to the policy as just another
variation (Tobin et al., 2017). Generative world foundation models such as
NVIDIA Cosmos (NVIDIA, 2025a) take this a step further: they turn
simulated footage into photorealistic variations that preserve its geometry and
motion, bringing the training data closer to what a robot’s cameras see in a
real facility.

Together, these advances make learned navigation policies the natural next step
for industrial navigation. A learned policy adapts to a new robot or a new site
through data and fine-tuning rather than manual re-engineering; it can use
camera images and the semantics they carry, not only geometry; and a single
training pipeline can serve a whole fleet of embodiments. Two questions stand
between this promise and industrial deployment: whether learned policies remain
reliable outside simulation, on real robots in real facilities, and whether they
can match the production navigation stacks they would replace on the metrics
that matter in operation, namely task success, efficiency, safety and onboard
compute.

NVIDIA’s X-Mobility (Liu et al., 2024) and
COMPASS (Liu et al., 2025) are a concrete instance of this approach.
X-Mobility learns an end-to-end navigation policy: a world model, trained on
random-exploration data, encodes camera images, route information and robot
state into a latent representation, and a policy head, trained by imitation on
Nav2 expert demonstrations, decodes this representation into velocity commands.
COMPASS freezes the X-Mobility policy and trains a residual policy on top of it
with reinforcement learning in Isaac Lab, learning only the corrections a given
embodiment needs, either as a specialist for one robot or as a
generalist distilled across several.

Idealworks develops autonomous mobile robots for intralogistics together with
the software that operates them. Its iw.hub is a differential-drive AMR that
navigates with the Idealworks navigation stack, its production navigation system, and its Humanoid Mobile Platform (HMP) is a humanoid robot on an
omnidirectional mobile base.
New navigation capabilities at Idealworks are developed and validated first in
simulation and then in the Idealworks R&D center, a facility used to test
robots under warehouse conditions before customer deployment. This makes the
Idealworks robots and the R&D center a natural testbed for the two questions
above.

This work evaluates whether the X-Mobility (Liu et al., 2024) and
COMPASS (Liu et al., 2025) navigation stack, combined with sim-to-real data
augmentation using NVIDIA Cosmos (NVIDIA, 2025a), can be adapted to
Idealworks robots and deployed in a real facility. We address this question in
two benchmarks, one in simulation and one on a real robot.

Simulation benchmark. We extend the simulation benchmark of COMPASS with two Idealworks embodiments,
the differential-drive iw.hub and the omnidirectional HMP,
and with a new evaluation environment, the digital twin of the Idealworks R&D
center (Section 2). Because the released
stack moves the robot with a kinematic controller that bypasses actuation
dynamics, we adapt physics-based controllers to both robots: a differential
drive controller for the iw.hub and an omnidirectional controller for the
HMP. The HMP is evaluated in simulation only.

Real-world benchmark. On a physical iw.hub in the Idealworks R&D center, we compare three COMPASS
policies with the Idealworks navigation stack, the production navigation system
of the iw.hub (Section 3). The three add training on
the R&D center step by step: NVIDIA COMPASS, the iw.hub Specialist of the simulation
benchmark, is trained only on NVIDIA’s environments; IW.COMPASS fine-tunes
X-Mobility on data generated in the digital twin of the R&D center and trains
its COMPASS residual there; and IW.CE-COMPASS does the same on a hybrid version of
that data extended with Cosmos-augmented sim-to-real variants. Each static
scenario is run both in a digital-twin replica and in the R&D center. For
NVIDIA COMPASS, this measures how it generalizes to a new facility, in simulation and
in the real world; for the policies trained in the digital twin, it exposes their
sim-to-real gap and how far Cosmos-enhanced data closes it. The systems are compared on task success,
efficiency, safety, motion smoothness and onboard compute. All learned policies
run on the iw.hub’s onboard NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier. For far and occluded
goals, a global planner integrated with the COMPASS ROS 2 node supplies the route
that the COMPASS policy cannot plan on its own; it is used with IW.CE-COMPASS on the
real robot.

Organization. Section 2 introduces the two
embodiments and the digital twin of the R&D center, and reports the simulation benchmark
across the original and new embodiments and environments.
Section 3 presents the real-world benchmark on the
iw.hub: the compared navigation systems, their training data, the scenarios, the
metrics, the onboard deployment and the results in the digital-twin replica and
in the R&D center.
Section 4 concludes and outlines future work. The appendices
follow the order of the main text and detail the controller type study
(Appendix A), the omnidirectional controller of the HMP
(Appendix B), the global planner integration
(Appendix C), the training datasets
(Appendix D) and training pipeline
(Appendix E) of the real-world models, samples of the
Cosmos sim-to-real augmentation (Appendix F), the
deployment on the Jetson AGX Xavier (Appendix G) and
the results of all metrics of the COMPASS policies in the digital-twin replica
(Appendix H).

title: Plausible Future, Wrong Choice: Steering World-Action Models toward Intended Future
authors: Zhuohao Li,Jiawei He,Yuxuan Yan,Lang Zhou,Yinghao Li,Yanrui Li,Tianyu Zhang,Yi-Yang Song,Xirui Wu andYi-Lin Wei,Fating Hong,Qing Zhang,Zhilin Zhao,Jingdong Wang,Wei-Shi Zheng
abstract:
World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied generalist policies by jointly modeling future world evolution and robot actions across diverse manipulation tasks.
However, representing diverse futures is only the first step: a capable WAM must also generate futures that match the requirements of the current task and execution progress.
In long-horizon manipulation where similar observation-action segments occur across different tasks and stages,
existing approaches may generate locally plausible yet misdirected rollouts to drift toward wrong task stage, i.e., a phenomenon we term Stage Confusion.
To address this problem, we propose TaskWAM, a closed-loop, stage-aware framework that represents fine-grained task requirements with Mode Tokens and tracks execution progress with State Tokens, forming a structured task state to steer world–action generation toward intended future.
We further introduce StageBench, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark with parameterized stage variations and automated evaluation.
Extensive experiments on both simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks demonstrate that TaskWAM effectively reduces confusion and achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods.
Moreover, TaskWAM provides strong plug-and-play transfer across heterogeneous WAM architectures and robot embodiments, including single-arm robots, dual-arm grippers, dexterous hands, and humanoid robots.
introduction:
Recently, World-Action Models (WAMs) (Bi et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a) have shown promise for embodied generalist policies by jointly modeling future world evolution and robot actions, with the goal of supporting diverse manipulation tasks in everyday environments(Zhu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026).
However, modeling diverse futures is only the first step.
Once models are capable of representing multiple possible futures, the next challenge lies in generating future that is consistent
with the task requirements and execution context.
Existing WAMs typically infer stage progression implicitly from task instructions, observations, and execution histories (Lin et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026).
This becomes particularly challenging in long-horizon household manipulation, where similar observation-action interactions can correspond to different next stages depending on fine-grained task requirements, e.g., ordering, timing, repetition, or embodiment assignment, as illustrated in Figure 1 (Top left).

Consequently, WAMs may generate futures that are visually plausible and physically feasible, yet lead execution to the wrong stage.
We refer to this failure as stage confusion in world-action modeling (hereafter, stage confusion).
A few recent WAMs Yang et al. (2026); Cai et al. (2026) have explored longer-term history modeling, but stage confusion is not merely a memory-length problem, leaving two key challenges:
(1) similar interaction histories may still require different next stages, making instruction-specific guidance essential for resolving stage ambiguity; and
(2) simply extending history introduces substantial redundant context, which can obscure critical execution cues for stage tracking while increasing the architectural burden of WAMs.

To address these challenges, we propose TaskWAM, a closed-loop, stage-aware framework that explicitly grounds world-action generation in both task requirements and execution progress for long-horizon manipulation.
Specifically, we introduce Structured Task-State Grounding with two complementary representations:
Mode Tokens retrieve mode representations from a learnable mode codebook and ground them with text context to encode fine-grained execution requirements, while State Tokens track execution progress through causal temporal modeling of closed-loop action-observation transitions.
We further propose Task-State Conditioned Future Steering, which steers future prediction by inject the structured task state into world and action generation through attention conditioning and residual flow correction.
TaskWAM thus bridges diverse future modeling and intended future generation, offering two main advantages:
(i) future generation grounding in closed-loop robot-environment interaction;
(ii) plug-and-play steering mechanism applicable across heterogeneous WAM backbones.

Additionally, existing benchmarks (Mees et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2026b; Nasiriany et al., 2026) has mainly evaluated tasks in relatively independent settings, lacking sufficient data and evaluation protocols to assess this capability.
To support systematic evaluation, we further introduce StageBench, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark built on LIBERO Liu et al. (2023) and RoboTwin Chen et al. (2026b).
StageBench constructs overlapping observation-action trajectories across tasks and execution stages by varying stage compositions and orders, covering visual grounding, sequential reasoning, embodiment coordination, etc.
Extensive experiments in simulation and diverse real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that TaskWAM significantly reduces stage confusion and improves multi-stage manipulation over state-of-the-art methods.
We further validate its generalization on RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark Chen et al. (2026b) and its plug-and-play applicability across heterogeneous WAM architectures.
Moreover, our method can be applied across diverse robot embodiments, including single-arm robots, dual-arm grippers, dexterous hands, and humanoid platforms.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We identify stage confusion in world-action modeling, where WAMs generate locally plausible yet stage-inconsistent futures under overlapping observation-action trajectories.

We propose TaskWAM, which explicitly grounds world-action generation in task requirements and execution progress through Structured Task-State Grounding and task-state-conditioned future steering for stage-consistent future generation.

We introduce StageBench, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark that systematically constructs overlapping trajectories through parameterized task-stage variations and provides automated stage-aware evaluation.

Extensive experiments across simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that TaskWAM significantly reduces stage confusion and improves multi-stage manipulation across heterogeneous WAM backbones and diverse robot embodiments.

1. We identify stage confusion in world-action modeling, where WAMs generate locally plausible yet stage-inconsistent futures under overlapping observation-action trajectories.

2. We propose TaskWAM, which explicitly grounds world-action generation in task requirements and execution progress through Structured Task-State Grounding and task-state-conditioned future steering for stage-consistent future generation.

3. We introduce StageBench, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark that systematically constructs overlapping trajectories through parameterized task-stage variations and provides automated stage-aware evaluation.

4. Extensive experiments across simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that TaskWAM significantly reduces stage confusion and improves multi-stage manipulation across heterogeneous WAM backbones and diverse robot embodiments.

title: CAPSafe: A Benchmark for Contextual Action and Plan Safety Reasoning in Embodied Agents
authors: Youmna Farag,Svetlana Stoyanchev,Simon Keizer,Mohan Li,Rama Doddipatla
abstract:
Reasoning about safety is essential for embodied agents powered by large language models (LLMs). We introduce the Contextual Action and Plan Safety benchmark (CAPSafe), designed to evaluate safety reasoning at two levels: (1) an action-level dataset that tests whether a single action is safe given its environmental context, and (2) a plan-level dataset that evaluates whether agents can generate safe long-horizon plans for complex hazardous household tasks. CAPSafe models safety conditions where hazards are situational (inferred from object properties), multiple hazards can co-occur within the same environment, and each is annotated with a relative severity level for fine-grained analysis.
Evaluating nine closed and open-source LLMs reveals a substantial gap between hazard recognition and safe long-horizon planning. Several models achieve high accuracy in recognizing unsafe actions (exceeding 90%90\% in the best cases), yet safe long-horizon planning remains substantially harder. Gemini-3-pro achieves the highest safe success rate (78.19%78.19\%), while other models remain below 65%65\%. These results highlight that robust safety reasoning over long action sequences remains an open challenge.
introduction:
Embodied agents powered by LLMs are increasingly used to perform complex tasks Huang et al. (2022a); Huang et al. (2022b); Ahn et al. (2022); Singh et al. (2023); Sarch et al. (2023). To operate safely, agents must not only interpret instructions and generate action sequences, but also ensure the safety of these actions. Unsafe actions, such as mishandling appliances or using contaminated objects, can cause physical harm to humans or property, making safety a key requirement for real-world deployment.
Recent work has begun to study safety-aware embodied AI Zhou et al. (2024b); Li et al. (2025); Zhou et al. (2024a); Khan et al. (2025); Son et al. (2025); Lu et al. (2025). However, existing benchmarks focus on explicitly dangerous instructions that agents can refuse, rather than situational hazards that must be inferred from the environmental context Yin et al. (2024); Liu et al. (2025). A few others evaluate safety only from final environment states, overlooking unsafe intermediate actions during execution Zhu et al. (2024); Sadhu et al. (2025). Additionally, these benchmarks consider relatively simple environments, involving a single hazard and a few objects, limiting the study of safety in long-horizon settings Zhu et al. (2024); Lu et al. (2025); Son et al. (2025).

Motivated by these limitations, we introduce the Contextual Action and Plan Safety (CAPSafe) benchmark, comprising two complementary datasets.11
1
https://github.com/Youmna-H/CAPSafe The action-level dataset evaluates whether agents can judge the safety of a single action given its environmental context, while the plan-level dataset evaluates long-horizon safety reasoning by assessing whether agents can generate safe successful plans.
Unlike prior benchmarks, CAPSafe environments contain multiple co-occurring hazards (12 on average), substantially larger scenes (96 objects), and longer tasks (21 steps on average), enabling evaluation of safety reasoning in complex environments. Hazards in CAPSafe are situational, inferred from object properties. We also introduce hazard severity as another dimension that is underexplored in existing benchmarks. A comparison with prior benchmarks is summarised in Table 1.

We focus on the reasoning required for safety-aware planning. To isolate this capability, we abstract away from perception and provide agents with structured environment descriptions. This setup enables systematic evaluation of models’ ability to reason about risks and generate safe plans even when the environment is perfectly specified Jia et al. (2024).
As our results show, models still struggle under these ideal conditions, indicating that safety-aware planning itself remains a challenge.

We evaluate nine LLMs (four proprietary and five open-source) under multiple prompting strategies. Our results show that strong action-level hazard recognition does not necessarily translate to safe long-horizon planning.
Our main contributions are as follows:

We construct a contextual action-level safety dataset where action safety depends on object properties and environment state, requiring agents to perform situational reasoning.

We introduce a long-horizon plan-level dataset where agents must complete household tasks in environments containing multiple co-occurring hazards across many objects. These hazards arise over extended action sequences, requiring sustained safety reasoning over long-horizon plans.

We annotate hazards with relative severity levels, enabling fine-grained analysis of model performance across different risk levels.

We systematically evaluate models under different prompting strategies, analyzing how implicit safety knowledge in demonstrations, explicit safety guidelines, and self-reflection affect safety reasoning.

We provide a text-based simulator to detect plan success and safety violations. It operates on structured environment descriptions, enabling controlled evaluation of models’ safety reasoning.

1. We construct a contextual action-level safety dataset where action safety depends on object properties and environment state, requiring agents to perform situational reasoning.

2. We introduce a long-horizon plan-level dataset where agents must complete household tasks in environments containing multiple co-occurring hazards across many objects. These hazards arise over extended action sequences, requiring sustained safety reasoning over long-horizon plans.

3. We annotate hazards with relative severity levels, enabling fine-grained analysis of model performance across different risk levels.

4. We systematically evaluate models under different prompting strategies, analyzing how implicit safety knowledge in demonstrations, explicit safety guidelines, and self-reflection affect safety reasoning.

5. We provide a text-based simulator to detect plan success and safety violations. It operates on structured environment descriptions, enabling controlled evaluation of models’ safety reasoning.

title: SPAR: Search-trained Push Action Ranker for Efficient Navigation Among Movable Obstacles
authors: Dhruv Metha Ramesh,Tri-An Nguyen,Junshan Huang,Jingjin Yu,Kostas E. Bekris,Abdeslam Boularias
abstract:
Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) requires a
robot to rearrange objects that block access to its goal.
For a pushing robot, progress may depend on a setup push
that enables a later opening without itself clearing a
passage. The number of candidate sequences can grow
exponentially with sequence length, making physics-based
search costly.
We introduce the Search-trained Push Action Ranker
(SPAR), which learns to prioritize push primitives
from simulated search outcomes. Searches over sequences
of up to two pushes per object provide supervision that
distinguishes immediate openings from setup pushes.
A transformer trained with regression and ranking losses
scores primitives using contact tokens conditioned on scene geometry and reachability
regions. The same model guides simulator evaluations
in SPAR Search and selects actions for direct execution
in SPAR Policy. Both modes solve successive keyhole
problems that open access to neighboring free-space
regions within a NAMO planner.
Across successful runs on 300300 simulated two-push keyhole
problems, SPAR Search reduces median simulator calls
by 7.0×7.0\times, leading to a 3.8×3.8\times reduction in
planning time relative to Random Search.
Without retraining, the same ranker guides search on
600600 keyhole problems which have no solution within two pushes. At a depth limit of five pushes, SPAR Search achieves 50.7%50.7\% success within 100100 simulator calls, compared with 20.2%20.2\% for Random Search.
These gains carry over to NAMO planning: on hard
simulated scenes, SPAR Search achieves 47%47\% success
within 100100 simulator calls, compared with 21%21\% for
Random Search. In real-robot experiments, SPAR Policy
succeeds in 37/4037/40 trials without a physics-based digital
twin, compared with 33/4033/40 for SPAR Search and 27/4027/40
for Random Search.
introduction:
Movable obstacles can easily bring a robot’s mission to
a halt. A warehouse inspection robot may need to push boxes aside to continue its route [1]; a robot delivering first aid may need to remove debris to reach a victim [2]. The ability to rearrange such obstacles gives robots a way to create passages through otherwise inaccessible environments.
Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) captures this
coupling between navigation and obstacle
relocation [3]. We address NAMO
for a mobile robot that makes progress toward its goal
through non-prehensile pushing.
Region-based planners organize these rearrangements into
keyhole problems, each requiring access to a
neighboring free-space region by moving one or more
blocking objects [3, 4].
Each opening extends the robot’s access to the workspace
and creates opportunities for further progress. Our focus
is to find useful push sequences for these local problems
with little simulation effort, then compose their solutions
to reach the navigation goal (Fig. 1).

A useful push can matter before it opens a passage.
For example, rotating a box may expose a previously
unreachable face, enabling a second push that clears the
doorway. Finding such setup pushes requires accounting for
contact location, push duration, and interactions with
walls or other objects to predict how the object moves
and which contacts the robot can reach
afterward [5].

Physics simulation lets a planner explore how the scene
evolves over successive pushes. However, the number of
candidate sequences can grow exponentially with sequence
length, making even two-push solutions costly to discover.
Prior work learns local pushing
policies [6] or guides sampling
in NAMO planning [7].
Our Search-trained Push Action Ranker (SPAR) instead
learns from the search itself, turning simulated keyhole
search outcomes into priorities for executable pushes.

Each push primitive specifies a contact point and duration.
We generate training data by searching over sequences
of up to two pushes per object. These searches identify pushes that open a passage immediately and setup
pushes that enable a second push to do so.
Regression and ranking losses train the model to
rank passage-opening pushes above setups, and both above
pushes with no successful continuation.
A transformer uses contact tokens conditioned on object
and obstacle geometry and the source and target free-space
regions to score all primitives for a selected object in
one forward pass, before candidate pushes are simulated.
Because scores depend on the current scene rather than search
depth, the model can be reapplied at each state to guide search
beyond the two-push training horizon.

These priorities support both planning and direct action.
SPAR Search simulates reachable primitives in learned
priority order, retaining alternative sequences when
a branch fails. SPAR Policy instead executes a push
selected from the same scores, then observes and rescores
the changed scene. We evaluate Policy in simulation before
deploying it on a real robot, where it requires no
physics-based digital twin. Both modes use the same
region-graph NAMO planner, extending the gains on local
keyhole problems to NAMO without
additional training.

On 300300 simulated two-push keyhole problems, SPAR Search
reduces median simulator calls and planning time over
successful runs by 7.0×7.0\times and 3.8×3.8\times, respectively,
relative to Random Search. Without retraining, the same ranker guides search on 600600 keyhole problems with no solution within two pushes
under the primitive library. At a depth limit of five
pushes, SPAR Search achieves 50.7%50.7\% success within
100100 simulator calls, compared with 20.2%20.2\% for Random Search.

These gains carry over to NAMO: on hard simulated
scenes, SPAR Search achieves 47%47\% success within
100100 simulator calls, compared with 21%21\% for Random Search.
In real-robot experiments, SPAR Policy succeeds in
37/4037/40 trials, compared with 33/4033/40 for SPAR Search
and 27/4027/40 for Random Search.

Our contributions are:

SPAR, a push ranker learned from simulated
keyhole searches, combining executable primitives,
contact-based spatial scoring, and regression and
ranking supervision that distinguishes immediate
openings from setup pushes.

Generalization beyond the training horizon:
priorities learned from searches of up to two pushes
per object guide search at depths three through five
on keyhole problems with no solution within two pushes,
improving success over Random Search at matched
depths and simulator-call budgets.

Integration of the ranker into search and direct
execution within a NAMO planner, with simulation
and real-robot experiments showing that keyhole-level
gains carry over to full navigation.

1. SPAR, a push ranker learned from simulated
keyhole searches, combining executable primitives,
contact-based spatial scoring, and regression and
ranking supervision that distinguishes immediate
openings from setup pushes.

2. Generalization beyond the training horizon:
priorities learned from searches of up to two pushes
per object guide search at depths three through five
on keyhole problems with no solution within two pushes,
improving success over Random Search at matched
depths and simulator-call budgets.

3. Integration of the ranker into search and direct
execution within a NAMO planner, with simulation
and real-robot experiments showing that keyhole-level
gains carry over to full navigation.

title: Reinforced Iterative Learning Control for elastic joint arms: Guaranteed cross-trajectory generalization under model uncertainties
authors: Yuri De Santis,Michele Pierallini,Franco Angelini,Manolo Garabini
comment: Accepted for publication in Control Engineering Practice, 2026.
abstract:
Trajectory tracking for compliant robots is challenging due to nonlinear dynamics and modeling uncertainties, often requiring learning-based methods to avoid explicit parameter identification.
Iterative Learning Control (ILC) ensures theoretically high precision and preserves the passive compliance of the robot. However, traditional ILC requires a separate learning phase for each new trajectory.
Conversely, Reinforcement Learning (RL) generalizes to new trajectories, but practically suffers from high sample complexity and limited tracking precision.
This work proposes Reinforced Iterative Learning Control (RILC) that combines the strengths of both approaches to achieve fast adaptation and guaranteed tracking convergence across diverse trajectories. By establishing a concurrent coupling between the two controllers, RILC overcomes the high initial errors and slow adaptation of traditional ILC, enabling high-performance tracking from the very first trials. In this architecture,
ILC provides high-quality samples, while RL contributes as a generalizing best-effort policy across iterations. Additionally, a theoretical proof is presented to show that the RL component preserves ILC stability and, under specific conditions, can also reduce the error bound asymptotically.
The efficacy of this framework is demonstrated through simulation and experiments on an underactuated 4-degree-of-freedom serial elastic robot using different trajectories and modeling mismatches.
introduction:
The recent successes of robots deployed in unstructured environments, such as environmental monitoring
Pierallini et al. (2025), and robot-human interactions Li et al. (2020) emphasize the scientific community’s interest in robots that operate with limited information. Furthermore, enhancing performance and safety involves compliant hardware elements to guarantee physical safety Angelini et al. (2018) and learning-based controllers Peters et al. (2016).
However, the intrinsic flexibility of these structures introduces complex nonlinear dynamics that make trajectory tracking control challenging De Luca and Book (2016); Shao et al. (2024).

Model-based control ensures performance but requires precise models, which are difficult to obtain for compliant systems De Luca and Book (2016); George Thuruthel et al. (2018). To handle modeling errors, high feedback gains are often used, effectively adding a virtual stiffness in parallel with the physical transmission and yielding an increased closed-loop stiffness that negates the safety advantages of the mechanical adaptability Angelini et al. (2018). This is particularly critical for collaborative robots with elastic elements and industrial arms with parasitic flexibility such as harmonic drives or belt transmissions De Luca and Book (2016). While data-driven identification can address these uncertainties, it remains costly and time-consuming Hollerbach et al. (2016).

Learning techniques obtain reliable models or data across diverse dynamic scenarios, see Sutton and Barto (2018); Pierallini et al. (2023). This approach can update and reshape the control directly from raw real-time data in a model-free and data-driven fashion.
However, data-driven approaches are time-consuming and need a large amount of data.
The combination of MB and data-driven control is a promising choice for obtaining good results with guarantees of MB while adding an auxiliary part with learning.

One example of learning controllers is Iterative Learning Control (ILC) Ahn et al. (1993); Bristow et al. (2006); Chen et al. (2020); Pierallini et al. (2021); Aarnoudse et al. (2024), which guarantees theoretically good performance using mostly feedforward actions while compensating for the reality gap by repeating the desired task, iteratively. Recent research has investigated multi-reference tracking through various generalization strategies, including parametric basis functions Blanken et al. (2016), combined trial-specific adaptations Tsurumoto et al. (2023); Tsurumoto et al. (2024), and non-parametric Gaussian Process methods Meindl et al. (2024); Sun and Freeman (2024). However, achieving fast adaptation across diverse trajectories remains a challenge, because these methods often restrict target trajectories to a narrow neighborhood of the nominal path to preserve stability.
Conversely, Reinforcement Learning (RL) generalizes across trajectories, enabling zero-shot transfer to new references Kaelbling et al. (1996); Schulman et al. (2017), but suffers from high sample complexity and policy chattering that limits tracking precision Kober et al. (2013); Pavlichenko and Behnke (2022).
While the similarities and differences in ILC and RL learning processes have generated interest Zhang et al. (2019), existing combinations treat the two controllers as functionally decoupled. Some employ additive blending with fixed weights Xu et al. (2020); He et al. (2025) or RL-based parameter tuning Soleimani et al. (2025), while others adopt sequential pipelines where ILC generates offline datasets for RL training Ma et al. (2023); Yang et al. (2026). None of these approaches provide formal convergence guarantees for the combined system, and the RL component remains blind to the trial-to-trial evolution of the ILC feedforward signal. Other works modify the RL algorithm itself by drawing inspiration from ILC, e.g., Gurumurthy et al. (2023). Our objective, however, is not to improve the RL algorithm internally, but rather to operate directly at the control level.

This paper proposes a new control framework, Reinforced Iterative Learning Control (RILC), which combines the ILC and RL contributions to achieve precise multi-reference tracking. RILC establishes a concurrent coupling where the RL policy observes the ILC historical states and actively shapes the feedforward signal in real-time, while the ILC loop provides a stable envelope that constrains RL exploration. This synergy overcomes the slow trial-by-trial adaptation of traditional ILC, enabling high-performance execution from the very first trials. As a practical benefit, accurate feedforward compensation reduces the reliance on aggressive active feedback, which is essential in collaborative robotics and contact-rich industrial tasks to maintain the hardware’s safety and mechanical adaptability.
We derive theoretical convergence guarantees and conditions that ensure tighter error bounds than baseline ILC.

We validate the effectiveness of the algorithm both in numerical simulations, to test robustness against strong modeling mismatches, and in real-world experiments using a 4-degree-of-freedom (DoFs) articulated soft robot Pratt and Williamson (1995). Results confirm the robustness of RILC on complex physical dynamics, outperforming baseline ILC and RL controllers.

This work is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the state-of-the-art learning frameworks used; in Section 3, we describe the control problem in a model-based and model-free paradigm; in Section 4 we derive the control architecture, and show how all the introduced issues can be addressed. In Section 5-6, the controller effectiveness and robustness are tested and discussed. Finally, in Section 7, we conclude.

title: Large Multimodal Models for Direct Robot Control: GPT-6 as a Beginning
authors: Youwei Zhou,Bohan Hou,Yankai Fu,Yaoxu Lyu,Yifan Ye,Shilin Shan,Chen Guo,Jiaming Liu,Ran He,Caifeng Shan,Shanghang Zhang,Jianfei Yang,Zhihe Lu
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Robot manipulation requires a tightly coupled set of capabilities: understanding language and visual scenes, reasoning about spatial relationships, generating physically grounded actions, and adapting to environmental feedback [2, 52].
Although general-purpose LLMs and VLMs excel at semantic understanding and high-level planning [1, 16], their limited spatial grounding [9] and closed-loop control preclude reliable action generation [26, 35, 32, 14].
LLM/VLM-based coding agents have likewise been explored for robotic manipulation [35]; however, they specify only high-level action logic, whereas precise manipulation points and target poses are still delegated to hand-engineered geometric computations and control primitives, which limits their flexibility.

In contrast, specialized action models, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) [6, 5, 30, 4, 20, 3, 55, 57] models and World Action Models (WAMs) [7, 51, 23], directly generate actions, but remain constrained by their embodied training distributions [56], which limits their generalization to unseen tasks and environments [17]. Agentic hybrid architectures [48, 63, 46] aim to combine the strengths of both families, using general models for planning and specialized action models for execution. However, these systems still rely on post-trained action policies, even for relatively simple manipulation tasks, and therefore inherit the same generalization and flexibility bottlenecks.

Recently, GPT-6 Astra [45] has emerged as a promising candidate, with strong visuospatial understanding, 3D reasoning, and agentic reasoning.
These capabilities suggest that a general-purpose model could directly generate executable actions through spatial reasoning and sustain closed-loop control through agentic reasoning—without the hand-engineered primitives or post-trained action policies required by existing hierarchical architectures.
Preliminary robotics studies [50, 62, 13, 37] offer initial evidence for this potential, reporting promising manipulation performance without specialized VLA or WAM policies.
Yet the boundaries of GPT-6 Astra’s embodied capabilities remain insufficiently characterized.
Existing studies focus on benchmark performance and selected failure cases, without establishing which capabilities the model executes reliably and where its limitations emerge across diverse physical demands; in particular, real-world evaluations have not systematically probed precise geometric constraints, complex motion coordination, or safety-critical interactions.
These gaps raise a fundamental question: What can GPT-6 Astra reliably achieve in manipulation, and where do its capabilities break down, particularly in the real world?

To answer this question, we conduct a comprehensive, capability-driven investigation of GPT-6 Astra spanning more than 2,000 trials across simulation and real-world environments. We first introduce GPT-Generalist End-effector Action Reasoning (GPT-GEAR), an agent execution framework that equips GPT-6 Astra with minimally engineered general-purpose tools for direct closed-loop robotic manipulation (Figure 1 (a)). Using GPT-GEAR, we isolate three capabilities that underlie successful manipulation—depth perception [25, 24], embodied in-context learning [13, 37], and tactile understanding [33, 8, 39, 18] (Figure 1 (b))—and show that the model can estimate and exploit depth, acquire simple motor skills from in-context demonstrations, and use tactile feedback to correct its actions during execution. We then evaluate GPT-6 Astra on five established benchmarks—LIBERO-Plus [17], RoboTwin 2.0 [11], RoboDojo [10], RoboCasa GR1 [43, 3], and UniVTAC [8] (Figure 1 (c))—providing a broad empirical baseline for general-purpose models in robotic manipulation. Characterizing performance along six capability dimensions reveals an uneven profile: without task-specific policy training, GPT-6 Astra exhibits strong task understanding, promising generalization, and superior memory and attains competitive results on several benchmarks, yet these strengths do not consistently translate into reliable physical execution—particularly in long-horizon manipulation, precision-sensitive tasks, and complex motion coordination—while substantial inference overhead further underscores the gap between general-purpose reasoning and efficient robotic control [31].

Geometry-constrained manipulation exposes this gap most clearly, as it requires precise pose control, coordinated translation and rotation, and anticipation of physical interactions. To probe these demands, we introduce LIBERO-GeoMotion, a targeted benchmark built on LIBERO [36] assets that emphasizes complex motion execution while minimizing semantic complexity (Figure 1 (d)). On LIBERO-GeoMotion, GPT-6 Astra exhibits substantial difficulties in satisfying geometric and sequential constraints, exposing a critical disconnect between understanding desired spatial configurations and generating physically feasible action sequences. We finally extend the evaluation to real-world zero-shot deployment: GPT-6 Astra reliably completes basic pick-and-place tasks, but its overall zero-shot success rate reaches only 40%, with some constrained tasks failing entirely, and persistent failures involving unsafe grasp configurations, motion feasibility, and precise alignment reveal substantial challenges in safety-aware planning and reliable physical execution. General-purpose models thus already exhibit meaningful zero-shot manipulation capabilities, but remain far from delivering consistently safe and reliable robotic control.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

We introduce GPT-GEAR, a lightweight agent execution framework that equips GPT-6 Astra with minimally engineered general-purpose tools, enabling direct closed-loop robotic manipulation with no specialized action policies.

We systematically investigate three fundamental embodied capabilities—depth perception, embodied in-context learning, and tactile understanding—revealing how diverse forms of embodied information support action generation and execution.

title: Safe Multi-Robot Collaboration With Uniform Exclusion Using Trust
authors: Thomas Kaminsky,Áron Vékássy,Hammad Izhar,Angelia Nedić,Stephanie Gil
abstract:
Robot swarms coordinate through directed, time-varying local communication links, some of which may be compromised to allow the transmission of arbitrary malicious data.
We provide an algorithm that acts as a wrapper around robot communication—when a robot seeks to update its state using data from some incoming links, our wrapper provides a subset of trusted links whose data can be safely incorporated. It selects these links by testing a stream of trust values—data collected from an anomaly detector on each robot—using Safe Anytime-Valid Inference. We require only that the detector be better than chance.
This wrapper ensures safe and performant autonomy by providing two powerful statistical guarantees: it uniformly excludes all compromised links for all time with high user-chosen probability, but nevertheless quickly learns to trust legitimate links. Both guarantees are vital to secure generic tasks, but no previous work provides them simultaneously without restrictive assumptions on connectivity structure or the number of compromised links that are not guaranteed in practice.
We study our Safe Wrapper’s performance in hardware for two contrasting tasks—neural implicit mapping and heading consensus—deploying on 3 LoCoBots and 8 GoPiGos, respectively. We provide simulations using trust values sampled from hardware to validate that our approach scales well to swarms of hundreds of robots.
introduction:
We associate the set of robots (and Sybil entities) in a swarm with vertices of a graph. We model communication among robots as a time-varying directed graph, where a directed edge indicates that a robot can send a message to another robot at the given time. From the point of view of a receiving robot, we call the sender of a compromised link a malicious neighbor, and the sender of a legitimate link a legitimate neighbor.

Following a class of previous works which use stochastic observations of trust (trust values) derived from physical sensors on robotic platforms [17, 18], we assume that each robot can leverage local sensor information to estimate whether its incoming links are compromised. In the case of a Sybil attack, such trust values can be derived from the channel state information of the wireless communication [15], and for injection attacks by looking at the transmission rates on the communication link [2]. We provide more details in Sections 3.2.5 and 3.1.2.

In this section, we will describe the capabilities of our framework through hardware experiments. In Supplementary Section 3.6, we also theoretically ground our empirical observations by providing proofs of safety and performance under mild assumptions, and provide a list of distributed algorithms that can be secured using our approach in Table S1.

Five legitimate robots try to agree on a common heading direction, with 3 malicious robots spoofing 2 additional malicious identities each, making the total number of malicious agents in the network 9. This resulted in legitimate agents having more compromised links than legitimate ones in nearly all timesteps of the consensus algorithm (Figure S2).
We test whether the swarm reaches safe consensus, meaning that its final heading direction is inside the convex hull of the initial headings of the legitimate robots. Because of the frequent malicious majority, existing intrinsic approaches cannot be guaranteed to reach a safe consensus in our setting. The consensus algorithm and online computation of trust values were run completely locally on the swarm. For more details see Section 3.2.

In Figure 3 we compare our approach to an unsecured run and a baseline algorithm [18] that uses trust values, but does not guarantee time-uniform exclusion of malicious agents from communication. We ran 18 separate runs of consensus using our approach and 17 using the baseline. We also collected all of the trust value sequences and evaluated the other approach with them, so both methods were compared on the same set of 35 sequences. Our wrapper uniformly excluded compromised links in 100% of the trials and reached safe consensus, with all legitimate links being identified after an average of 40.3 samples per link at significance level γ=0.05\gamma=0.05 (Table 1). The reference baseline eventually learned to exclude the compromised links. However, an average of 70.3 malicious messages were included in legitimate updates before exclusion, causing the legitimate swarm to converge to a heading outside the convex hull in all trials (Figure 4). We report the histogram of aggregated trust observations collected over all malicious and legitimate links in Figure 5.

To test the generality of our safe wrapper, we ran additional experiments with a team of 3 robots learning a neural implicit reconstruction of their environment using UDON [24].
In this algorithm, the swarm tries to jointly learn a neural network representation of the environment by iteratively exchanging networks trained on local RGB-D datasets collected online. In our setup, a malicious robot attempts to overwrite messages sent along one robot’s outgoing links by injecting a network trained on an adversarially altered environment, overwriting each message with high probability (p=0.9p=0.9). Since these learned representations are non-interpretable, this message is difficult to distinguish from legitimate network updates. Details of the method, attack, and trust values are provided in Section 3.3.

Without our wrapper, the legitimate robots’ mesh reconstruction includes the malicious model’s fictitiously added and removed objects (Figure 1) as well as adversarial replacements (Figure S1). Quantitatively, the attacked model converges almost exactly to the malicious model, with a weight-space distance of dθmal=0.028d_{\theta}^{\text{mal}}=0.028 (versus 0.9120.912 for the nominal model, where no attack occurs). Using our safe wrapper, the learned model uniformly excludes malicious messages. Though it has a weight-space distance of dθnom=0.508d_{\theta}^{\text{nom}}=0.508 to the nominal model since both reach different local minima, the reconstructed maps are close, with a Chamfer distance of only 2.302.30 cm. Visually, we see that the reconstructed meshes have no hallucinations (Figures 1 and S1).

We seek to examine how our wrapper scales to large robot swarms that are difficult to evaluate in hardware due to time, battery, and space constraints. To do so, we collect trust values along all links for the distributed consensus hardware experiments, yielding a large dataset of empirical trust values (Figure 5). Sampling trust values directly from these empirical distributions for all simulated links, we evaluate detection performance on swarms of up to 500 robots. Details are provided in Section 3.4.1.

We consider two important times: when perfect classification is achieved, meaning that all links are correctly identified for all subsequent timesteps, and when strong connectivity is achieved, meaning that the legitimate robots can all communicate on a strongly connected subgraph. Results are reported in Table 2.
We find that the number of malicious robots has almost no impact on these times, since they are already uniformly excluded with high probability.
Even when M=L=500M=L=500, and thus 250,000 links are compromised, we do not observe a single false positive in these experiments.
More legitimate robots yield slower perfect classification times since more tests must all pass, but this delay grows very slowly. For example, even though 187,250187{,}250 new links are added between the L=250L=250 and L=500L=500 cases, fewer than 10 more samples are required on average to achieve perfect classification. Moreover, we see that the time to learn a trusted subgraph actually decreases with L,L, since there exist more simultaneous paths available to trust. Additional simulations are provided in the Supplementary Materials with trust values collected from sparse deterministic graph links (Table S3) and sparse random graph links (Table S4).

In hardware experiments, no compromised links were trusted under our safe wrapper.
However, an understanding of the per-compromised-link false positive rate is useful for understanding how the false-trust rate increases with larger swarms.
Thus, we consider the false positive rate for one malicious link, under varying levels of detector quality (Figure 6). We see that even with a trivial detector that performs entirely at chance (trust values drawn from Bernoulli​(0.5)\text{Bernoulli}(0.5)), the false positive rate remains below half of the significance level, and often far below it. When the detector has reasonable quality, no false positives are recorded. Our trust values for the consensus case are closest to the (p=0.25,γ=0.05)(p=0.25,\gamma=0.05) case; we see here that no false positives are recorded across 5,000 trials.

title: Perceives but Doesn't Brake: A Perception-Action Binding Gap in Reasoning Driving VLAs
authors: Matteo Cercola,Katie Z Luo,Simone Formentin,Marco Pavone
abstract: Reasoning-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) driving models can perceive and reason about safety-critical hazards yet fail to translate that evidence into safe actions. We characterize this failure as a perception–action binding gap: hazard information is available inside the model but exerts insufficient control over trajectory generation. Using matched simulated counterfactuals and logged driving replay, we show that in-path hazards are actually encoded in the visual representation, but longitudinal plans are dominated by ego-speed history and respond only weakly to hazard proximity or the model’s own reasoning trace. Further analysis shows that the trajectory generator is capable of braking but sometimes fails to do so due to the perception-action binding gap. Without retraining or modifying any weights, we inject a hazard-conditioned energy into the frozen flow-matching sampler of Alpamayo-1.5, restoring the missing coupling at generation time. With exact obstacle geometry, guidance cuts footprint intrusion from 58.1% to 14.5% and recovers safe braking whenever sufficient stopping distance remains, eliminating collisions entirely in our braking-relevant closed-loop battery. It also reverses the diagnosed dependence of the plan, from tracking ego speed to responding to obstacle range. These results separate hazard perception from hazard control in driving VLAs, show that unsafe behavior can arise even when the model has both the evidence and the ability to act on it, and propose a simple fix for bridging this binding gap.
introduction:
Reasoning-augmented vision–language–action (VLA) models are increasingly
designed to do more than map observations directly to actions: they perceive
the scene, produce an explicit reasoning trace, and then generate a driving
trajectory. This architecture suggests a natural safety premise: if the model
correctly identifies a hazard and reasons that the vehicle should respond, that
evidence should influence the resulting action.
However, on simulated scenes containing a stationary obstacle in the ego
lane, a state-of-the-art
reasoning VLA [1] generates trajectories that enter the
obstacle footprint on 58.1% of samples, and its selected actions collide
with a reconstructed version of that obstacle in most closed-loop rollouts, even though a comfortable stop was still possible. Crucially, the failure does
not arise because the hazard is absent from the model. The obstacle is
recoverable from the visual representation and is often explicitly
identified in the model’s own reasoning, yet neither source of evidence
exerts sufficient influence on the generated longitudinal plan. Instead,
the plan remains strongly governed by the supplied ego-speed history. We
call this dissociation between accessible hazard evidence and its influence
on action a perception–action binding gap (Figure 1); here
perceives means recoverable from the model’s representation
(formalized as availability, Section IV), not awareness.

This distinction matters because an unsafe action can have at least three
different causes. First, the relevant hazard may not be represented at all
(availability). Second, the trajectory generator may be incapable of
producing an appropriate response even when the hazard is known
(action-side sufficiency). Third, the evidence may be available and a
safe action may be expressible, but the evidence may have insufficient
action authority: changing the hazard does not sufficiently change the
generated plan. These cases imply different remedies, yet standard driving
metrics typically conflate them.

We disentangle them with matched simulated interventions that vary
visual hazard content, obstacle range, ego-speed history, and textual reasoning
while holding competing inputs fixed. Hazard information is available
throughout, yet longitudinal behavior is far more sensitive to ego history than
to the hazard itself, under closed-loop control in AlpaSim/NuRec [2] as well as
open-loop scoring.

Next, we ask whether the missing coupling can be restored without retraining the
policy. We inject a differentiable hazard energy into the frozen
flow-matching sampler of Alpamayo-1.5, steering trajectory generation during
flow integration while leaving all model parameters unchanged. Supplied exact
obstacle geometry, this reduces footprint intrusion from
58.1% to 14.5% and changes the governing dependence of the generated plan:
trajectory reach becomes primarily responsive to obstacle range rather than ego
speed. Controlled CARLA sweeps further show that the remaining failures are
those in which insufficient stopping distance remains.

Finally, we ask how far this intervention can be driven by signals
already present in the frozen model, rather than by privileged geometry.
Lightweight readouts of the visual cache estimate both when an in-path
hazard is present and where it lies. The key is to preserve the spatial
structure needed for that estimate: on sites held out in both geometry
and appearance, a spatially aware readout reduces footprint intrusion
from 65.0% to 11.7%, approaching the
6.0% obtained with exact geometry, with no measured
reach loss on matched clear scenes. Thus, much of the safety constraint
needed to restore perception-action binding is already recoverable from the model’s own
representation.
Autonomous binding is therefore feasible within
the evaluated visual domain, while robust semantic triggering under
domain shift remains open.

Our contributions are threefold. First, our primary contribution is to identify and causally diagnose a perception–action binding gap in a reasoning driving VLA.
Across logged driving, matched counterfactuals, and closed-loop replay, we
separate hazard availability from action authority and show that
longitudinal planning is dominated by ego-speed history; to our knowledge,
this is the first causal, rather than correlational, separation of hazard
availability from action authority in a reasoning driving VLA. Second,
we show that the missing coupling can be enforced at inference time without
retraining. A differentiable hazard-conditioned energy steers the frozen
flow-matching sampler toward safe braking and, when supplied an accurate
constraint, shifts the plan’s dependence from ego speed toward obstacle
range, demonstrating action-side sufficiency. Third, we show why standard logged evaluation can miss such a
failure. Because a binding gap is a failure of hazard-conditioned action response rather
than average prediction quality, standard logged evaluation can miss it:
safety-critical states in which a moving ego must brake for a stationary
in-path obstacle are rare because human drivers typically avoid them.

title: Reasoning as a Distribution: Generative Plan Latents for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Matteo Cercola,Katie Z Luo,Milan Ganai,John Alora,Simone Formentin,Marco Pavone
abstract: Vision–Language–Action (VLA) policies increasingly reason before acting, but existing reasoning models compress this intermediate decision into a single representation. When several plans are valid, this commitment hides alternatives that could otherwise be selected or revised. We introduce the Generative Plan Latent (GPL), which represents the reasoning state as a low-dimensional conditional distribution over plans, such as which object, grasp, or route to use. This makes the reasoning state addressable: without retraining the VLA, plans can be sampled (coverage), selected on request (steering), and reweighted by deployment outcomes (outcome adaptation). We test all three on SimplerEnv manipulation with π0\pi_{0}, and extend the analysis to RoboCasa, LIBERO, and a maze domain. Steering the plan raises the fraction of executions that follow the request from 0.48 to 0.94, while the same guidance on the native action distribution shows no reliable gain. Finally, we show that an explicit plan is most useful when it carries decision information not already determined by the observation.
introduction:
Vision–Language–Action (VLA) policies increasingly place a reasoning stage
between perception and action
(Zawalski et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026a), and this intermediate state empirically
improves policy success rate. This intermediate state is attractive because it can separate what the robot decides to do from the motor trajectory that realizes that decision. Yet existing reasoning models represent this state as one vector per observation. This raises the question: should a model expose one committed decision per observation, or
a distribution over valid ones?

The distinction matters whenever the observation leaves more than one decision valid. Consider a robot facing two identical cubes, with an instruction that names neither: nothing favors one target over the other. The same ambiguity is pervasive in everyday tasks: whether to pick up a can or push it aside, how to grasp a mug, or which route to take. A reasoning state that must produce a single decision necessarily collapses these alternatives. Averaging them may yield an invalid plan between the cubes; choosing one avoids this failure but still hides the equally valid alternative. The missing property is therefore not simply validity, but a representation that preserves the alternatives so they remain accessible at inference time, allowing preferences or outcomes to dynamically select the most viable strategy at deployment without retraining (Figure 1). We call a reasoning state addressable when, at inference time, the policy can be: sampled to obtain distinct valid decisions (coverage), conditioned to select among them a single decision (steering), and reweighted by outcome to adapt the decision in closed-loop (outcome adaptation).
The limitation of prior
designs is therefore a lack of addressability.
This is not the usual action-multimodality problem: robot learning has
already developed generative action models precisely to avoid averaging
incompatible motor trajectories (Section 2).
The unresolved question is whether the upstream decision
should itself also be represented as a distribution.

We introduce the Generative Plan Latent (gpl), which replaces a
deterministic plan readout with a conditional distribution pθ​(z∣c)p_{\theta}(z\mid c) of plans zz given a VLA representation cc. This distribution can be sampled, steered toward a requested mode, and reweighted from
deployment experience, all without retraining the underlying VLA. We show that the plan provides a substantially stronger handle than the action distribution for expressing an external preference. Under matched executors, selecting a requested plan increases the fraction of executions that follow it from 0.48 to 0.94, whereas applying the same inference-time intervention to π0\pi_{0}’s native action distribution yields no reliable improvement. Because these alternatives remain explicit, deployment outcomes can also change which plans are preferred without updating the plan generator or VLA. This benefit is conditional: an explicit plan can influence behavior only when it carries decision information that the executor cannot already recover from the observation. We call this the redundancy principle. In a controlled test, changing only the demonstrations to reduce this redundancy increases the plan-selection effect from +0.19 to +0.65. Finally, these capabilities do not depend on hand-designed plan coordinates: they persist when the plan representation is learned directly from demonstrated behavior.

Our contributions are:

We identify the decision bottleneck as a distinct locus for multimodality in VLAs and define addressability, the capacity to preserve alternative decisions so they can be sampled, selected, and revised. Matched plan- and action-level interventions show that the decision bottleneck provides the stronger handle for controlling behavior.

We introduce gpl, a distribution over task-level plans,
instantiated by a rectified-flow head and integrated into π0\pi_{0} with
frozen base weights and a small adaptation.

We propose the redundancy principle: an explicit plan should affect behavior only when it carries decision information not already determined by the observation.

title: From Predictive Geometry to Action: Learning Complementary Predictive Representations for Embodied Manipulation
authors: Xiaoxu Xu,Hao Li,Hongtao Zhang,Yili Tang,Jiafei Cao,Junhao Cai,Haoxiang Ma,Weixin Li,Weinan Zhang
abstract: Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. Existing approaches either augment policies with geometric information from current observations or introduce future prediction as auxiliary supervision, leaving open how predictive geometry should be represented for action generation. Therefore, we propose a two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations from multi-view video clips. During pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model provides dense geometric features that are compressed into predictive geometric representations and optimized to preserve scene structure and its temporal evolution. Action supervision is then applied to geometric transitions to extract a complementary motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant transitions. During downstream post-training, predictive geometry is transferred through geometry queries, while the motor representation guides intermediate features along the action-generation pathway. Future observations are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm tasks, our approach consistently improves downstream policies, including an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points on the WidowX evaluation. We further demonstrate transfer across multiple VLA architectures and WAMs, with improvements in both future-world and action prediction. The code will be available at https://github.com/xuxiaoxxxx/CPR.
introduction:
Anticipating how the physical world will evolve(Assran et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2023) under interaction is becoming increasingly important for vision-language-action (VLA) models(Ma et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026) and world action models (WAM)(Li et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2026). Such predictive capability allows an agent to reason about the consequences of interaction, rather than mapping only its current observation to an immediate action. Yet effective manipulation requires more than temporal foresight alone: it also depends on a precise understanding of how the scene is spatially organized. Geometry specifies object layouts, spatial relationships, and robot-scene configurations, while dynamics describe how these structures evolve as an interaction unfolds. For action generation, these two aspects play distinct but complementary roles: geometry provides the spatial structure within which actions are executed, while its evolution provides cues about how the scene may change over time. This naturally raises a central question: how should geometric structure and its predicted evolution be represented so that they can more effectively support action generation?

Recent efforts to incorporate geometry into predictive policy learning follow two directions. As shown in Fig.1, input-centric approaches(Sun et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026c; Zhang et al., 2025b) augment observations with depth, point clouds, 3D coordinates, or pretrained geometric features. These methods improve spatial grounding, but use geometry as additional context for describing the currently observed scene and may rely on sensing or geometry-estimation pipelines. Prediction-centric approaches(Yang et al., 2026a; He et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025c; Su et al., 2026) instead supervise models with future RGB-D observations, future geometric states, or other world-prediction targets, explicitly exposing the policy to future scene structure. However, such targets are represented as dense observations or holistic latent states, requiring the learned representation to retain geometric information whose relevance to control may vary substantially. More broadly, these approaches primarily organize geometry to represent the scene and its evolution. They leave less explicit how action-relevant information should be distinguished from geometry needed for a coherent world representation. This creates a gap between predictive geometric modeling and action-oriented motor representation learning.

A natural way to bridge this gap is to recognize that predictive geometry and action generation place different preferences on learned representations. Predictive geometric modeling benefits from preserving a sufficiently complete and coherent account of scene structure. Action generation, in contrast, benefits from emphasizing geometric variations that are informative for motor commands while reducing the influence of static or action-irrelevant scene content. Rather than forcing these roles to be served in exactly the same representation, we introduce two complementary representations with distinct but related purposes: a predictive geometric representation that provides a compact and structured description of scene geometry and its evolution, and a motor representation that emphasizes action-aware information from geometric transitions. The former provides structured predictive context, while the latter focuses this predictive information toward control.

Building on this observation, we propose the two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations (CPR) from large-scale heterogeneous interaction videos(Collaboration, 2023; Jin et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2024; Goyal et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2025a) and transfers them to downstream policies. As illustrated in Fig. 1, our framework first constructs a predictive geometric representation from dense geometric features and then extracts action-aware information from the temporal evolution of scene geometry across video clips, providing complementary guidance for downstream action generation. Specifically, as shown in Fig.2, during representation pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model (Wang et al., 2025) extracts dense geometric features from multi-view video observations, which are progressively compressed by a hierarchical query-based encoder into compact temporal states. Geometry reconstruction, masked representation prediction, and geometric transition prediction encourage the predictive geometric representation to preserve scene structure while capturing its evolution over time. We then apply action supervision to transitions between consecutive predictive geometric states, yielding a motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant geometric transitions. The predictive geometric representation therefore captures structured information about the evolving scene, while the motor representation focuses on transitions that are more directly informative for action. During post-training, as shown in Fig.3, these two representations are transferred through role-specific supervision pathways. Dedicated geometry queries are trained to infer the predictive geometric representation from current-time inputs, while intermediate features along the action-generation pathway are aligned with the motor representation. Importantly, future observations and the pretrained representation model are used only to construct privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. We evaluate CPR on both multiple VLA architectures and WAM across diverse simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks, demonstrating consistent improvements across different robot embodiments and action-generation paradigms. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We identify complementary roles for predictive geometric and motor representations in predictive policy learning: predictive geometric modeling benefits from preserving structured scene geometry, while action generation benefits from emphasizing control-relevant geometric transitions.

We identify complementary roles for predictive geometric and motor representations in predictive policy learning: predictive geometric modeling benefits from preserving structured scene geometry, while action generation benefits from emphasizing control-relevant geometric transitions.

We develop a two-stage framework that learns and transfers these complementary predictive representations. Hierarchical geometric tokenization and predictive objectives learn geometric states, while action supervision extracts action-aware information from their transitions; the two representations are transferred through geometry-query and motor-alignment pathways.

Extensive experiments across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent improvements across policy architectures and robot embodiments. CPR yields a 10.4% absolute gain on the WidowX evaluation and improves future-world and action prediction in WAM.
