title: De-Diffusing WAMs: Action-Sufficient Direct Prediction for Robot Control
authors: Shaoyi Zheng,Zhongtao Jiang,Yue Peng,Wenbo Lu,Shunchi Zhang,Xi Wang,Shengji Wan
abstract:
Cascade world-action models (WAMs) use predicted visual futures to condition robot actions, but inherit costly iterative inference from diffusion-pretrained experts.
We ask what a single-step predicted future must preserve to support accurate single-step action prediction.
In the evaluated WAM, resampling video noise has little effect on downstream actions, yet naively truncating both streams to one step substantially reduces task success.
Video-space supervision only partially closes this gap, and a local sensitivity analysis shows that vision prediction errors have highly unequal consequences for action accuracy.
These findings motivate DirectWAM, which converts pretrained video and action experts into single-step predictors without stochastic sampling through action-sufficient distillation, while retaining the explicit future-to-action cascade.
After learning a one-step action model, we train the future predictor by decoding actions from its own predicted futures and backpropagating demonstration action error through the expert, with an optional future-latent reconstruction loss.
The resulting objective evaluates the student-generated future through its downstream control consequences rather than relying on representation matching alone.
DirectWAM achieves 97.1% average success across four LIBERO suites and 85.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, outperforming Flash-WAM at the same one-evaluation-per-stream budget.
This advantage has also extended to three real-world tasks that we designed.
Compared with the full iterative teacher, it reduces inference latency by 28.0×28.0\times.
introduction:
Cascade world-action models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video models to predict visual futures, which then condition an inverse dynamics model (IDM) for action generation.
Unlike standalone video generation, the predicted future is not the final output but an intermediate representation for robot control.
This causal future-to-action relationship allows a robot policy to utilize world prior from video while retaining futures that can be decoded for inspection.
However, diffusion-based video and action experts realize this computation through repeated denoising, introducing a substantial inference cost.
We study how to retain the pretrained experts and explicit future-to-action interface while replacing their iterative inference procedure with direct prediction.

Recent acceleration methods either modify the future-to-action interface or compress its computation.
Fast-WAM retains video co-training but removes explicit future prediction at deployment Yuan et al. (2026); Motus supports action-only inference alongside other joint and conditional modeling modes Bi et al. (2026).
Among methods that retain the cascade, Flash-WAM Akbari et al. (2026) uses modality-aware consistency distillation to achieve one-step inference in both the video and action streams.
DIDO Lyu et al. (2026) concentrates supervision on control-relevant visual regions to learn single-step future prediction, while retaining iterative action generation.
These advances establish that cascade inference can be accelerated.
However, a more basic question is largely overlooked in WAM acceleration: what must a single-step future preserve to support accurate downstream action prediction?
As the future serves only as an intermediate representation, the reconstruction objective of video diffusion may not naturally align with the control objective of the downstream IDM.

We first disentangle the roles of stochastic sampling and iterative refinement, using LingBot-VA as our experimental instantiation.
Varying only the video noise produces limited changes in downstream actions, and fixing it throughout an episode barely affects closed-loop success.
Stochasticity can therefore be removed, yielding a deterministic future predictor that nonetheless still relies on the teacher’s multi-step computation.
Removing this iteration is non-trivial: naively reducing the steps degrades control, and learning a one-step predictor with video-space supervision recovers only part of the gap.
Therefore, these results motivate learning the direct future predictor through the action model that consumes its predictions, rather than relying on video-space supervision alone.

To understand how the remaining prediction errors affect control, we selectively correct components of the future-representation error under a frozen action expert.
Correcting only a small, locally action-sensitive component recovers a disproportionate share of the achievable offline action-error reduction.
The complementary component still contributes, but the imbalance shows that representation-error magnitude is a poor proxy for downstream importance.
This motivates action sufficiency as the learning principle for single-step prediction: the predicted future should be optimized according to the action decoded from it, rather than through representation matching alone.

We implement this principle in DirectWAM through action-sufficient distillation.
Starting from diffusion-pretrained video and action experts, we first train a single-step action expert with the video expert fixed.
We then train the single-step future predictor end-to-end through this action expert: actions are decoded from the student’s own predicted futures, and the demonstration action error is backpropagated into the future predictor.
An optional future-latent reconstruction loss anchors predictions to the demonstrated future.
Because both objectives supervise final predictions rather than intermediate denoising states, the pretrained experts are converted into a direct cascade without the student having to reproduce the teacher’s denoising trajectory.

In experiments, DirectWAM achieves 97.1% average success on LIBERO and 85.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, outperforming cascade baselines at the same compute budget and substantially narrowing the single-step control gap. These gains further carry over to three real-world manipulation tasks.
Inference latency decreases from 5042 ms for the full iterative teacher to 180 ms for DirectWAM, a 28.0×28.0\times speedup.
Together, these results demonstrate a practical route to retaining explicit future prediction while replacing iterative diffusion inference with direct computation trained for downstream control. Our contributions are threefold:

Separating stochastic sampling from iterative refinement.
We characterize their distinct roles in the evaluated cascade WAM: video-noise resampling has limited downstream effects, whereas naively truncating both streams to one step causes control drops.

Action sufficiency as a learning criterion.
We show that the magnitude of future-prediction error is a poor proxy for its effect on action accuracy, motivating a training objective that supervises the student-generated future through the actions it induces online.

A deterministic single-step future-to-action cascade.
We introduce DirectWAM, a one-step de-diffused cascade WAM that preserves explicit future prediction while achieving strong control performance both in simulation and in the real world.

title: FIT-MAC: A Closed-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Robust Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Jiatong Li,Jisheng Dang,Qiangqiang Ma,Bimei Wang,Jingwen Zhao,Wenjun Ma,Juncheng Li,Hong Peng,Bin Hu
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on standard robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, their reliability can degrade substantially when task conditions deviate from the nominal setting. Perturbations in object positions and task instructions may lead to complete task failure. Existing VLA policies generally lack an explicit runtime mechanism for distinguishing these failure modes and selecting an appropriate recovery strategy.
To systematically mitigate this issue, we propose FIT-MAC, a failure-aware, closed-loop multi-agent control framework for improving the robustness of VLA policies at inference time.
FIT-MAC augments a VLA policy with an inference-time control layer. First, the Planner Agent parses the language instruction into a structured task specification that captures the manipulation goal and spatial constraints, and the Grounder Agent resolves each instruction-level reference to a visual target. Next, the Verifier Agent tracks phase-specific execution progress, distinguishes target-binding errors from local execution failures, and determines whether intervention is warranted. The Correction Agent then routes permitted interventions to target rebinding or bounded grasping or placement recovery, depending on the failure type. When no intervention is required, the pretrained VLA remains the default action generator.
Extensive experiments on LIBERO-PRO demonstrate that FIT-MAC improves robustness across multiple VLA backbones, consistently increasing success rates and achieving state-of-the-art performance under diverse perturbations. Code11

introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception and language understanding to generate actions for robotic manipulation. OpenVLA provides an open-source foundation for generalist robot control (Kim et al., 2024), while π0\pi_{0} uses flow matching to generate continuous actions (Black et al., 2024). Its successor, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, further improves open-world generalization through heterogeneous co-training (Intelligence et al., 2025). Recent models pursue complementary directions, NORA reduces the computational cost of generalist VLA policies (Hung et al., 2025), while X-VLA targets scalable cross-embodiment transfer (Zheng et al., 2026). MolmoAct incorporates structured spatial reasoning between perception and low-level control (Lee et al., 2025). Other methods improve predictive modeling and long-horizon execution through world-knowledge modeling, future-goal prediction, and phase-aware policies (Zhang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026b; Fan et al., 2025). Collectively, these advances highlight the potential of VLA models for generalist robot control.

However, strong benchmark performance does not necessarily translate into reliable execution under distribution shift. AGNOSTOS reports limited zero-shot generalization across tasks, while SAFE identifies frequent failures on novel tasks, underscoring the need for runtime failure detection (Zhou et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026). Broader evaluations show substantial sensitivity to perturbations in actions, instructions, observations, and environments (Guo et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2025). VLATest documents similar robustness gaps under variations in clutter, lighting, viewpoints, and instructions, as well as in the presence of unseen objects (Wang et al., 2025b). Adversarial evaluations further expose vulnerabilities to digital and physical perturbations (Wang et al., 2025a). Together, these findings highlight the challenges of robust VLA execution.

Addressing these challenges requires both reliable temporal visual evidence and
effective runtime recovery. Reasoning-based video segmentation improves
language-conditioned grounding by decoupling textual semantics from dynamic
visual representations (Dang et al., 2026a). At the control level, RACER
combines a VLM supervisor with an actor trained on automatically generated
recovery trajectories (Dai et al., 2025). Sparse spatio-temporal propagation
strengthens object correspondence across frames (Dang et al., 2026b), while
COME-robot uses execution feedback for closed-loop failure diagnosis and
recovery (Zhi et al., 2025). Frame-relation mining reduces redundant memory
and mitigates error accumulation (Dang et al., 2023), whereas TCoT
integrates hierarchical reasoning with global–local recovery
(Li et al., 2026). Parallel temporal–spatial memory further captures
complementary motion and contextual cues (Dang et al., 2024).

We study a complementary runtime decision problem of distinguishing incorrect target binding from local execution failure and selectively applying the appropriate recovery mechanism. The pretrained VLA remains the default action generator.
As illustrated in Figure 1, we aim to improve the robustness of pretrained VLA policies through runtime recovery without modifying the underlying policy. Our key observation is that perturbations induce distinct failure types. Target failures arise when incorrect grounding of the language-specified target object or reference relation directs the policy toward the wrong object instance before grasping. Execution failures occur when the target is correctly identified, but local control becomes unstable during grasping, transport, or placement. These failures manifest as empty grasps, failed lifts, unstable releases, or stalled execution. Distinguishing between these failure types allows an external controller to select targeted recovery mechanisms rather than apply generic retries.

Building on this observation, we propose FIT-MAC, a failure-aware, closed-loop multi-agent control framework for improving the robustness of VLA policies at inference time. Specialized agents coordinate task parsing, visual grounding, execution monitoring, and recovery through a shared execution state. FIT-MAC retains the pretrained VLA as the default action generator and intervenes only when task progress, target visibility, or grasping and placement signals indicate failure. It distinguishes incorrect target binding from local execution failure and routes them to target rebinding or bounded local recovery, respectively. This design enables selective, interpretable correction while limiting disruption to nominal execution and leaving the pretrained policy unchanged.

Experiments on LIBERO-Object and LIBERO-Spatial show that FIT-MAC consistently improves the robustness of OpenVLA, π0\pi_{0}, and π0.5\pi_{0.5} across diverse perturbations. The largest gains occur under position, task, and environment perturbations, where successful execution often requires target rebinding and stage-wise recovery. FIT-MAC also maintains high success rates under object and semantic perturbations, demonstrating its effectiveness across perturbation types. Our contributions are as follows:

Specialized agents coordinate monitoring, diagnosis, routing, and correction through a shared execution state, while the pretrained VLA remains the default action generator.

title: Temporal Difference Learning of Probabilistic Reach-Avoid Value Functions
authors: Elias Fontanari,Pietro Noah Crestaz,Matteo Saveriano,Andrea Del Prete
abstract: Reach-avoid sets, defining the states from which a task can be completed while avoiding unsafe regions, are fundamental tools for deploying robots in environments subject to disturbances and uncertainty, as well as for runtime task-feasibility monitoring, allowing prediction of whether a state is safe and will lead to successful task completion. Classical Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability (HJR) and its recent neural extensions (e.g., Lipschitz Continuous Reachability Learning, DeepReach) treat disturbances adversarially, computing the reach-avoid set under worst-case disturbances from a bounded set. This guarantees safety but can yield overly conservative sets when disturbances are stochastic rather than adversarial, and additionally requires the disturbance set to be known or specified in advance.
introduction:
Autonomous robotic systems are increasingly deployed to perform complex tasks in environments subjected to different sources of noise and uncertainty. Determining, from a given state, whether a task of interest can be completed while satisfying critical safety constraints can often be framed in terms of the Reach-Avoid set: the set of states from which the system can reach a target region while avoiding an unsafe one. Avoid and Reach-Avoid sets are essential in runtime safety monitoring, as done in model predictive shielding [1]. Reach-avoid sets are also a useful tool for computing Control Invariant Sets (CIS) [2]: if the target set used to compute a reach-avoid set is itself control invariant, the resulting reach-avoid set is also control invariant, and typically larger. CISs are essential tools in safe control methods such as Model Predictive Control (MPC) [3], since constraining the terminal state of the associated optimal control problem to lie in a CIS ensures recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction.
Therefore, the accurate computation of reach-avoid sets is extremely useful for deploying robots in safety-critical settings.

Existing approaches to computing reach-avoid sets are predominantly grounded in Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability (HJR) [4], which treats disturbances as an adversary selecting the worst-case action from a bounded set.
This comes with two main drawbacks: i) these methods cannot be applied to disturbances with unbounded support, such as a Gaussian distribution, and ii) when the disturbance is random they tend to be extremely conservative.
Classic HJR methods rely on grid-based dynamic programming over the state space, which scales exponentially with the system’s dimensionality, rendering them intractable for high-dimensional systems.

For this reason, the computation of reach-avoid sets has been addressed mainly by two lines of work, alleviating the curse of dimensionality: physics-informed neural networks such as DeepReach [5], and reinforcement learning [6, 7].
DeepReach learns the reach-avoid set through a curriculum learning procedure that enforces the conditions of the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs partial differential equation (PDE).
RL-based methods, instead, learn a critic that encodes the safe set, replacing the PDE-based Hamilton-Jacobi formulation with a Bellman recursion that can be solved via RL algorithms.
However, in the adversarial setting the disturbance policy must be learned jointly with the control policy, turning training into a min-max optimization problem that is notoriously unstable and slow to converge.
In addition, the theoretical guarantees typically rely on regularity assumptions on the dynamics, most commonly Lipschitz continuity, which may not hold for hybrid or contact-rich systems.
DeepReach has been tested on large nonlinear systems such as quadrotors, but, unlike RL methods, it cannot be applied to non-differentiable dynamical systems, such as legged robots or black-box systems, since the dynamics is needed in the computation of the Hamiltonian.

A separate line of work, stochastic reachability analysis [8], [9], addresses reach-avoid problems directly as probabilities of success under a stochastic disturbance model, formulated via dynamic programming over the system’s transition kernel in a measure-theoretic setting.
While closer in spirit to our probabilistic formulation, these approaches rely on the numerical solution of the associated Bellman recursion over a gridded or otherwise explicitly represented state space, which precludes their use with the high-dimensional, black-box dynamics typical of robotic simulators.

In another line of work [10] the authors used actor-critic RL to learn a safe policy, where the critic expresses a pseudo-probability of future failure.
However, several aspects of this formulation limit its use as a set-computation method.
First, the critic addresses only the avoid component: it estimates the probability of failure with no notion of task completion and cannot distinguish states from which the task is achievable from states that are merely never-failing.
Second, the critic is defined with respect to the policy induced by the critic itself, a self-referential construction that the authors report to be excessively pessimistic early in training and that requires implementation-level corrections, namely computing Bellman targets under the unconstrained policy and maintaining a separate near-on-policy replay buffer.

Another method capable of computing reach-avoid sets, specifically used to compute CISs, is Viability Boundary Optimal Control (VBOC) [11], which avoids resorting to HJR by directly identifying states on the boundary of the reach-avoid set and training a neural network to represent it. The target set corresponds to the system’s equilibria, while the avoid set represents collisions with the environment or joint limit violations. By directly learning the boundary of the reach-avoid set, VBOC achieves higher data efficiency compared to HJR, but its main drawbacks are that it does not account for disturbances and can only handle fully-actuated systems.

We introduce PVF (Probabilistic Reach-Avoid Value Functions), addressing the typical drawbacks of HJR methods in settings where there is no adversary, but simply non-adversarial stochastic noise, as is often the case in robotics scenarios, wind disturbances acting on an aerial vehicle being a representative example.
By learning a value function that expresses, for each state, the probability of reaching the target set without ever entering the failure set, we are able to assess safe target reaching in a graded fashion: states that succeed under most disturbance realizations, and fail only under a highly unfavourable sequence of disturbances, are distinguished from states that fail under typical conditions.

Crucially, the entire procedure treats the system as a black box: it requires only the ability to sample transitions from the environment, with no access to an analytical model, no differentiability of the dynamics, and no knowledge of the disturbance distribution.
This makes the approach directly applicable to contact-rich and hybrid systems, such as legged robots, for which a closed-form model is either unavailable or non-differentiable, and where PDE-based methods cannot be applied. Fig. 1 provides an overview of the proposed method.

Additionally, our value function provides interpretable probabilities, as opposed to those computed by HJR methods, which provide either the worst-case constraint violation the trajectory will incur, or the value of the target-set membership function at the time the target is reached.

Summarizing, the contributions are the following: (i) a novel self-supervised method for computing probabilistic reach-avoid sets under stochastic disturbances with potentially unbounded support, without assuming worst-case behavior; (ii) a comparison against HJR-based baselines on systems of increasing complexity, up to a Hopper locomotion task, showing that the resulting sets are more interpretable, less conservative and more accurate under non-adversarial disturbances.

title: PACT-VLA: Speculative Action-Chunk Verification with Pre-Commit Observations
authors: Yixiang Zhu,Ruilong Wu,Yonghao Chen,Jiaxiang Zou,Yusong Hu,Xinyu Chen
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are commonly deployed with asynchronous inference in real-world settings, where the next action chunk is generated while the robot is still executing the previous one. By the time the new chunk is committed, the robot and scene have changed, so the chunk is conditioned on a stale observation and task success drops sharply as this inference delay grows. Generating multiple candidate chunks could let newer observations inform the final choice, but existing multi-candidate methods either rank candidates
with the stale inference-start observation or repeatedly switch between
candidates during execution, which can make the executed action sequence
discontinuous. Our key insight is that inference delay can be used as decision time. While
candidate generation is still underway, candidate selection can reuse the VLA
itself to choose the complete action chunk that best fits a later observation. We propose PACT-VLA, a training-free framework that generates candidates from the inference-start observation and selects one using this pre-commit observation. Its scoring function, FlowRes, measures the residual between each candidate’s implied flow direction and the velocity predicted by the frozen policy under the pre-commit observation, requiring no separate verifier. A pipelined implementation overlaps observation processing with candidate generation and batches scoring, so selection adds no control-step delay on the evaluated hardware. At a four-step delay, PACT-VLA improves average success by 15.0 percentage points over RTC on Kinetix and by 5.2 points over single-candidate asynchronous execution with GR00T N1.7 on LIBERO, and it further improves existing delay-robust methods. On three real-robot tasks, it raises average success from 60% to 82% over naive asynchronous execution with the same frozen π0.5\pi_{0.5} checkpoint.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2024) increasingly predict action chunks rather than individual actions (Li et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a; Black et al., 2024; Team et al., 2024), allowing several control steps to be executed from a single policy inference and preserving temporal coherence across consecutive actions (Black et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025). However, action-chunk generation is not instantaneous. While inference is running, the robot continues to act and the surrounding scene may change. Consequently, by the time a newly generated chunk is ready for execution, the observation from which it was generated may already be stale, and the chunk may no longer fit the scene (Black et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2025; Agouzoul, 2026).
The challenge is that action generation begins before later changes are observed.

Existing approaches address this challenge in different ways. Future-state methods use information available at inference start to
anticipate the conditions under which the next action chunk will be executed (Tang et al., 2025).
However, these methods determine the next action chunk before changes during
the current inference interval are observed, so the conditions at execution
may differ from what was anticipated. A natural alternative is to postpone
this decision by keeping multiple candidate action chunks available until more
information about the upcoming execution conditions becomes available. However, some test-time
sampling methods still rank these candidates using the inference-start
observation (Kwok et al., 2025; Jang et al., 2026), so the final choice
remains fixed before later changes are observed.

DreamChunk (Chen et al., 2026)
goes further by using a learned world model to predict a trajectory for each
candidate. As new observations arrive during execution, it compares them with
these predicted trajectories and repeatedly reselects which candidate to
follow.
This allows the choice to respond to newly observed changes, but keeping the
decision open during execution can cause repeated candidate switching, making
the executed action sequence discontinuous, which can hurt task performance. However, sensing
continues while the next chunk is being generated, so an observation arriving
during inference can already be available before commitment. This leaves open
whether such an observation can be used to finalize one complete action chunk
before commitment, without switching between candidates during execution.

Our key insight is that inference delay can be used as decision time. While
candidate generation is still underway, candidate selection can reuse the VLA
itself to choose the complete action chunk that best fits a later observation.
We propose PACT-VLA, which realizes this principle by generating a fixed
candidate pool from the inference-start observation and selecting one candidate
using a pre-commit observation received shortly before execution. To choose among the candidates, PACT-VLA uses the original
flow-based VLA policy (Lipman et al., 2022; Black et al., 2024) to evaluate each
candidate under the pre-commit observation. We introduce FlowRes, which
measures the mismatch between the flow direction implied by each candidate
and the direction predicted by the frozen policy under this observation.
The candidate with the lowest FlowRes score is selected, and the controller
executes actions from the selected chunk until the next planned chunk switch.

Using a pre-commit observation leaves only a short interval for candidate selection before the planned chunk switch. PACT-VLA therefore processes the pre-commit observation while candidate generation is still running and scores all candidates in a single batch. On the evaluated hardware, the full generation-and-selection cycle remains in the same control-step delay bucket as single-candidate generation. Experiments on Kinetix, LIBERO, and three real-robot tasks demonstrate the benefit of this design. At a four-step delay, PACT-VLA improves average success by 15.0 percentage points over RTC on Kinetix and by 5.2 points over single-candidate asynchronous execution with GR00T N1.7 on LIBERO. Across the three real-robot tasks, average success increases from 60% to 82% using the same frozen π0.5\pi_{0.5} checkpoint.

Our contributions are as follows.

We propose PACT-VLA, a training-free framework for action selection
under inference delay. PACT-VLA uses observations arriving during inference
to select one complete action chunk before commitment, reducing the
prediction–execution mismatch.

We introduce FlowRes, a candidate-verification method that reuses the
frozen VLA to rank candidates under the pre-commit observation, without
additional training or a separate verifier.

We design a pipelined implementation that overlaps pre-commit observation processing with candidate generation and batches candidate verification.

Experiments on Kinetix, LIBERO, and real robots show gains across multiple flow-based VLA policies and further improvements when combined with existing delay-robust methods.

1. We propose PACT-VLA, a training-free framework for action selection
under inference delay. PACT-VLA uses observations arriving during inference
to select one complete action chunk before commitment, reducing the
prediction–execution mismatch.

2. We introduce FlowRes, a candidate-verification method that reuses the
frozen VLA to rank candidates under the pre-commit observation, without
additional training or a separate verifier.

3. We design a pipelined implementation that overlaps pre-commit observation processing with candidate generation and batches candidate verification.

4. Experiments on Kinetix, LIBERO, and real robots show gains across multiple flow-based VLA policies and further improvements when combined with existing delay-robust methods.

title: Knowing When to Stop Thinking: A Dissection of Expected Free Energy as a Test-Time Compute Controller for Latent World-Model Planning
authors: Tong Zhang,Zhiyuan Shi,Yun Peng,Tao Xie
abstract: A planner using a learned world model can improve its predicted outcome while choosing a worse action. We study when expected free energy (EFE) can help decide how much computation to spend on a plan. An EFE-inspired objective combines goal distance with disagreement among stochastic predictions. We test candidate scoring, stopping, and online predictor updates separately. Stopping when elite cost stalls reduces refinement on tasks whose success plateaus with depth, with mean success close to fixed-depth references. At the larger tested weights, rewarding disagreement lowers success with a frozen model. Penalizing it helps at some task and weight settings but harms others. When training data omit a region needed to reach the goal, online updates recover part of the resulting loss. The tested cost-stall rule can fail when further optimization exploits model errors, because predicted cost keeps falling after task success peaks. Cost progress can guide computation on a plateau, but protecting performance after a peak requires information about the consequences of the chosen actions.
introduction:
A robot planning from images can improve its next action by repeatedly imagining and comparing possible futures. Each refinement step costs computation. Stopping too early may leave a useful action undiscovered. Continuing too long can favor an action that exploits errors in the learned dynamics. The planner must decide whether further optimization will improve the action it executes.

Test-time computation has improved iterative reasoning and model-based control. Recurrent language models refine internal representations before producing an answer (Geiping et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025). World-model agents predict future states to evaluate candidate actions (Hafner et al., 2023; Assran et al., 2025). A larger optimization budget gives the planner more opportunities to improve a plan. Its objective, however, remains a prediction of task performance. A fixed budget cannot respond to differences between instances, and convergence of the objective does not establish that the predicted consequences are correct.

Expected free energy (EFE) connects goal achievement and information seeking (Friston, 2010; Parr et al., 2022). Its pragmatic component favors preferred outcomes, and its epistemic component values information. These components suggest ways to control planning. Goal progress may indicate when refinement has stalled. Prediction uncertainty may change which plan the agent selects. New observations may improve the model before the next decision. Disagreement-based exploration methods collect information during learning (Sekar et al., 2020), whereas uncertainty penalties discourage plans that rely on unreliable predictions (Yu et al., 2020). Whether disagreement helps immediate task execution with a frozen predictor remains unclear. Internal progress may also fail to reveal when more planning becomes harmful.

We test these decisions with a compact latent world model and a sampling planner. In Figure 1, candidate trajectories provide goal cost and disagreement among stochastic predictions. We vary the disagreement weight and stopping statistic with the model frozen. We then test stopping in additional planner families and remove training data from a required region to study online learning. These comparisons separate the effects of reducing refinement, changing action selection, and updating the predictor.

Cost-stall rules reduce refinement on tasks whose success plateaus with depth, with mean success close to fixed-depth references. A best-elite baseline is competitive and often stops earlier. On tasks whose success declines after a peak, falling cost sustains harmful refinement. Rewarding disagreement reduces frozen-model planning success, whereas penalties help at selected task and weight settings. Online updates improve success when the agent must enter a region missing from its training data.

Our experiments address the stopping decision and the uses of prediction uncertainty.

We separate candidate scoring, stopping, and online adaptation in a common world-model planning protocol.

We measure when cost-stall controllers reduce planning effort and when model exploitation defeats the tested stopping signals.

We measure the task-dependent effects of disagreement penalties and test online learning by removing training data from a required region.

1. We separate candidate scoring, stopping, and online adaptation in a common world-model planning protocol.

2. We measure when cost-stall controllers reduce planning effort and when model exploitation defeats the tested stopping signals.

3. We measure the task-dependent effects of disagreement penalties and test online learning by removing training data from a required region.

title: LocoPilot: Single-Operator Bilateral Teleoperation for Loco-Manipulation Policy Learning
authors: Antonio Langella,Giovanni Minelli,Giovanni B. Dessy,Lorenzo Amatucci,Giulio Turrisi,Victor Barasuol,Claudio Semini
abstract:
Learning loco-manipulation policies requires demonstrations that
capture coordinated base and arm motion on the target embodiment.
Robot-free interfaces allow demonstrations to be collected
independently of the target robot, increasing flexibility but
without directly capturing platform-specific commands, proprioception, and
body-mounted observations. On-robot teleoperation allows to capture these signals directly, but requires an interface capable of commanding the complete system concurrently.
This paper presents LocoPilot, a single-operator bilateral teleoperation and
data-collection framework implemented on a 12-DoF Unitree Go2
quadruped equipped with a 6-DoF AgileX Piper L manipulator, an Intel
RealSense D435 wrist camera, and an Intel RealSense D405 head
camera. A second 6-DoF Piper L arm, used as the leader and two
handheld controllers provide simultaneous control of the base,
body posture, manipulator, and gripper. The follower arm interaction forces are estimated without a
dedicated force/torque sensor and rendered to the operator through a
passivity-constrained haptic channel. A ROS 2 pipeline records
synchronized multimodal observations together with a unified
11D action shared by teleoperation and
policy deployment. Compared to prior work, LocoPilot uniquely unifies robot-in-the-loop legged data collection,
force feedback without motion-capture instrumentation, and the
same action interface at deployment. We evaluate the interface across multiple
loco-manipulation tasks and validate the complete
collection-to-deployment pipeline by fine-tuning MolmoAct2 [1] on
pick-and-place demonstrations and deploying on
the physical robot without action retargeting or additional inverse
kinematics.
introduction:
Robots capable of both locomotion and manipulation extend physical interaction beyond the workspace of fixed-base manipulators. Arm-equipped quadruped robots are particularly suited to unstructured environments, where they combine legged mobility with physical interaction capabilities. Prior work has explored legged loco-manipulation through model-based whole-body control [2], or learned
coordination of locomotion and manipulation [3, 4].
More recently, generalist
Visual Language Action (VLA) models have gained increasing attention
for learning manipulation behaviors from multimodal demonstrations,
leveraging large-scale visual and language representations [5, 6, 7, 8]. For loco-manipulation, however, such
demonstrations must capture both base and arm actions on the target
embodiment. Ideally, the collection interface should therefore
minimize the collection–deployment gap while preserving direct
operator authority over all task-relevant commands.

Existing systems trade off these requirements in different ways:

Teleoperation systems place a human directly in the control loop of the physical robot, combining the operator task understanding with the constraints of the target embodiment. Leader-follower interfaces with direct joint correspondence provide intuitive control of fixed-base manipulators [9, 10], while mounting the same kind of interface on a wheeled base extends the concept to mobile manipulation, recording base motion alongside bimanual manipulation [11]. XR-based systems provide more general cross-embodiment interfaces
[12, 13], and DROID demonstrates the use of teleoperation for standardized large-scale data collection [14].
Immersive interfaces additionally stream the robot’s own onboard imagery to the operator [12], allowing real-time inspection of the visual inputs that will directly condition the downstream policy.
For arm-equipped quadrupeds, previous systems have used wearable motion capture, joysticks, haptic devices, or hand gestures [15, 16, 17, 18]. Collecting directly on the target robot reduces observation and action mismatch, but simultaneously commanding all task-relevant DoFs becomes increasingly difficult for a single operator.

Robot-free interfaces make the opposite trade-off. The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) [19] records demonstrations using a sensorized handheld gripper, allowing the operator to demonstrate manipulation without the kinematic constraints of the target robot. This improves collection flexibility, but omits embodiment-specific signals such as base
commands, proprioception, and body-mounted observations. Deployment therefore requires an additional mapping from demonstrated
end-effector motion to the target embodiment, as in UMI on Legs [20].

This work aims to combine the collection-deployment consistency
of on-robot teleoperation with the flexibility of learning-based
interfaces for arm-equipped quadrupeds. As illustrated in
Fig. , both the human operator and the
learned policy act through the same loco-manipulation interface,
while the resulting demonstrations are collected directly on the
target platform. Achieving this requires addressing two main
challenges.

The first challenge is enabling a single operator to command the
entire loco-manipulation action concurrently. Reaching and grasping
may require the robot to translate, rotate, or change body posture
while the arm is moving, so sequential base and manipulator control
produces segmented demonstrations rather than the smooth continuous
coordination desired from the final policy. Existing systems address
this through multiple operators, wearable instrumentation, or
partial autonomy, introducing additional coordination or removing
task decisions from the demonstrator.

To retain these decisions under single-operator control, we propose a bimanual interface design where a handheld controller is mounted on the end-effector handle of the leader arm. The dominant hand articulates the manipulator while
operating the mounted controller, and the non-dominant hand provides
the remaining base commands through a second controller. Together,
the two interfaces provide concurrent control of planar base
velocity, yaw rate, body pitch, arm configuration, and gripper
aperture. Interaction forces at the follower are additionally
estimated online and rendered through the leader arm, providing
contact feedback without a dedicated force/torque sensor.

The second challenge is maintaining consistency between collection
and deployment. On a legged manipulator, high-level commands are
executed through a locomotion and manipulation stack whose behavior
also shapes the recorded motion. Replacing this stack at deployment
can therefore shift the distribution of observations and executed
motions away from the demonstrated one, even when the high-level
action representation is unchanged.
We avoid this by using the same 11-dimensional loco-manipulation
action in both regimes and by keeping the same downstream execution
modules: the locomotion policy and leg controller, the arm controller,
and the gripper interface.
During collection, the action is generated by the
operator, whereas at deployment it is generated by the learned
policy; the locomotion policy, arm controller, and gripper interface
remain unchanged.
Table I compares LocoPilot with the closest prior
systems in terms of the teleoperation and data-collection properties
discussed above.
The contributions of this work can be summarized as follows:

A single-operator bilateral teleoperation interface for
arm-equipped quadrupeds, combining concurrent base, body, arm,
and gripper control with sensorless force reflection and an
operator-side passivity layer.

A unified 11-dimensional action interface shared between
teleoperation and learned-policy deployment, with the same
locomotion and manipulation controllers used in both regimes.

A synchronized learning-oriented data pipeline recording
multi-camera RGB-D observations, robot state, odometry, and
commanded actions, validated through multiple teleoperation
tasks and real-robot deployment of a fine-tuned MolmoAct2 policy.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows:
Section II presents the hardware and
software architecture. Section III the
teleoperation mapping and unified command.
Section IV reports the teleoperation
experiments and validates the collected demonstrations through
real-robot deployment. Section VI draws the final conclusions.

1. A single-operator bilateral teleoperation interface for
arm-equipped quadrupeds, combining concurrent base, body, arm,
and gripper control with sensorless force reflection and an
operator-side passivity layer.

2. A unified 11-dimensional action interface shared between
teleoperation and learned-policy deployment, with the same
locomotion and manipulation controllers used in both regimes.

3. A synchronized learning-oriented data pipeline recording
multi-camera RGB-D observations, robot state, odometry, and
commanded actions, validated through multiple teleoperation
tasks and real-robot deployment of a fine-tuned MolmoAct2 policy.

title: Learning Tactile-Aware Hand Representations from Human Hand-Object Interaction Data
authors: Yeonguk Yu,Jaehong Kim,Byungok Han
abstract: Tactile representation learning for dexterous manipulation often requires substantial robot-side data collection, limiting its scalability across different hands and sensors. We explore whether large-scale human hand-object interaction (HOI) data can provide a useful prior for robotic tactile learning. To this end, we propose HuTact, a framework that pretrains tactile-aware hand representations from human HOI data without requiring real tactile signals during pretraining. HuTact transfers the interaction structure learned from human hand motions to robotic tactile observations and can be further adapted with a small amount of unlabeled robot interaction data. We evaluate HuTact on tactile perception and manipulation tasks, including grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and tactile-conditioned policy learning. Across these tasks, human HOI pretraining improves data efficiency and provides a strong initialization for downstream learning. Notably, with HOI pretraining followed by midtraining on unlabeled robot play data, HuTact achieves 88.26% Macro-F1 on grasp prediction using only 25% of the labeled downstream data, comparable to training from scratch on the full labeled dataset (88.23%). These results suggest that human interaction data can serve as a scalable complementary source for robotic tactile representation learning.
introduction:
Tactile sensing enables humans to perceive and interact with the physical world, providing direct information about contact, force, texture, and motion that is difficult to obtain through vision alone [1].
Inspired by this remarkable human capability, tactile sensing has emerged as a critical modality for robotic manipulation, enabling robots to perceive subtle contact interactions, infer local physical properties, and regulate contact forces during complex manipulation tasks that demand precise and adaptive physical interaction [2, 3, 4].

Accordingly, a wide range of tactile sensors have been developed to capture rich information arising from physical contact, including vision-based sensors (e.g., GelSight [2], DIGIT [5]) and magnetic-based sensors (e.g., AnySkin [4], ReSkin [6]).
Beyond advances in tactile sensing hardware, the growing availability of large-scale tactile interaction data has further motivated learning-based approaches to extract generalizable representations from raw tactile observations [7]. In particular, recent works have explored self-supervised pretraining using large-scale tactile interaction data collected with respective tactile sensors, learning representations that can be transferred to downstream manipulation tasks [8, 9, 10, 11].

Learning generalizable tactile representations can reduce the amount of task-specific data required for downstream tasks. For vision-based tactile sensing, Feng et al. propose AnyTouch [12], which learns transferable representations from a sensor-aligned dataset collected across multiple visuo-tactile sensors. For non-vision-based tactile sensing, Sharma et al. [8] apply DINO-based self-distillation to masked tactile sequences collected from a dexterous hand, while Guzey et al. [9] pretrain tactile representations using task-agnostic robotic play data. However, existing approaches for non-vision-based tactile sensors still largely require real tactile interaction data collected directly with the target robotic hand and sensing hardware. As a result, adapting representation learning to a new robotic platform or tactile sensor requires additional data collection, introducing substantial time and cost for pretraining.

As an alternative, human hand-object interaction (HOI) data provide a promising source of pretraining supervision, where they contain large-scale and diverse interactions across objects, hand configurations, and manipulation behaviors [13, 14, 15, 16]. These datasets are particularly attractive for learning transferable hand representations because they provide (1) interaction patterns that can be shared across different hand embodiments, (2) large-scale interaction data that would be costly to collect on robotic platforms, and (3) an opportunity to reduce embodiment-specific data collection when adapting to a new robotic hand. Many of these datasets also provide temporally aligned 3D reconstructions of human hands and manipulated objects, allowing fingertip configurations and their evolution during interaction to be recovered without collecting data on a robotic platform. Although HOI datasets do not contain real tactile signals, their hand–object trajectories encode spatial and temporal structure associated with physical interaction. We hypothesize that this structure can serve as a transferable prior for robotic tactile representation learning and reduce the amount of robot-side tactile data required for adaptation.

In this work, our research question is: Can human hand-object interaction (HOI) data provide a transferable prior for robotic tactile representation learning? To answer this question, we propose HuTact, a framework for learning tactile-aware robot hand representations from human HOI data.
Rather than attempting to reconstruct real tactile signals from human data, HuTact learns the spatial and temporal structure of hand interactions from wrist-local fingertip trajectories.
To bridge human HOI pretraining and robotic tactile sensing, we separately tokenize fingertip coordinates and tactile observations, allowing the coordinate representation and shared Transformer backbone learned from HOI data to be retained while adapting the sensor-specific tactile input embedding. We further incorporate geometry-derived pseudo-contact signals as an auxiliary cue, encouraging the model to capture the relationship between fingertip coordinates and their corresponding tactile-like signals. This framework enables large-scale human interaction data to provide a transferable initialization for tactile-aware robot learning while reducing the amount of robot-side tactile data required for adaptation.

To validate the effectiveness and transferability of HuTact, we evaluate it on tactile-sensitive downstream tasks, including grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and policy learning on tactile-sensitive tasks, and analyze the factors that enable transfer from human HOI data to robotic tactile sensing. In summary, our contributions are as follows:

We propose HuTact, a framework that uses large-scale human hand-object interaction data to pretrain tactile-aware robot hand representations without requiring real tactile signals during the initial pretraining stage.

We show that representations learned from HOI data transfer to robotic tactile perception and manipulation, improving grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and tactile-conditioned policy learning.

We provide systematic analyses of the transfer mechanism through architectural ablations and data-efficiency experiments, studying the roles of temporal modeling, token separation, pseudo-contact cues, and robot-side midtraining. Our results show that HOI pretraining can substantially reduce the amount of task-specific robotic tactile data required for downstream adaptation.

1. We propose HuTact, a framework that uses large-scale human hand-object interaction data to pretrain tactile-aware robot hand representations without requiring real tactile signals during the initial pretraining stage.

2. We show that representations learned from HOI data transfer to robotic tactile perception and manipulation, improving grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and tactile-conditioned policy learning.

3. We provide systematic analyses of the transfer mechanism through architectural ablations and data-efficiency experiments, studying the roles of temporal modeling, token separation, pseudo-contact cues, and robot-side midtraining. Our results show that HOI pretraining can substantially reduce the amount of task-specific robotic tactile data required for downstream adaptation.

title: EventSync: Event-Driven Memory Updates for History-Dependent Manipulation
authors: Jingjiao Zhao,Dong Jing,Mingyu Cao,Ruochuan Shi,Xiansheng Chen,Pengwei Wang,Zhiwu Lu
abstract:
History-dependent robotic manipulation requires task context and interaction history, as the current observation alone is insufficient to determine the next action.
Hierarchical frameworks use task memory for high-level subgoal reasoning and low-level policies for execution.
However, memory updates require accurate completion assessment: similar observations may correspond to different execution phases, and prematurely recording completion can mislead subsequent subgoal reasoning.
We present EventSync, a hierarchical framework that coordinates task reasoning and action execution through event-driven memory updates.
A vision-language model generates subgoals from task plans and interaction history, while a vision-language-action model executes them.
A lightweight Event Monitor combines visual observations with end-effector trajectories to determine whether the current subgoal is complete.
The framework records the current subgoal in its completed-subgoal history and triggers subsequent reasoning only after obtaining completion evidence.
With visual history in the executor, EventSync achieves 64.5% overall success on RoboMME, exceeding the best baseline reported in the benchmark by 20.0 percentage points.
Further analysis shows that this update mechanism helps build a reliable completed-subgoal history.
Experiments on four real-robot tasks with different memory requirements validate the framework’s effectiveness in real-world robotic manipulation.
introduction:
Real-world robotic manipulation often requires decisions based on previous interactions.
In assembly, tidying, and everyday service tasks, earlier requirements and interaction outcomes can determine what the robot should do next [19].
History may also be needed to interpret the current phase of an ongoing operation.
Such tasks are non-Markovian with respect to instantaneous observations: robots must retain task context and interpret execution history to select subsequent goals and actions [18, 31, 11, 9].

Prior work introduces memory into vision-language-action (VLA) models to use historical information [23, 31, 39, 38], while other approaches assign task memory to a high-level reasoner that guides action execution through subgoals [36, 7].
We argue that hierarchical frameworks are well suited to history-dependent manipulation.
The limited performance of hierarchical methods reported in existing evaluations [9] motivates us to revisit memory updates within this framework.
As illustrated in Fig. 1, an instruction issued by the high-level reasoner does not imply that the corresponding operation has been completed, and similar current poses may correspond to different execution phases.
If an unfinished operation is recorded as completed, subsequent reasoning may rely on an incorrect estimate of task progress and advance to the next subgoal prematurely.
For task-memory updates, completion judgments must be accurate enough to avoid premature goal transitions and timely enough to keep subsequent reasoning and actions aligned with execution progress.

We propose EventSync, a hierarchical framework that coordinates task reasoning and action execution through event-driven memory updates.
A Memory Reasoner built on a vision-language model (VLM) obtains a task plan and combines it with interaction history to generate subgoals, which a VLA-based Action Executor executes.
EventSync maintains an event state for the current operation, and a lightweight Event Monitor with 87.39M total parameters estimates completion from visual observations and end-effector trajectories.
The framework adds the current subgoal to the completed-subgoal history and triggers high-level reasoning for the next subgoal only after obtaining completion evidence.

With visual history in the executor, EventSync achieves a 64.5% overall success rate on RoboMME, exceeding FrameSamp+Modul, the best baseline reported in the benchmark, by 20.0 percentage points [9].
Our variant without visual history in the executor achieves 94.0% on SwingXtimes, compared with the 7.3% reported for the hierarchical framework GroundSG + QwenVL [9].
Analysis of execution records further shows that updates guided by completion evidence help reduce premature progression and build a reliable completed-subgoal history.
Experiments on four real-robot tasks further demonstrate the effectiveness of combining task-memory reasoning with event-driven memory updates.

Our contributions are as follows:

A hierarchical memory framework for history-dependent manipulation.
We introduce EventSync, in which a high-level reasoner manages task memory and generates subgoals, a low-level policy executes actions, and an independent lightweight monitor provides completion feedback.

Event-driven task-memory updates.
We design a lightweight Event Monitor that combines visual observations with end-effector trajectories to assess operation completion, using the resulting evidence to trigger updates to the completed-subgoal history and subsequent high-level reasoning.

Empirical evaluation in simulation and on real robots.
We evaluate EventSync on the RoboMME simulation benchmark and real-robot tasks to assess its effectiveness in history-dependent manipulation, with comparisons and ablations examining the role of event-driven memory updates.

1. A hierarchical memory framework for history-dependent manipulation.
We introduce EventSync, in which a high-level reasoner manages task memory and generates subgoals, a low-level policy executes actions, and an independent lightweight monitor provides completion feedback.

2. Event-driven task-memory updates.
We design a lightweight Event Monitor that combines visual observations with end-effector trajectories to assess operation completion, using the resulting evidence to trigger updates to the completed-subgoal history and subsequent high-level reasoning.

3. Empirical evaluation in simulation and on real robots.
We evaluate EventSync on the RoboMME simulation benchmark and real-robot tasks to assess its effectiveness in history-dependent manipulation, with comparisons and ablations examining the role of event-driven memory updates.

title: What Novice Operators See Changes What the Policy Learns: A User Study of Keypoint Hand Visual Representation for Teleoperated Demonstration
authors: Amane Yamaguchi,Shohei Kamiguchi,Masashi Hamaya,Shigeo Yoshida,Takuji Narumi,Mai Nishimura
abstract:
Imitation learning increasingly relies on novice operators, whose demonstrations fall short of experts’ in number and inter-trial consistency.
Operators act on what they are shown, yet how the rendering of the robot affects their demonstrations, and the policies trained on them, has not been examined.
We study this question with PointHand, a teleoperation interface that renders a multi-fingered robot hand as sparse keypoints at its fingertips and joints, the same keypoints a policy can observe.
In a simulated mug-in-box task, 18 novices and 4 experts collected 2,200 trials under three renderings: the real shape of the hand, all keypoints emphasized, or the thumb and index finger alone emphasized.
The novices shown the thumb and index finger emphasized collected 441 successful demonstrations from 600 trials, against 320 for those shown the real shape.
We then trained diffusion policies on these demonstrations, replacing the scene point cloud and proprioceptive state they observe with the hand keypoints and two object keypoints.
Within 400 steps these demonstrations went from the weakest of the three novice conditions under the point-cloud policy (46.3%) to the strongest under the keypoint policy (57.3%), a gain of +11.0+11.0 percentage points in all five seeds.
Those collected with all keypoints emphasized changed by at most +0.7+0.7 percentage points, and in no more than three seeds.
The value of a demonstration therefore depends on the rendering shown during collection and on what the policy observes together.
A shared representation can pay off on both sides, in the number of successful demonstrations and in the success rate of the policy trained on them.
Project page: https://omron-sinicx.github.io/point-hand/.
introduction:
In imitation learning for multi-fingered robot hands, the quality of the demonstrations collected by novice operators limits the performance of the policy.
As policies and datasets scale up [1, 2], imitation learning is expected to rely increasingly on novices who have no knowledge of policy learning or robot kinematics.
Multi-fingered hands make this especially visible: teleoperation constrains observation and action more than one’s own body [3], and the number of possible postures is vast, so consistent control takes practice.

What makes a demonstration good is inter-trial consistency, and it has to hold with respect to what the policy observes rather than to the operator alone.
Sakr et al. define the quality of demonstration data by how repeatably the operator performs the same task [4], and a policy can only learn from repetitions it can tell apart in its own observation [5].
Operators act on what they are shown, so the rendering of the robot decides which cues they rely on.
When those cues are absent from the policy’s observation, demonstrations that were consistent for the operator can look inconsistent to the policy, an effect related to the imitation gap [6].
How the rendering shown to the operator affects the demonstrations and the policies trained on them has nevertheless not been examined.

This paper investigates this question with PointHand, a teleoperation interface that renders the robot hand to the operator as sparse keypoints at the fingertips and at the joints that bend each finger (Fig. What Novice Operators See Changes What the Policy Learns:
A User Study of Keypoint Hand Visual Representation
for Teleoperated Demonstration), a keypoint hand visual representation.
Unlike the real shape, which occupies much of the view, the keypoints remove occlusion and limit the operator’s cues to these parts, so we expect the task to become easier and the number and inter-trial consistency of demonstrations to increase.
We compare three renderings of the hand: its real shape (Baseline), all 11 keypoints emphasized (KP-Standard), and only the five keypoints on the thumb and index finger emphasized (KP-Salient).
In a user study, each novice collected demonstrations under one of the three renderings, and the experts under the real shape as a reference.
We train the same diffusion policy under two observation representations and compare them.
DP3 [7] observes the dense scene point cloud with the proprioceptive state.
DP-KP replaces both with a sparse set of 13 points, the same hand keypoints and two object keypoints on the symmetry axis of the object.

We ask three questions.
RQ1: does the keypoint hand visual representation bring the number and inter-trial consistency of novice demonstrations closer to the expert level?
RQ2: how does the collection condition change the performance of policies trained on these demonstrations?
RQ3: does the effect of switching the policy’s observation from the scene point cloud and proprioceptive state to the hand and object keypoints depend on how the demonstrations were collected?
Our contributions are as follows.

We built PointHand, a teleoperation interface that varies the hand rendering shown to the operator while giving the same keypoints to the policy.

We show that emphasizing only the thumb and index finger yielded the most successful novice demonstrations, 441 of 600 trials against 320 for the real shape, and the most consistent on four of the five kinematic metrics (Study 1).

We find that in the fraction of episodes that place the mug within 400 steps, these demonstrations were the weakest of the novice conditions under DP3 and the strongest under DP-KP, so the rendering at collection and what the policy observes are worth choosing together (Study 2).

1. We built PointHand, a teleoperation interface that varies the hand rendering shown to the operator while giving the same keypoints to the policy.

2. We show that emphasizing only the thumb and index finger yielded the most successful novice demonstrations, 441 of 600 trials against 320 for the real shape, and the most consistent on four of the five kinematic metrics (Study 1).

3. We find that in the fraction of episodes that place the mug within 400 steps, these demonstrations were the weakest of the novice conditions under DP3 and the strongest under DP-KP, so the rendering at collection and what the policy observes are worth choosing together (Study 2).

title: High-Precision RCM Motion for Ophthalmic Robotics via Hierarchical QP Control and Authority-Guided Recovery Planning
authors: Huanyu Tian,Adriana Namour,Lingyun Zeng,Zicong Wu,Sebastien Ourselin,Lyndon da Cruz,Christos Bergeles
abstract:
General-purpose manipulators can position ophthalmic instruments under a software Remote Centre of Motion (RCM). However, at some reachable configurations that are nonsingular for the tip task alone, the RCM and tip-tracking objectives conflict and the servo oscillates.
We formalise this failure as a constraint-induced task singularity: the RCM-projected tip Jacobian loses rank while the unprojected tip Jacobian stays well conditioned. Thus, the effective tip authority collapses although the target remains reachable.
We present a high-precision RCM servo architecture with built-in singularity recovery: for each commanded target, an authority-guided planner selects a well-conditioned arm configuration that reaches it and plans an RCM-consistent route, executed by a fixed hierarchical-QP controller.
On a 200-scenario kinematic benchmark, the complete nominal-and-recovery protocol reaches 128/128 near-singular targets and 71/72 near-joint-limit targets (100% and 99%, respectively), with the software-RCM residual below 0.142 mm.
On a physical 6-DOF arm it executes across four RCM entry points, with a worst-case kinematically reconstructed RCM residual of 178 μ​m\mu m and a median tip-regulation error of 32 μ​m\mu m, within the 200 μ​m\mu m control requirement adopted for the ophthalmic task.
introduction:
Robot-assisted vitreoretinal surgery is a keyhole task: a slender instrument is steered inside the eye while its shaft pivots about a fixed scleral entry, the Remote Centre of Motion (RCM) [1].
In vitreoretinal surgery, both the robot tip error and the RCM residual must be held to maximum 200 µ​m200\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}, against retinal structures only a few hundred micrometres thick, leaving little margin to trade between the two objectives [2, 3].
Purpose-built platforms realise the RCM through a mechanical linkage [4, 5, 6, 7, 8], which may also be adaptable [9, 10]. A general-purpose manipulator, e.g. such as that used in [11], however, enforces it through software and control, and the constraint becomes coupled with tip tracking and competes for the same joint velocities.

At certain reachable configurations that are nonsingular for the unconstrained tip-position task, this coupling becomes a constraint-induced task singularity: the joint motion that advances the tip is the same motion that sweeps the shaft laterally through the sclera, i.e. the tip-progress gradient aligns with the RCM constraint directions. In such a case, no RCM-consistent joint velocity produces the required first-order tip progress (Fig. 1).
Partial alignment can be accommodated within the residual null space by a prioritised controller [12, 13]. As the alignment approaches completion, however, the available first-order tip authority vanishes.
A loose RCM tolerance may absorb the conflict through temporary constraint violation, whereas the tight ophthalmic tolerance leads to oscillatory tip motion or loss of tip progress toward the target (Sec. II-B).

In prior work, programmable RCM enforcement is realised with task-priority (hierarchical) control and solved by hierarchical quadratic programming (HQP). The RCM residual is imposed as the high-priority level, and tip tracking is resolved on the remaining subspace. The constraint is written as an equality in the hierarchy or as an inequality in a positional- or velocity-level QP [14, 15, 16, 17, 18]. The residual null space is used for a redundancy resolution, typically toward a manipulability/conditioning measure [19, 18].
Because this resolution is local and provides no path-level lookahead, it cannot route around a singularity lying on the nominal path. The underlying projected-Jacobian rank loss is known in task-priority control as an algorithmic singularity [20].

Two gaps therefore remain. First, software-RCM work reports RCM and tip accuracy, but rarely analyses the closed-loop oscillation produced by constrained-induced task singularity under a strict tolerance. Second, redundancy-resolution studies typically involve more redundant degrees of freedom and looser task tolerances, so the constrained null space retains enough dimensions, and the solver enough slack, to absorb the conflict, which then never appears as a task singularity.

We study a representative challenging case: a 66-DOF arm performing 3D point positioning under a high-priority RCM constraint with bounded slack, where a single redundant degree of freedom (roll about the shaft) leaves little room to reconcile the RCM and tip objectives once joint limits are active.
The contributions of this work are:

A bounded-slack HQP controller that enforces the RCM while servoing the tip.

An authority-guided recovery planner, built on our characterisation of the constraint-induced task singularity, that acts only on the reference the controller tracks.
