title: Enumeration-Guided Training of Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Safety Certificates
authors: Mihaela-Larisa Clement,Tosca Pierro,Ezio Bartocci,Luca Marzari
abstract: Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis offers formal safety guarantees for control systems, but training accurate neural certificates remains difficult, particularly when unsafe regions are hard to characterize. We propose a verification-guided training framework that addresses this by using probabilistic enumeration of safety constraints to detect forward-invariance violations, i.e., states where the learned certificate incorrectly classifies unsafe behavior. This produces a compact, targeted set of counterexamples that more precisely captures the failure boundary than inputs generated by standard adversarial attack methods. Crucially, using this representation to fine-tune a pretrained HJ value function yields larger certified regions and reduces certification time across all tested benchmarks. We further introduce a shielding mechanism based on the refined certificates to enforce safety constraints at deployment time. We evaluate the proposed safety filter in a realistic, physics-based Isaac Sim environment and through real-world autonomous racing experiments, achieving zero safety constraint violations compared to a nominal controller and a backup policy based on Linear Quadratic Regulation (LQR). These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed shielding mechanism in ensuring safe operation under high-speed, safety-critical conditions.
introduction:
For control systems interacting with the physical world, safety is a primary concern in controller design, as controllers must satisfy safety constraints at all time steps over an infinite horizon. Consider, for example, a robot locomotion task where safety requires maintaining a positive clearance from surrounding obstacles at all times. Two distinct challenges arise in such settings. The first is identifying the set of states from which long-term constraint satisfaction is guaranteed, the so-called feasible region, since the deployment of a controller should be restricted to this set. The second is actively enforcing safety at runtime, as even when a controller is initialized within the feasible region, it may issue actions that push the system toward constraint violations, and an explicit safety mechanism is required to intercept and correct such actions before they are executed. Addressing both challenges simultaneously is essential for deploying safety-critical controllers in realistic environments.

A widely adopted approach to enforce safety constraints is based on Model Predictive Control (MPC) [1]. Nominal MPC incorporates state and input constraints directly into a finite-horizon optimal control problem solved repeatedly online. Under suitable assumptions, nominal MPC can exhibit a degree of robustness; however, when hard state constraints are present, these safety margins can become very small. To account for bounded disturbances and model uncertainty, robust MPC variants such as tube-based methods [2, 3] confine the system trajectory to a tube around the nominal trajectory, ensuring constraint satisfaction through tightening of the nominal problem. Nonetheless, constraint tightening can introduce conservatism that degrades performance in demanding tasks, and the finite planning horizon limits the scope of safety guarantees that can be provided.

A more principled framework for characterizing safety over an infinite horizon is Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis [4], which offers a formal setting for computing feasible regions of control systems subject to safety constraints. HJ reachability defines the feasible region as the zero-sublevel set of a value function V⁡(x)V(x), representing the worst-case constraint violation along an optimally controlled trajectory originating from state xx. Compared with MPC-based approaches, HJ reachability provides direct global safety guarantees rather than relying on finite-horizon optimization and repeated replanning. This makes VV a natural candidate not only for certifying the feasible region, but also for constructing a runtime safety filter, namely a shield, that corrects unsafe control actions by substituting a verified backup policy whenever a nominal controller would violate the safe set boundary. However, this increased rigor comes at a high computational cost, as the underlying HJ partial differential equations suffer from the well-known curse of dimensionality, making exact solutions intractable for high-dimensional systems.

To address this limitation, several recent works have proposed neural HJ certificates, leveraging function approximation to scale reachability analysis to more complex systems [5, 6]. Nevertheless, learned certificates do not inherently guarantee that the resulting zero-sublevel set defines a sound feasible region and therefore require formal verification to confirm that safety guarantees are preserved. This limitation motivated the approach of Yang. et al. [7], which integrates neural value function learning within a training loop guided by adversarial search and formal verification. While this approach improves scalability and enables learning of provably safe certificates, it faces three critical challenges that we aim to address in this work.
First, the adversarial procedure is empirical and relies on sparse, locally generated counterexamples as gradient-based attacks explore only a narrow neighborhood of the current iterate and may therefore miss failures located in other regions of the state space. As a result, the search may report no violation even when unsafe states remain in the fine-tuned certificate, not because these states are genuinely safe, but because the search did not reach them. This false negative prematurely triggers the formal verifier, which, being NP-hard [8], can incur substantial computational cost. The verifier then identifies the violation that the adversarial search missed, generates additional counterexamples, and initiates another fine-tuning cycle. This process can repeat over many iterations, leading to significant verification overhead before convergence. The inefficiency becomes particularly acute in high-dimensional systems, where the local coverage of adversarial search can be small relative to the global extent of the failure set. Second, even after a verified certificate has been obtained, the question of how to exploit it as a practical runtime safety filter for a learned controller operating in a complex environment remains unaddressed: translating the certified feasible region into an effective shielding mechanism requires additional design choices that the learning procedure alone does not resolve.

This paper addresses both limitations by introducing a novel enumeration-guided training strategy depicted in Fig. 1. At the core of our approach is the enumeration of compact unsafe regions, which replaces purely local counterexample search with a more structured exploration of the state space based on preimages of the unsafe set in deep neural networks [9, 10]. The underlying intuition is that isolated local violations provide only limited information about the geometry of the failure set, whereas counterexamples drawn from a globally organized, spatially distributed exploration better characterize its shape and extent, offering a richer training signal to the learning algorithm. Crucially, our enumeration-guided training is not a substitute for formal verification; it improves the quality, diversity, and coverage of the counterexample set during training, while verification retains its role as the provable safety certification. In addition to this new training strategy, and building on the least-restrictive safety framework of Fisac et al. [11], we introduce a shielding mechanism that leverages the refined neural HJ certificate to enforce safety at deployment time. The proposed shield acts as a safety filter between a nominal controller and the plant: at each time step, it checks whether the intended action preserves forward invariance of the certified safe set and, if necessary, overrides it with a safe recovery action provided by a backup policy based on Linear Quadratic Regulation (LQR) [12]. Unlike existing HJ-based safety filters, which typically rely on grid-based value functions or learned approximations without formal safety guarantees, our approach introduces a formally verified neural HJ certificate that, by construction, ensures forward invariance of the certified safe set under the verified system dynamics. This enables the deployment of formally certified safety filters in complex systems where closed-form safety certificates are unavailable.

Our empirical evaluation spans four safe-control verification benchmarks from [7], covering systems with both linear and nonlinear dynamics, as well as a new obstacle-avoidance benchmark based on the RoboRacer platform (formerly F1TENTH) [13]. Enumeration-guided training yields faster convergence times and, in general, larger certified regions across all benchmarks, with the largest gains on higher-dimensional and more complex tasks. The verified RoboRacer certificate is first evaluated in a realistic, physics-based Isaac Sim environment to assess its robustness against different track geometries, corridors, and heading disturbances. We further validate its effectiveness under real-world conditions by deploying it on a physical RoboRacer platform on an unseen real racing circuit. This deployment confirms the effectiveness of the proposed solution for complex safety-critical tasks.

title: Frontier LLMs Enter the World of Robotics: A Cross-Model Evaluation on RoboColiseum
authors: Da Huang,Jichao Wang,Junhui Wu,Tong Ran,Linting Guo,Siying Zhang,Chuang Men,Sukai Wang,Yue Zhou,Maoqing Yao,Mo Wu
abstract: Recent studies have explored the potential of multimodal large language models for robot control, yet the models’ embodied capabilities remain insufficiently characterized across models, tasks, and execution settings. We conduct a multidimensional comparative evaluation on RoboColiseum across four tracks: Instruction Following, Spatial Reasoning, General Manipulation, and Robustness. We implement Agent2Act, a control harness that integrates GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon into the evaluation environment through shared observation, action execution, and feedback interfaces. Under common task settings and scoring criteria, all four models exhibit a consistent capability profile: high instruction-following scores, with three approaching perfect performance; strong spatial reasoning; and general manipulation scores below those of the other three tracks. Within the evaluated configurations, Astra leads instruction following and robustness, while Opus leads spatial reasoning, general manipulation, and overall performance. These results reveal complementary strengths across models and a persistent gap between task understanding and reliable physical execution. Component comparisons on selected tasks further show that harness design affects task success, planning cost, and execution time. Additionally, case studies with Astra examine whole-body coordination, manipulation across robot embodiments, precision manipulation, dexterous-hand manipulation, and real-robot tasks, providing further insight into the model’s capabilities and limitations across embodied tasks.
introduction:
The release of GPT-6 Astra [1] raises a practical question: what can a
multimodal large language model achieve when it directly controls a robot?
A growing body of work explores how large language models (LLMs) can use
observations to control robots.

In simulation, W. Zhang et al. evaluate LLMs as manipulation policies and
identify a gap between semantic task understanding and precise physical
control [2]. GPT-as-Policy compares Astra-generated
end-effector actions with a hybrid controller in which Astra reviews and
corrects π0.5\pi_{0.5} action proposals [3]. Galbot’s study
examines direct and hybrid control across simulated manipulation and other
embodied domains, distinguishing model-generated commands from actions
provided by learned policies or whole-body controllers
[4]. Y. Yao et al. evaluate tabletop and mobile
manipulation in Ebench, where Astra generates end-effector waypoints,
gripper targets, and base targets through a fixed execution interface
[5].

On real hardware, RoboCurve compares Astra with a VLA policy on bimanual
tabletop tasks using YAM robot arms. Astra issues absolute end-effector
poses through action tools [6]. RoboICL evaluates
both simulated tasks and three real-robot tasks on a Franka Research 3
arm. Its frozen Astra model uses demonstrations and interaction memory
to generate numerical action chunks through a fixed tool schema
[7].

These studies provide initial evidence of LLM-driven robot control across
different tasks and control configurations. Building on this work, we
compare four frontier multimodal large language models across
RoboColiseum’s four tracks, using shared sensing and execution interfaces
to examine their strengths and limitations.

Our evaluation covers GPT-6 Astra [1], GPT-6.1
Sol [8], Claude Opus 5.5 [9], and
Gemini 4 Argon [10]. To integrate these models into
RoboColiseum, we implement Agent2Act, a harness that provides a unified
interface for interaction with robotic environments and action execution.
RoboColiseum’s consistent task settings and scoring criteria allow us to
systematically examine the models’ relative strengths, weaknesses, and
capability boundaries in embodied tasks.

RoboColiseum is a multidimensional benchmark for embodied model
capabilities. It supports vision-language-action (VLA) models, world/action
models (WAM), and agent-based systems. Its four tracks assess complementary
dimensions of embodied performance:

Instruction Following: evaluates instruction understanding
across ten dimensions, including color, size, quantity, semantics, and
logical conditions.

Spatial Reasoning: evaluates understanding of spatial
relations, including relative and absolute positions, sorting, and stacking.

General Manipulation: evaluates a range of manipulation
skills, including grasping, placing, insertion, twisting, pouring,
scooping, and bimanual coordination.

Robustness: evaluates performance under changes in robot
state, camera mounting position, image quality, instruction wording,
environmental conditions, and lighting.

Strong instruction following, spatial reasoning, and
robustness, but weaker manipulation. All four models exhibit a common
capability profile: their instruction following, spatial reasoning, and
robustness scores exceed their general manipulation scores. Strong
zero-shot instruction following has not yet translated into reliable
complex physical manipulation.

Different models have different strengths. Among the four
multimodal models, Astra leads instruction following and robustness,
while Opus leads spatial reasoning, general manipulation, and Overall.
No single model leads every dimension. These complementary strengths
show why Overall scores alone cannot fully characterize model capabilities.

Cost and latency remain bottlenecks. Despite strong
benchmark performance, high inference costs and long waits for model
responses continue to limit the practical use of multimodal models for
embodied robot control.

Harness design matters. A well-designed harness helps
models make full use of their capabilities in robot control. Agent2Act
provides a shared control harness for evaluation across four capability
dimensions. Comparisons on a limited test set illustrate how observation
inputs, feedback, history, and control interfaces affect task completion
and execution efficiency.

Case studies reveal the scope and limits of model
capabilities. Case studies with GPT-6 Astra demonstrate that multimodal
large language models can control whole-body motion, manipulate objects
across robot embodiments, combine mobile navigation with interaction,
and perform selected tasks on real robots. Dexterous-hand control and
fine-grained physical interaction remain challenging.

title: RoboCasa-Shift: Stage-Aware Robustness Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Policies in Long-Horizon Household Manipulation
authors: Haocheng Wang,Youquan Liu,Weiyu Guo,Aokai Zhang,Donghang Wu,Hongyu Liu,Sha Zhang,Weidong Yang,Ben Fei
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) robustness is commonly summarized by aggregate task success, which obscures how individual executions change under distribution shifts and where failures emerge in long-horizon tasks. We introduce RoboCasa-Shift, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 that combines controlled single-factor shifts, matched clean-perturbed rollouts in which each pair shares the same underlying settings and differs only in the target shift, and simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics. We evaluate GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon tasks that pass a predefined clean-performance gate under four perturbation factors and three calibrated severity levels, including conditions that drive the evaluated policy to complete task failure, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts. Robustness responses vary substantially across factors and tasks, and increasing severity does not always produce monotonic degradation. For example, one camera condition yields Δ​SR=0\Delta\mathrm{SR}=0 despite 8 of 80 matched episodes changing outcome. Stage-aware analysis further shows that the same end-to-end degradation can correspond to different execution-depth profiles. Camera L2L_{2} and Gaussian blur L1L_{1} both yield Δ​SR=0.188\Delta\mathrm{SR}=0.188, yet their first-stage failure rates are 19.0% and 36.4%, respectively. Our findings suggest that VLA robustness should be viewed as a multi-dimensional property of execution rather than a single end-to-end performance measure, motivating evaluation protocols that jointly capture outcome degradation, paired outcome sensitivity, and failure progression.
The code is publicly available at https://github.com/HaochengWang23/RoboCasa-Shift.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become an increasingly important paradigm for robotic manipulation by integrating visual observations, language instructions, and robot actions within unified policy frameworks [1, 2]. Despite their growing capabilities, maintaining reliable behavior under distribution shifts remains a key challenge for deployment, as robots may encounter variations in observations, environments, and physical states that differ from those seen during training.
Systematically evaluating VLA robustness under such distribution shifts is important for understanding the reliability of these models in robotic applications.

Recent robustness benchmarks have expanded the evaluation of VLA policies beyond nominal task settings through diverse controlled distribution shifts and increasingly systematic evaluation protocols [3, 4, 5].
Despite this broader coverage, robustness is still commonly summarized at the task or evaluation-condition level through aggregate metrics such as success rate. Such summaries do not reveal how individual executions change under a distribution shift or where failures emerge within long-horizon task execution, leaving a need for more diagnostic evaluation at the execution level.

Such diagnosis requires controlling episode-level variation for meaningful comparison, since clean and shifted evaluations with different task instances or initial conditions may confound episode difficulty with the target distribution shift.
We therefore compare each perturbed execution with a corresponding clean execution under the same underlying task conditions, changing only the target perturbation. This counterfactual pairing provides a controlled basis for identifying episode-level outcome changes associated with the evaluated shift.

Even under such controlled comparisons, a binary task outcome provides only a coarse description of failure in long-horizon manipulation. These tasks unfold through a sequence of semantically meaningful subgoals [6, 7], so two failed executions may terminate after very different amounts of task progress.
Stage-aware evaluation can therefore complement final success or failure by tracking semantic progress and identifying the first incomplete subgoal, providing a clearer view of where robustness failures emerge during execution.

We introduce RoboCasa-Shift, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 [3] for evaluating VLA policies under controlled distribution shifts in long-horizon household manipulation, as illustrated in Figure 1.
The benchmark defines controlled single-factor shifts at multiple frozen severity levels and a matched clean-perturbed protocol for episode-level counterfactual comparison.
It further incorporates simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics to track semantic execution progress and localize where failures emerge during long-horizon task execution. RoboCasa-Shift characterizes robustness from complementary perspectives, including end-to-end task outcomes, episode-level outcome changes, and stage-aware execution behavior.

Our evaluation reveals that robustness responses vary across perturbation factors and tasks, and that increasing calibrated severity does not always lead to monotonic degradation in end-to-end performance.
Aggregate success rates can also mask considerable episode-level outcome changes, while similar end-to-end degradation can correspond to failures emerging at different semantic depths of task execution.
Stage-aware analysis further shows that perturbation severity can alter the semantic depth reached by failed executions, with stronger shifts in some conditions associated with earlier incomplete milestones.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We develop RoboCasa-Shift, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 for long-horizon household
manipulation. The benchmark defines controlled single-factor distribution shifts at multiple frozen severity levels under an
episode-level clean-perturbed counterfactual protocol, enabling robustness changes to be examined under matched task conditions.

We develop RoboCasa-Shift, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 for long-horizon household
manipulation. The benchmark defines controlled single-factor distribution shifts at multiple frozen severity levels under an
episode-level clean-perturbed counterfactual protocol, enabling robustness changes to be examined under matched task conditions.

We introduce a simulator-grounded stage-aware robustness diagnostic that complements final task success with semantic execution information. Long-horizon tasks are represented through ordered semantic
subgoals evaluated by simulator-state predicates, allowing execution progress and the first incomplete subgoal to be tracked for failure localization.

We conduct a controlled robustness study on four clean-qualified long-horizon RoboCasa tasks across four perturbation factors and three severity levels, jointly analyzing end-to-end task outcomes, counterfactual episode-level changes, and stage-aware execution depth. The analysis reveals
robustness behaviors not captured by aggregate success alone, including heterogeneous severity responses and differences in
the semantic depth reached by failed executions.

title: Agentic discovery of interpretable car-following laws from multi-source trajectory data
authors: Jiamei Xu,Jie Sun,Keshuang Tang,Jian Sun
abstract: Car-following (CF) models is a fundamental component of microscopic traffic simulation and underpin the analysis of collective traffic dynamics, while its modeling becomes more challenging due to diverse human driving behaviors and the increasing presence of automated vehicle. Analytical CF models offer interpretable representations of longitudinal vehicle interactions, but their prescribed functional structures may limit the representation of heterogeneous driving behavior. This study proposes an agent-centered, physics-aware framework for the empirical discovery of CF laws from multi-source trajectory data. The framework iteratively combines agent-guided hypothesis generation, informed by traffic flow knowledge and state-dependent reconstruction errors, with evolutionary symbolic search and physics-aware multi-objective evaluation. Using NGSIM US-101, highD, and exiD, the framework discovers the Adaptive Equilibrium Response Model (AERM), which couples state-dependent relative-speed response with spacing-dependent equilibrium-speed restoration. AERM admits analytical equilibrium speed–spacing and flow–density relationships; its stability conditions are derived for the zero-delay formulation, and platoon simulations examine disturbance propagation. Evaluated against seven classical CF models on Shanghai naturalistic driving data, NGSIM I-80, and Waymo trajectories, AERM attains the lowest spacing and speed reconstruction errors under trajectory-specific calibration, reducing spacing RMSE by 9.11%, 7.59%, and 21.73% relative to the strongest baselines, and remains competitive under dataset-level shared parameters. These results demonstrate the fitting flexibility and analytical tractability of the discovered CF law, providing an interpretable basis for microscopic traffic simulation.
introduction:
Car-following (CF) models describe how a follower vehicle adjusts its longitudinal motion in response to its leader and the prevailing traffic state. They constitute the fundamental component of microscopic traffic simulation and underpin the analysis of collective traffic dynamics (Brackstone and McDonald, 1999; Treiber et al., 2000; Jiang et al., 2001). Their importance rests on a simple observation that the local acceleration response of a vehicle governs not only its own trajectory but also the formation and propagation of traffic disturbances, so that errors in the assumed longitudinal interaction can amplify into large-scale congestion patterns. An accurate yet tractable CF law is therefore a prerequisite for reproducing and explaining realistic traffic behavior. This raises a twofold requirement for such laws, as they must capture nonlinear, condition-dependent vehicle interactions with sufficient accuracy, and they must retain enough analytical structure that their traffic flow implications (e.g., equilibrium states, fundamental diagrams, and stability) can be derived and interpreted.

Classical CF modeling has produced a family of interpretable equations built on distinct behavioral hypotheses: stimulus–response relations (Gazis et al., 1961), safety-based speed constraints (Gipps, 1981), relaxation toward a spacing-dependent desired speed (Bando et al., 1995), relative-speed feedback (Jiang et al., 2001), and free-flow and desired-spacing interactions (Treiber et al., 2000). These formulations connect microscopic behavior to traffic flow theory, but they are developed in a structure-first fashion that the functional form is fixed by behavioral assumptions, and trajectory data are used only to calibrate its parameters (Kesting and Treiber, 2008). Extensions with heterogeneous parameters or added behavioral terms improve flexibility, yet they remain confined to the analytical skeleton that was assumed in the first place (Ossen and Hoogendoorn, 2011; Saifuzzaman and Zheng, 2014). With increasingly heterogeneous traffic, the natural question is whether the governing functional relationship itself (not just its parameters) can be determined from observed behavior.

High-resolution trajectory data and machine learning have made this question tractable. Nonparametric and neural CF models approximate complex responses without committing to a prescribed equation (Papathanasopoulou and Antoniou, 2015; Huang et al., 2018), although an implicit predictor is less convenient for extracting an explicit mechanism or deriving equilibrium and stability conditions, and dedicated methods are required to analyze its dynamics (Zhang et al., 2024). Symbolic regression offers a complementary route by searching for compact, inspectable expressions. Within traffic research, SciNet-CFM discovers tractable CF relations through neural-symbolic regression (Li et al., 2025); SR-LLM combines LLM-assisted knowledge retrieval with incremental symbolic regression (Guo et al., 2025b); deep symbolic regression with variable-selection regularization has been applied to identify CF dynamics from trajectories (Angah et al., 2024); and NOVA investigates structural recurrence and residual-guided refinement at scale (Abassi et al., 2026). Together these studies establish that empirical CF-law discovery is feasible, and they sharpen the question of how discovery can remain accurate and physically meaningful across heterogeneous observations.

More importantly, what existing methods leave under-specified is not the search itself but the loop that surrounds it. First, although these methods perform residual analysis and iterative feedback, they rarely convert persistent, state-dependent reconstruction errors (which are concentrated in specific driving regimes) into concrete, testable structural modifications, and they seldom verify such modifications across heterogeneous trajectory sources. Second, when the functional form emerges from open-ended search, physical admissibility and behavioral interpretability are usually imposed as post-hoc filters rather than treated as explicit objectives in model selection. Third, a discovered law is only as useful as the theory it supports, where its analytical consequences, such as equilibrium relations, fundamental diagrams, and stability regimes, must remain derivable. These gaps motivate a discovery framework that couples structural hypothesis generation, cross-source verification, and physics-aware selection into one evidence-driven process.

To fill the gap, we propose an agentic CF law discovering framework, which couples an agent-guided hypothesis generator, which draws on traffic flow knowledge and on diagnosed state-dependent reconstruction errors, with evolutionary symbolic search, and it ranks candidates under a physics-aware, multi-objective scheme in which physical admissibility and interpretability enter explicitly. Applying the framework to NGSIM US-101, highD, and exiD yields an explicit CF law—the Adaptive Equilibrium Response Model (AERM)—that pairs state-dependent relative-speed response with spacing-dependent equilibrium-speed restoration, and whose structure admits closed-form equilibrium and fundamental-diagram relations as well as local and string stability conditions. We evaluate AERM against seven established CF models on Shanghai naturalistic driving data, NGSIM I-80, and Waymo trajectories under both dataset-level and trajectory-specific calibration, and we examine its dynamical behavior through equilibrium, stability, and platoon analyses.
The main contributions are summarized as follows:

An evidence-driven structural-evolution framework. We develop an iterative loop in which an agent translates persistent, state-dependent reconstruction errors into testable structural hypotheses, evolutionary search explores the resulting candidates, and physics-aware multi-objective evaluation selects and refines them, with candidate laws verified across heterogeneous trajectory sources without prescribing the final equation in advance.

An evidence-driven structural-evolution framework. We develop an iterative loop in which an agent translates persistent, state-dependent reconstruction errors into testable structural hypotheses, evolutionary search explores the resulting candidates, and physics-aware multi-objective evaluation selects and refines them, with candidate laws verified across heterogeneous trajectory sources without prescribing the final equation in advance.

An interpretable empirical CF law. The framework identifies AERM, an explicit acceleration law with state-dependent relative-speed sensitivity and nonlinear equilibrium-speed restoration, whose analytical structure permits the derivation of steady-state relationships, the associated fundamental diagram, and traffic flow stability.

Behavioral and dynamical evaluation. We assess the discovered law against seven classical CF models using real-world trajectory reconstruction under both common- and trajectory-specific parameter calibration, complemented by equilibrium analysis, stability analysis, and platoon simulations of its dynamical properties.

We develop an iterative loop in which an agent translates persistent, state-dependent reconstruction errors into testable structural hypotheses, evolutionary search explores the resulting candidates, and physics-aware multi-objective evaluation selects and refines them, with candidate laws verified across heterogeneous trajectory sources without prescribing the final equation in advance.

title: Multi-View Latent Action Pretraining for Cross-Embodiment Robot Learning from Videos
authors: Oliver Hausdörfer,Felix Minzenmay,Mani Majd,Maximilian P. Christof,Shiyuan Zhang,Angela P. Schoellig
abstract: Action-free videos are an appealing substitute for costly teleoperated data. Latent action models (LAMs) turn videos into a supervision signal by inferring abstract actions between frames. Existing LAMs observe a single camera view, which resolves 6D robot actions only ambiguously missing out-of-plane movements and potential occlusions. We propose a LAM that ingests synchronized multi-camera views using cross-attention to resolve depth and occlusions before compressing them into latent actions. The latent actions are fed into a policy in which a latent expert and an action expert are coupled by sequential flow matching around a frozen VLM backbone. We further evaluate in strict cross-embodiment settings where task-specific demonstrations come from other embodiments. We show that dual-view LAM pretraining improves the decodability of ground-truth 6D actions by 17% compared to single-view, while scaling single-view data by two orders of magnitude is not sufficient to fully recover out-of-plane motions. The downstream policy improves success rate by +13.5%+13.5\% compared to +6.2%+6.2\% for single-view LAM. A single cross-embodiment is sufficient for skill transfer, and adding a second viewpoint outperforms adding up to four further embodiments. The results transfer to hardware where demonstrations come from a human hand improving success rate by +20%+20\% over action-only policies in 850850 rollouts. We show that video and robot data are complementary, and that benefits of learning from video are task-dependent. Qualitative results are in the suppl. video. Website: https://learnsyslab.github.io/multiview_latent_action_pretraining/.
introduction:
Data availability remains a limiting factor for learning robot policies. Recent works propose leveraging action-free video data that contains semantically rich information, which can aid robots in long-term task planning. One
approach infers latent actions from videos using an inverse dynamics model
(IDM), and conditions a downstream policy on
those latents [1, 2, 3]. The latent actions are an abstract representation describing the transition dynamics in the video. Downstream policy success highly depends on how well the latent actions predict real robot actions. A number of approaches have been proposed to improve this transferability, including grounding latent actions in real robot actions or states[4, 5] and visual pre-processing approaches [6, 7, 8]. However, we show that existing single-view approaches cannot sufficiently recover the full 6D poses that define robot actions. Single views capture actions only ambiguously: out-of-plane motion is underdetermined and parts of the scene may be occluded.

We therefore propose a Latent Action Model (LAM) that ingests synchronized multi-camera
views and attends to image patches across viewpoints—recovering depth and occlusion a single camera leaves ambiguous—before compressing them into a latent action. We demonstrate that this spatial awareness leads to better recoverability of 6D robot actions compared to single-view approaches. Crucially, multiple views are only required during LAM pretraining to improve latent action quality, but not during the policy learning stage where only a single external camera and wrist view are used.

A key advantage of learning from video is the ability to leverage cross-embodiment demonstrations, with the ultimate goal of learning from human demonstrations. Most existing works use only videos from the target robot embodiment, or leverage large-scale public datasets that confound different embodiments, tasks, and visual diversity [3, 4, 8], making performance attribution to cross-embodiment transfer difficult. We specifically evaluate our policy under cross-embodiment demonstrations, where task-specific demonstrations come from other robots in simulation or humans on hardware. We then add a small number of demonstrations on the target embodiment and investigate performance as we scale. We find that a single cross-embodiment video source already enables transfer learning both in simulation and on hardware. Adding a second viewpoint consistently outperforms adding cross-embodiments, establishing multiple viewpoints as an affordable lever for policy performance.

We propose to combine our LAM with a lightweight policy training jointly on the small action-labeled dataset and the much larger video-only set using sequential flow-matching experts. The sequential design provides a strong inductive prior, enabling the action expert to effectively leverage the latent plan. We benchmark our method on LIBERO [9], LIBERO-Plus [10], and MimicGen [11], and a real robot using 850 rollouts. Our main contributions are:

We propose an approach for multi-view IDM-style video pretraining and a downstream policy improving action-only learning by +13.5%+13.5\% in simulation and +20%+20\% on hardware.

Training LAMs on in-domain multi-view videos raises the decodability of ground-truth actions by 17%17\% and policy success rate by +7.3%+7.3\% over single-view LAMs, and outperforms large-scale single-view pretraining, which does not fully recover out-of-plane motions.

We show that a single cross-embodiment already enables skill transfer, and that videos from a second viewpoint outperform adding embodiments.

On hardware, dual-view pretraining improves policy success rate by +20%+20\%, and we demonstrate skill transfer from human-only demonstrations for novel tasks.

1. We propose an approach for multi-view IDM-style video pretraining and a downstream policy improving action-only learning by +13.5%+13.5\% in simulation and +20%+20\% on hardware.

2. Training LAMs on in-domain multi-view videos raises the decodability of ground-truth actions by 17%17\% and policy success rate by +7.3%+7.3\% over single-view LAMs, and outperforms large-scale single-view pretraining, which does not fully recover out-of-plane motions.

3. We show that a single cross-embodiment already enables skill transfer, and that videos from a second viewpoint outperform adding embodiments.

4. On hardware, dual-view pretraining improves policy success rate by +20%+20\%, and we demonstrate skill transfer from human-only demonstrations for novel tasks.

title: AWLS: Advantage-Weighted Latent Steering for One-Step Generative Robotic Manipulation Policies
authors: Jiahong Tang,Jiaju He,Zhiyuan Yang,Ruyang Han,Haiyue Zhu
abstract:
Human-collected real-world robotic manipulation demonstrations often contain
mixed-quality trajectories, including hesitant, indirect, or inefficient
action segments.
While diffusion- and flow-based policies can model such multimodal data,
standard behavior cloning (BC) assigns equal likelihood to all demonstrated
actions and may therefore reproduce suboptimal modes.
Offline RL value estimates offer a natural signal for biasing policies
toward higher-value behavioral modes, but directly fine-tuning the
generative policy or using critic gradients for policy steering can amplify
critic errors and induce prior drift.
We propose Advantage-Weighted Latent Steering (AWLS), an offline
post-training method for improving frozen one-step generative manipulation
policies without updating their decoders.
AWLS learns a residual noise shaper, an observation-conditioned residual
correction to the policy’s latent noise, and trains it with an
advantage-weighted action reconstruction objective.
The advantages are detached, scale-normalized, and used only as supervised
weights on demonstrated actions, avoiding critic-gradient policy updates
while preserving fast single-step inference.
We further introduce a rollout-free decoder-sensitivity criterion for
selecting pretrained checkpoints that remain responsive to latent-noise
perturbations.
Experiments on simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks with
clean and mixed-quality demonstrations show that AWLS improves over the
frozen base policy while limiting drift from the pretrained behavior prior.
Project page: https://awls-corl2026.github.io/.
introduction:
Generative policies based on diffusion and flow
matching [1, 2, 3] have become a
standard approach to imitation learning for robotic manipulation.
They are typically trained by behavior cloning (BC), which fits the policy to
human-collected demonstrations and therefore inherits their quality.
Yet even successful demonstrations are rarely uniformly optimal.
Some trajectories are smooth and efficient, while others are hesitant,
indirect, or unnecessarily long [4, 5].
Standard BC does not distinguish between these quality levels, so it
reproduces hesitant behavior as faithfully as efficient behavior
(Figure 1, left).
Can a policy trained on such data instead be steered toward the better
behavior in those demonstrations?

Offline reinforcement learning (RL) offers an answer: value estimates learned
from the same demonstrations can identify higher-advantage demonstrated
actions in their respective contexts.
The question then becomes how to inject this signal into a pretrained
generative policy.
Guiding the sampling process with the value
signal [6, 7, 8] keeps the
critic in the loop at inference time, and fine-tuning the decoder with value
gradients can amplify offline critic errors while eroding the pretrained
prior [9, 10].
This makes frozen-decoder latent steering an appealing interface: the
pretrained decoder is kept fixed, and improvement is attempted by reshaping
the latent noise.
Yet this interface exposes two hidden failure modes.
First, critic-gradient (Q-maximization) steering in latent
space [11, 12, 13, 14]
can still chase extrapolated value artifacts rather than demonstrated
high-value behavior (Figure 1, middle).
Second, latent steering is only effective if the frozen decoder remains
sensitive to its latent noise, a property that behavior cloning may weaken
during training.

We propose Advantage-Weighted Latent Steering (AWLS) to mitigate both failure
modes simultaneously.
AWLS post-trains the policy with the pretrained decoder frozen, learning only
a residual noise shaper that applies observation-conditioned corrections to
the latent-noise input.
These corrections are initialized near zero to bias post-training toward the
original latent prior.
Critically, the offline critic never provides a gradient to the policy:
advantages estimated via implicit Q-learning (IQL) [15]
are detached and enter
training only as scalar weights on demonstrated
actions [16] (Figure 1, right)—critic errors
may change which demonstrated actions are emphasized without directly
providing gradients toward potentially unsupported actions.
Two additional mechanisms help make this interface practical across tasks:
scale-normalized advantage weighting bounds weight concentration
independently of reward magnitude, and a rollout-free decoder-sensitivity
diagnostic selects frozen checkpoints that remain responsive to latent-noise
perturbations.

Our contributions are:
(i) we identify two reliability issues in frozen latent steering
for one-step generative manipulation policies, critic-gradient failure
modes and decoder-sensitivity degradation, and address them with detached
advantage weights and decoder-sensitivity checkpointing;
(ii) we propose AWLS, a residual noise shaper trained by
advantage-weighted reconstruction with scale-normalized weights while
keeping the decoder frozen;
(iii) we evaluate AWLS on simulation benchmarks, controlled
mixed-quality demonstrations, and real-world robot tasks.

title: Prescribed Performance Guided Safe Reinforcement Learning for Roundabout Navigation of Autonomous Vehicles
authors: Wenhan Li,Yangrui Zhang,Hang Zhou,Peiran Liu,Yiding Ji
abstract: Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) face significant challenges in roundabout navigation due to dense traffic interactions and unpredictable agent behaviors, necessitating high levels of adaptability and safety. While the combination of Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Model Predictive Control (MPC) offers a promising approach, existing frameworks suffer from a structural mismatch where pointwise RL decisions fail to align with MPC’s trajectory level optimization, and often lack rigorous safety guarantees. This work proposes RLTrajGen-PPMPC-CBF, a hierarchical framework for safe, smooth and comfort roundabout navigation, which regulates the coupling between RL-based planning and MPC-based control. We employ Prescribed Performance Constraints (PPC) to enforce a gradual, stable convergence between reference trajectories and control outputs, ensuring MPC tracking performance remains consistent with intended behavior from RL. Additionally, a Control Barrier Function (CBF) layer provides real-time safety corrections that are fed back into the RL process. Simulation results in the MetaDrive environment demonstrate that our method achieves a 6.25% increase in average success rate and a 65.87% reduction in Motion Sickness Dose Value (MSDV) compared to the optimal baseline, meanwhile accelerating training convergence.
introduction:
The advancement of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) has accelerated the deployment of Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs), enabling them to navigate diverse urban environments [1, 2, 3, 4]. Significant progress has been achieved in standard driving tasks, including lane keeping [5, 6, 7], lane changing [8, 9], and adaptive cruise control [10, 11]. However, roundabouts remain particularly challenging due to dense vehicle interactions and rapidly changing traffic conditions, where planning or control failures may compromise both safety and ride comfort [5, 12].

Current autonomous driving approaches mainly fall into learning-based and model-based methods. Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated strong capability in high-dimensional perception and decision-making [13, 14, 15, 16]. However, its model-free nature makes it difficult to explicitly incorporate vehicle dynamics and safety constraints [17, 18]. In contrast, Model Predictive Control (MPC) explicitly considers system dynamics and constraints, while Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) have been widely integrated into MPC to provide formal safety guarantees [19, 20, 21, 22]. Nevertheless, model-based approaches generally exhibit limited adaptability in highly dynamic environments.

To combine the adaptability of RL with the capability to enforce safety and other constraints of MPC, hybrid RL-MPC frameworks have recently attracted increasing attention [23, 24, 25, 26]. Oliveira et al. [25] employed RL to determine discrete decision variables to accelerate MPC optimization, while Lubars et al. [26] combined DDPG with MPC, where MPC served as a safety backup for potentially unsafe RL actions. Zhang et al. [8] further incorporated a CBF safety filter into an RL-MPC framework (Fig. 1(b)). Nevertheless, these methods still suffer from a structural mismatch: RL produces pointwise decisions whereas MPC optimizes trajectories, limiting MPC’s ability to accurately realize the planning intent and resulting in less smooth trajectories in complex driving scenarios.
Zhang et al. [8] introduced a CBFG-PPO framework (Fig. 1 (b)), where RL provides target states for MPC, and CBF filters unsafe actions and feeds corrections back to RL.
Nevertheless, RL produces pointwise decisions while MPC optimizes over trajectories in this framework, which results in structural mismatch and limits MPC’s ability to accurately realize RL intent, producing less smooth trajectories for CAVs in complex environments.

To address the mentioned issues, we propose a novel RLTrajGen-PPMPC-CBF framework, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (c), and validate its effectiveness in a roundabout scenario. The proposed framework consists of three key components: an RL-based Trajectory Generator (RLTrajGen) that facilitates high-level decision making by producing reference trajectories, a prescribed performance MPC (PPMPC) that dynamically adjusts trajectory tracking within a predefined performance envelope, and a CBF-based safety filter that corrects unsafe behaviors. Specifically, we first introduce a trajectory generator that transforms the pointwise outputs of RL into reference trajectories for MPC tracking. In addition, we incorporate a prescribed performance constraint (PPC) mechanism to progressively reduce the tracking error, enabling MPC to more accurately follow the trajectories generated by RL. This design improves the consistency between planning and control, facilitating more stable policy learning and enhanced navigation performance. The main contributions of this work are summarized below:

We design a trajectory generation mechanism that converts single-step outputs from RL into trajectories with adaptive parameters for MPC tracking, thereby effectively resolving the structural mismatch between RL and MPC and significantly accelerating the convergence of training.

We design a trajectory generation mechanism that converts single-step outputs from RL into trajectories with adaptive parameters for MPC tracking, thereby effectively resolving the structural mismatch between RL and MPC and significantly accelerating the convergence of training.

We utilize PPC to regulate the coupling between RL-based planning and MPC-based control, which is the first one in RL-MPC hierarchical framework to our best knowledge. Our method facilitates the progressive reduction of trajectory tracking errors between the planning and control layers, thus balancing the adaptability to complex scenarios and the safety for autonomous systems, and improving ride comfort by producing smoother trajectories.

The remaining sections are organized as follows. Section II introduces the dynamic model of CAVs, prescribed performance constraints, control barrier functions, and formulates the safe navigation problem. Section III presents the RLTrajGen-PPMPC-CBF framework. Section IV includes simulation results and compares our approach with baselines. Section V concludes the paper and outlines future directions.

title: Adaptive Traversal Tubes for Posture-Aware Navigation of Bipedal Humanoids
authors: Zijian Ge
abstract:
Bipedal humanoids can change their effective footprint by adjusting body yaw, enabling both narrow-passage traversal and socially aware yielding.
This paper presents a posture-aware navigation framework centered on Adaptive Traversal Tubes (ATT), Interval Velocity–Heading (IVH) control, and a sidestep-enhanced AMP locomotion prior.
ATT represents a behavior-feasible corridor width field along a reference path, unifying geometric clearance and social comfort into a continuous signal.
IVH maps this width to a continuous frontal-to-sidestep posture schedule and omnidirectional velocity commands.
A velocity-conditioned AMP policy, trained with GVHMR-retargeted frontal/sidestep motions and coupled (vx,vy)(v_{x},v_{y}) tracking rewards, is designed to improve transition stability over a generic locomotion controller while remaining interchangeable with the default onboard policy.
This preprint presents the full method; a planned evaluation protocol on a Unitree G1 is outlined, with quantitative results to follow.
Demo videos of MuJoCo simulation and real-robot deployment are available at:
https://github.com/lborogzj997/Humanoid-Navigation-in-Crowds-and-Narrow-Spaces.
introduction:
Indoor service settings—offices, hospitals, apartments, and retail floors—are built around the human body:
doorways, corridors, and furniture clearances are often only marginally wider than a person’s shoulders, while the same spaces are shared with pedestrians who expect socially acceptable distances and yielding [1, 2, 3].
Bipedal humanoids are uniquely well matched to this ecology.
Unlike wheeled platforms, whose chassis footprint is essentially fixed in the horizontal plane, a humanoid can reshape its effective passage width by changing body yaw and locomotion style—walking face-forward in open space, then rotating into a lateral (sidestep) posture when the corridor tightens [4, 5].
The same posture change also supports socially polite yielding: by presenting a thinner frontal profile and shifting sideways, the robot can open a lane for a person without abandoning the intended route.
This combination of geometric squeeze-through and socially aware lateral yielding is difficult to realize with classical wheeled navigation stacks, which typically inflate a disk or polygon footprint and either declare a passage infeasible or merely slow down [6].

Realizing that potential, however, exposes several general challenges that cut across applications.
First, posture-dependent footprint ambiguity: the clearance that matters is not raw wall-to-wall distance, but whether the robot’s current (and scheduled) body orientation makes the passage behaviorally feasible.
A frontal shoulder width that is safe in a hallway may be too large for a door, while the same door may be passable in a sidestep posture; treating the robot as a fixed disk therefore both over-rejects and under-explains failures [4, 7].
Second, unified geometric and social constraints: in human environments, free space is further compressed by comfort and proxemic expectations [1, 2].
Prior social-navigation work—including our own congestion-aware and spatial–temporal routing methods for mobile robots [8, 9, 10]—has largely addressed crowd-aware path selection and speed adaptation for platforms with essentially fixed footprints.
For bipeds, social compression should instead trigger the same continuous posture response as a physical bottleneck: earlier sidestepping and lateral yielding, not only detours or slowdowns.
Third, navigation-layer posture scheduling under locomotion interfaces: modern humanoids often expose omnidirectional velocity commands to a learned or commercial locomotion policy.
Contact-level footstep and whole-body planners can traverse tight spaces [7, 5], but their computational focus is on footholds and balance rather than on an explicit, tunable mapping from corridor or social width to body yaw.
Conversely, wheeled stacks such as Nav2 [6] provide mature map-based planning yet lack a first-class notion of frontal-to-sidestep posture.
The general concern is therefore not merely find a collision-free path, but schedule posture and omnidirectional velocity so that the path remains behavior-feasible as clearance and social comfort vary along it.

This paper argues that posture should be elevated to the navigation layer through a shared width signal (Fig. 1).
We introduce Adaptive Traversal Tubes (ATT): a path-parameterized width field that represents an effective passage width along a reference path for frontal walking decisions, rather than the raw gap between walls.
Far from obstacles this width saturates at a nominal upper bound wnomw_{\mathrm{nom}}; it shrinks when geometric clearance or social comfort tightens, thereby unifying static squeeze-through and dynamic yielding in one continuous scalar signal.
We then introduce Interval Velocity–Heading (IVH) tracking, which maps the tube width to a continuous frontal-to-sidestep posture schedule and the corresponding omnidirectional velocity and heading commands for bipedal locomotion.
To execute these commands stably, we further train a sidestep-enhanced AMP locomotion prior from custom human videos (GVHMR capture and GMR retargeting), with task rewards that explicitly couple frontal and lateral velocity tracking during yaw transitions.
ATT and IVH remain compatible with a generic onboard controller; the enhanced prior mainly improves transition smoothness and lateral tracking when IVH requests nonzero (vx,vy)(v_{x},v_{y}) jointly.

ATT: a behavior-feasible traversal tube along a reference path that unifies static geometric clearance and dynamic social compression into one posture-relevant width field.

ATT: a behavior-feasible traversal tube along a reference path that unifies static geometric clearance and dynamic social compression into one posture-relevant width field.

IVH: a continuous frontal–sidestep posture schedule driven by the tube width, producing omnidirectional velocity and heading commands for bipedal locomotion.

Sidestep-enhanced AMP prior: a velocity-conditioned locomotion policy trained with frontal/sidestep reference motions and coupled (vx,vy)(v_{x},v_{y}) tracking objectives, intended to improve stability of frontal–sidestep transitions relative to a generic locomotion controller while remaining drop-in interchangeable with it.

Evaluation protocol: a planned simulation and real-robot comparison on a Unitree G1 against a frontal-only navigation baseline, to be reported in an updated version of this preprint.

title: CovNav: Conformal Prediction-Guided Adaptive Inference for Object Goal Navigation
authors: Pengying Wu,Zhejia Wen,Kang Ding,Kangjie Zhou,Chunxuan Jiao,Wei Pan,Xiangli Nie,Chang Liu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: In object goal navigation (ObjectNav), an embodied agent must find a target object (e.g., “find a bed”) in a previously unseen environment, relying on spatial commonsense such as object co-occurrence. Large Language Models (LLMs) encode this commonsense, but deploying them on robots exposes a trade-off between reasoning quality and efficiency: cloud-based models incur latency and privacy risks, whereas small on-device LLMs are fast but prone to hallucinated spatial judgments. Hybrid reasoning LLMs offer both a fast non-thinking mode and a slow thinking mode, which raises a key question for embodied agents: when is slow thinking worth its cost? We propose CovNav, a training-free framework that answers this question with Conformal Prediction (CP), turning dual-process (System 1 / System 2) inference into an uncertainty-aware decision. Much like recent decision models such as Jev, CovNav casts each spatial query as a structured binary decision rather than free-form generation: a local LLM in fast mode judges whether the target is likely near an observed object, CP converts its token probabilities into a prediction set, and only ambiguous queries are escalated to slow chain-of-thought reasoning. The object-pair formulation keeps calibration tractable and supports open-set objects through off-the-shelf detectors. Experiments on Gibson and HM3D show that CovNav surpasses the strongest zero-shot baseline by 0.8 and 1.7 percentage points in success rate on HM3D v1 and v2, while invoking slow reasoning for only 12.4% of queries and retaining most of the gain of always-on thinking at a fraction of its latency. Real-robot experiments on a TurtleBot 4 further validate the approach. CovNav shows how calibrated uncertainty can decide when an embodied agent should think slowly, offering a principled form of adaptive test-time reasoning for LLM-based robots.
introduction:
Recent advances in large foundation models have achieved remarkable success across language understanding, visual reasoning, and knowledge-intensive tasks. A pivotal next step for artificial intelligence is to ground these capabilities in the physical world, building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act within complex, unstructured environments [1]. Among the core competencies required for such agents, the ability to autonomously navigate to semantically specified targets is both fundamental and practically significant, underpinning applications from domestic assistance to search and rescue.

Object goal navigation (ObjectNav) serves as a representative testbed for this capability. Given a semantic target (e.g., “find a bed”), an agent must explore and navigate through a previously unseen environment without any prior map [2, 3]. A key enabler for efficient exploration is commonsense spatial knowledge, that is, the understanding that functionally related objects tend to co-locate within the same room (e.g., beds and nightstands in bedrooms, sofas and televisions in living rooms). Large Language Models (LLMs), which encode vast commonsense knowledge from pre-training, have recently emerged as a powerful tool for providing such spatial priors without task-specific training [4, 5, 6], motivating a growing body of work on LLM-based object goal navigation.

Existing LLM-based navigation approaches face significant deployment challenges. First, many state-of-the-art methods rely on cloud-based APIs (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude) [5, 7], which introduces network latency, raises privacy concerns, and limits deployment in offline or network-constrained scenarios. Second, directly deploying smaller open-source LLMs on resource-constrained robot platforms often leads to performance degradation, manifesting as hallucination and unreliable spatial judgments when processing complex relationships. Third, existing approaches lack adaptive mechanisms to dynamically adjust inference depth based on problem difficulty, resulting in either consistently invoking large models (incurring high computational costs) or relying exclusively on small models (sacrificing accuracy). This raises a critical question: How can we achieve both efficient and accurate spatial reasoning on resource-constrained robotic platforms?

To address this challenge, we propose an adaptive inference framework that dynamically adjusts inference depth based on problem difficulty, utilizing LLM prediction uncertainty as a core metric. A key insight driving our work is that not all spatial reasoning problems require deep deliberation, as illustrated in Figure 1. For instance, judging the spatial proximity between a television and a sofa is straightforward, given their typical co-occurrence in living rooms. However, determining the relationship between a sofa and a bed requires cross-room reasoning to recognize they belong to distinct functional spaces. Crucially, the output confidence produced by small LLMs, specifically the logits generated during deployment, serves as an effective indicator of problem difficulty, reflecting how well the input aligns with the training corpus. We leverage Conformal Prediction (CP) [8], a statistically rigorous uncertainty quantification framework, to assess this confidence without requiring additional model training. CP constructs prediction sets based on model outputs: when the model is highly confident, the prediction set contains a single answer, indicating that the fast direct inference mode is sufficient. Conversely, when uncertain, the prediction set contains multiple possible answers, indicating the model’s inability to identify a unique solution, which triggers a slow deliberative reasoning mode. This mechanism mirrors human cognitive processing: System 1 thinking (fast, intuitive) handles routine decisions, while System 2 thinking (slow, analytical) engages for complex problems [9].

This perspective also connects CovNav to two recent trends in LLM reasoning. First, hybrid reasoning models such as Qwen3 [10] expose both a fast non-thinking mode and a slow thinking mode, and recent work trains such models with reinforcement learning to decide when to think [11, 12]; CovNav makes this decision without any training, using a statistically calibrated criterion. Second, decision models such as Jev [13, 14] answer queries with structured choices, binary judgments, or scores instead of free-form text, trading open-ended generation for speed and reliability. CovNav’s fast mode follows the same principle by casting each spatial query as a binary object-pair decision with a confidence score, and adds a CP gate that escalates to System 2 reasoning only when this System 1 decision is uncertain.

Building on this insight, we design a CP-guided navigation framework (CovNav) where the robot constructs an object-wise semantic map using off-the-shelf detection models. For each newly observed object, it queries the LLM to assess spatial relationships with the target object. CP analyzes the response confidence to determine whether the fast direct inference mode can reliably answer the question. If confidence is sufficient, the system directly utilizes the response; otherwise, it activates the slow deliberative reasoning mode for more thorough analysis. The resulting semantic value map, weighted by these assessments, guides the robot toward high-potential exploration regions. Two key design choices facilitate this framework: (1) formulating queries as object-pair relationships rather than open-ended visual question answering makes the problem space more tractable for CP calibration, and (2) leveraging open-source detection models enables open-set semantic understanding without task-specific training.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We propose a novel fast-slow inference paradigm for robotic navigation that adaptively switches between fast direct inference and slow deliberative reasoning based on LLM response uncertainty, effectively achieving a balance between computational efficiency and decision accuracy on resource-constrained platforms.

We propose a novel fast-slow inference paradigm for robotic navigation that adaptively switches between fast direct inference and slow deliberative reasoning based on LLM response uncertainty, effectively achieving a balance between computational efficiency and decision accuracy on resource-constrained platforms.

We introduce the first use of Conformal Prediction to gate between the fast and slow reasoning modes of an LLM for object navigation, providing a theoretically grounded and training-free switching mechanism. We further design an object-pair-based query formulation that makes CP calibration tractable while enabling open-set semantic understanding through off-the-shelf vision models.

We validate our approach through extensive simulated and real-world robot experiments, demonstrating significant improvements in both navigation efficiency and success rate compared to existing methods.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work in zero-shot object navigation, LLM-based navigation and uncertainty quantification in Embodied AI. Section III provides the problem formulation and details our proposed methodology, specifically the object-based semantic mapping and the CP-guided fast-slow switching mechanism. Section IV presents extensive experimental results, including simulation comparisons and ablation studies. Section V details real-world validations, demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach in physical environments. Section VI concludes the paper and discusses future directions.

We propose a novel fast-slow inference paradigm for robotic navigation that adaptively switches between fast direct inference and slow deliberative reasoning based on LLM response uncertainty, effectively achieving a balance between computational efficiency and decision accuracy on resource-constrained platforms.

2. We introduce the first use of Conformal Prediction to gate between the fast and slow reasoning modes of an LLM for object navigation, providing a theoretically grounded and training-free switching mechanism. We further design an object-pair-based query formulation that makes CP calibration tractable while enabling open-set semantic understanding through off-the-shelf vision models.

3. We validate our approach through extensive simulated and real-world robot experiments, demonstrating significant improvements in both navigation efficiency and success rate compared to existing methods.

title: PLaCA: Learning Patch-Level Future Latent Change for Action Generation
authors: Zhan Yi,Yuchen Wang,Chao Li,Lei Hong,Boyuan Yang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot
actions from visual observations and language
instructions, but effective manipulation also
requires anticipating how the environment will
change. Existing world-action models explore future
image prediction and latent dynamics modeling.
However, generating complete future images can be
computationally expensive, while highly compressed
latent representations may obscure local changes.
To address these challenges, we propose PLaCA,
a world-to-action framework built around future
latent change. PLaCA directly predicts spatially
structured patch-level future latent change from
the current multimodal input, preserving local
information about expected environmental changes.
We introduce patch-level change-aware supervision
to emphasize regions undergoing larger changes
and a future-to-action interface that explicitly
incorporates predicted future latent change into
action generation.
Experiments on LIBERO-Long show that PLaCA achieves
a 79.0% success rate, improving upon the Action-only
baseline by 5.0 percentage points. On CALVIN, PLaCA
improves the average sequence length from 2.784 to
3.564. These improvements are achieved while updating
only 2.95% of the model parameters during the second
training stage, demonstrating the effectiveness of
future latent change modeling for downstream robotic
manipulation.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically generate robot
actions from current visual observations and language
instructions [7, 15, 30]. However, in manipulation tasks such as grasping,
pushing, and placing, effective action generation requires
more than understanding the current environment. A policy
must also consider how its actions may change object positions,
contact relations, and local environmental states. To
incorporate such future information, recent studies have
explored integrating world modeling with VLA policies,
motivating the development of world-action modeling (WAM)
 [10, 40].

Existing approaches represent future information in different
ways. Some predict future images or videos [8, 55],
while others model future states or temporal dynamics in latent
space [16, 2].
Recent studies have further explored compact latent motion
representations [29, 46, 47].
Latent-space modeling has become a widely adopted approach
in world modeling and robot learning [16, 2, 46].
While pixel-level future prediction provides rich visual
details, generating complete future images often involves
reconstructing substantial redundant visual content,
leading to additional computational costs [44, 46].
In contrast, latent-space modeling avoids explicit pixel-level
reconstruction, yet choosing an appropriate future representation
for robotic manipulation remains an important question.
For action generation, it may not be necessary to recover
the complete future state or all intermediate dynamics.
Instead, a policy may benefit from information about
how the environment is expected to change.

Recent work has shown that differences between latent states
can capture information related to robot motion. StaMo [29] learns
highly compressed latent state representations and uses
the latent displacement between states to represent robot
motion. It also explores latent motion prediction for world
modeling. However, latent representations differ
in how they preserve spatial information. As illustrated in
Fig. 1(a), when a robot places an object into
a box, the changes are mainly concentrated around the robot
arm and the object, while much of the background remains
unchanged. Highly compressed state representations can encode
such changes, but they do not explicitly preserve the
correspondence between spatial locations and their latent
changes. In contrast, retaining the patch-level spatial
structure allows future changes at different image locations
to be represented separately, as shown in
Fig. 1(b). Moreover, the magnitude of future
change can vary considerably across patches, while uniform
patch supervision does not specifically emphasize regions
undergoing larger changes. This motivates our first research
question: How can we preserve the spatial structure
of future latent change and learn local changes more
effectively by accounting for their different magnitudes?

Another important question is how future modeling can be effectively coupled with action generation. Prior work has explored different approaches, including jointly learning future prediction and action policies within shared architectures [40, 46], using predicted future images or video plans to guide downstream control [52, 14], and leveraging learned latent or interaction dynamics for action inference [37, 41]. These studies provide different ways of using future information to inform robotic behavior. For the spatially structured future latent change considered in this work, the predicted representation preserves local information about expected environmental changes across image regions. This motivates investigating how such spatially organized predictions can be incorporated into action representations to support action generation. We therefore pose our second research question: How can predicted future latent change be effectively used to support action generation?

To address these questions, we propose PLaCA,
a world-to-action framework built around
future latent change. PLaCA directly predicts
spatially structured patch-level future latent change
from the current multimodal input and employs
patch-level change-aware supervision to emphasize
regions with larger changes. We further introduce a
future-to-action interface that incorporates the
predicted future latent change into the action representation,
allowing it to directly contribute to full action-chunk
generation.

We evaluate PLaCA on LIBERO-Long, achieving a 79.0% task success rate. Ablation studies demonstrate that preserving fine-grained spatial structure, employing change-aware supervision, and incorporating predicted future latent change into action generation through the future-to-action interface contribute to improved downstream manipulation success rates.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We investigate patch-level future latent change
modeling, which directly predicts future latent change
from the current multimodal input while preserving its
spatial structure, providing local future information
for action generation.

We propose patch-level change-aware supervision,
which adjusts the supervision weights according to the
magnitude of ground-truth future latent change.
Ablation results show that this approach improves
closed-loop manipulation performance compared with
uniform patch supervision.

We design an explicit future-to-action interface
that incorporates the final predicted future latent
change into the action representation, allowing future
information to directly contribute to full action-chunk
generation.

1. We investigate patch-level future latent change
modeling, which directly predicts future latent change
from the current multimodal input while preserving its
spatial structure, providing local future information
for action generation.

2. We propose patch-level change-aware supervision,
which adjusts the supervision weights according to the
magnitude of ground-truth future latent change.
Ablation results show that this approach improves
closed-loop manipulation performance compared with
uniform patch supervision.

3. We design an explicit future-to-action interface
that incorporates the final predicted future latent
change into the action representation, allowing future
information to directly contribute to full action-chunk
generation.
