title: Minimum-Time Escape from the Conic Field of View of a Reeds-Shepp Pursuer: Classification and Game Value for a Slower or Equally Fast Evader
authors: Ubaldo Ruiz
abstract:
We study minimum-time escape of an omnidirectional evader from the forward conic field of view of a Reeds–Shepp pursuer with minimum turning radius rr. For speed ratio ν
u and cone half-angle 0<α<π/20<\alpha<\pi/2, we prove a global escape/holding classification: straight reversal holds the whole cone for ν≤sin⁡α
u\leq\sin\alpha, escape is confined to a barrier-bounded dart for sin⁡α<ν≤1\sin\alpha<
u\leq 1, and escape is possible from every state for ν>1
u>1. For the slower or equally fast evader, sin⁡α<ν≤1\sin\alpha<
u\leq 1, we construct the solution with Isaacs’ characteristics and verify it in feedback form, using a Filippov pursuer relay and a one-sided evader branch. The finite escape time is the first root of one scalar equation, and the holding region is bounded by the nonusable parts of the rays and a barrier that closes with a convex corner on the front axis. Sample-and-hold counter-controls show that this escape time is the value of the game in nonanticipative strategies at every state except the corner. There the two strategy values differ: the pursuer’s is infinite, whereas an evader that chooses which barrier branch to cross from the initial germ of the pursuer’s control escapes before the barrier time τI	au_{I}, which is the evader’s exact strategy value. An independent level-set solver, refined on fixed comparison points, agrees with the closed-form escape time and reproduces the holding region at the tested parameters.
introduction:
A directional sensor attached to a moving vehicle observes only part of the plane. Escaping surveillance therefore requires leaving its field of view, rather than outrunning the observer. We study minimum-time escape from an unbounded forward cone of half-angle 0<α<π/20<\alpha<\pi/2, with an omnidirectional evader and a Reeds–Shepp pursuer that can drive forward or in reverse but cannot rotate in place (Reeds and Shepp, 1990). The evader minimizes the exit time and the pursuer maximizes it.

The closest forward-only model is the conic surveillance–evasion game of Lewin and Olsder (1979). Reverse motion changes its geometry: backing away reduces the evader’s bearing without turning and can preserve observation indefinitely.

Our analysis uses Isaacs’ characteristics and singular surfaces (Isaacs, 1965; Lewin, 1994). Related surveillance games include circular detection regions (Dobbie, 1966; Lewin and Breakwell, 1975), an isotropic rocket (Lewin and Olsder, 1989), two identical cars (Greenfeld, 1987; Ruiz, 2026), an agile pursuer (Braun et al., 2025), and a fixed-course target (Weintraub et al., 2023). Differential-drive capture and surveillance games are developed in several works (Ruiz et al., 2013; Ruiz and Murrieta-Cid, 2016; Ruiz, 2022; Saavedra and Ruiz, 2024), including escape from a conic field of view (Ruiz, 2023). Their velocity set is a diamond, allowing rotation in place; the Reeds–Shepp set is a bow tie, allowing full speed and full turn rate simultaneously. The Hamiltonians and characteristics therefore differ.

The contributions are the game-of-kind classification for all speed ratios ν=Vemax/Vpmax\nu=V_{e}^{\max}/V_{p}^{\max} and the solution for ν≤1\nu\leq 1. The solution is constructed from the usable boundary and the primary characteristics, verified in feedback form with the pursuer’s relay understood in the sense of Filippov, and identified with the strategy values by sample-and-hold counter-controls and an explicit evader strategy at the corner. An independent level-set solver, refined on fixed comparison points, agrees with the closed-form escape time. The main results are the following.

For ν≤sin⁡α\nu\leq\sin\alpha, straight reversal holds the whole cone (Proposition 3).

For sin⁡α<ν≤1\sin\alpha<\nu\leq 1, the escape region is a dart bounded by the usable parts of the rays and a closed barrier with a corner cc on the front axis, and the escape time WW is the first root of one scalar equation (Proposition 6 and Theorem 6.1).

WW is the value of the game in nonanticipative strategies at every state except cc; at cc, VP​(c)=+∞V_{P}(c)=+\infty while VE​(c)=τIV_{E}(c)=\tau_{I} (Theorem 6.2).

For ν>1\nu>1, escape is possible from every state (Proposition 3).

For ν>1\nu>1 the minimum escape time has a different structure: the characteristic analysis indicates a universal line on the front axis, along which the evader chases the reversing pursuer, and a barrier that ends at a cusp. Its verification requires other arguments and is the subject of ongoing work; here the case ν>1\nu>1 only completes the classification.

Sections 2–5 formulate the game, derive its characteristics and solve the game of kind. Section 6 constructs and verifies the synthesis for the slower or equally fast evader, Section 7 compares it with an independent numerical solution, and Section 8 compares the geometry with the forward-only game. Appendix A proves Lemma 1, and Appendix B proves Theorem 6.2.

title: A Head Camera Is (Almost) All You Need: An Electronics-Free UMI Glove Labelled and Observed by One Moving Camera
authors: Yosub Shin,Yuan Liu,Igor Molybog
abstract: Handheld demonstration devices decouple data collection from the robot, but conventional designs burden the hand with a wrist camera, cables and a pose tracker (SLAM, an IMU, a VR controller, or a fixed external camera that the collector’s body occludes), and burden the pipeline with as many data streams to timestamp, synchronise and cross-calibrate. We show that a single egocentric camera ($122) worn on the collector’s head replaces both the camera and the tracker, and the streams with one. It reads printed fiducials on an electronics-free glove ($22) against paper tiles taped around the workspace, giving the 6-DoF gripper pose and the jaw width from the same frames the policy will see; at deployment the same camera rides a low-cost ($120) arm beside the robot that mimics the collector’s head from the robot’s joint state. Against the robot’s encoders the labels are accurate to 6.5 mm6.5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m} and 1.6 °1.6\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} median with 93 93\text{\,}–100 %100\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} frame coverage, and a policy trained on them instead of encoders pays 3 %3\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} in validation loss. Adding 194 glove demonstrations to 48 teleoperated episodes lifts rollout success from 10/25 to 17/25, level with 172 teleoperated episodes alone (18/25), and the full co-trained head-camera policy succeeds in 20/25 against 15/25 for the wrist-camera recipe, whose policies drop the object when the goal leaves their view, and 12/25 for a fixed camera.
introduction:
Teleoperation occupies a robot and an operator for every demonstration. Handheld devices decouple collection from the robot: with ours a collector records 2.0–3.1 demonstrations per minute against 1.6 by teleoperation on the same task (§2), in parallel and without robot time, with a $22 printed glove, a $122 wearable camera and four paper tiles. The glove is purely mechanical, a replica of the robot’s gripper carrying fiducials and nothing else, and the one head-worn camera is at once the policy’s observation and the source of the gripper’s pose and jaw width, so there is no second sensor stream to synchronise or calibrate against.

Every UMI-style device answers two questions: what does the policy see, and how is the gripper tracked? The conventional answer puts both on the wrist. SLAM on the wrist camera [7, 4] needs a mapping pass and textured scenes and loses track under occlusion or fast motion; a visual-inertial sensor adds a second device [26]; a VR controller adds weight (119 g119\text{\,}\mathrm{g} of YUBI’s 319 g319\text{\,}\mathrm{g} [16, 23]) and external tracking infrastructure [2, 5]; a fixed overhead camera [20] avoids drift but ties collection to a mount and loses the hand behind the body in 8 8\text{\,}–22 %22\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of frames (§2). Each tracker is a second stream beside the camera, with its own clock and calibration to reconcile, and the wrist camera itself adds cable and weight while its view is tied to the hand: even through UMI’s 155 °155\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} fisheye the frame holds what the jaws face, so a drop-off bin leaves it once the hand lifts or turns [11].

We answer both with one head-worn camera, addressing two challenges this workshop names [1]: tracking without SLAM and the human-to-robot viewpoint gap. Gaze precedes the hand [14], so the head keeps the gripper at arm’s length, unoccluded by the torso, with the workspace around it. From that vantage an 11-face fiducial ball gives the pose, tags on the jaws the opening, and four AprilTag tiles [17] the world frame. At deployment the camera rides a small printed servo arm beside the robot that imitates head motion from the robot’s joint state, identically in teleoperation and rollouts, so glove, teleoperated and rollout data share one viewpoint. EgoMimic [13] co-trains on egocentric human video with the hand pose estimated from the video; our collector holds a replica of the robot’s gripper, so contact and jaw width are the robot’s. Active-vision teleoperation [8, 6] steers a robot camera from a VR headset; our positioner needs neither operator nor headset.

title: JARVIS: From Visual Manuals to Autonomous Robotic Assembly
authors: Fan Ding,Fucai Ke,Kevin Yuchen Ma,Xuewen Luo,Wenyu Liang,Vishnu Monn Baskaran,Hamid Rezatofighi,Yan Wu
abstract: Visual manuals communicate procedural knowledge through stepwise diagrams, but translating these instructions into reliable long-horizon robotic execution remains challenging. We introduce JARVIS, a method-agnostic benchmark for autonomous visual-manual-guided execution without additional language instructions. JARVIS comprises 236,679236{,}679 LEGO assembly tasks across 8,9878{,}987 scenes, with a carefully curated JARVIS-v1 suite of 5050 tasks for interactive robotic evaluation. Tasks span varying initial structural complexities and assembly horizons, requiring agents to interpret manuals, ground actions in an evolving workspace, and execute the intended procedure. A structure-aware evaluation protocol captures geometric accuracy, structural relations, construction order, partial progress, and completion. We further introduce JARVIS-agentic, a tool-grounded embodied agent that composes robot primitives into executable programs and uses execution feedback for verification and recovery, without task-specific action trajectories or model parameter updates. Across nine multimodal and reasoning models, task-oriented primitives increase the average assembly score. Performance nevertheless declines sharply with assembly horizon, and execution errors remain difficult to correct. Prior-task experience improves initial performance, while repeated reflection provides inconsistent benefits, highlighting persistent limitations in connecting visual procedural reasoning with reliable physical execution.
introduction:
Across many everyday activities, people learn how to build, assemble, and operate things by following visual manuals. These manuals organize tasks into standardized step-by-step diagrams, providing a compact and transferable representation of procedural knowledge that conveys both the desired outcome and the process required to achieve it [31]. Following such manuals requires humans to interpret the visual instructions, align each illustrated step with the current physical state, and translate the inferred procedure into concrete actions. This ability goes beyond visual recognition alone, requiring visual reasoning to be tightly coupled with sequential decision-making and physical execution [32]. As multimodal models increasingly move beyond passive perception toward embodied interaction [16, 12, 17], a fundamental question is whether machines can interpret procedural knowledge from visual manuals and autonomously translate it into action.

Recent studies have taken initial steps toward this capability, particularly in manual-guided robotic assembly [31, 39, 9, 15]. Existing approaches have primarily developed task-specific solutions for extracting assembly structures, predicting part poses, and generating assembly plans [31, 28, 18, 32, 36, 22].
Many therefore stop before physical execution; when execution is included, it is often realised through predefined or manually engineered control pipelines. As a result, they do not directly evaluate whether a model can autonomously close the loop from visual manual understanding to physical construction. Benchmarking this capability further requires end-to-end execution tasks and metrics that capture partial progress and structural correctness beyond binary task success [11, 33]. Consequently, it remains unclear how well current multimodal models can use a visual manual as the task specification and autonomously carry out a complete procedure over multiple steps.

To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce JARVIS, a method-agnostic benchmark for autonomous visual-manual-guided execution. We construct a large-scale task collection comprising 236,679236{,}679 assembly tasks across 8,9878{,}987 LEGO scenes, spanning diverse initial structures and assembly horizons. From this collection, we curate JARVIS-v1, a suite of 5050 tasks across three difficulty levels for interactive robotic evaluation. As shown in Fig. 1, an agent receives a visual assembly manual and workspace observations, infers the intended procedure, and executes it while adapting to the evolving physical state. Each manipulation affects subsequent steps, requiring coherent planning and execution throughout assembly. We further introduce a structure-aware evaluation protocol that measures relative geometry, structural relations, and completion, capturing partial progress and accumulated errors beyond binary task success.

Turning manual understanding into physical execution poses a separate practical challenge. Learned control policies typically require task-specific robot action supervision, as low-level trajectories are tied to the robot’s kinematics and control interface. Collecting dedicated demonstrations or trajectories for each new construction task is therefore costly. We introduce JARVIS-agentic, a tool-grounded embodied agent that bridges manual-derived reasoning and physical execution without task-specific action trajectories. Equipped with a compact library of verified robot primitives, the agent grounds the manual, composes executable behaviours, and uses execution reflection for verification, recovery, and replanning.

Using JARVIS, we evaluate 9 multimodal and reasoning models on manual-guided assembly tasks spanning different structural complexities and assembly horizons. Task-oriented robot skills raise the average assembly score from 7.887.88 to 14.7114.71 without task-specific action trajectories, demonstrating the value of tool-grounded execution. Nevertheless, performance declines sharply with assembly horizon, and improvements in intermediate grounding do not reliably translate into successful assembly. Prior-task experience improves first-round performance, whereas repeated reflection and recovery from execution errors remain unreliable. These findings expose the difficulty of connecting procedural reasoning, physical execution, and reflection-based correction in long-horizon assembly.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We formulate autonomous visual-manual-guided execution for long-horizon robotic assembly and introduce JARVIS, comprising 236,679236{,}679 tasks across 8,9878{,}987 scenes, with a curated JARVIS-v1 suite for interactive evaluation. A structure-aware protocol measures geometric and relational correctness, partial progress, and completion.

We introduce JARVIS-agentic, a tool-grounded embodied agent that translates visual assembly instructions into executable programs through reusable robot primitives. The framework integrates planning, execution verification, and recovery without task-specific action trajectories or model parameter updates.

We evaluate nine multimodal and reasoning models, revealing persistent difficulties in translating manual understanding into reliable long-horizon execution. Our analysis shows that task-oriented tools and prior-task experience improve performance, while online reflection provides inconsistent benefits and error recovery remains limited.

A structure-aware protocol measures geometric and relational correctness, partial progress, and completion.

2. We introduce JARVIS-agentic, a tool-grounded embodied agent that translates visual assembly instructions into executable programs through reusable robot primitives. The framework integrates planning, execution verification, and recovery without task-specific action trajectories or model parameter updates.

3. We evaluate nine multimodal and reasoning models, revealing persistent difficulties in translating manual understanding into reliable long-horizon execution. Our analysis shows that task-oriented tools and prior-task experience improve performance, while online reflection provides inconsistent benefits and error recovery remains limited.

title: EchoNav: Evidential BEV Completion from Historical Observations for Visual Navigation
authors: Diwen Liu,Yiyang Shao,Borui Wang,Chi Zhang,Yunhui Liu
abstract: Visual navigation in cluttered environments requires robots to recover previously observed structure and infer obstacles and free space that remain occluded. We present a framework that combines temporal aggregation and occupancy completion in an evidential bird’s-eye-view (BEV) representation predicted from short RGB sequences. A decoder adapts frozen VGGT-Omega features and combines historical residual proposals using cellwise weights and a learned no-update option. The BEV predictor produces a local map in the latest ego frame without depth or camera-pose inputs or explicit geometric warping. The evidential model treats observed free space separately and predicts occupancy with associated confidence across the remaining supported region. We train the predictor on simulated RGB sequences paired with complete and visibility-masked occupancy annotations. Our experiments evaluate navigation in simulation and on a wheeled robot, with additional demonstrations on quadruped and humanoid robots. In simulated sequential two-goal navigation, our system achieves 89.6% success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 32.5 percentage points. Across 60 wheeled-robot trials in 20 scenes, it achieves 73.3% success, compared with 33.3% for the strongest evaluated baseline.
introduction:
Mobile robots navigating cluttered environments must make spatial decisions from incomplete visual observations (Fig. ). Each camera view reveals only part of the surrounding layout. Relying only on the latest view can cause a robot to revisit unproductive routes or become trapped in local minima and fail to reach its goal. Observations retained within the RGB window provide evidence about nearby regions that are no longer visible in the current image. The more complete map gives the planner additional local context to choose more efficient paths. Yet some obstacles and free space remain hidden behind furniture and walls throughout this process. Predicting these hidden regions can inform planning, but the robot must account for the uncertainty of those predictions. The challenge is therefore to build a local BEV map that retains useful information across time, distinguishes observed space from inferred structure, and indicates how reliable its predictions are.

Learned occupancy anticipation has demonstrated that visual context can help predict unseen structure [1]. In autonomous driving, occupancy completion has shown strong results in scene understanding by predicting occupancy in both visible and occluded regions [2, 3]. For mobile robots, anticipating obstacles and free space beyond current observations can similarly provide a more complete map for planning, supporting exploration and navigation before those regions are directly observed [1, 4].

BEV occupancy maps place obstacles, free space, and candidate paths in a common top-down frame. This representation makes the basis of motion decisions transparent. The map describes the environment, while the planner and controller handle robot footprints, clearance margins, and motion constraints. This separation leaves the choice of planning algorithm open to the task and robot platform.

To address these challenges, we propose an RGB-based framework for temporal BEV mapping and occupancy completion. It combines evidence from earlier observations with predictions of persistently hidden obstacles and free space, producing occupancy and reliability estimates for local planning. The BEV predictor requires neither depth nor camera-pose inputs and uses no explicit geometric warping.

The main contributions are:

Spatially selective temporal BEV fusion. We propose a framework that integrates RGB histories into an ego-centric occupancy BEV. Historical residual proposals from a shared decoder are weighted independently at each map location. The fusion includes a learned no-update option that allows the anchor representation to be retained.

Observation-aware evidential occupancy completion. We develop an occupancy-learning formulation that distinguishes observed free space from inferred occupancy and predicts spatial support and confidence for planning. Visibility-aware supervision supports completion of occluded obstacles and free space while regularizing evidence assigned to incorrect predictions.

Navigation integration and physical validation. We integrate predicted occupancy and reliability with established local motion planners. Experiments show higher navigation success rates than the evaluated baselines in simulation and wheeled-robot trials. Additional quadruped and humanoid demonstrations illustrate deployment on other embodiments.

title: Embodied Task Agents Can Perform Fine Manipulation through Tactile In-Context Learning
authors: Yubang Wang,Zezheng Huai,Yifei Zhang,Jinhao Wu,Yitong Chen,Haozhe Zhang,Sixian Li,Jingjing Gong,Zhenyang Lin,Ziyang Chen,Xipeng Qiu
abstract: Can embodied task agents use tactile experience to perform fine manipulation without task-specific model training? We investigate this capability through Tactile-ETA, a system that incorporates tactile experience into an embodied task agent through in-context learning. Successful expert demonstrations show how contact changes during manipulation. We pair each recorded robot movement with its camera views and bilateral tactile observations. We keep tactile observations at the start and end of each movement and add two neighboring time points when the tactile images change markedly in between. The agent combines these demonstrations with current vision, tactile observations, and proprioception to select actions through general-purpose robot tools, without updating model parameters. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, adding tactile observations to the same two expert demonstrations increases average success from 15.75% to 24.00%, with current sensing and execution interfaces held fixed. Further experiments show that performance depends on the sensory content and representation of demonstrations, while comparing agent models on Lift Bottle reveals substantial differences under the same system configuration. On the real-robot tasks, demonstrations with aligned visual and tactile observations increase the task success rate from 0% to 60%. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of using tactile experience in context for fine manipulation and suggest a path toward extending embodied task agents to additional sensory inputs.
introduction:
Embodied task agents such as ETA (Chen et al., 2026d),
Show-Harness (Chen et al., 2026c), and
RoboDawn (Guo et al., 2026)
demonstrate that general-purpose models can execute robot tasks through
observations, reasoning, and robot commands.
However, fine manipulation remains challenging.
Recent real-robot evaluation also shows a substantial performance
gap between pick-and-place tasks and fine insertion tasks
(Menon et al., 2026).
Such manipulation requires adjusting actions to contact conditions,
which can be difficult to infer reliably from vision alone.
Tactile feedback provides complementary information for these adjustments
(Bi et al., 2025).
In-context learning further allows demonstrations to provide task guidance
at deployment without additional parameter updates
(Palo and
Johns, 2024b; Yin et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026).
This creates an opportunity to extend the sensory information these agents
can use: can embodied task agents similarly use tactile experience
in context to perform fine manipulation that requires contact-sensitive
adjustments? We investigate this question through Tactile-ETA
(Figure 1), which incorporates expert tactile experience
into an embodied task agent that acts through general-purpose robot tools,
without task-specific fine-tuning.

Current tactile
observations describe ongoing contact, whereas expert demonstrations can
provide a reference for how contact evolves during movement. For example,
during rotation or insertion, a demonstration can show how an expert
continues moving, adjusts its pose, or changes manipulation stages around
a contact transition. Visual–motion records capture what the expert did, but not how contact evolved during the demonstrated actions. We organize expert demonstrations so that the agent can see each movement
together with the visual and tactile changes that accompany it.

Tactile-ETA divides successful expert demonstrations into action-aligned
interaction segments, each containing robot motion, before-and-after
camera observations, and bilateral tactile sequences from the same interval.

Full tactile sequences can contain many observations within one movement,
while the endpoints alone can miss changes during contact. We therefore
retain tactile observations at motion boundaries and, when a change
threshold is met, add an adjacent pair spanning the selected change.
Complete demonstrations are provided in interaction order as references
for execution. The agent combines them with current visual and tactile observations, proprioception, and
execution feedback to select motion and
gripper commands. Model parameters remain unchanged: task guidance is
provided through context, while general-purpose tools and the underlying
controller execute the selected actions.

We evaluate the system on four UniVTAC simulation tasks
(Chen et al., 2026a), with 100 trials per task
and condition. Adding tactile observations to the same two visual–motion
demonstrations increases average success from 15.75% to 24.00%, with current
sensing and execution interfaces held fixed. Content ablations reveal
task-dependent contributions from demonstration vision and tactile
observations, while representation ablations show that retaining more
tactile frames does not automatically improve performance. A comparison of agent models
on Lift Bottle also reveals substantial differences under the
same system configuration. Execution statistics and cases illustrate
behavioral differences in contact-guided corrections and stage transitions.
On two real-robot tasks, a single multimodal demonstration enables three
successful trials out of five per task, compared with zero without demonstrations.
Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of using tactile
experience in context for embodied task agents and suggest a path toward
extending them to additional sensory inputs.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce Tactile-ETA, a system that incorporates expert tactile
experience into embodied task agents through context for fine manipulation,
without task-specific parameter updates.

We construct action-aligned visual–motion–tactile demonstrations
that compactly retain motion boundaries and intermediate contact changes.

We show that tactile demonstration experience can improve
manipulation performance, with outcomes depending on context organization
and the underlying agent model. Execution records illustrate associated
differences in contact adjustment and stage transitions.

1. We introduce Tactile-ETA, a system that incorporates expert tactile
experience into embodied task agents through context for fine manipulation,
without task-specific parameter updates.

2. We construct action-aligned visual–motion–tactile demonstrations
that compactly retain motion boundaries and intermediate contact changes.

3. We show that tactile demonstration experience can improve
manipulation performance, with outcomes depending on context organization
and the underlying agent model. Execution records illustrate associated
differences in contact adjustment and stage transitions.

title: Sensitivity-Orthogonal Residual Learning for Adaptive Sideslip and Cornering Stiffness Estimation
authors: Kyoungtae Ji,Dongyeol Won,Kyoungseok Han
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract:
Online adaptation of the cornering stiffness keeps a model-based sideslip estimator
valid as tires change, but competes with learned model correction for the same
filter innovation. A corrector with enough parameters can absorb the innovation pattern
that a stiffness change produces, and adaptation is suppressed while the fit
improves. We propagate the stiffness sensitivities of the predicted measurements through
the vehicle states and construct a corrector orthogonal to them. A null-space parameterization enforces the constraint without a penalty
coefficient and preserves the static least-squares stiffness estimate on each
identification segment. In full-vehicle simulation, the stiffness response of the
unconstrained corrector declines as its parameter count grows, whereas the orthogonal
corrector responds at least as fully as the uncorrected filter at all sizes and lowers
sideslip error by 12.7%12.7\% to 22.0%22.0\%. In a simulated drive with a stiffness step, the
orthogonal corrector adapts as quickly as the uncorrected filter and lowers sideslip
error during and after the transient. On public real-vehicle data, the 430-parameter
unconstrained corrector loses most of its response to deliberate offsets of the filter’s
nominal stiffness, whereas the orthogonal corrector of the same size retains most of it, with a sideslip
error slightly above the uncorrected filter’s.
introduction:
Vehicle sideslip angle is a key input to stability control, yet it is not measured in
production vehicles [1], and the axle cornering stiffnesses that govern its dynamics drift
in service with tire wear, inflation pressure, load, and temperature [2]. Joint estimation
addresses both problems at once. A model-based filter estimates the sideslip angle
while adapting the stiffness parameters online from the yaw rate and lateral
acceleration. The adapted stiffness has diagnostic value of its own and keeps the
sideslip estimate consistent as the tires change. Holding it constant instead exposes the sideslip
estimate to stiffness mismatch, which raised the error by an order of magnitude in a
simulation study [3].

The single-track model at the core of such filters is kept simple to limit computation and
the number of parameters to be identified, and its discrepancy from the real vehicle is
systematic rather than random [4]. Methods that combine learned
components with physics-based filters have been proposed to account for this discrepancy
[5, 6, 7, 8]. These
augmentations reproduce the measurements more closely than the physical model alone. In
the vehicle state estimator closest to ours [8], the network
is trained with the stiffnesses fixed at offline-identified values. Its sideslip
estimation error increased when both axle cornering stiffnesses in the model were
increased by 10%10\%.

As Figure 1 illustrates, a mismatch between the measured and the predicted
output can be explained either by a change of the cornering stiffness or by a learned map
of the measured signals, and both explanations reproduce the measurement. A corrector, a learned term added to the model prediction,
absorbs whatever it can predict from its inputs. This includes the component that a
stiffness deviation produces, so the adaptation is suppressed while the fit to the
measurements still improves. This is the confounding between physical parameters and model discrepancy that
is well known in static Bayesian calibration
[9, 10]. In a sequential filter it appears
as a reduced response of the adapted stiffness to a real stiffness change. The more
parameters the corrector has, the less the filter responds to a real change. The
corrected filter still fits the identification data despite this reduced response, and
the adapted stiffness is rarely compared with an independent reference. Without such a
reference, the adapted values alone do not show whether the response to a stiffness
change is preserved.

The method proposed here constrains the corrector so that its output contains no
component of the form that a stiffness change produces, that is, so that it is orthogonal
to the sensitivities of the predicted outputs to the stiffness. The constraint is enforced
through the parameterization of the corrector. This paper makes three contributions.

We show that the parameter–discrepancy confounding known from static Bayesian
calibration appears in joint sideslip and cornering stiffness estimation as a reduced
response of the adapted stiffness to a real stiffness change.

We introduce a residual corrector whose output is orthogonal by construction to
the stiffness sensitivities of the predicted outputs along the state trajectory. The
constraint is built into a null-space parameterization and needs no penalty coefficient.
We show in closed form that the correction leaves the static least-squares stiffness
estimate unchanged.

We evaluate stiffness response, axle separation, and transient adaptation together
with sideslip accuracy in full-vehicle simulation. Real-vehicle data with an optical
sideslip reference further test the response to offsets of the nominal stiffness.

title: Velocity Optimization via Thermal Imaging Enhances Autonomous Tumor Resection
authors: Naveed D. Riaziat,Jiawei Ge,Ethan Kilmer,Michael W. Mikula,Paul Maria Scheikl,Michael Kam,Leila J. Mady,Axel Krieger,Jeremy D. Brown
abstract:
Objective: To demonstrate and evaluate THERMO, a thermal-velocity optimization algorithm for autonomous electrosurgery, in ex vivo porcine tissue using the UR10e-based ASTR system.
Methods: Thermography for Electrosurgical Rate Modulation via Optimization (ThERMO), a closed-loop algorithm that uses real-time thermal imaging data to minimize thermal injury while ensuring accurate cut margins, was tested on ex vivo porcine tissue. Histological analysis was performed to detect thermal injury extent at a cellular level, and 3D photogrammetric measurement was used to verify margin accuracy. ThERMO’s performance was compared against two previously used fixed velocity methods.
Results: ThERMO outperformed both fixed velocity comparison methods without requiring data-driven training or iterative tuning, reducing thermal injury by up to 52%, improving cut accuracy by up to 59%, and maintaining task completion speed.
Conclusions: Closed-loop thermal feedback via ThERMO improves autonomous robotic electrosurgery by simultaneously reducing thermal injury and improving margin accuracy, reinforcing its value over fixed velocity approaches for tumor resection applications.
Significance: This work advances autonomous robotic tumor resection by demonstrating that real-time closed-loop thermal feedback control can substantially reduce collateral tissue damage and improve surgical margin accuracy.
introduction:
Oral cavity cancer (OCC) is cancer of the mouth, tongue, lips, and cheeks. Approximately 377,000 new OCC cases are diagnosed each year globally, leading to 178,000 deaths. Tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and human papillomavirus (HPV) are risk factors for developing OCC. Over 90% of OCC cases are squamous cell carcinoma, or cancer of the cells that line the outer layer of the tongue, cheeks, gums, and throat [1]. For treatment of pre-metastatic oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), surgical intervention is often the most effective treatment [2].

The standard surgical approach is the partial glossectomy procedure, where the portion of the tongue consisting of the OSCC tumor is removed. Cancer recurrence rates are minimized if the surgical margins (the region between the tumor and the cut boundary) reach 5 mm5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} [3]. The term negative margin indicates that no cancer cells were found in the margin, while positive margin indicates the opposite. Though positive margins increase recurrence risk, excess negative margins indicate excess healthy tissue removal and worsen post-operative recovery and quality of life [4, 5]. Therefore, it is critical to ensure accurate surgical margins during tumor resection.

Electrosurgery is a common technique for removing tumor tissue, wherein a surgical tool conducts electricity to generate heat in tissue, thereby causing it to denature. The heat-induced tissue denaturation reduces mechanical cutting effort while controlling bleeding. Monopolar electrosurgery directly heats the tissue by passing current from the tool tip through the body to an alternate-site grounding pad. Excess application of electrosurgery, however, may cause trauma to the lingual nerve in the tongue and permanently impair tongue sensory function. Insufficient application, by contrast, reduces cut accuracy by causing tissue snagging, which negatively impacts surgical margins and outcomes. As such, electrosurgery requires surgeons to diligently monitor tissue conditions to prevent adverse outcomes.

Monitoring and safely controlling electrosurgery becomes increasingly difficult in the tight constraints of the oral cavity. Consequently, robotics has provided advances in ergonomics and visualization during oral surgeries [6, 7]. Systems like the da Vinci Single Port (Intuitive Surgical Inc., Sunnyvale, California, USA) have made trans-oral robotic surgery (TORS) possible by reducing tool size while maintaining high-quality stereoscopic vision. The application of robotics to head and neck surgery offers the possibility of procedural enhancements with sensing, feedback, and automation.

Though current commercial soft tissue surgical robots have little to no autonomous capability, increased electrosurgical autonomy could greatly reduce surgeon workload and improve surgical outcomes [8]. In the few early demonstrations of autonomous tumor resection has been an active research field, a discrepancy exists between the surgeon’s technique and the robot’s. While experienced surgeons adjust their cutting speed based on visual feedback of cut accuracy and thermal injury, current autonomous electrosurgical robots do not.

Autonomous surgical debridement of bone tissue was first demonstrated in human cadavers by Sefati et al. [9]. They used a hybrid continuum robot on a UR10 robot to perform osteolytic debridement in the pelvis using a surgeon-approved preoperative plan. Autonomous cutting of hard tissue like bone does not face many of the challenges of cutting soft tissue. Autonomous surgical cutting has typically run in an open-loop fashion, using a velocity predetermined via trial-and-error tuning or simulation. Studies have shown that autonomous robotic electrosurgery of this form causes more cellular injury than manual electrosurgery, indicating that the fine adjustments surgeons make during surgery have a substantial impact on excess heat injury [10]. In past demonstrations of autonomous tumor resection, researchers have prioritized cutting accuracy over thermal injury and manually selected low cutting speeds. For instance, Opfermann et al. first demonstrated a visual servoing approach for electrosurgical cutting on the Smart Tissue Autonomous Robot (STAR) [11, 12]. Saeidi et al. similarly showed that STAR could perform tissue-cutting tasks using a predetermined cut speed [13]. Ge et al. introduced the Autonomous System for Tumor Resection (ASTR) system for fully autonomous tumor resection and demonstrated successful cutting at 2 mm/s2\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}\text{/}\mathrm{s} [14]. Ge et al. later proposed that for faster velocities that excessively deform tissue, simulation-based trajectory augmentation could reduce spatial error [15]. However, soft tissue simulation is both challenging and not patient-specific, potentially limiting robustness, optimality, and safety without additional feedback mechanisms.

Closed-loop sensing has shown promise in optimizing electrosurgical performance. Since thermal injury is largely invisible to the naked eye until permanent damage has been done, researchers have used thermal imaging to measure electrosurgical thermal spread [16, 17, 18]. Recent works have developed miniaturized endoscopic thermal cameras as well, which are compatible with the laparoscopic surgery workflow [19, 20, 21]. Bao and Mazumder showed that thermal imaging can control the denaturation zone using a novel computer-controllable electrosurgical unit (ESU) [22]. Surgeons, however, typically employ a fixed power level, and most ESUs are not capable of real-time power modulation. El-Kebir et al. instead used thermal sensing to train a data-driven non-linear autoregressive exogenous input (NLARX) model to determine when a static surgical tool should move to the next waypoint [23]. It is still unclear, however, if these data-driven models generalize from laboratory settings to the complex surgical environment. Some researchers instead have developed methods to estimate soft tissue parameters online, including by use of thermography, Bayesian and Gaussian Estimation, and finite element models [24, 25, 26, 27, 28].

While these prior works have demonstrated the potential benefits of thermal injury measurement and control, electrosurgery is more appropriately solved as an optimal control problem with competing goals of limiting thermal injury and maximizing cut accuracy, which is significantly impacted by tissue deformation. In an attempt to maximize accuracy, Shademan et al. used near-infrared fluorescent markers to track tissue deformation during autonomous porcine intestinal anastomosis [12]. Kam et al. showed promising results controlling electrosurgical cut velocity with tracker-based tissue deformation feedback [29]. Similarly, Ferrari et al. used deformation modeling and feedback to track and therefore more accurately target tumor biopsy sites [30]. Giannarou et al. utilized microscopy images during retinal surgery to estimate tissue deformation and tool forces [31]. Despite these advancements, the combination of deflection and thermal injury feedback has yet to be demonstrated. Without considering both deflection and thermal injury, the above approaches to autonomous electrosurgical control cannot achieve optimality, especially in the highly muscular and therefore tough tissue found in the tongue.

Our previous work demonstrated optimal autonomous electrosurgical cutting speed in tissue phantoms using a thermal-feedback algorithm, Thermography for Electrosurgical Rate Modulation via Optimization (ThERMO). ThERMO improved resistance to disturbances, reduced thermal injury, and minimized tool deflection without the need for simulation or model training [32]. ThERMO prevented the need for trial-and-error speed selection by using online tissue parameter identification. However, up to this point, autonomous cutting under visual thermal feedback has not yet been demonstrated for 3D cutting in biological tissues with a multi-DoF robotic system. Testing in ex vivo tissue is a critical step towards eventual cadaveric and in vivo studies. Likewise, the connection between thermal feedback and cell death and the relationship between tool deflection and margin accuracy have not been validated through histological analysis or post-hoc margin measurement. Validating these outcomes is critical for the eventual clinical translation of autonomous thermal-feedback electrosurgical technologies.

Here, we evaluate adaptive velocity control using ThERMO on the Autonomous System for Tumor Resection (ASTR) system, an autonomous robotic surgery platform with an electrosurgical tool and RGB-D camera (see Fig. 1) [14]. Our contributions are threefold. First, we validate ThERMO’s effectiveness in improving margin accuracy while minimizing thermal spread in an ex vivo porcine tissue model. Second, we present histological analysis quantifying thermal injury in relation to cutting accuracy during a simulated electrosurgical tumor resection. Third, we provide a comparative study measuring thermal injury and cut accuracy against fixed-speed robotic methods, highlighting the benefits of thermal feedback in surgical performance. These results underscore the promise of intelligent electrosurgical automation for improving tumor resection outcomes in future surgeries.

title: Robot-Task Suitability in Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Task Allocation
authors: Daniel Weiner,Raj Korpan
comment: Accepted at Workshop on Foundation Models for Multi-Robot Systems (FM-MRS), IROS 2026
abstract: Heterogeneous multi-robot task allocation depends on estimates of how suitable individual robots are for candidate tasks, yet suitability can be defined in substantially different ways. We compare ten deterministic methods and two LLM-based variants spanning rule-based, similarity-based, requirement-oriented, fuzzy, and semantic approaches. Using common robot and task profiles, we compare how the methods score and rank candidate robots, identify feasibility, and select a top robot, while examining how these outcomes change with team composition, scale, spatial context, capability uncertainty, and task representation. The methods frequently disagree despite operating on identical scenarios. Generic similarity measures can violate properties expected under a one-sided requirement-satisfaction interpretation of suitability, while LLM-based scoring introduces additional stochastic and linguistic sensitivity. These results show that robot–task suitability should be treated as an explicit modeling choice whose assumptions, robustness, and decision-level consequences should be considered before allocation.
introduction:
Multi-robot task allocation (MRTA) concerns assigning tasks to robots subject to constraints on resources, timing, motion, and team objectives. MRTA has been studied through centralized optimization, market- and auction-based methods, distributed coordination, heuristics, and learning-based approaches [1, 2, 3, 4]. The problem is especially challenging for heterogeneous teams, whose robots may differ in mobility, sensing, manipulation, payload, reach, endurance, communication, and environmental tolerance [5]. Existing heterogeneous MRTA approaches represent these differences through capability constraints, utilities, energy-aware allocation, resilience mechanisms, or task-specific requirements [6, 7, 8, 9]. Regardless of the allocation mechanism, however, the system must determine how appropriate each robot is for each task [10, 11]. We use the term robot–task suitability to describe how well a particular robot matches the requirements of a particular task, including considerations such as feasibility, specialization, and expected performance.

Constructing suitability values is itself a nontrivial modeling problem. Robot capabilities and task requirements may be numerical, categorical, contextual, unstructured, or uncertain, and some requirements are mandatory while others permit partial satisfaction or tradeoffs. A robot with the necessary hardware may nevertheless be a poor candidate under current conditions because of travel distance, endurance, or environmental constraints [10, 11, 12, 13]. Prior work has considered uncertain or changing capabilities and task requirements [14, 15], while adaptive specialization methods model robot efficacy as initially unknown or changing during deployment [11, 8]. Reducing these factors to a scalar therefore requires assumptions about hard vs. soft constraints, capability weighting, surplus vs. deficient capability, and whether operational context is part of suitability.

Different methods encode these assumptions differently. Rule-based methods can explicitly evaluate requirements and reject infeasible pairs; vector-based approaches compare robots and tasks through geometric similarity; requirement-oriented methods measure satisfaction or deficiency; and fuzzy methods allow gradual satisfaction near numerical thresholds. Multi-objective MRTA likewise reflects the need to balance competing aspects of robot suitability [16, 17, 18, 19]. More recently, large language models (LLMs) have been used to reason over heterogeneous robot capabilities and natural-language task descriptions [20, 21, 22]. Such methods offer semantic flexibility but introduce stochasticity and sensitivity to linguistic representation. These approaches encode different notions of compatibility, making their effects difficult to isolate when they are evaluated using different robot, task, and allocation models.

This work therefore examines suitability estimation as a distinct component of heterogeneous MRTA rather than proposing a new allocation algorithm. We compare ten deterministic methods, including rule-based, similarity-based, requirement-oriented, set-based, and fuzzy approaches, together with two LLM-based variants, using common robot and task profiles. We evaluate agreement and robustness under changes in team composition, scale, robot-to-task ratio, spatial scale, and capability perturbations; test five one-sided suitability properties; examine task-dependent behavior; and evaluate LLM repeatability and semantic robustness. The experiments show that suitability method affects feasibility judgments and robot rankings, that several generic similarity measures exhibit behaviors inconsistent with one-sided requirement satisfaction, and that semantic scoring introduces additional uncertainty. These findings motivate treating suitability estimation as an explicit modeling decision rather than an assumed input to downstream task allocation.

title: Evaluating Social Reasoning in Embodied Vision-Language Models
authors: Daniel Weiner,Raj Korpan
comment: Accepted at Workshop on Foundation Models for Multi-Robot Systems (FM-MRS), IROS 2026
abstract: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person’s internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.
introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have quickly moved from perception and planning aids to the reasoning core of robot autonomy [1, 2].
A distinct class of embodiment-specialized models for robotic reasoning has emerged, targeting spatial grounding, pointing, affordance and trajectory prediction, and success detection [3].
Such models are natural candidates for high-level reasoning about what a robot should do from multimodal observations. Increasingly, those decisions are made among people, and by teams of robots: guides in airports, assistants in hospitals, service fleets in malls.
For such teams, coordination quality hinges on a shared assessment of human social state, such as who is engaged, who is confused, who is disengaging, or whether a robot has made a social error, so the team can determine which robot should approach, continue an interaction, or withdraw.
We refer to this as a social-perception layer: a semantically rich estimate of the humans in view produced from each robot’s observations and made available to the coordination layer.

Recent work has begun evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can provide such social information. SHREC benchmarks foundation models on real human-robot interactions (HRI), including recognition of social errors, competencies, and social attributes such as engagement, and reports substantial variation across models and tasks [4]. HRIBench similarly evaluates VLMs on interaction-relevant human perception, including nonverbal cues and other visual signals [5], while complementary work studies broader interaction-centric human-robot collaboration capabilities [6]. VLMs have also been used directly as proxies for social intelligence [7] and to determine whether and when a robot should initiate interaction [8].

Embodiment-specialized models are appealing candidates for the social-perception layer: one pretrained model, no per-deployment training, outputs already expressed in language the rest of the robotics stack uses [3].
Existing HRI benchmarks primarily evaluate general-purpose VLMs, while embodiment-specialized models are primarily evaluated on physical and spatial capabilities. To our knowledge, the relative social-reasoning performance of an embodiment-specialized VLM has not been evaluated against general-purpose VLM baselines on the same HRI benchmark.

Concretely, we evaluate whether Gemini Robotics-ER, a model tuned for embodied robotic reasoning, can identify human social states, such as engagement, robot social competencies, and social errors, on the SHREC benchmark [9], and compare its performance with the general-purpose VLMs reported by SHREC. SHREC’s social labels vary in how directly they can be supported by observable interaction evidence, thus, we examine performance along a gradient from externally grounded to internally inferred. Externally grounded tasks can be resolved from the observable structure of an interaction, such as turn-taking and response timing evident in the transcript. Internally inferred tasks require stronger inference about affect, intention, or mental state. Our hypothesis is that Gemini Robotics-ER will perform better on externally grounded tasks than internally inferred ones.

Furthermore, foundation models are increasingly being placed directly inside multi-robot decision-making loops. RoCo uses language-model agents to negotiate collaborative plans [10]; SMART-LLM decomposes natural-language tasks and forms robot coalitions based on robot capabilities [11]; and COHERENT coordinates heterogeneous teams through LLM-mediated task assignment and feedback [12].
Recent work applies conformal prediction and uncertainty-aware reasoning to robot planning [13, 14, 15], while embodied-agent evaluations show that models may fail to abstain appropriately under ambiguous or infeasible conditions [16]. Recent work also argues for deployment-specific evaluation when selecting foundation models for social robots [17]. Against this background, we ask whether an embodiment-specialized robotics VLM preserves the social-reasoning capabilities needed for human-aware robotic systems.

We make three contributions. First, we formulate the question of whether an embodiment-specialized robotics foundation model preserves social reasoning capability, particularly in the context of human-aware multi-robot systems. Second, we define a benchmark-aligned evaluation of Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, validating our modified evaluation pipeline against an established general-purpose VLM baseline. Third, we analyze the implications of any observed capability gap for model reliability across multi-robot teams.

title: HATCH: Hardware-Attested Task Chains for Verifiable Manipulation
authors: Shiza Charania
comment: . Accepted at the 5th Workshop on Open Robotics Software, IROS 2026, Pittsburgh, PA, USA. Benchmark repository:this https URL
abstract: Capability claims in robot manipulation are unverifiable, and existing leaderboards are each closed, simulated, or gameable. We propose HATCH, a robot escape room: an openly specified, physically replicable, sensor-scored, and unrehearsable benchmark, released under an open license.
introduction:
Capability claims in robot manipulation are, at present, unverifiable. Results arrive as curated demonstration videos, run on hardware no other lab owns, in environments no other lab can recreate, against self-defined success criteria. Vision and language compounded progress on shared benchmarks; ImageNet is the defining case. Manipulation never acquired one, in part because physical evaluation is expensive: hardware, resets between runs, and human labor.

The leaderboards that do exist achieve at most two of the three properties a trusted benchmark requires: openness, physical evaluation, and trustworthy results. RoboLab-120 [1] evaluates entrants in-house, in simulation, which resists gaming but is neither open nor physical: the entrant pool is small, and as of mid-2026, the operating vendor’s own model topped the leaderboard [5]. RoboArena [2] distributes real-world evaluation across volunteer institutions—an open and physical design—but its team recently disclosed that volunteer evaluators had not completed some assigned evaluations, pulling affected results and flagging low-sample entries [3]; the failure was in the trust layer, not the robots. MolmoSpaces [4] is fully open but simulation-only, and simulated success does not certify physical capability [7]. Nothing available today is simultaneously open, physical, and trustworthy [5, 6], so we propose one that is: HATCH, a robot escape room.

title: Towards Autonomous Bricklaying Using Boston Dynamics Spot
authors: Karl-Johan Sorensen,Nico vom Hofe,Frank H. P. Fitzek
comment: . Published in the Proceedings of the 43rd International Symposium on Automation and Robotics in Construction (ISARC 2026), Singapore
abstract: Mobile legged robots offer unique advantages for on-site construction, including the ability to traverse unstructured terrain, climb stairs, and operate independently between spatially separated work zones. This paper presents a proof-of-concept system for autonomous brick stacking using a Boston Dynamics Spot quadrupedal robot equipped with a manipulator arm. The system operates between a supply area and an assembly area, using AprilTag fiducials for localization and autowalk missions for navigation. Target brick positions and orientations are specified in CAD software and exported directly for robotic execution. We evaluate placement accuracy through ten repeated assemblies of a curved four-layer wall comprising 14 wooden bricks. Results show mean translation errors below 10 mm and mean yaw errors below 1.5°, while the overall RMSE across all runs is 27.72 mm (translation) and 2.06° (rotation). The system was also tested outdoors with stairs between the two areas. The workflow is modular and easily extendable to different wall geometries.
introduction:
The construction industry is undergoing a transition towards greater automation, driven by rising housing demand, skilled labor shortages, and persistent safety concerns on construction sites. Yet, compared to sectors such as automotive and logistics, construction has seen limited productivity gains, with annual improvement rates of only 1 %1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} against an industry average of 2.8 %2.8\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} [1]. On-site robotic automation has been proposed as one means to address these challenges [2].
Despite this potential, the deployment of robotic systems on construction sites remains limited [3]. Existing approaches face significant constraints. Large gantry systems require infrastructure that often exceeds the scale of the structure being built. Wheeled and tracked mobile platforms struggle with rough terrain, stairs, and cluttered site conditions. These constraints have confined most successful automation efforts to off-site prefabrication; yet construction fundamentally remains an on-site process where varying conditions resist complete pre-planning.
Recent advances in commercial legged robotics have produced platforms capable of traversing stairs, uneven terrain, and human-centric spaces [4]. This makes them suited to the multi-level, cluttered environments of real construction sites, where wheeled and tracked platforms face fundamental access constraints. Prior work has demonstrated legged manipulation for general pick-and-place tasks [5, 6], but application to construction assembly has not been explored. To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has quantitatively evaluated the accuracy with which a legged robot can execute a brick-stacking task.

This paper presents a proof-of-concept for what we term the  MARA (MARA) workflow: a distributed construction process in which a legged mobile manipulator autonomously traverses between spatially separated supply and assembly areas, picking and placing bricks according to a specified layout. The approach is evaluated using a Boston Dynamics Spot quadrupedal robot equipped with a manipulator arm. Target brick positions are modeled in Rhino, a  CAD (CAD) program, and exported directly for robotic assembly. The system localizes by referencing each manipulation operation to a locally visible fiducial marker, thereby decoupling placement accuracy from global odometry drift. Placement accuracy is evaluated through ten repeated assemblies of a curved four-layer wall, reporting translational and rotational errors across layers.

title: Real-Time Disturbance-Aware Koopman Model Predictive Control for Quadrotors in Spatially Varying Winds
authors: Stella Kombo,Masih Haseli,Alejandro A. Stefan-Zavala,Peter I. Renn,Morteza Gharib,Joel W. Burdick
abstract:
Reliable quadrotor flight in disturbed environments requires predictive models that remain accurate as unmodeled aerodynamic effects change during deployment. We introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) framework that preserves an offline-identified nominal model while learning only
a disturbance-induced correction online. A reference-dependent KCF is first learned from simulation data and calibrated using limited hardware data. During deployment, the nominal KCF remains fixed while a lightweight residual ensemble learns a low-dimensional disturbance correction from causal state–command–state transitions. The Adaptive DA-KCF model is incorporated into MPC, where disturbance corrections are evaluated along the prediction horizon to optimize position and yaw references sent to the onboard stabilizing controller. Hardware experiments on a nano-quadrotor under uniform wind and a spatially varying wake demonstrate that online adaptation improves multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, while satisfying real-time control requirements.
introduction:
Autonomous aerial robots are increasingly being considered for inspection, delivery, monitoring and human mobility tasks in densely built environments [1]. Such missions require multi-rotors to operate around buildings, above rooftops, through corridors and other confined structures while maintaining accurate trajectory tracking and satisfying state and actuation constraints. Reliable flight in these settings remains challenging since quadrotors are nonlinear, underactuated systems whose performance can degrade when aerodynamic effects are not adequately represented by the prediction or control model [2, 3]. The challenge is particularly pronounced in urban environments, where interactions between incoming flow and surrounding structures generate spatially varying wakes, vortices, recirculation zones and accelerated flows around building edges [4]. Consequently, the disturbances experienced by the aerial vehicle can vary significantly along a single flight trajectory.

Aerodynamic disturbances have previously been addressed at several levels of aerial-robot modeling and control. Classical approaches mainly rely on feedback to reject external disturbances and modeling errors during flight [5]. Analytic aerodynamic models, such as linear/quadratic rotor-drag terms, augment nominal dynamics with low-order aerodynamic effects while remaining compatible with real-time control [6]. Data-driven approaches instead learn residual dynamics or full-state transition models from flight data, capturing complex effects that are difficult to model analytically. These learned effects can improve prediction and control for high-performance drone flight [7, 8, 9]. Although such models can be identified offline and used efficiently online, their accuracy degrades when the vehicle encounters dynamics not represented in the identification data.

A complementary line of work uses measured or predicted spatial flow information to aid wind-aware trajectory planning and penalize paths that enter adverse flow regions [10]. High-fidelity computational fluid dynamics can resolve complex urban flow structures [11], but their computational costs limit direct use in online prediction and high-rate control [12]. Learned flow surrogates provide a tractable alternative for wind-informed planning [13, 14]. However, disturbed regions cannot always be avoided when geometric constraints, mission requirements or unknown wakes force the vehicle to traverse them. When this occurs, unmodeled disturbances can induce persistent mismatch between nominal predictions and the realized vehicle response, degrading tracking and stability. Adaptive, observer-based and learning-based controllers compensate for these effects by estimating disturbances, adapting model parameters or learning residual corrections online [15, 16, 2]. For predictive control, these corrections must also be propagated over the prediction horizon without requiring online retraining of the full dynamics model. This motivates learning a nominal model offline from broad system excitation, while adapting to unmodeled disturbance-induced discrepancies during deployment.

Koopman-based models provide a structured nominal predictor that can be learned offline and used efficiently online, making them potentially suitable for disturbance augmentation. By representing nonlinear dynamics through observables in a function space, finite-dimensional approximations can be incorporated into model predictive control [17, 18] and have been applied to quadrotor prediction and trajectory tracking [19, 20]. The Koopman Control Family (KCF) [21] represents nonlinear and state-dependent control systems via a family of linear operators parameterized by the control input. However, existing KCF methods do not explicitly represent disturbances that arise during deployment [22].

Koopman methods have also been extended to disturbance estimation and online adaptation. Disturbance-observer approaches learn disturbance models for online compensation [23], while adaptive Koopman methods update residual or lifted dynamics [24, 25]. For quadrotors, related work either switches among pre-identified Koopman models across operating conditions [26] or augments nominal predictors with residual corrections [27]. These approaches do not formulate online adaptation as a disturbance-dependent extension of an input-dependent KCF. This leaves open how to preserve a pretrained nominal KCF while adapting only to disturbance-induced discrepancies online within real-time predictive control, without retraining the full model.

To address this gap, we introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) and apply it to real-time predictive control of multi-rotors. We first identify a nominal KCF from simulation data and calibrate it using hardware data, capturing the coupled vehicle-onboard controller response while keeping the nominal model fixed during deployment. We then adopt a structured separable approximation A⁡(u,d)≈Ac​(u)+Ad​(d)A(u,d)\approx A_{\mathrm{c}}(u)+A_{d}(d), where Ac​(u)A_{\mathrm{c}}(u) is the nominal reference-dependent KCF and Ad​(d)A_{d}(d) is a disturbance-dependent modification. For real-time deployment, the disturbance-dependent effect is realized through a low-dimensional correction learned online and propagated through the predictive horizon, while the calibrated nominal KCF and onboard stabilization controller remain fixed. We validate the method on a nano-quadrotor under previously unmodeled aerodynamic disturbances. Experiments include figure-eight tracking in uniform fan-array flows and traversal through a spatially varying wake generated by a building-like obstacle. The results demonstrate online adaptation of the predictive dynamics, improved trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, and real-time execution within the control deadline.

title: Training Controllable World Models via Action Influence Maximization
authors: Samuel M. Bateman,Tenny Yin,Chongyi Zheng,Lei Huang,Brian Wang,Benjamin Eysenbach,Jaime Fernández Fisac,Dhruv Shah
abstract:
Action-conditioned video generative models trained on successful, goal-directed demonstrations tend to ignore the commanded action, rendering a plausible expert-like future regardless of what is asked of them. We trace this failure to training data that lack sufficient action influence. We analyze this metric and prove that it upper bounds the action influence that any model trained on that data can express. Expert demonstrations, whose narrow action distributions let next states be predicted without attending to the action, set a low ceiling that no amount of model capacity alone can raise. Raising it requires collecting different data. We introduce Action Influence Maximization (AIM), an algorithm for actively collecting training data for improving dataset action influence.
We compare the performance and data-efficiency of AIM against exploration heuristics and intrinsic-motivation methods on simulated navigation and manipulation tasks. In pixel-based manipulation, AIM is the only method that consistently improves controllability: 500 actively collected episodes added to 3k demonstrations match a world model trained on 300k expert episodes on end-effector controllability, an 85×85\times reduction in data.
introduction:
Action-conditioned world models promise to predict what would happen if a robot took different actions at a given state, enabling policy improvement in novel problems.
Yet, when queried with out-of-distribution actions, models trained on expert demonstrations can predict expert-like futures or hallucinate implausible alternatives.
This failure of controllability (the ability to faithfully predict how changing actions affect outcomes) limits their usefulness for improving robot policies.

Scaling the quantity and diversity of training data can mitigate this [1, 2], but is limited by the cost of collecting robotics data.
To make world models competitive with on-robot experience, the practical question is how to obtain the most useful world-model training data from each real robot interaction.
Despite this, optimal data collection for robotic world models is relatively underexplored compared to policy improving data [3, 4, 5].
This paper investigates two key hypotheses: Does the data collection distribution strongly influence the downstream world model controllability and fidelity? And, supposing it consequential, can we optimize the data collection distribution to directly improve world model controllability and fidelity?
This work suggests that the answer to both questions is yes.

This has a plausible and intuitive explanation: expert demonstrations in high-dimensional action spaces (e.g. human teleoperation) achieve their goals through a narrow sequence of actions.
The more sensitive success is to action variability, the more deterministic expert demonstrations must be.
Successful demonstrations can thus provide insufficient variation in actions to reveal evidence of how alternative actions would change outcomes.
A world model fitting this data can rationally ignore action influence and usually predict expert-like outcomes regardless of action command [1].
In contrast, a non-expert learner may visit different states and try actions underrepresented in expert demonstration.
Predicting consequences of varying actions in these states are precisely the situations where downstream policy improvement stands to benefit the most and where the world model has the least data support.
We see evidence for this (Figures 6 and 8): scaling passive data collection improves controllability for different eval distributions, but the most efficient collection strategy is eval-distribution dependent.

To address this, we propose Action Influence Maximization (AIM), an active data collection algorithm that uses a data-derived intrinsic reward.
Put simply, AIM estimates which variations in action consequences would be poorly explained by the current dataset using a theoretically-motivated, learned intrinsic reward, and then focuses data collection on those state-action pairs as a form of embodied active learning.
To do this, we connect conditional dataset mutual information (MI) to the controllability of any downstream world model, and derive a tractable learned pointwise reward estimator using data density estimation to optimize this property directly.
AIM achieves up to an 85×85\times improvement in data efficiency in a high-dimensional, robot manipulation task: adding just 500 actively collected episodes to 3k expert demonstrations matches the end-effector controllability of a world model trained on 300k expert episodes.

title: Refuses When Asked, Complies When Acting: A Runtime Safety Check for Robot Control Loops
authors: Arnav Grover
comment: plus references. Submitted to the Science of Physical AI Safety (SPAIS) workshop at CoRL 2026
abstract: Frontier models can control robots through agent harnesses that loop on one question: what motion comes next toward the user’s goal? We show that this default loop carries out harmful instructions. With GPT-6 Astra controlling a low-cost SO-101 arm through the Inspect Robots harness on three household tasks whose hazard is common knowledge, such as “put the knife in the toy basket”, the policy refused 0% of 15 trials, attempted the harm every time, and completed it in 27%. Its one exit, give_up, is meant for goals that cannot be achieved, and it never cited the hazard. We add an optional runtime safety check to the loop: before the first motion, the model is asked whether it would carry out the instruction, given the same camera frames. The check would have stopped all 15 hazardous instructions, including the 4 that completed the harm, and flagged none of the 15 harmless controls. Code and data: https://github.com/Arnav-Gr0ver/Refuses-When-Asked-Complies-When-Acting.
introduction:
Before acting, a person considers the harm an action could do to those it affects, but a robot control loop that works toward the user’s goal has no step where that consideration happens. Ask a frontier model whether it would put a knife in a toy basket that children reach into, and it says no. Give the same model the same instruction as the control loop of a robot arm, and it reaches for the knife to put it in the basket.

RoboHarm [1] showed that frontier robot policies fail this check on hardware: GPT-6 Astra refused 2% of harmful instructions (2 of 100) and carried out 60%, including 17 of 20 attempts to stab a baby doll. We study why in one widely used harness. The Inspect Robots harness [2] runs the policy in a loop in which every call returns one motion toward the user’s goal. Its safety approvers only clamp out-of-bounds and too-fast motion, and its one exit, give_up, is for goals that cannot be achieved, not for goals that should not be pursued. Nothing in the loop asks whether the instruction should be carried out, so a harmful instruction proceeds like any other.

We show that the default loop does carry out the harm: on three household tasks, GPT-6 Astra refused none of 15 trials and completed the harm in four. We then add an optional runtime safety check to the loop. Before the first motion, the check asks the policy model whether it would carry out the instruction, given the camera frames. It would have stopped all 15 hazardous instructions and flagged none of the harmless controls (Fig. 1). The check reuses the policy’s model and adds one call, with no second model and no safety specification, unlike prior safeguards that add safety specifications [3] or a separate monitoring model [4]. We also introduce three household tasks, each with a named hazard, a safe alternative, and a harmless control, and describe the policy’s reasoning across 464 robot calls.
