title: Determination of the Human-Robot Interaction Workspace for Robot Assisted Head Stabilization Control
authors: Xinmin Liu,Alexander L. Van Slyke,Destinee Holloman,Ahmad Sakaamini,Rodney D. Wiersma
abstract:
Accurate head immobilization is critical for medical procedures such as neuroimaging and intracranial radiation therapy, where even minor motion can compromise precision. Traditional methods, such as rigid stereotactic frames and thermoplastic face masks, are invasive, uncomfortable for patients, and require a time-consuming setup. To overcome these limitations, a novel approach employs a 6-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) robotic head holder that is integrated with real-time optical motion tracking, enabling dynamic compensation for head movements without physical restraint. However, implementing this system requires a detailed biomechanical understanding of skull-cervical spine interactions to define safe and effective motion limits. In this study, we conduct a human volunteer investigation using a 6DoF Stewart platform robot to characterize biokinematic workspace of the head-neck system and establish foundational data for
human-robot interaction in precision head stabilization.
introduction:
There has been significant interest in achieving high-precision positioning of the head in medical applications 41, 11, 34. In diagnostic brain imaging, head motion can lead to movement-related artifacts such as blurring and ghosting, which can hinder clinical diagnosis 25. This is especially true for imaging modalities such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET), where the collection of data required for 3D image reconstruction requires patients to lie still for long periods of time 45, 16. This issue is especially challenging when scanning children or adults who exhibit involuntary motion 10, 40, 23.
Prospective motion correction (PMC) is a popular technique that updates the image acquisition in real-time to keep the field of view constant relative to the moving object in brain MRI. However, PMC has some limitations. It cannot correct higher-order effects such as changing magnetic field inhomogeneities and gradient imperfections. When using multiple receiver coil arrays for better signal quality, motion can change the coil sensitivities relative to the moving object. Motion during image acquisition can cause blurring and spatial distortion because data is collected from different positions within the nonlinear gradient fields. Even with accurate real-time pose correction, motion can still cause magnetic field changes due to inhomogeneities and object-induced field changes. These local magnetic field changes are often the main source of remaining artifacts 14, 43, 39, 3, 36. Therefore, it is desirable to use a robotic platform to stabilize the head position.

Although computed tomography (CT) can typically acquire images faster than MRI or PET, in certain cases, head motion artifacts have been reported 29, 30. In therapeutic applications, accurate head positioning is essential for procedures involving the treatment of the brain using conventional surgery or radiation therapy 21, 12, 15. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is a treatment modality employed for managing brain disorders by utilizing highly precise radiation dose placement. SRS has been used to treat benign or metastatic brain tumors 13, arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) 18, 6, trigeminal neuralgia 44, 9, and acoustic neuromas 24. For SRS, accurate head positioning is needed to avoid damaging critical neural and vascular structures within the brain.

The most common approach to stabilize the head position is the use of stereotactic frames. In this approach, a metal ring is attached to the patient’s skull using screws, and then the frame is bolted to the treatment table, see top row in Fig. 1 8, 27. The invasive nature and discomfort associated with the frame have been identified as a central cause of poor patient compliance and poor clinical efficacy. Another approach involves thermoplastic face masks, as shown in the bottom row of Fig. 1. However, such masks have decreased accuracy due to patient-induced mask flex and can suffer from material changes over time, such as shrinkage 35.

Even with the mask in place, a patient’s head can still drift laterally due to rotational movement around the fulcrum at the back of the skull. In some cases, this has resulted in systematic shifts of up to 2 mm from the initial target setup position 26. A recent study reported significant errors, which were attributed to improper patient setup stemming from factors such as limitations in mask manufacturing quality, loosening or shrinkage of the mask during treatment, or physical changes in the patient’s head due to facial swelling or weight loss19. Moreover, many patients find the thermoplastic mask invasive and psychologically confining, as it severely restricts natural head motion. These factors can contribute to unsafe conditions, potentially leading to treatment interruptions for patient realignment to ensure proper target coverage27.
The clinical significance of localization inaccuracies in frameless stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) remains a subject of debate. For critical applications—such as treating acoustic neuromas, pituitary adenomas, trigeminal neuralgia, or lesions adjacent to vital structures—frameless SRS methods have not yet achieved the same level of confidence as frame-based approaches. To mitigate this concern, image-guided radiotherapy (IGRT) is commonly used to monitor patient positioning, complemented by 6D robotic couch adjustments to reduce setup errors in frameless SRS33, 17, 2. However, IGRT is typically performed intermittently and does not compensate for real-time patient motion deviations during radiation delivery.

In general, the accuracies of masks are not suitable for deep tumors located near critical structures, such as in trigeminal neuralgia cases.

One recent method that allows highly accurate human head positioning without the use of head frames or thermoplastic masks is through the use of a 6-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) robotic head holder 4, 37. By performing real-time 6DoF patient head motion tracking through a suitable camera system that is used as an input into a control system, it was demonstrated that a Stewart platform (hexapod) type of robot can be used to continuously correct the head target position both translationally and rotationally during treatment (Fig. 2). The
system efficacy was evaluated on healthy volunteers and indicated that head motion remained under a 0.5mm/0.5deg threshold >> 99% of the time, compared to less than 10% of the time without the use of robotic stabilization demonstrating that the robotic SRS has potential to match or exceed the accuracies of frame based procedures.

Currently, robotic head position stabilization systems do not consider the biokinematics of the head and neck, but rather treat the head as a rigid body object that can freely move in space. This control method can therefore lead to robot head correction trajectories that do not follow natural head-neck motion and can be uncomfortable for patients.

The use of an accurate biomechanical model of the head and neck could allow for improved patient comfort and more effective robotic head motion correction. However, such kinematic modeling of the human head and neck is a complex subject that requires a multidisciplinary approach, combining knowledge of anatomy, biomechanics, and engineering. The study 28 aimed to examine the three-dimensional kinematics of the cervical spine during maximal passive head rotation, with a focus on coupled motion, using low-dose CT scans of twenty healthy volunteers in both neutral and maximum axial rotation positions. The study employed the finite helical-axis method to describe the 3D motion between the discrete positions of each separated vertebra. In another work, investigating the spine’s role during walking, a 3-dimensional multi-segment kinematic spine model 20 was developed for noninvasive analysis of spinal motion during walking. Validation of the kinematic model was carried out by comparing the calculated angles to the known angles from a mechanical model. The study involved collecting data on the motion of the spine from volunteers walking at their self-selected speeds. Kinematic modeling can also be useful in the development of devices aimed at addressing issues in the head and neck region. A novel study 46 was reported where a dynamic neck brace was utilized to analyze the head movements of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) while also recording the surface electromyography (EMG) of their neck muscles. The ALS participants were instructed to perform three head-neck movements in a single plane: flexion-extension in the sagittal plane, lateral bending in the coronal plane, and axial rotation in the transverse plane. These movements were repeated five times at self-selected speeds. There are also many studies on occupational neck disorders as a result of the workforce shifting from industry to sedentary office work, and on the mechanical behavior of the cervical vertebra under normal conditions and under conditions that result in minor or major injuries 1, 7, 31.

In this work, we present results from a healthy volunteer study investigating head and neck reaction to a 6DoF robot that is aimed for potential use in SRS radiation therapy. Optical camera monitoring was used to track the real-time response of the human head to various translational and rotational input trajectories induced by a compact 6DoF robot located behind the head. Analysis of motion data allowed for determination of general kinematic parameters as needed for the development of a head-and-neck biomechanical model. Knowledge of the head’s dynamic motion constraints is an important considerations for the interaction between humans and robots, not only in the medical space but potentially in other research areas such as the development of head motion control through robotic exoskeletons.

title: Design and Control of a Multimodal Legged-Aerial Robot Through Separate Control Contraction Metrics
authors: Kaushik Venkatesh Krishnamurthy,Eric Sihite,Alireza Ramezani,Morteza Gharib
comment: Presented at 2026 IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems, Pittsburgh PA
abstract: The integration of dynamic legged locomotion and aerial mobility offers versatility that is deterred by challenges in payload distribution, actuation, and the contrasting requirements of both domains. In this paper, we present the design and operation of a multimodal quadrupedal aerial-legged robot. The presence of legged aerial systems also allows for thruster-assisted legged locomotion, which we make possible with a unified control framework using Control Contraction Metrics (CCM). We search for separate domain-specific contraction metrics for walking and flight independently offline and unify them using an online energy-based Control Lyapunov Function Quadratic Program (CLF QP). This enables optimal, cross-domain control allocation, which we show using simulations. We also show experimental results that validate the mechanical viability of our hardware and the paradigm of thruster-assisted trotting. The stability of said experiments motivates the deployment of the control framework for multimodal operations.
introduction:
Robotic biomimicry of birds’ dynamic bipedal and flight locomotion can be a significant ordeal. The prohibitive design restrictions, such as a tight power budget, limited payload, complex multi-modal actuation and perception, an excessive number of active and passive joints involved in each mode, sophisticated control, and environment-specific models, just to name a few, have alienated these concepts. It is worth noting that, as multi-modality has secured birds’ (and other species) survival in complex environments, similar manifestations in mobile robots [7] can be rewarding and important.

In this work, we will report our legged-aerial quadrupedal robot’s first multi-modal operations, including thruster assisted dynamic trotting and hovering. Our long-term objective has remained to integrate dynamic legged locomotion and aerial mobility in a single platform. Our robot design primarily focused on mass allocation to minimize the total cost of transport, which consequently yields smaller actuation bulk in the system, and component selection for the flight unit was systematically made to achieve successful lift-off while not too much negatively affecting dynamic legged mobility.

Standard control theory have struggle with dynamic, changing trajectory tracking. A contraction metric is a Riemannian metric, with respect to which the distance between any two solutions of a differential equation is decreasing. Unlike a Lyapunov function, which measure the decreasing generalized distance between a point and an attractor such as an equilibrium, contraction does not require any knowledge about the position of the attractor. Simply, contraction ensures incremental stability between two trajectories, instead of the stability of an equilibrium point.
Control Contraction Metrics (CCM) ensures that small displacements in directions orthogonal to the span of the control inputs must be contracting.
The existence of a CCM can be formulated as a convex problem as specified in previous works [8, 18]. To overcome the computational bottleneck of global stability analysis for this coupled hybrid system, we propose a unified control framework inspired by CCMs.

We outline this work’s contributions as follows:

The design and operation of a multimodal legged-aerial robot.

A proposed control framework using contraction theory to create separate metrics for walking and flight, which are then unified online using an energy-based control Lyapunov function quadratic programming (CLF-QP).

Experimental results on hardware, with a decoupled heuristic control policy to demonstrate the capabilities of thruster-assisted trotting and flying. These experiments seek to prove that the physical paradigm of combining thrusters with legs is robust.

1. The design and operation of a multimodal legged-aerial robot.

2. A proposed control framework using contraction theory to create separate metrics for walking and flight, which are then unified online using an energy-based control Lyapunov function quadratic programming (CLF-QP).

3. Experimental results on hardware, with a decoupled heuristic control policy to demonstrate the capabilities of thruster-assisted trotting and flying. These experiments seek to prove that the physical paradigm of combining thrusters with legs is robust.

title: RadGeoLoc: Radar Geolocalization via Particle Filtering
authors: Shaunak Kolhe,Peng Jiang,Kasi Viswanath,Srikanth Saripalli
abstract: In real-time autonomous field applications, GNSS is often unreliable and inaccurate. A possible solution is localizing against a prebuilt map like a satellite image, as it is georeferenced and already surveyed. In this work, we localize a spinning radar measurement against overhead RGB imagery with a learned observation model. We use a radar representation pretrained by masked reconstruction and align it to features from a satellite image. A particle filter propagated by radar odometry proposes candidate poses, and our observation model provides a likelihood over these poses. We evaluate our method over 31 distinct routes, over 8 datasets spanning both urban and offroad conditions using only ground radar and a coarse local prior. We also examine the robustness over changing weather using repeated traversals over the same route over 13 months, in both urban and offroad conditions.
introduction:
Reliable robot localization in operating environments is essential for their effective operation. In GPS-denied environments, this proves to be difficult. A common remedy to this problem is to localize against a prior map, often built by a previous field deployment. This approach limits localization to pre-mapped areas, and is vulnerable to scene changes over time. Additionally, if such a prebuilt map is to be built at runtime[1], [2], these methods scale poorly with the size of the environment. Satellite and aerial orthophotos instead provide a useful map, since they are georeferenced, widely available, and globally consistent.

Localizing against a satellite image introduces its own set of challenges. For instance, with cameras, the gap between a top-down orthophoto and the forward camera measurement must be bridged by a view transform, termed as crossview localization [3]. While this gap is reduced significantly with other sensors that measure radially, such as LiDAR [4], there is also the temporal gap from the time of capture of the satellite image. What both sensors also lack is robustness to weather, which can be bridged by using Radio Detection and Ranging (radar). Radar sensors prove to be suitable for detection in these scenarios and yield geometric features over a longer range due to their longer wavelength [5].

Spinning radar [6] presents a practical alternative to the geolocalization problem. A radar measurement is already metric and in BEV form. Existing methods that localize radar against a public map build an explicit intermediate representation first, and then solve for a geometric alignment against it using OpenStreetMap routes and semantic layers [7], or points extracted from overhead imagery and registered against radar-derived points [8], [9], [10], [11]. Each of these commits to a class label or a fixed structural representation derived from the satellite images. However, performance of such methods in unstructured environments is not explored.

In this work, we instead pose a learned, shared representation for this task. A radar encoder pretrained by masked reconstruction is aligned by a contrastive objective to features of the satellite image on a shared metric grid, and the model is then asked the question: given a candidate pose, how compatible are the two representations? We use this to score pose hypotheses derived from a particle filter. We achieve a median per-frame ATE of 2.9m and 5.17m on urban and offroad routes respectively.

Our main contributions are:

An observation model for particle filtering which computes pose likelihoods by matching learned features from a radar image and a satellite image, by explicitly learning scene structure from radar.

An exhaustive evaluation, to the best of our knowledge, of over 8 of 10 published datasets11
1
                  
                  
                  
                We exclude the BoreasRT [12] and MOANA [13] datasets, since BoreasRT provides only Doppler radar and MOANA provides marine scenarios showing very sparse returns spanning over 31 distinct routes in both urban and offroad scenarios.

An analysis of what radar reconstruction pretraining contributes, by ablating the pretrained weights.

title: What Would Removing This Corruption Change? Failure Attribution for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Carson Sobolewski,Anjali Parashar,Fei Chen,Yingke Li,Chuchu Fan
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are sensitive to visual corruptions, but knowing that a corruption is typically harmful does not establish whether removing it would benefit the current episode. Furthermore, when several corruptions co-occur, deciding what to correct requires understanding which ones contribute to failure risk and how much their removal would help. We define this problem as failure attribution. Detecting corruption presence alone cannot answer this question, as corruptions can be present but relatively harmless, while directly measuring removal benefits requires costly paired policy rollouts with and without the corruption present. To address this, we introduce a factorized risk model that learns separate representations of the scene and corruptions, allowing us to estimate removal benefits through latent intervention from the current image and task instruction, without paired clean images or additional counterfactual rollouts. We evaluate our approach on OpenVLA and π0.5\pi_{0.5} in simulation and π0.5\pi_{0.5}-DROID on a Franka robot. Our method outperforms monolithic and vision-language-model (VLM) baselines, including achieving approximately 3x lower attribution error than frontier VLMs. We also demonstrate our method adapts to execution context and corruption intensity, and can be used for online failure monitoring on hardware.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [1, 2, 3] have emerged as generalist robotic policies capable of performing manipulation tasks directly from images and natural language instructions. However, their reliance on visual input makes them sensitive to visual corruptions [4]. For example, viewpoint changes and sensor noise have considerable impact on OpenVLA’s performance, reducing success rate from 76.5% to 1.1% and 19.3%, respectively [4]. These effects motivate knowing how each corruption influences a policy during execution. A straightforward approach is to estimate average failure rates for each corruption combination based on historical data. However, these averages assign the same prediction to episodes with the same corruption combination, regardless of corruption intensity or the current scene context. Knowing that a corruption is harmful on average therefore does not establish whether removing it would reduce failure risk in the current episode.

When several corruptions co-occur, this problem is compounded: we need to determine which corruptions contribute to the current failure risk and which would offer the greatest benefit if removed. We call this failure attribution: quantifying each corruption’s contribution by asking, “How much would failure risk decrease if this corruption were removed?”
Answering this question can guide whether and how to correct an execution failure.

However, failure attribution presents two challenges.
First, corruption presence alone does not establish its effect on performance. A corruption may be clearly visible yet have little impact on a particular policy, so detecting it does not indicate whether correcting it would help.
Prior works address neighboring problems, including improving robustness through corruption-inclusive training [4, 5] or input restoration [6], and predicting failure through online monitoring [7, 8, 9, 10]. However, these approaches do not directly answer the attribution question of how much removing each corruption would reduce failure risk.

Second, directly measuring this removal benefit requires intervention: executing the policy repeatedly with and without each corruption from the same underlying state. Because a corruption’s effect depends on which others remain present, exhaustively characterizing these interactions requires covering a large majority of combinations, rather than just single corruptions. Such comparisons are expensive in simulation and difficult to reproduce during deployment, where repeated failed executions can also put hardware at risk. We therefore seek to estimate removal effects from the available observation, without executing these counterfactual rollouts.

To address these challenges, we introduce a factorized risk model that estimates each corruption’s contribution to failure risk from the current image and task instruction alone.
The model learns separate latent representations of the scene and corruptions. By intervening on the corruption latent while holding the scene latent fixed, it estimates how failure risk would change if a corruption were removed (Figure 3), without modifying the physical scene or rerunning the policy.

We evaluate the model on OpenVLA and π0.5\pi_{0.5} in simulation and π0.5\pi_{0.5}-DROID on hardware. Our experiments validate that our approach accurately estimates per-corruption attributions, captures interactions between co-occurring corruptions, and learns sensitivity to scene context and corruption intensity. Under co-occurring corruptions, it achieves approximately 3x lower attribution error than frontier VLMs. Hardware experiments demonstrate our approach can be used for online monitoring () as corruptions change during an episode. In summary, we:

Formulate failure attribution for VLA models as estimating the reduction in failure risk from removing individual visual corruptions.

Introduce a factorized risk model that estimates these removal effects through latent interventions, using only the current image and task instruction.

Evaluate the method on OpenVLA and π0.5\pi_{0.5} in simulation and π0.5\pi_{0.5}-DROID on hardware, demonstrating attribution under co-occurring corruptions, sensitivity to execution context and corruption intensity, and online failure monitoring.

title: On Maximum Clique and Maximum Consensus Formulations in Point Cloud Registration
authors: Abolfazl Babanazari,Kaveh Fathian
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: . Interactive examples and Lean proof verification:this https URL
abstract:
Maximum clique and maximum consensus are widely used formulations for robust point cloud registration in robotics.
Maximum consensus seeks one transformation that aligns as many matches as possible, while maximum clique selects matches through pairwise distance tests.
Maximum clique is often used as a substitute for or an approximation to maximum consensus, with empirical evidence suggesting a close relationship.
However, how closely the two formulations agree is not fully understood.
We study this relationship theoretically.
We show that a maximum clique can have arbitrarily large alignment error and be arbitrarily larger than the maximum consensus set at any fixed positive tolerance, and derive geometric conditions that bound this error.
When rotation is fixed, we derive sharp error bounds and tests that exactly characterize maximum consensus for the translation subproblem.
Finally, we study group-kk consistency, which tests groups of kk matches, and determine the smallest group sizes that guarantee alignment error bounds independent of point cloud scale and geometry.
These are d+1d+1 for rotations and translations and d+2d+2 when reflections are allowed, in dimensions d≥2d\geq 2.
Interactive examples and proof verification using the Lean theorem prover are available at https://ariarobotics.github.io/mc-vs-mc-registration/.
introduction:
To build a map or localize within one, a robot needs to align 3D environment scans taken from different viewpoints [3, 4].
Point cloud registration estimates the alignment between the scans when they are represented as point clouds.
When no initial alignment is available, registration pipelines begin by matching local features across the scans, providing a set of tentative correspondences [1].
Repeated structures and limited overlap can make many of these matches incorrect, so registration must identify reliable matches for an alignment.

Maximum consensus and maximum clique are two widely used formulations for selecting reliable matches.
Maximum consensus seeks one transformation that aligns as many correspondences as possible within a prescribed tolerance.
Maximum clique selects a largest set that passes all pairwise distance tests, without estimating a transformation.
The two are closely related, and maximum clique is often used as a substitute for maximum consensus, but how far their solutions can differ is not fully understood.

At matched tolerances, maximum clique is a relaxation of maximum consensus.
Any set that one transformation aligns within the point tolerance passes every pairwise test and therefore forms a clique, so maximum clique size gives an upper bound on maximum consensus.
The converse does not hold in general [5, 6].
This upper bound alone does not tell us the clique’s alignment error or how many of its matches can be aligned within the prescribed tolerance.
Fig. 1 shows an example in practice, where a maximum clique and a maximum consensus set of similar sizes have few matches in common and produce very different registration results.

Testing larger groups offers a way to narrow this gap by detecting inconsistencies that pairwise tests miss.
In group-kk consistency, every group of up to kk matches must admit an alignment within the prescribed tolerance, although different groups may use different transformations [7].
Fig. 2 compares these three selection approaches on a small example.

In this paper, we study the theoretical relationship between these three formulations, independently of a specific registration pipeline.
We begin with the simpler problem of known rotation, where pairwise tests bound the translation error and testing larger groups gives an exact characterization of maximum consensus.
When rotation must also be estimated, we show a maximum clique can have arbitrarily large alignment error and be arbitrarily larger than a maximum consensus set.
We derive bounds that explain how this error depends on point cloud geometry.
We then show how group-kk tests give alignment error guarantees without assumptions on point cloud scale or geometry, and determine the smallest group sizes needed.
In summary, the contributions of this paper are as follows:

We show that maximum clique and maximum consensus methods for point cloud registration can give different results in general.
In particular, for certain point clouds, maximum clique can produce matches that cannot be obtained through maximum consensus, regardless of the chosen tolerance.

When the rotation that aligns two point clouds is fixed, we provide sharp lower and upper bounds on the maximum consensus solution size in terms of the maximum clique size.
In particular, in a dd-dimensional space, we show that maximum clique using group-(d+1)(d+1) consistency is equivalent to maximum consensus.

In the general case with unknown rotation, we show that d+1d+1 is the smallest group size for which maximum clique using group consistency can provide lower and upper bounds on the maximum consensus solution size.
When reflections are allowed, the smallest such group size is d+2d+2.

title: XoNav: An Exoskeleton as a Personalized Haptic Interface for Assisted Navigation
authors: Debadrata Sarkar,Soumen Sen,Aman Arora
comment: A supplementary video illustrating the XoNav hardware, haptic cues, Wizard-of-Oz trials and autonomous navigation is available atthis https URL
abstract: Walking without vision requires timely, unambiguous guidance, yet many wearable aids encode directions as audio or vibrotactile signals that users must translate into movement. We present XoNav, a four-actuator hip exoskeleton that renders guidance cue directly at the hip joint. It renders Advance cue and two-level Braking cues through sagittal-plane actuators and two-level Steering cues through frontal-plane actuators. A bilateral LSTM-based gait-state classifier uses two thigh-mounted IMUs to identify gait states, enabling haptic cues to be delivered in coordination with the wearer’s gait while suppressing them during standing. The classifier generalized to unseen users with recalls of 95.2–97.9%, with mean detection delays of 38.6 and 63.1 ms for stance-to-swing and swing-to-stance transitions respectively. Constrained human-in-the-loop Bayesian optimization personalized Braking for minimum resistance and Steering for maximum comfort while ensuring detectability and safety. All participants reliably distinguished between grades of their personalized cues and the firmest Braking cue remained below 53% of the safety limit. In blindfolded Wizard-of-Oz navigation trials along three paths, the participants kept 98.8% of the walked distance within a 0.75 m wide passage, with a 4.9% increase in mean progression speed per trial. A body-worn camera, RTAB-Map and Nav2 further enabled a feasibility study of autonomous navigation and detours around previously unmapped obstacles.
introduction:
Navigating without vision requires guidance about both direction and movement. Canes, guide dogs and electronic aids serve people with visual impairment, while comparable needs arise when sight is obscured or occupied, such as for firefighters in smoke [1] or industrial workers engaged in visually demanding tasks. A wearable RGB-D, audio and vibrotactile system improved navigation for blind and low-vision users [2], and bone conduction preserves awareness of environmental sounds [3]. Personalized smartphone audio has also guided blind users outdoors with performance comparable to a human guide [4]. Robotic canes [5] and quadruped guides [6] provide physical guidance but occupy a hand and act from outside the body.

Body-worn haptic interfaces offer hands-free guidance, although a survey found that many walking aids still depend on Wizard-of-Oz operators and are not ready for daily use [7]. Vibrotactile belts reduce collisions during training [8], instrumented walker handles can improve confidence [9], and textile interfaces distribute haptic feedback across the body [10, 11]. Vibrotactile directions nevertheless require interpretation as locomotor actions, while audio competes with ambient cues. Kinesthetic interfaces instead communicate movement through force, as demonstrated by the resistance and pulling rendered by the Kinethreads exosuit [12].

Lower-limb exoskeletons can convey guidance at the joints responsible for walking. Recent works include multi-activity [13] as well as task-agnostic [14] joint-moment assistance, data-driven community ambulation [15] and online personalization [16], frontal-plane control of step width and balance [17, 18], and improved haptic transparency [19]. Variability in individual responses have motivated human-in-the-loop optimization (HILO) [20, 21], including Bayesian optimization [22] and preference-based methods [23, 24]. Adding vibrotactile signals to exoskeleton torques can modulate walking speed but may increase cognitive load [25].

Closest to our work, Carrasquillo et al. [26] used artificial potential fields to modulate lower-limb exoskeleton impedance for obstacle avoidance. In virtual reality with occluded vision, this increased clearance and reduced collisions, demonstrating the potential of exoskeleton force feedback for human navigation. However, four gaps remain for real-world wayfinding. First, directional cueing through the hip’s frontal-plane degrees of freedom, which govern mediolateral foot placement and heading, remains unexplored. Second, guidance has not been phase-locked to gait events, potentially displacing an unloaded swing limb and overriding, rather than informing, motor intent. Third, navigation cues have used fixed parameters despite individual differences in perception and comfort, while HILO has not been formulated to jointly satisfy detectability, safety and comfort. Finally, reliance on external tracking leaves untested whether egocentric localization from a body-worn camera, despite gait-induced sway, can couple a navigation stack [27] with a human walker.

Here, we present XoNav, a hip exoskeleton serving as a personalized haptic interface for assisted navigation (Fig. 1). XoNav renders Advance and two-level Braking cues in the sagittal plane and two-level Steering cues in the frontal plane. Each cue is gait-informed, being released at its gait event and withheld while the wearer stands, so that the exoskeleton guides the movements the wearer initiates and never overrides them. The graded cues are personalized for reliable detection at the lowest intensity, within safety limits and in the profile the wearer finds most comfortable. The main contributions are: (i) a four-actuator hip exoskeleton realizing gait-informed haptic navigation cues, timed by a classifier that uses only two thigh IMUs and generalizes to unseen users; (ii) a constrained HILO framework that balances detectability, safety and comfort through a detection constraint, an analytic safety screen and duel-based comfort scoring; (iii) a blindfolded Wizard-of-Oz navigation study, using motion capture and user ratings to evaluate haptic guidance independently of robotic perception and planning errors; (iv) an autonomous navigation feasibility study integrating a body-worn camera with a ROS 2 navigation stack, demonstrating guidance and detours around unmapped obstacles. Our results show that wearers navigate reliably with personalized cues of minimal intensity, a step towards exoskeletons that guide human locomotion rather than driving it.

title: EmbodyHOI: Embodiment-Aware Generation of Hand-Object Interactions for Humanoid Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Chaitanya Chawla,Kartik Sharma,Ananya Bal,Laszlo A. Jeni,Guanya Shi
abstract:
Humanoid dexterous manipulation needs reference motions that are both semantically rich and
kinematically feasible for the target robot.
Text-conditioned hand–object interaction (HOI) generators supply diverse, language-specified
demonstrations, but they synthesize motion in human (MANO) space.
The embodiment gap is therefore deferred to post-hoc retargeting, where trajectories deployed on the robot can fail to maintain contact with objects and also degrade policy learning.
Our key idea is that robot reachability should constrain the interaction trajectories while they are being
generated.
We present EmbodyHOI, which runs a differentiable inverse-kinematics (IK) solver for a specific humanoid embodiment inside the
sampling loop of a frozen flow-matching HOI trajectory generator. We feed back gradients from the embodiment-aware IK solver into the HOI sampler and jointly optimize the position of the humanoid with respect to the object.
Because guidance acts only at inference, one HOI trajectory generator trained on human hand poses transfers across humanoid embodiments without
retraining.
On ARCTIC trajectories with two contrasting humanoids (Unitree G1 and H1-2), our proposed guidance-based method cuts the retargeted
wrist error from 8.9 cm to 0.6 cm while leaving text-to-HOI generation quality intact, and
raises task success from 68% to 79% on 50 random G1 tasks
and from 62% to 76% on a four-task H1-2 suite.
Critically, cheaper alternatives for bridging the embodiment gap fail to beat EmbodyHOI. Post-hoc wrist refinement and
compute-matched best-of-NN selection both reach lower IK energy than our guidance yet
train worse policies. For simulation results, see our website: https://embodyhoi.github.io/
introduction:
Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands remains difficult for humanoids that can reliably walk and loco-manipulate [1, 2, 3, 4].
A robot must coordinate reaching, finger contact, and whole-arm motion under embodiment-specific kinematic constraints to execute trajectories that actually manipulate objects.
A human trajectory when kinematically retargeted to a humanoid is often not executable, due to differences in finger morphology, joint limits, and wrist reachability.

We study how to generate human interactions which can easily close the above gap. Given a language prompt and an
articulated object, we produce bimanual hand–object trajectories specific to a humanoid, which are easily executable by the robot.

A natural route to this goal of end-to-end policies is generate-then-track, but today’s Hand-Object Interaction (HOI) generators have no notion of the robot that will execute their output. In this route, a generator proposes diverse task-conditioned reference motions and a physics-based RL policy learns to track them under contact and actuation limits [5].

Hand-centric HOI generators are the natural source of dexterous references as they model finger-object contact, but they generate in MANO [6] space with no term that couples the wrist to a robot’s kinematic chain. This mismatch only surfaces during retargeting, after the finger and object motions are committed, and the tracking policy inherits wrist targets that the arm cannot reach. Previous works resolve this on either side of generation. Training the motion prior in robot space [7] yields one generator per robot, which rules out cross-embodiment reuse. Whereas repairing a generated human motion [8, 9] only makes delta modifications, and cannot always rectify retargeted wrist trajectories unreachable for the robot. Tracking systems such as DexMachina [10] and ManipTrans [11] sidestep the question by commanding a floating wrist with no arm.

We take a different approach: keep a frozen MANO HOI generator as a reusable motion prior and make its samples embodiment-aware during generation (Fig. ).
We build on MAD-HOI [12], a text-conditioned HOI generator that fills object and hand tokens over a sequence of unmasking steps, integrating a flow-matching ODE for the unmasked tokens at each step. Inside every ODE step, we decode the current wrist trajectories, solve a differentiable IK problem on the target humanoid, and add a gradient of the IK residual (IK energy) to the learned velocity field, in a manner of classifier guidance. A wrist correction made in one unmasking step conditions the finger and object tokens generated in later ones, so the interaction re-forms around the corrected wrist instead of being patched afterward.

A full humanoid raises another problem that floating hands and fixed-base arms do not, where the robot stands. The base placement decides whether both arms stay reachable over the whole interaction, and a fixed-base IK cannot differentiate between a feasible interaction performed from the wrong standing position from an infeasible one. We therefore solve for the base translation together with the arm joints, and re-solve it at every unmasking step so that the base follows the partially generated motion. Finally, we retarget the guided motions and train a PPO tracking policy with separate imitation rewards for arm and hand, as they differ in error scale and contact requirements.

IK energy is a diagnostic, not a quantity to minimize on its own.
Guidance costs 32×32\times a native sample (5 s to 160 s on an A100), paid once per reference, so we compare it with alternatives that lower the energy after generation at the same or lower cost.
Post-hoc IK refinement of a finished sample reaches the lowest energy of any method, and compute-matched best-of-NN selection also beats guidance on energy, yet both train worse policies (Table I).
Refinement moves the wrists after the fingers and object are fixed, and selection returns a different interaction instead of correcting the requested one.
Reachability has to be imposed while the interaction is still being generated.

Our contributions are as follows.

Training-free IK guidance for a frozen HOI generator.
A differentiable IK solve on the target humanoid runs inside every ODE step of the sampler, and its gradient steers the hand tokens.
One objective with one set of weights serves the Unitree G1 and H1-2, and it also lowers the IK energy of a second generator, Text2HOI [13], without modification.

Base placement inside guidance.
Solving for the base removes near-singular G1 arm configurations (2.6% to 0.2% of test samples) even when applied once to a finished sample, and re-solving it at every unmasking step accounts for 2.8 of the 5.7 success-rate points that guidance adds over post-hoc base optimization on the four-task G1 suite (Table III).

Lower IK energy after generation does not give better references.
Post-hoc refinement and compute-matched best-of-32 selection reach lower energy than guidance (0.35 and 1.21 vs. 1.81), yet their policies succeed less often (32.8% and 74.0% vs. 79.7%, Table I).

Downstream gains on two humanoids.
Policies trained on guided references with decoupled hand and arm reward streams, raise success from 68% to 79% on 50 randomly drawn ARCTIC tasks on the G1 and from 62% to 76% on a four-task H1-2 suite.
We will release the guidance code, the generated references and the trained policies.

A differentiable IK solve on the target humanoid runs inside every ODE step of the sampler, and its gradient steers the hand tokens.
One objective with one set of weights serves the Unitree G1 and H1-2, and it also lowers the IK energy of a second generator, Text2HOI [13], without modification.

2. Base placement inside guidance.
Solving for the base removes near-singular G1 arm configurations (2.6% to 0.2% of test samples) even when applied once to a finished sample, and re-solving it at every unmasking step accounts for 2.8 of the 5.7 success-rate points that guidance adds over post-hoc base optimization on the four-task G1 suite (Table III).

3. Lower IK energy after generation does not give better references.
Post-hoc refinement and compute-matched best-of-32 selection reach lower energy than guidance (0.35 and 1.21 vs. 1.81), yet their policies succeed less often (32.8% and 74.0% vs. 79.7%, Table I).

4. Downstream gains on two humanoids.
Policies trained on guided references with decoupled hand and arm reward streams, raise success from 68% to 79% on 50 randomly drawn ARCTIC tasks on the G1 and from 62% to 76% on a four-task H1-2 suite.
We will release the guidance code, the generated references and the trained policies.

title: Which Depth Estimator for Jetson AGX Orin? A 2026 Benchmark of Monocular and Stereo Methods
authors: Leaf Jiang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: . Code and per-scene results:this https URL
abstract:
The Jetson AGX Orin is a common computer for robots and vehicles, yet measured accuracy, speed and
energy of current depth estimators on it are hard to find. We benchmark nine model families as of
October 2026: the monocular Depth Anything V2 and 3, Depth Pro, MoGe-2, Metric3D v2 and UniDepth V2,
and the stereo methods libSGM, NVIDIA ESS and Fast-FoundationStereo. Every method runs on the Orin as a
TensorRT FP16 engine or native CUDA code at up to three input sizes, up to the full 5.7 MP, and is
scored for metric accuracy against Middlebury 2014 ground truth (non-occluded pixels of the 10 scenes
whose disparity stays below 256 px), GPU time, energy and licence. Stereo is far more accurate. At
30 fps, NVIDIA’s ESS reaches 0.70% AbsRel in 8.6 ms and libSGM 0.73% in 25 ms; with more compute,
Fast-FoundationStereo reaches 0.33%. The best monocular models reach 12% with the true focal length
(Depth Anything 3 Metric-L in 33 ms, Depth Pro in 803 ms), and 3.8–4.0% only with an oracle per-image
scale (MoGe-2-L, UniDepth V2-B, Metric3D v2-L). Stereo error falls as the input resolution grows; no
monocular model improves, and the metric scale of most drifts away from the truth outside their training
resolution. At depth discontinuities, which AbsRel barely registers, the monocular models scatter
17–46% of the edge points between foreground and background, learned stereo 2–9% and libSGM at full
resolution 1%. We give recommendations per frame-rate budget and release all code, per-scene results
and engine build scripts.
introduction:
Dense metric depth is a core input for driving, robotics and industrial automation, and the NVIDIA
Jetson AGX Orin is one of the most common computers on which it runs. Two families of camera-based
methods compete for it. Monocular depth networks such as Depth Anything
V2 [1] and 3 [2], Depth Pro [3],
MoGe-2 [4], Metric3D v2 [5] and UniDepth
V2 [6] infer metric depth from a single image with large vision
transformers. Stereo methods triangulate depth from two calibrated cameras, with classical
matching such as semi-global matching (SGM) [7] or with learned matchers such as
NVIDIA’s ESS [8] and Fast-FoundationStereo [9].

Choosing among them for an Orin is hard. Papers report accuracy on desktop GPUs, at the networks’
training resolution and often after aligning the prediction to the ground truth; embedded timings, if
any, come from different devices, precisions and input sizes; and licences differ from permissive to
non-commercial. This paper is a practical benchmark for that choice. We run every method on the same
Jetson AGX Orin 64GB as a TensorRT FP16 engine (accuracy from FP32 where FP16 is unreliable) or as native
CUDA code, at up to three input sizes from its native or smallest input to the full 5.7 MP, and score
every output against the same full-resolution Middlebury 2014 ground truth [10]
on the 10 scenes whose disparity stays within the 256-level range of the semi-global matcher. We report
metric accuracy, GPU time, energy and licence, and derive recommendations per frame-rate budget.

(i) Measured metric accuracy, GPU time and energy on Jetson AGX Orin for nine current monocular and
stereo model families, each at up to three input sizes (table 7).
(ii) Recommendations: the most accurate stereo and monocular configuration for each frame-rate budget,
with licences (section 5).
(iii) A resolution-scaling study: stereo error falls with resolution, monocular error does not, because
the monocular metric scale drifts outside the training resolution and the shape does not improve
(section 6.1).
(iv) An analysis of depth discontinuities, where AbsRel is blind to the “flying” points that the
networks produce and a classical matcher can be the better choice (section 6.3).
(v) All code, per-scene results, engine build scripts and this paper’s source, released at
https://github.com/nodarhub/orin-depth-benchmark.

title: Learning to Be Different: Component Specialization for Compositional Diffusion Policies
authors: Alec Laprevotte,Haonan Chen,Xiaoshen Han,Yilun Du
abstract: Diffusion policies with linearly composed scores have emerged as a promising approach to multitask robotic learning by combining separate factors to enable modular, task-wise adaptation, compositional generalization, and interpretable functional decomposition. However, current training objectives do not encourage factor specialization, often resulting in uninterpretable denoisers whose composed prediction is an average over identical copies, undermining their architectural premise. To address this, we propose a drop-in score-decorrelation auxiliary loss, motivated by projective composition theory. Our approach encourages specialization by penalizing overlap directly between component noise predictions, with little architectural change or computational overhead. We demonstrate across multiple benchmarks that our decorrelation loss consistently reduces measurable double-counting between components, improves task decomposition, and produces behaviorally meaningful specialization without compromising multitask performance. Website: https://al3cl1.github.io/robotics-score-decorrelation.
introduction:
Offline imitation learning has become one of the dominant paradigms to replicate complex robotic manipulation skills [12, 36, 29]. However, as the diversity of tasks scales, their action distributions become highly multimodal. Monolithic policies model these behaviors jointly, merging them together and complicating both specialized skill interpretation and recombination across tasks [56, 29, 10].

To address these limitations, a growing line of work instead breaks down larger monolithic policies into smaller, composable generative models for better interpretability and test-time generalization [16]. Particularly, many robotics models sum multiple diffusion components via linear score combination, breaking down complex action distributions into simpler, specialized factors that are aggregated at inference time [47, 42, 48, 9, 31, 25]. While these methods provide architectural factorization, their training objective supervises only the composed sum of component scores, leaving the decomposition itself weakly constrained. As a result, components often collapse into overlapping predictors [31, 48], undermining the modular adaptation, compositional generalization, and interpretability that motivated factorization in the first place.

We propose an auxiliary loss that directly encourages the components of a compositional diffusion policy to specialize. During training, it penalizes overlap between the noise predictions of each pair of components, pushing them toward distinct contributions to the composed score. The loss is a drop-in addition to the standard denoising objective: it requires no change to the component networks and is discarded at inference. Our approach is motivated by recent theory on projective composition of diffusion models [5], in which Factorized Conditionals, a sufficient condition for projective composition, imply orthogonality between background-relative score deltas. Because compositional policies rarely include an explicit background model, we use output decorrelation as a practical proxy for this structure. Unlike orthogonality regularizers for mixture-of-experts models, which act on hidden activations [20, 22], our loss acts directly on the score outputs, where overlap between components has a direct generative meaning.

We validate our approach on Factorized Diffusion Policy (FDP) [31] across RLBench [27], RoboCasa [35], and LIBERO [30], and further demonstrate its benefits on a real-world cup-flipping task. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We introduce a training-time decorrelation loss that encourages specialization among the components of compositional diffusion policies, motivated by projective composition theory. (2) We show that it consistently reduces redundancy between components across factor counts and outperforms alternative decorrelation objectives, while maintaining or improving task success, especially on diverse and multi-step tasks. (3) We show that the resulting components specialize to behaviorally meaningful parts of the action space, such as the mobile base and the gripper, without supervision over the action space.

title: Visual Task Modeling and Automated Planning for Humanoid Robots in Education of Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder
authors: Lada Kudláčková
comment: presented at conference AICCONF 2026 in Prague, Czech Republic
abstract: In robot-assisted education, a robot must understand how to complete a task in order to effectively guide a student through it. We present a novel method that enables a semi-autonomous, camera-equipped robot to recognise the task goal and plan actions to achieve it. Our work focuses on Shoebox Tasks, an activity commonly used in the education of individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). These tasks are designed so that the goal can be inferred directly from their visual structure. We have developed a solver that uses a vision-based Large Language Model to convert photos of a Shoebox Task into a Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) representation and generate action plans for solving it. We have also implemented a robotic interface that enables a Nao robot to autonomously execute various Shoebox Tasks and assist a student by suggesting next steps or signalling detected failures through action demonstrations, voice commands, or gestures. With an adapted robotic interface, the solver can be integrated into a variety of educational robots. No programming expertise is required from teachers, and the solver operates exclusively on captured images as input. Research in special educational needs indicates that students with ASD can benefit substantially from robot-assisted teaching, and our system aims to strengthen these learning opportunities while also fostering interest in robotics among individuals with ASD.
introduction:
We build a system that enables a robot to autonomously solve Shoebox Tasks and assist students in completing them. The automated task analysis relies entirely on visual input. We develop a task solver for Shoebox Tasks, an activity widely used in the education of individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). These tasks are intentionally highly visual, as learners with ASD often excel at visual learning but may struggle to follow spoken or textual instructions. Shoebox Tasks are therefore designed so that all information necessary to solve them can be inferred directly from their visual structure [1].
Our approach leverages this property by using Vision–Language Models (VLMs) to analyze images of the task, generate a corresponding Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) problem representation and action plan, and verify the plan execution through sequential image captures. We have implemented a simple robotic interface that allows a Nao humanoid robot to execute the generated plan autonomously or guide a student through the steps.
Robot-assisted education has the potential to enhance learning outcomes for people with ASD [2]. Learners may benefit from the robot’s predictability and consistency, and often respond positively to interaction with robots [3].
Our work builds on a recently introduced method observing that the strong visual structure of Shoebox Tasks—and similar educational activities—makes them well suited for VLM-based analysis [4]. Initial experiments in that work used photos of the tasks with prompts and output examples as input to a VLM (e.g., ChatGPT-4o), producing a formatted analysis log and a PDDL problem file. This file was then passed to the Fast Downward planner to generate an action plan. After each executed action, a new image was captured, and the PDDL description and plan were updated iteratively until the task was completed.
We extend this idea by providing a simple, practical implementation of a task solver. The system incorporates a PDDL validator to enable automatic regeneration of output in cases of model false-positive refusals, and introduces image comparison technique to detect not just a single action but a sequence of executed actions.
Photos can be captured via a PC-connected camera or uploaded from a mobile phone through a web interface. Both task analysis and plan generation are executed directly by the VLM, which outputs a single PDDL problem file containing the action plan as a comment.
In the robotic setting, solving a Shoebox Task can be viewed as performing an unordered sequence of Pick-and-Place actions leading from an initial configuration to one of the allowed goal states. We have implemented a Nao robot interface enabling the robot to autonomously execute these actions or assist a student in solving selected types of Shoebox Tasks (Fig. 1).
We further observe that the proposed approach naturally supports the robot’s learning by demonstration: users can teach the robot by manipulating objects while the system continuously updates its visual interpretation of the scene. This image-based control mechanism creates additional opportunities for robotics education, particularly for learners with ASD, as it enables the translation of physical demonstrations into PDDL-encoded actions. For example, each action can be represented by a card with a pictogram, allowing the robot to be controlled by presenting cards rather than through direct programming.

Shoebox Task is a visually structured educational activity consisting of a small number of movable items and clearly defined storage areas. The task is designed such that the student can infer both the required work and task completion solely from the visual structure, without textual or verbal instructions. Rather than a fixed task set, the Shoebox Task represents an approach for adapting general educational activities for students with ASD.
A simple example is a sorting task in which items placed on a table must be grouped by shape. In a Shoebox-style implementation, a box contains multiple smaller containers: one initial container holding the items and separate target containers marked with symbols corresponding to each shape.
The strong visual structure supports learners with ASD, who are predominantly visual learners, and also makes the task suitable for automated vision-based analysis.
ShoeboxTasks© were originally developed in the 1990s by Ron Larsen as part of the TEACCH methodology [1], an educational framework widely used worldwide in the education of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We had the privilege of collaborating with Ron Larsen to ensure that the proposed system closely aligns with the underlying educational principles of this methodology.

The robot acts as a teacher assisting the student during a Shoebox Task. In the standard setting, the student solves the task by manually moving items to their target containers, while a teacher provides assistance when needed by demonstrating actions, giving verbal instructions, pointing to relevant
items and containers, or alerting the student in case of an incorrect action.
The robot provides analogous, but simplified, feedback. It uses the solver to evaluate the validity of the current state and to generate an action plan. Based on the selected educational mode, the robot can alert the student about incorrect actions, demonstrate actions manually, or suggest the next action via voice commands or pointing gestures.
We implemented a solver prototype together with a basic robotic interface on the Nao robot to
demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed concept.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

Integration of vision-language reasoning with PDDL-based planning for Shoebox Tasks using a VLM (ChatGPT), without reliance on an external PDDL planner.

Integration of vision-language reasoning with PDDL-based planning for Shoebox Tasks using a VLM (ChatGPT), without reliance on an external PDDL planner.

End-to-end detection and validation of complete action sequences directly from images, enabling reasoning over both initial and intermediate Shoebox Tasks states.

A simple interface for the Nao robot, allowing autonomous execution or assisted solving of Shoebox Tasks within the proposed framework.

2. End-to-end detection and validation of complete action sequences directly from images, enabling reasoning over both initial and intermediate Shoebox Tasks states.

3. A simple interface for the Nao robot, allowing autonomous execution or assisted solving of Shoebox Tasks within the proposed framework.

title: Towards Interaction State Recognition in Sensorized Gecko-Inspired Adhesive Interfaces for Orbital Servicing
authors: Eduart Abdullahu,Francesco Grella,Carol Martinez
abstract: Reliable contact establishment remains a critical challenge for autonomous on-orbit servicing (OOS), particularly when interacting with non-cooperative targets. Gecko-inspired dry adhesives provide a lightweight, passive, and residue-free solution for robotic capture in space, yet current systems operate in open loop, without the ability to estimate their own contact or adhesion state during interaction. This paper presents a real-time interaction-awareness framework that enables sensorized gecko-inspired adhesive interfaces to estimate their contact state throughout the adhesion lifecycle using embedded capacitive sensing. Five discrete interaction states (idle, proximity, contact, engaged, and disengaged) are classified using experimentally collected and augmented sensor data, enabling a comparative evaluation of six lightweight machine learning models suitable for embedded deployment. Among the evaluated models, Random Forest achieved the highest offline classification accuracy of 95.65%. For online deployment, combining Random Forest with a rule-based state machine improved accuracy from 78.02% to 93.14%, achieving a macro F1-score of 0.9343 while maintaining a 53 ms inference cycle. These results demonstrate that incorporating physics-consistent state constraints significantly improves robustness during real-time inference, representing a step toward interaction-aware capture in future autonomous orbital servicing missions.
introduction:
Since the launch of Sputnik-1, Earth orbits have become increasingly congested [1]. The planned deployment of megaconstellations is expected to intensify this congestion and increase the risk of collisions and debris generation [2]. Addressing this challenge and ensuring long-term orbital sustainability require advanced debris-removal and on-orbit servicing (OOS) systems capable of establishing safe and reliable initial contact with non-cooperative targets.

Gecko-inspired dry adhesives offer a promising solution for first contact with space structures. Unlike conventional mechanisms, they require no suction or mechanical interlocking, can attach and detach from unprepared surfaces without leaving residue, and can operate in vacuum environments  [1] with demonstrated performance under space-relevant thermal conditions [3]. Inspired by the hierarchical setae structure of gecko feet, these materials rely on van der Waals interactions, enabling adhesion without chemical bonding, contamination, or consumable materials. In particular, wedge-type architectures require only low normal preload combined with controlled shear displacement, minimising reaction forces during contact and making them well-suited for repeated attachment cycles when interacting with free-floating targets.

Despite successful space demonstrations [4][5], reliable use of gecko adhesives remains challenging because of sensitivity to contact trajectory, misalignment, and variability in applied normal and shear loads [6]. Most systems are open-loop and lack awareness of contact state, thereby limiting autonomy and making recovery from partial engagement or premature release difficult. Moving from passive interfaces toward intelligent adhesive systems, therefore, requires real-time interpretation of the contact interface during interaction.

Integrating sensing into gecko-inspired adhesives can address this gap. Capacitive sensing with embedded flexible electrodes enables mechanically transparent measurement without affecting adhesion [7]. However, the resulting signals are complex and capture multiple overlapping interaction phenomena (proximity effects, initial contact, conformational engagement, and shear loading), requiring data-driven methods to extract meaningful information.

This paper presents an initial step toward intelligent gecko-inspired interfaces by enabling real-time interaction-state estimation in sensorized adhesives. As shown in Fig. 1, such awareness of the interaction can provide feedback on the state of the adhesive interface during capture, supporting higher-level decision-making in future autonomous OOS missions. Using a wedge-shaped gecko-inspired adhesive equipped with an embedded interdigitated capacitive sensor developed by the Stanford Biomimetics and Dexterous Manipulation Lab (BDML) [6][3], we collect experimental data throughout the adhesion lifecycle, including approach, contact, engagement, and release. We apply signal processing and feature extraction methods to characterize the evolving adhesive interaction, then evaluate six lightweight machine learning models for real-time contact-state classification. To improve robustness during dynamic operation, classifier predictions are combined with a state machine that enforces physically consistent interaction transitions.

The main contribution of this work is a real-time interaction-state recognition framework for sensorized gecko-inspired adhesive interfaces, combining lightweight machine learning with physics-informed state-transition constraints for robust online deployment. Experimental validation demonstrates that incorporating these constraints improves online inference robustness, increasing classification accuracy from 78.02% to 93.14% during real-time operation, enabling reliable recognition of the adhesive interaction throughout the contact lifecycle.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work enabling real-time interaction awareness in sensorized gecko-inspired adhesive interfaces for autonomous space robotic applications, moving adhesive-based capture systems from passive mechanisms toward interaction-aware autonomous operation.

title: ACE-Brain-0.6: Scaling Spatial Grounding for Physical Foundation Models
authors: Yinhe Wang,Tao Tao,Zexin He,Shuang Luo,Wei Mao,Yao Mu,Feng Pan,Hanming Deng,Lewei Lu,Zhi Hou,Xingang Pan,Dahua Lin,Dacheng Tao,Xiaogang Wang
abstract:
General-purpose multimodal models, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, demonstrate broad capabilities in embodied manipulation.
Our analysis indicates that this generality is accompanied by strong spatial perception, as Astra can determine where to interact with task-relevant entities amid visual distractors.
Because spatial perception connects high-level reasoning to the physical scene, we investigate scaling visual grounding to strengthen the perceptual foundation of general embodied operation.
We develop a unified data pipeline that combines robot manipulation recordings with complementary visual data from diverse sources.
After automatically annotating the robot recordings, the pipeline converts the collected data into verifiable grounding supervision.
Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on approximately 1.5 million samples produced by this pipeline yields ACE-Brain-0.6.
The model outperforms GPT-6 Astra on four of seven public grounding benchmarks, with an overall average score of 75.41 compared with Astra’s 73.68.
Under a fixed Qwen3.5-9B fine-tuning setup, aggregate grounding performance improves steadily as successive data releases expand the training collection to cover a broader range of grounding scenarios.
These results show that scaling verifiable grounding supervision from diverse sources can strengthen the spatial perception of an open 9B model for general embodied operation.
introduction:
General-purpose reasoning models are beginning to generalize across diverse embodied settings.
GPT-6 Astra [1], in particular, demonstrates strong performance in embodied manipulation.
A closer examination of its behavior shows that this embodied competence is accompanied by strong spatial perception.
It can localize task-relevant interaction targets in cluttered scenes despite the presence of visually similar distractors.

This observation highlights the role of spatial perception in translating high-level reasoning into physical action.
Grounding provides this connection by linking natural-language descriptions to their visual referents in an image [2, 3].
Reliable grounding requires precise localization of all image regions that satisfy a description, with explicit recognition when no match exists [4].
In embodied environments, clutter and occlusion make this correspondence particularly difficult to establish [5].
A grounding error can therefore misdirect an agent’s actions even when its high-level reasoning is sound.

We therefore examine Astra’s spatial grounding capabilities in greater detail.
Our analysis in Section 3 illustrates its ability to handle diverse grounding queries, while also revealing localization errors in tasks with precise spatial requirements.
Using Astra as a reference, we ask whether an open 9B-parameter vision-language model can match or surpass Astra’s grounding performance by expanding the scale and coverage of grounding supervision, with the model architecture and training recipe held fixed.

To investigate this question, we develop a unified pipeline for constructing grounding supervision from existing open datasets.
The pipeline combines robot manipulation recordings from more than thirty dataset families with complementary visual data to broaden task coverage.
We automatically annotate the robot recordings to supply the object-level labels they generally lack.
All sources are then converted into question–answer supervision that is verifiable against the supporting annotations, with controls to reduce shortcuts between question wording and answer format.
This pipeline yields approximately 1.5 million training samples, which we use to fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B [6] for a single epoch, producing ACE-Brain-0.6.
Figure 1 provides an overview of our approach.

We evaluate ACE-Brain-0.6 on seven public grounding benchmarks.
The model outperforms the Qwen3.5-9B baseline on six benchmarks and remains behind on PixMo-Count.
It exceeds GPT-6 Astra on four benchmarks and achieves a slightly higher seven-benchmark average (75.41 versus 73.68), while remaining behind on PixMo-Count, RefSpatial, and PointArena.
These results suggest that a 9B open model trained with diverse, verifiable grounding supervision can match Astra’s aggregate performance on the evaluated benchmarks.

We further examine data scaling by fine-tuning from the same base checkpoint with a fixed training recipe for each data release.
Across releases that expand both sample count and supervision coverage, the seven-benchmark average increases approximately linearly with the logarithm of sample count over the evaluated range, slightly exceeding Astra’s average at about 1.5 million samples.
In a control experiment, adding samples only from existing sources improves this average by less than one point, suggesting that broader supervision coverage contributes to the observed gains.

Our contributions are threefold:

A data pipeline for grounding. We collect large-scale open-source robot, egocentric, object-centric, and spatial data, automatically annotate robot recordings, and convert these sources into verifiable question–answer supervision for target identification, complete instance coverage, and precise localization.

An empirical study of grounding-data scaling. Through a controlled series of training runs, we show that grounding performance improves steadily with data scale and that expanding the coverage of supervision contributes substantially more than increasing the volume of existing sources.

ACE-Brain-0.6. By scaling verifiable grounding data to approximately 1.5 million samples, we train a 9B model that exceeds GPT-6 Astra on four of seven grounding benchmarks and achieves a higher overall average.

We collect large-scale open-source robot, egocentric, object-centric, and spatial data, automatically annotate robot recordings, and convert these sources into verifiable question–answer supervision for target identification, complete instance coverage, and precise localization.

2. An empirical study of grounding-data scaling. Through a controlled series of training runs, we show that grounding performance improves steadily with data scale and that expanding the coverage of supervision contributes substantially more than increasing the volume of existing sources.

3. ACE-Brain-0.6. By scaling verifiable grounding data to approximately 1.5 million samples, we train a 9B model that exceeds GPT-6 Astra on four of seven grounding benchmarks and achieves a higher overall average.
