title: Embodied Playground: A Long-Horizon Agentic Robotics Benchmark for Physical, Strategic, and Spatial Reasoning
authors: Feng Chen,Pei Zhou,Lixuan He,Yunchao Yao,Li Sun,Shenghua Gao,Mingyu Ding,Kaifeng Zhang,Kaichen Zhou,Yi Ma
abstract:
Foundation models offer a promising basis for robotic agents, but long-horizon tasks require them to sustain coherent reasoning and reliable physical execution across interdependent stages. We introduce Embodied Playground, a benchmark for evaluating how foundation-model agents coordinate physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning throughout such tasks. Agents must track task progress, satisfy intermediate constraints, and revise their plans using execution feedback as earlier actions shape subsequent decisions. The playground comprises 410 task environments spanning basic manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi-stage household activities, with variations in planning depth, geometric constraints, and physical execution demands. We curate EP-100, a representative selection of 100 tasks across five suites and 16 task types, together with the EP-Easy and EP-Hard difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection. A shared protocol specifies observation and tool access, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent checks of goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity. Embodied Playground provides a unified framework for studying whether foundation-model agents can sustain effective reasoning and action over extended task horizons.
The project website is available at
Embodied Playground Website.
introduction:
Foundation models have shown promising capabilities in robotic tasks, supported by their ability to interpret visual observations, reason about spatial relationships and physical interactions, and formulate strategies. [1, 2, 3, 4] Existing robotics benchmarks largely emphasize the performance and generalization of control policies. [5, 6, 7, 8] This leaves a complementary question: can a foundation-model agent sustain these capabilities over long-horizon robotic tasks, where actions must establish the conditions for later stages and execution errors can affect subsequent decisions? Addressing this question requires evaluating how an agent tracks task progress, satisfies intermediate constraints, and adapts its plan throughout physical execution.

We introduce Embodied Playground, a benchmark for studying long-horizon robotic problem solving by foundation-model agents. Tasks couple physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning across dependent stages: an agent must determine what to do next, execute it through the robot interface, and use the resulting observations to update its understanding of the remaining task. Earlier actions can change object configurations, consume resources, or constrain later choices, making sustained coordination between planning and execution central to successful completion. Given a task description, permitted observations, and a specified set of tools, the agent must ground its decisions in the observed scene and revise its plan using execution feedback. Success requires achieving the final goal while respecting task rules and physical constraints throughout the episode.

Embodied Playground comprises 410 robotic task environments, ranging from basic object manipulation to long-horizon planning and dexterous coordination. These tasks vary in planning depth, geometric constraints, and physical execution demands. Tower of Hanoi requires executing legal move sequences while preserving valid intermediate configurations; cube puzzles require keeping track of puzzle states and object orientations through successive physical turns; and Kongming locks couple assembly or disassembly order with geometric feasibility and contact-rich manipulation. Multi-stage household tasks combine ordered interactions with object-placement and final-scene requirements. Launcher tasks connect trajectory prediction and causal effects with finite ammunition and, in selected scenes, target-order constraints. Shorter manipulation, precision, and dynamics tasks complement these extended sequences by probing constituent capabilities across multiple robot embodiments.

To facilitate evaluation, we curate EP-100, a representative selection of 100 tasks organized into five subsets: Launch, Tower, Lock, Cube, and Home. Together, these subsets cover 16 task types and provide focused evaluations alongside the full playground. EP-100 is divided into EP-Easy and EP-Hard by ranking the tasks of each type according to their workload, and EP-20 offers a compact selection that spans both splits. All tasks follow a common interaction interface and evaluation protocol, with specified observation and tool access, execution budgets, repeated trials, and task-specific physical success criteria.

Our contributions are threefold:

An agent-centered perspective on long-horizon robotic problem solving. We evaluate a foundation-model agent’s ability to sustain coordinated perception, reasoning, tool use, and action across interdependent task stages, using execution feedback to track progress, revise plans, and satisfy task constraints throughout an episode.

A diverse playground spanning task horizons and execution demands. We introduce 410 robotic task environments spanning basic manipulation and multi-stage problem solving, with variations in planning depth, geometry, and physical execution requirements. EP-100 provides a representative selection across five suites and 16 task types, complemented by two difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection.

An episode-level protocol for evaluating completion and validity. We specify observation and tool-access levels, resource budgets, and repeated-trial conditions, with independent checks of final goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity over the executed trajectory.

We evaluate a foundation-model agent’s ability to sustain coordinated perception, reasoning, tool use, and action across interdependent task stages, using execution feedback to track progress, revise plans, and satisfy task constraints throughout an episode.

We introduce 410 robotic task environments spanning basic manipulation and multi-stage problem solving, with variations in planning depth, geometry, and physical execution requirements. EP-100 provides a representative selection across five suites and 16 task types, complemented by two difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection.

3. An episode-level protocol for evaluating completion and validity. We specify observation and tool-access levels, resource budgets, and repeated-trial conditions, with independent checks of final goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity over the executed trajectory.

title: Replan for Error Recovery: Training Embodied VLMs through Verifiable Interaction with Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO
authors: Zhuoran Wang,Keqing Fan,Yang Li,Jinbo Su,Ke Wang,Sijia Luo,Yuanzheng Tan,Junken Peng,Jing Zhang
abstract:
Embodied VLMs can execute increasingly complex manipulation tasks, yet execution errors can leave the environment in states that require replanning for recovery.
Existing recovery methods either rely on inference-time mechanisms with fixed policies or learn from failure examples and reference corrections rather than verified action outcomes.
To enable recovery learning through verifiable interaction, we introduce the Embodied Replanning for Recovery Environment (ERR-Env), which provides feedback on task progress and execution errors.
We further construct ERR-Bench, a benchmark with held-out tasks spanning nominal, intermediate, and error states for evaluating recovery capability and execution reliability.
We then propose Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO (AGT-GSPO), an online reinforcement learning method combining turn-level rewards for task progress and error states with action-grouped advantage estimation, and use it to train ERR-VLM, a compact 2B embodied VLM.
Evaluation on ERR-Bench reveals a mismatch between task progress and execution reliability across diverse VLMs. AGT-GSPO improves ERR-VLM by 10.25 percentage points in Strict Success Rate for error-free completion and 22.95 percentage points in Recovery Rate, while ablations and zero-shot transfer further validate the effectiveness of our method.
introduction:
Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as high-level
decision makers for embodied agents, enabling multi-step manipulation through visual observations, language goals, and semantic action interfaces (Driess et al., 2023; Tan et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026).
During execution, errors, limited visibility, or unexpected scene conditions can leave the task in a state for which the original plan is no longer appropriate.
Reliable task completion therefore requires the model to recognize these deviations and replan from the resulting state to recover and continue execution.

To support recovery from execution errors, inference-time approaches equip VLMs with prompting strategies, external monitors, or specialized mechanisms to detect errors and trigger replanning (Chen et al., 2025b; Zhou et al., 2025; Ahmad et al., 2025).
But with the policy fixed, recovery is limited to existing model capabilities.
Recovery-oriented post-training instead uses error cases and reference corrections to improve error recognition and corrective action selection (Ye et al., 2026; Pacaud et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026).
However, reference-based supervision does not optimize the policy against verified outcomes of recovery actions, leaving a gap between imitating corrections and resolving execution errors.
This motivates training through environment interaction, where action outcomes are verified for error correction and task progress to improve recovery decisions.

In this paper, we aim to train embodied VLMs to recover from execution errors through verifiable interaction and evaluate their recovery capability and execution reliability. Interaction-based recovery learning requires explicit feedback on errors and task progress, which existing embodied benchmarks typically lack (Yang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a).
To address this gap, we develop the Embodied Replanning for Recovery Environment (ERR-Env), an executable and verifiable interaction environment built on RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025c).
ERR-Env uses task-specific checkers to verify task progress, completion, execution errors, and visibility, supporting recovery-oriented data generation, online reinforcement learning, and evaluation.
To assess recovery capability and execution reliability beyond task progress alone, we construct ERR-Bench based on ERR-Env, a controlled benchmark with held-out tasks spanning nominal, intermediate, and error states.

To learn recovery from verifiable interaction in ERR-Env, verified action outcomes need to be translated into signals that reinforce effective corrections and discourage error-inducing actions.
However, a trajectory-level signal cannot assign distinct feedback to error-inducing and corrective actions.
Therefore, we propose Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO (AGT-GSPO), an online reinforcement learning method that uses turn-level rewards capturing task progress and error states after each executed action.
AGT-GSPO further estimates advantages within action groups, avoiding comparisons across action types.
Using AGT-GSPO, we train ERR-VLM, a compact 2B embodied VLM that learns to recognize execution errors and select corrective actions through replanning.

Evaluation of diverse VLMs on ERR-Bench shows that high task progress does not guarantee reliable execution. Against this backdrop, training ERR-VLM with AGT-GSPO improves both task completion and recovery, raising Strict Success Rate for error-free task completion by 10.25 percentage points and Recovery Rate by 22.95 percentage points over its supervised initialization. Ablations and zero-shot transfer to external simulators and a physical robot further validate our approach.

In summary, our principal contributions comprise:

We introduce ERR-Env, an executable and verifiable interaction environment with feedback on task progress and execution errors, supporting recovery data generation, online RL, and evaluation. We further construct ERR-Bench to evaluate recovery capability and execution reliability.

We propose AGT-GSPO, an online RL method that learns from verifiable interaction by combining turn-level rewards for task progress and error states with action-grouped advantage estimation. Using AGT-GSPO, we train ERR-VLM, a compact 2B embodied VLM for error recovery.

Evaluation on ERR-Bench across diverse VLMs reveals a clear mismatch between task progress and reliable execution, while ERR-VLM, trained with AGT-GSPO, substantially improves both recovery capability and execution reliability.

1. We introduce ERR-Env, an executable and verifiable interaction environment with feedback on task progress and execution errors, supporting recovery data generation, online RL, and evaluation. We further construct ERR-Bench to evaluate recovery capability and execution reliability.

2. We propose AGT-GSPO, an online RL method that learns from verifiable interaction by combining turn-level rewards for task progress and error states with action-grouped advantage estimation. Using AGT-GSPO, we train ERR-VLM, a compact 2B embodied VLM for error recovery.

3. Evaluation on ERR-Bench across diverse VLMs reveals a clear mismatch between task progress and reliable execution, while ERR-VLM, trained with AGT-GSPO, substantially improves both recovery capability and execution reliability.

title: DexGraspFlow: Topology-Aware SE(3) Flow Matching for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasp Generation
authors: Bin Zhou,Boyu Ma,Xinyu Zhou,Jiahua Dong,Chuhao Zhou,Yizhou Liu,Hao Wan,Jianfei Yang
abstract: Differences in hand geometry, joint parameterization, and kinematic topology pose challenges for cross-embodiment dexterous grasp generation. However, spatial relations among links alone are insufficient to fully capture the hand’s kinematic topology. We propose DexGraspFlow, a conditional link-level SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) flow-matching framework integrating geometric relations and kinematic topology. The framework encodes local object geometry, link geometry, and current poses. A dual-stream DiT models link–link coordination and link–object interaction, while attention biases derived from kinematic-tree distances provide explicit structural information for modeling evolving geometric interactions. The model jointly learns translational and rotational velocity fields, integrates them to generate link poses, and recovers joint configurations through inverse kinematics. Additionally, inference-time palm-orientation guidance enables controllable grasp generation without retraining. Across three robotic hands and 30 object–hand pairs, DexGraspFlow achieves a 95.33% average simulation success rate, with an average generation latency, including inverse kinematics, approximately 49% lower than that of a state-of-the-art baseline. Further experiments demonstrate zero-shot adaptability to seven finger-removal variants and palm-orientation control. A model trained on demonstrations for the deployed hand achieves a 91% success rate over 100 real-robot grasping trials, supporting the framework’s applicability to physical grasp execution.
introduction:
Dexterous hands are robotic end-effectors that interact directly with the physical world, performing the last centimeter of robotic manipulation. Through coordinated finger motions, they enable versatile grasping and precise manipulation, supporting the practical deployment of embodied intelligence (Dong et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Reliable dexterous grasping requires jointly accounting for object geometry, hand–object interactions, and kinematic constraints (Wang et al., 2023). Differences in link geometry and kinematic topology across hands further complicate cross-embodiment grasp generation. Embodiment-specific joint representations differ in dimensionality and physical meaning, making it difficult to learn a unified model directly from grasp demonstrations collected across different hands (Li et al., 2023). Training a separate model for each hand also increases training and deployment costs. These challenges motivate cross-embodiment dexterous grasp generation methods that share grasping knowledge while accommodating differences in hand morphology and kinematics, facilitating the reuse of grasping capabilities across robotic platforms.

Existing approaches address cross-embodiment grasp synthesis through optimization or shared interaction representations. Optimization-based methods require computationally intensive iterative search for each grasp instance (Liu et al., 2021), while contact- and distance-based formulations necessitate auxiliary matching or complex reconstruction to recover executable configurations (Li et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2025). Recently, 𝒯⁡(ℛ,𝒪)\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{O}) Grasp (TRO-Grasp) introduced a transformation-graph diffusion model via object-centric link poses and relative spatial relations without requiring a shared joint parameterization (Fei et al., 2026). However, relying solely on continuous spatial relations ignores kinematic topology: spatially adjacent links across diverse hands may belong to distant topological branches with fundamentally different kinematic meanings. GraspGraphNet (Lee et al., 2026) incorporates kinematic structure through local message passing, but propagating information between distant links along the kinematic tree requires multiple graph hops. Beyond unconditioned synthesis, practical deployment also requires efficient control over grasp approach orientations while maintaining grasp stability across different hand embodiments.

To this end, we propose DexGraspFlow, a cross-embodiment dexterous grasp synthesis framework that unifies continuous SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) flow matching with URDF-derived kinematic topology (Fig. 1). To resolve structural ambiguities across heterogeneous hands, DexGraspFlow augments dynamic link states and spatial relations with kinematic-tree shortest-path distances, providing complementary geometric and structural information that explicitly separates spatial arrangement from kinematic connectivity. Grasp synthesis is formulated as link-level flow matching with separate translational reference paths in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} and geodesic rotational reference paths on SO⁡(3)\mathrm{SO}(3) (Lipman et al., 2023; Chen and Lipman, 2024). This formulation preserves valid link orientations and supports inference-time palm-orientation guidance through tangent-space velocity corrections without retraining. A geometry- and topology-aware dual-stream DiT (Peebles and Xie, 2023) predicts these coupled velocity fields, followed by batched inverse kinematics (Kim et al., 2025) to recover executable joint configurations.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on cross-embodiment grasp representations and geometric generative models. Section 3 presents the grasp representation and geometry- and topology-aware dual-stream DiT architecture of DexGraspFlow. Section 4 evaluates DexGraspFlow through grasp generation on unseen objects, zero-shot generation on finger-removal variants, and palm-orientation-conditioned generation, along with ablation studies and real-robot experiments. Section 5 concludes the study and discusses the limitations of the proposed framework and directions for future research.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We address the core discrepancy that geometric spatial relations do not reflect kinematic topological connectivity across diverse embodiments, proposing a topology-aware link representation that couples dynamic spatial interactions with kinematic-tree distances to preserve structural coordination under hand topology changes.

We formulate grasp synthesis via link-level SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) flow matching that couples Euclidean translation with Riemannian rotation on SO⁡(3)\mathrm{SO}(3), and design a geometry- and topology-aware dual-stream DiT, demonstrating superior grasp success with substantially reduced generation latency compared to diffusion baselines in our empirical evaluations.

We propose a training-free directional grasp guidance formulation. By injecting geodesic velocity corrections directly into the tangent space of the continuous flow during inference, DexGraspFlow achieves high-precision, user-specified palm-orientation steering without requiring conditional retraining or auxiliary classifiers.

We conduct extensive empirical evaluations across multi-embodiment simulations, zero-shot generalization to seven finger-removal variants, and 100 real-robot physical trials (91% success rate), demonstrating the superior adaptability and physical viability of DexGraspFlow.

3. We propose a training-free directional grasp guidance formulation. By injecting geodesic velocity corrections directly into the tangent space of the continuous flow during inference, DexGraspFlow achieves high-precision, user-specified palm-orientation steering without requiring conditional retraining or auxiliary classifiers.

title: Joints, Camera, Action! Co-Generating 3D Motion and Video for Arbitrary Rigs
authors: Noam Rotstein,Yoad Tewel,Chen Tessler,Haggai Maron,Gal Chechik,Or Litany,Yoni Kasten,Yuval Atzmon
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Graphics (cs.GR); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Video generation models can now depict remarkably realistic motion.
Yet it is unclear how to use this motion beyond pixels: to animate a specific 3D asset and replay the animation in its 3D scene.
For instance, a video model can show a monkey jumping over a crossbar, but it cannot return that jump as replayable 3D motion placed in the 3D scene.
Here we present a model that directly co-generates the video and 3D motion for any supplied rig, along with a camera that registers this motion to the scene. Prior video–motion models either handle only human skeletons, often adding billions of parameters, or triangulate 3D motion from generated 2D pose maps. We instead keep 3D motion in a separate model that supports arbitrary skeletons, and connect it to a pretrained video model through a small set of cross-attention layers. This separation lets the motion model first learn how skeletons move from motion-only data, which is easier to obtain and augment than paired video. Additionally, our model learns to locate each joint in the video frames, which lets us recover the camera and place the 3D motion in the scene. To train across many skeletons, we use a generative video editor to place animated 3D assets in scenes suited to their actions, curating the edits so their known motion remains valid. Together with human and robot video, this yields nearly 200K training pairs. Our evaluations demonstrate that our model animates diverse rigs from text more faithfully than video-first pipelines, and its motion responds to the surrounding scene. It also turns video into rig motion, rig motion into video, and enables keyframe-based control of the 3D motion.
Videos and additional results are available on our
project page.
introduction:
Video generation models capture complex real-world dynamics, making them promising world models for animation, robotics, and synthetic data generation. Yet they produce only pixels, so their motion cannot directly drive a 3D asset or robot. Imagine placing a monkey asset in front of a crossbar in a 3D scene, asking a video model to make it jump over, and replaying the resulting jump on the monkey’s rig inside that scene. Current video models deliver only the first step: a convincing video of the jump, with no 3D motion for the rig and no way to place that motion in the scene.

Replaying a generated motion on an arbitrary rig in a 3D scene requires two things: 3D motion that matches the video and a camera transformation that registers that motion to the generated scene. One natural approach is to recover the motion from a generated video post hoc (Sabathier et al., 2026; Song et al., 2025), but lifting motion from pixels may introduce errors that can make the animation drift from the video. Alternatively, generating video and motion together aims to avoid this post-hoc step, yet no joint model animates an arbitrary rig directly in 3D, and none registers its motion to the scene it generates. Existing ones either handle only human skeletons (Pang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026a), or triangulate 3D motion from 2D pose maps learned from multi-view videos (Huang et al., 2025).

In this work, we present Joints, Camera, Action! (JCA), a model that co-generates a video, motion for any supplied 3D rig, and a camera that places the 3D motion in the generated scene. To support arbitrary rigs, a dedicated motion model treats a rig skeleton as a graph, with joints as nodes and bones as edges. We pretrain it on motion alone, including motions retargeted to randomized skeletons. We then connect it to a pretrained video model through a few cross-attention layers, keeping the added parameters small. Zero-initializing these layers preserves the behavior of both pretrained models at the start of coupled training.

Through these layers, video and motion shape each other’s generation throughout denoising; two components strengthen this interaction and place the motion in the scene. First, we introduce a novel bridge guidance mechanism. At inference, we contrast predictions made with the connections enabled and disabled, then amplify the change caused by their interaction. Co-generating the motion with the video, however, does not determine where that motion lies in the depicted scene. Second, to solve this registration problem, we introduce learned localization of the rig’s joints: the model predicts where every generated 3D joint appears in the image. These 2D locations and the generated 3D positions provide correspondences from which we fit a camera that registers the motion to the generated scene.

Training the model poses a challenge: no corpus pairs natural video with 3D motion across many rigs. We start from human video, which offers rich motion and rich backgrounds, but only a single skeleton. To cover many rigs, we turn to animated 3D assets (Deitke et al., 2023b; Deitke et al., 2023a), which offer diverse rigs and precise labels, but simple actions and plain renders. Rather than build a 3D scene for every asset, a generative video editor (Liu et al., 2026) places our animated-asset renders in scenes suited to their actions. Editing may move the subject or camera, invalidating 3D labels; we verify results and regenerate failures. Together, the two sources combine the rich motion and scenes of human video with the rig diversity of assets. With additional robot video, our corpus reaches 200K video–motion pairs in total.

We evaluate the model on text-driven animation of diverse rigs and demonstrate motion that responds to the surrounding scene (fig. 1). The same model can recover motion for a supplied rig from video or generate video from prescribed rig motion. From a few reference image keyframes, it generates a complete 3D rig trajectory and matching video, providing image-based control over 3D motion.

Our contributions are: (1) JCA, the first model to directly co-generate video and 3D joint motion for arbitrary rigs, with motion that responds to the surrounding scene and can be controlled by image keyframes; the same model also generates either modality from the other; (2) a parameter-efficient architecture that represents arbitrary rigs as graphs, with bridge guidance amplifying video–motion agreement; (3) learned scene registration that recovers the camera needed to replay generated 3D motion in the scene; and (4) a data pipeline that places labeled asset animations in scenes suited to their actions and, together with human and robot video, yields 200K video–motion pairs spanning diverse rigs.

title: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators
authors: Michael Chen,Hong Chul Nam,Xi Deng,Anima Anandkumar
abstract: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt), to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95–100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D (λ=4\lambda=4), PUN achieves 10.7–60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29–32.15×\times faster.
introduction:
Planning (Latombe, 1991) is one of the most fundamental problems in robotics. Given a robot’s configuration space (LaValle, 2006), planning computes a path from the current configuration to a goal that is optimal under a given cost function. Real robots do not execute a commanded motion exactly (Thrun, 2002). These errors accumulate along a motion, so a route planned with a few centimetres of clearance can be executed into a wall. Sampling-based planners such as PRM (Kavraki et al., 1996) and RRT (LaValle and Kuffner, 2001), and graph search such as A⋆ (Hart et al., 1968), plan for a nominal system that executes commands exactly and leave the noise to a tracking controller. Sampling-based methods such as MPPI (Williams et al., 2017a) and PI2-CMA (Stulp and Sigaud, 2012) optimize control sequences or policy parameters using sampled trajectory costs. Optimal feedback under execution noise can be derived from a value function, which gives the minimum expected cost of reaching the goal from each configuration and satisfies the nonlinear Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation (Fleming and Soner, 2006). Solving this equation on a grid scales exponentially with the dimension of the configuration space (Bellman, 1957; Han et al., 2018).

While the problem can be converted into a linear screened Poisson equation (Theodorou et al., 2010) under control–noise matching (Assumption 1), a central difficulty in Poisson-based planning is specifying boundary conditions that produce a reliable value field across varying geometries.

Conventional mesh-based numerical methods can solve the screened Poisson equation efficiently in two and three dimensions. However, a robot with dd degrees of freedom (DoF) induces a dd-dimensional configuration space, making volumetric discretizations and numerical PDE solution increasingly expensive. Planning must also accommodate complex and previously unseen obstacle geometries, for which constructing a new mesh and solving the PDE from scratch can be costly. Mesh-free Monte Carlo methods (Muller, 1956; Sawhney and Crane, 2020; Sawhney et al., 2023; Jambon et al., 2026) support PDE solution on complex geometries, motivating their use for planning in higher-dimensional configuration spaces.

Among these, Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) (Muller, 1956) estimates the solution at a point by jumping repeatedly to a uniformly sampled point on the largest ball fitting in free space, until it reaches a boundary of known value, which requires every reachable boundary to be Dirichlet. Walk-on-Stars (WoSt) (Sawhney et al., 2023) accommodates reflecting obstacles by replacing that ball with a star-shaped region that may contain part of the obstacle boundary, keeping every boundary point visible from the center so that one ray continues the walk instead of branching at each contact. The screened kernels for Walk-on-Stars have been derived only in two and three dimensions (Sawhney et al., 2023). Moreover, directly planning with Monte Carlo estimates is unreliable: trajectories depend on local value gradients, and even modest estimator noise can corrupt or reverse the estimated direction, leading to planning failure.

Neural operators (Kovachki et al., 2023) can amortize expensive PDE solves by learning mappings from input geometries directly to solution fields. Moreover, prior work has shown that fully converged labels are unnecessary when training from Monte Carlo simulations: neural operators can recover accurate predictions from noisy, partially converged estimates (Viswanath et al., 2026). This enables training of neural operators with inexpensive Monte Carlo supervision while providing fast, smooth value-field predictions at inference time.

We propose Planning Under Noise (PUN), shown in Fig. 2, an operator-learning framework that maps environment geometry to value fields that account for control noise. Boundary conditions can be understood through a heat analogy. With unit desirability at the goal and zero desirability on obstacle boundaries, the goal acts like a hot source, while the obstacle walls act like cold sinks. The zero-Dirichlet condition fixes the field to zero along each obstacle surface, making the entire obstacle boundary a heat sink. In a long or narrow passage, heat spreading from the goal therefore leaks into the walls along the route. The farther the goal’s influence must travel, the more it is attenuated, leaving a weak signal in distant parts of free space that discretization, sampling, or learning errors can obscure. Narrow passages make this particularly pronounced because the absorbing walls remain close on both sides. This attenuation is visible in Fig. 1(c), where the weak goal signal provides insufficient directional guidance for starting points far from the goal, making it difficult to navigate toward the target. Moreover, the screened Poisson equation already includes decay throughout free space through its screening term; absorbing obstacle boundaries introduce an additional source of attenuation. We therefore keep a Dirichlet condition at the goal but impose homogeneous Neumann (zero-flux) conditions on obstacle boundaries. The walls now act like insulation: they prevent heat from escaping through the boundary without forcing the desirability itself to vanish there. Heat can spread along a corridor without continually draining into its walls, allowing the goal’s influence to reach farther into free space. Screening still causes decay, but the additional loss through obstacles is removed. This is precisely the effect illustrated in Fig. 1(d): compared with the absorbing Dirichlet field in Fig. 1(c), the mixed-boundary field extends the goal’s influence much farther through the environment, preserving a stronger signal for planning along long routes. The Neumann condition also makes the value gradient parallel to smooth obstacle boundaries; therefore, gradient-based planning directs motion along walls rather than into them. This permits guidance along walls in narrow passages without the strong repulsion induced by zero-Dirichlet conditions. Under our regularity assumptions, the value field and control remain bounded at obstacles, whereas zero-Dirichlet desirability makes both diverge there (Appendix C.4).

We first derive dimension-general Poisson kernels and Monte Carlo weights, extending mesh-free supervision beyond three dimensions for scalability. This enables supervision generation without a volumetric configuration-space mesh. We then train PUN using noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo estimates in the weak supervision paradigm. By amortizing the PDE solution across geometries, PUN produces spatially coherent value fields that guide gradient following and local search without requiring a fully converged Monte Carlo solve for every environment. We evaluate PUN across 2D–4D environments and compare its planning success and runtime with nominal planners and stochastic controllers under execution noise. In the experiments varying the execution noise level λ\lambda, we plan a path from the current state at each control step, follow it briefly, and repeat from the updated state; we refer to this as replanning. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We formulate Poisson-based path planning as a mixed boundary-value problem, imposing a Dirichlet condition at the goal and homogeneous Neumann conditions on obstacle boundaries.

We formulate Poisson-based path planning as a mixed boundary-value problem, imposing a Dirichlet condition at the goal and homogeneous Neumann conditions on obstacle boundaries.

We introduce an operator-learning framework that maps environment geometry to noise-aware value fields, enabling zero-shot planning in unseen complex geometries without per-instance retraining or numerical PDE solves.

We generalize the mesh-free Monte Carlo solver WoSt beyond three dimensions by deriving the dimension-dependent Green’s function and step weights for the screened Poisson equation.

We introduce a test-time scaling strategy that evaluates reachable candidate states on a local lattice using a fixed global learned field, without retraining, improving planning success over direct gradient following in the reported 2D–4D evaluations (Tables 1 and 11).

On 2D application benchmarks, zero-shot WoSt-supervised FNO reaches 93.62% local-search success, up from 83.87% with gradient following on the same fields (Table 1). With the same local-search, FNO-based PUN achieves approximately 941×941\times and 58×58\times speedups over direct WoSt on the 2D zero-shot application benchmarks and 4D manipulator test set, respectively (Table 12). In 4D replanning, PUN achieves 95.00–100% success at 10.51–11.66 ms/start across the tested noise levels (Table 5; Fig. 1(a)). At λ=4\lambda=4, PUN is 3.29×3.29\times faster than RRT and 5.095.09–32.15×32.15\times faster than A⋆, Dijkstra, MPPI, and PI2-CMA. FNO also maintains over 90% local-search success across resolutions up to 4096×40964096\times 4096 (256×256\times as many grid points as used in training) without retraining (Fig. 1(b)).

1. We formulate Poisson-based path planning as a mixed boundary-value problem, imposing a Dirichlet condition at the goal and homogeneous Neumann conditions on obstacle boundaries.

2. We introduce an operator-learning framework that maps environment geometry to noise-aware value fields, enabling zero-shot planning in unseen complex geometries without per-instance retraining or numerical PDE solves.

3. We generalize the mesh-free Monte Carlo solver WoSt beyond three dimensions by deriving the dimension-dependent Green’s function and step weights for the screened Poisson equation.

4. We introduce a test-time scaling strategy that evaluates reachable candidate states on a local lattice using a fixed global learned field, without retraining, improving planning success over direct gradient following in the reported 2D–4D evaluations (Tables 1 and 11).

title: CoGaussian: Open-Vocabulary Gaussian-based Collaborative 3D Scene Understanding
authors: Om Shivam Verma,Shaya Farahmand,Lingjun Zhao,Lu Gan
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Collaborative perception enables agents to retrieve the scene semantics and geometry beyond the field of view of any individual agent. This broader scene understanding enhances transportation safety and improves efficiency in multi-robot systems. However, existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods rely on dense 3D voxel annotations and are limited to recognizing objects within a predefined set of semantic classes. To overcome these limitations, we present CoGaussian, an open-vocabulary Gaussian-based collaborative semantic occupancy prediction framework. CoGaussian represents a scene as a set of foundation model-aligned sparse 3D Gaussians, which serve as a compact representation for communicating and fusing geometric and semantic information across multiple agents. On the Semantic-OPV2V benchmark, our method outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of open-vocabulary collaborative scene understanding.
introduction:
Collaborative perception enables local agents to exchange information that may be occluded or beyond their field-of-view, improving geometric and semantic understanding of their environment, and enabling safer and more reliable decision making in autonomous driving and robot navigation. Semantic occupancy prediction (SOP) is a representative and challenging task in 3D spatial understanding, which aims to predict voxel-wise occupancy status and semantic class. Recently, 3D Gaussian-based methods [1] have been shown to be effective for SOP. The GaussianFormer family [2, 3, 4, 5] represents scenes as 3D Gaussians, supervised by dense occupancy labels. VOGS-CP [6] extends GaussianFormer to collaborative SOP which communicates Gaussian primitives between neighboring agents. However, these methods are limited to predicting semantics within a closed vocabulary and heavily rely on densely annotated 3D occupancy labels that are expensive to obtain.

Vision foundation models (VFMs), such as DINO [7] and CLIP [8] have demonstrated strong open-vocabulary capabilities in 2D perception. In addition, Talk2DINO [9] and DINO.txt [10] further align 2D VFM features with natural language.
Building on the above VFMs, GaussTR [11] represents scenes as a set of sparse open-vocabulary 3D Gaussians that are predicted in a feed-forward manner and can be queried via natural language. The Gaussians are encoded with geometry and semantic information by splatting into 2D views and aligning rendered features with foundation model-derived depth [12] and semantics [8, 7]. However, GaussTR is designed for single-agent perception and cannot leverage information that is visible only to neighboring agents.

Based on these observations, we propose CoGaussian, the first open-vocabulary multi-robot collaborative perception framework. We represent scenes as sets of sparse VFM-aligned 3D Gaussians, which also serve as the communication primitives among agents. We also explore and develop three different algorithms to aggregate and fuse information from neighboring agents. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

Open-Vocabulary Collaborative Perception: We propose CoGaussian, the first framework for open-vocabulary collaborative perception (e.g. 3D semantic occupancy prediction) in outdoor environments.

Open-Vocabulary Collaborative Perception: We propose CoGaussian, the first framework for open-vocabulary collaborative perception (e.g. 3D semantic occupancy prediction) in outdoor environments.

Multi-Robot 3D Gaussian Representation: We develop a foundation model-aligned 3D Gaussian representation for collaborative perception, along with fusion strategies to enhance information transfer among agents.

Zero-Shot Benchmarking: We evaluate CoGaussian on the Semantic-OPV2V [13, 14] dataset in a zero-shot manner. Without any task-specific supervision, our approach achieves impressive performance for semantic occupancy prediction, highlighting the potential for open-vocabulary collaborative perception.

1. Open-Vocabulary Collaborative Perception: We propose CoGaussian, the first framework for open-vocabulary collaborative perception (e.g. 3D semantic occupancy prediction) in outdoor environments.

2. Multi-Robot 3D Gaussian Representation: We develop a foundation model-aligned 3D Gaussian representation for collaborative perception, along with fusion strategies to enhance information transfer among agents.

3. Zero-Shot Benchmarking: We evaluate CoGaussian on the Semantic-OPV2V [13, 14] dataset in a zero-shot manner. Without any task-specific supervision, our approach achieves impressive performance for semantic occupancy prediction, highlighting the potential for open-vocabulary collaborative perception.

title: CLOSER: Evidence-Aware Active Visual Verification for Embodied Object-Goal Navigation
authors: Pengying Wu,Mingye Jiang,Yunze Hu,Zhejia Wen,Kangjie Zhou,Zongru Yang,Zhe Peng,Chang Liu
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) requires an embodied agent to find an instance of a specified category in an unseen environment and stop near it. The agent typically relies on an object detector but must judge online from a limited egocentric video stream, sometimes a single frame, whether a detected candidate is the target. Detectors often confidently mistake similar objects, such as a sofa for a bed, and stopping at a false positive fails the episode. Prevailing systems also approach candidates greedily, leaving them occluded or partially observed. We present CLOSER, an evidence-aware active verification framework that treats stopping as closed-loop evidence acquisition, coupling vision–language model (VLM) verification with active perception. CLOSER fine-tunes an open-source VLM to label each view of a candidate tracked across frames as target, non-target, or uncertain, selects complementary views with an embedding-based diversity gate, and fuses their per-view probabilities with a lightweight network. If the fused judgment remains uncertain, a diffusion policy drives the agent toward the candidate using only the tracked mask and depth until the decision becomes decisive. CLOSER runs locally and plugs into existing ObjectNav systems without retraining them. On Gibson and Habitat-Matterport 3D, it raises average success rate by 3.6 points and success weighted by path length by 2.0 points, showing that verifying evidence before committing improves embodied navigation.
introduction:
Object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) is a fundamental task in embodied AI [1] in which an agent searches an unseen environment for an object of a specified target category and stops near it [2, 3]. To find the target, the agent must explore the environment efficiently and infer where the target is likely to be located. When an object resembling the target comes into view, the agent must further judge whether it is the target. ObjectNav therefore demands both efficient exploration and reliable perception from its online egocentric video stream, and remains a challenging problem despite extensive study [4].

To meet these demands, prevailing modular systems adopt an exploration strategy to search promising regions and an off-the-shelf object detector to recognize the observed objects [2, 5, 6]. Whenever a candidate for the target category is detected, the agent must decide from limited local observations whether the candidate is the target and hence whether to stop; in the worst case, only a single partial view is available. Since the episode ends once the agent stops, a wrong stop cannot be corrected, and this stopping decision has been identified as a major bottleneck of modular systems [7, 8]. Although modern open-vocabulary detectors such as YOLO-World and Grounded-SAM [9, 10] achieve high recall on common indoor categories, they frequently mistake semantically similar objects for the target. For example, a sofa observed from a distance may be detected as a bed (Fig. 1), and a stool partially occluded by a table may be detected as a chair. Such confusers are often detected with tight bounding boxes and high confidence, so raising the confidence threshold removes true targets before it removes these errors. Therefore, each detected candidate needs to be further verified before the agent commits to a stop.

To this end, recent systems introduce a closed-source vision–language model (VLM) such as GPT-4o-mini as a verifier that confirms or rejects each detected candidate [11]. Such a model provides open-world visual reasoning that the detector lacks, and can reject confusers even when the detection confidence is high. However, the verifier is accessible only through a remote API, which incurs per-query cost and latency and leaves its weights unavailable for local adaptation. A smaller open-source VLM avoids these constraints, yet its verification accuracy drops markedly on hard cases such as distant or partially occluded confusers. Moreover, existing verifiers are binary and must decide even when the current view supports neither confirmation nor rejection. Such a forced decision may stop the agent at a non-target or reject a candidate that a closer view could confirm. Recent work has proposed ternary uncertainty scores and explicit not-found outcomes [12, 13], but neither mechanism moves the agent to acquire more views of the candidate for verification.

In this paper, we propose CLOSER (Closed-Loop Observation Sensing for Embodied veRification), an evidence-aware active verification framework in which the agent decides whether to stop by reasoning over the visual evidence on a candidate and acting to improve it. Our key insight is that a reliable stopping decision depends not only on what the candidate appears to be but also on whether the available views suffice to identify it, and this sufficiency depends on the spatial relationship between the agent and the candidate, including its distance, viewing angle, and degree of occlusion. The agent therefore commits to a decision only when the evidence suffices and otherwise approaches the candidate to acquire more informative views (Fig. 1). Realizing this closed loop poses two challenges. First, the agent must learn when its evidence is insufficient, which confidence cannot reveal since distant or occluded views often yield confident predictions. Second, it must learn how to reach a more informative view without a complete map of the unseen environment.

To learn when the evidence is insufficient, CLOSER fine-tunes an open-source VLM with LoRA [14] to assess both the identity of the candidate and the sufficiency of each view. During navigation, CLOSER tracks the candidate across egocentric frames with ByteTrack [15] and caches complementary views of it, and a lightweight MLP fuses the per-view assessments of the VLM to decide whether the evidence suffices. To learn how to reach a more informative view, CLOSER imitates an expert that plans maximum-clearance paths along the Voronoi medial axis of the complete map and smooths them into Bézier trajectories, so that walls are less likely to occlude the candidate along the way. To eliminate this dependence on the map, we distill the expert trajectories into a Diffusion Transformer policy [16, 17] that conditions only on the tracked candidate mask and depth, which encode the distance and visibility of the candidate relative to the agent. As the agent follows this policy, verification and active perception form a closed loop, in which every view cached along the trajectory refines the assessment and the approach phase ends as soon as the evidence supports a decision. CLOSER is invoked only when a candidate for the target category is detected and leaves the exploration and mapping components of existing ObjectNav systems unchanged. It can therefore be inserted into these systems as a plug-in verification layer without retraining them.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We propose CLOSER, a plug-in layer for existing ObjectNav systems that formulates the stopping decision as an active verification problem. Closer judges not only whether a candidate is the target but also whether its views suffice for that judgment, and it drives the agent to acquire more views by approaching the candidate when the current views are insufficient.

Since a confident prediction on a distant or occluded view can be wrong, we design the verifier in Closer to assess the sufficiency of each view in addition to the identity of the candidate. We fine-tune an open-source VLM for this assessment under a closed-source VLM teacher and train a lightweight MLP that fuses the assessments of complementary views into a single decision.

We train a map-free approach policy by distilling an expert into a Diffusion Transformer that generates a trajectory toward the candidate from its tracked mask and depth. To keep the candidate in view throughout the approach phase, the expert plans each path along the Voronoi medial axis of the free space for maximum clearance from walls and smooths the path into a Bézier trajectory.

Simulation experiments confirm that CLOSER improves ObjectNav performance. Across diverse ObjectNav systems on Gibson, HM3D v1, and HM3D v2, CLOSER improves success rate (SR), with an average gain of 3.6 points and a maximum gain of 4.9 points. CLOSER also improves success weighted by path length (SPL) by 2.0 points on average.

title: Distributed Platoon Control for Safe and Smooth Crossing at an Unsignalized Intersection-Part I: Stability Analysis
authors: Bin-Bin Hu,Shuwei Pei,Saeed Ahmed,Bayu Jayawardhana
abstract:
We propose a distributed platoon controller that guarantees safe and smooth crossing of multi-vehicle systems at an unsignalized intersection. To support the stability analysis, we consider a multi-vehicle platoon maneuvering along a closed path with a single unsignalized intersection.
Unlike traditional bi-level decoupled designs on open paths, which primarily focus on intersection control while neglecting its coupling with platoon convergence, and thus hindering rigorous convergence analysis, the closed-path setting allows us to analyze the asymptotic behavior of the platoon.
The local exponential convergence analysis of the switched closed-loop system, induced by repeated vehicle switching at the intersection, is presented. Under some mild conditions on the controller gains, we show that safe intersection crossing is ensured during the transient phase and smooth crossing is achieved in steady state, where all vehicles travel at a common constant speed while avoiding collisions at the intersection. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed distributed controller is demonstrated in a high-fidelity CARLA simulator using multiple commercial vehicle models.
introduction:
With advances in connected and autonomous vehicle (CAV) technologies, multi-vehicle coordination has become increasingly important in urban transportation [1, 2]. Among cooperative scenarios, connected vehicle platooning has attracted significant attention because it enables vehicles to maintain desired inter-vehicle spacing, improving traffic efficiency, energy consumption, and safety [3, 4]. However, urban intersections remain challenging, as vehicles from different directions must share conflict regions safely and efficiently. Frequent deceleration, acceleration, and stopping may disrupt platoon continuity, causing platoon splitting or performance degradation. Therefore, cooperative intersection control (CIC) for multi-vehicle platooning has emerged as a promising approach to improving future intelligent transportation systems [5].

Depending on whether traffic signals are used to manage traffic at intersections, existing studies can be divided into two categories, namely, signal-based and unsignalized methods [6].

Following the signal-based CIC research line, the seminal work [7] studied intersection control for a personal rapid transit system. Later, a isolated controller
based on max-plus models was proposed to reduce energy consumption at homogeneous intersections [8], while a multi-agent reinforcement learning method was proposed for heterogeneous intersections by modeling intersections as basic agents [9]. However, these methods require physical traffic signals, leading to high installation and maintenance costs. This motivates unsignalized approaches with virtual infrastructure and fast computation.

Unsignalized methods have emerged as a promising alternative to signal-based control by reducing unnecessary stops through flexible vehicle coordination. Based on how decision-making, computation, and coordination responsibilities are allocated between infrastructure and vehicles, existing methods can be classified into three categories: centralized, decentralized, and distributed approaches [10]:
(i) For centralized methods where vehicles obtain traffic schemes from the intersection unit, a conflict-duration graph-based framework was designed to improve safety and capacity at unsignalized intersections [11]. To reduce computational burden, an abstraction-based supervision framework was adopted in [12]. For mixed traffic, deep reinforcement learning was used to enable connected autonomous vehicles to yield right of way and optimize traffic flow [13]. For safety guarantee and performance, a polling-systems-based coordination control algorithm was proposed in [14] with rigorous upper bound.
However, these methods directly transmit acceleration commands to individual vehicles, making the system sensitive to disturbances. To improve robustness, a CIC controller was proposed in [6], assigning each CAV a safe reference path and desired speed based on its state, onboard controller response, and origin–destination pair; (ii) For decentralized methods where vehicles distribute tasks across multiple computing nodes, a virtual platooning approach was proposed to map two-dimensional vehicle motions onto a one-dimensional virtual platoon for efficient intersection operation [15]. To handle inaccuracies and disturbances, a hybrid CIC framework was developed by integrating microscopic virtual platooning with traffic-flow regulation [16]. Later, a constraint-coupled bi-level optimization method was designed to balance performance and computational efficiency [17].

In contrast to the centralized and decentralized methods  [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17] in (i)-(ii), the distributed control policies in (iii) have also attracted considerable attention. Along this line, a distributed optimization algorithm was proposed in [18] to schedule conflict-free arrival times for trajectory planning at intersections. To minimize travel time and speed variations simultaneously, a mixed-integer nonlinear optimization method was developed in [19] to avoid near-crash conditions. Moreover, a graph-based cooperation method was proposed in [20] to formulate the conflict-free scheduling problem at unsignalized intersections, which enhances control flexibility.

However, most existing CIC methods [6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20] provide only limited rigorous analysis, mainly due to their bi-level decoupled designs for intersection control and platoon convergence on open paths. To facilitate stability analysis and safety guarantee, we consider a setting in which the platoon maneuvers along a closed path with a single unsignalized intersection, enabling the platoon to be analyzed as an integrated team. Compared with open-path scenarios, this closed-path setting introduces two challenges: (i) Vehicles repeatedly enter the intersection, which causes persistent coupling between intersection control and platoon convergence and invalidates decoupled optimization designs; (ii) Repeated intersection entries transform the closed-loop dynamics into a switched system, which makes the convergence analysis challenging.

To tackle these challenges, we propose a distributed controller that enables multiple vehicles to cross the intersection safely and converge to the steady-state platoon, where all vehicles travel at a common constant speed and achieve collision-free crossing.
The local exponential convergence of the switched closed-loop system, induced by repeated vehicle switching at the intersection, is rigorously analyzed. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated.

Contribution: The contribution is summarized as follows.

We propose a distributed smooth-crossing controller that enables multiple vehicles to spontaneously form a platoon on a closed path with a single intersection;

We enable smooth constant-speed crossing without acceleration or deceleration in steady state by introducing a sensing barrier function for incoming vehicle pairs approaching the intersection;

We rigorously establish the local exponential convergence of the switched closed-loop system induced by vehicle switching at the intersection on a closed path.

The proposed algorithm is not intended to replace general-purpose intersection scheduling methods. Rather, it provides a control-theoretic model in which the interaction between intersection safety and platoon convergence remains active indefinitely, which leads to a switched closed-loop system under repeated intersection crossings. This allows the switching dynamics to be included in the rigorous convergence analysis.

title: Interruption-Aware Recurrent Reinforcement Learning for UAS Navigation Under Temporary Overrides
authors: Christopher Conrad,Deepak Panda,Weisi Guo,Antonios Tsourdos
comment: This work has been submitted to IEEE for possible publication
abstract: Safe autonomous navigation of unmanned aircraft systems (UASs) requires tactical deconfliction to address conflicts that strategic coordination cannot fully prevent. This task is challenging under partial observability, when sensor or traffic data are missing, delayed, or degraded. Geometry-based methods can offer separation assurances but face limitations in dense encounters. Recurrent reinforcement learning (RL) has therefore been proposed to learn navigation policies that integrate observation-action histories to optimise long-term safety-efficiency trade-offs. However, operational safeguards may require a remote pilot, onboard detect-and-avoid (DAA) system, or runtime assurance (RTA) mechanism to temporarily override the learned policy. A research gap remains in understanding how these interruptions affect recurrent policies when the agent regains authority. Benchmark evidence shows that interruptions make task variables less decodable from the recurrent hidden state and increase post-interruption collision risk. The findings suggest that altered recurrent context prolongs post-handback degradation through an action-observation feedback loop, in which changed actions alter the flight path and subsequent recurrent updates. To address this vulnerability, we propose three interruption-aware architectures that condition recurrent processing on interruption context through separate feature streams, dedicated interruption memory, or gated environmental features. Across simulations, all three architectures preserve more decodable task information than a standard recurrent policy. Moreover, the strongest architecture reduces post-interruption collisions by 74% and interruption-induced mission failures by 69% relative to the recurrent baseline, without degrading interruption-free performance. These results show that safe interruption does not guarantee safe handback, and support interruption-aware recurrent design for resilient UAS autonomy.
introduction:
Unmanned aircraft system (UAS) traffic management (UTM) frameworks support flight planning, strategic deconfliction and information exchange for UAS navigation [1, 2]. Nonetheless, the UAS operator or remote pilot remains responsible for flight safety, and strategic coordination cannot eliminate every conflict that develops during a flight. Aircraft may deviate from their submitted intents, surveillance information may be delayed or degraded, and non-cooperative aircraft or other hazards may be absent from networked information. Tactical deconfliction is therefore required to address emerging conflicts and complement strategic UTM services [3, 4, 5, 6]. Moreover, additional safeguards are required when the tactical navigation algorithm encounters unreliable information or conditions outside its validated operating envelope. An onboard detect-and-avoid (DAA) system, runtime-assurance (RTA) mechanism or remote pilot may temporarily override nominal autonomy to resolve an emerging hazard [3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 5]. Additionally, interruptions may arise from command-and-control (C2) link disruptions or malicious cyberphysical interference [10, 11]. The reliability of the nominal algorithm after it regains authority, hereby referred to as handback, is therefore part of the safety problem.

Within this operational framework, tactical deconfliction has traditionally relied on geometry-based methods, including velocity-obstacle and potential-field algorithms [12, 13]. These approaches often leverage rule-, search- or optimisation-based planning to provide predictable behaviour under explicit assumptions about aircraft dynamics, traffic behaviour and environmental conditions [14, 15]. Advanced air mobility (AAM), however, will increase the volume, heterogeneity, and autonomy of aircraft in the airspace, creating denser and more uncertain traffic interactions [1, 16]. These conditions make the behaviour of interacting aircraft harder to model and increase the computational cost of repeatedly solving multi-aircraft deconfliction problems online [14, 15].

Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a complementary approach by learning navigation policies through simulated conflict encounters [17]. It can optimise safety-efficiency trade-offs while shifting much of the computational burden to offline training [18, 19, 20, 21]. However, finite sensor coverage, noise, occlusion and degraded traffic information make tactical deconfliction partially observable [1, 3]. Recurrent RL addresses this limitation by maintaining a hidden state that summarises task-relevant history to inform current decisions [22, 23, 24]. Notably, Lambrechts et al. [24] show that recurrent memory encodes information correlated with beliefs over latent task variables, with more informative representations resulting in better task performance. Recurrent memory can therefore be interpreted as a learned, task-dependent information state.

Temporary overrides introduce a distinct challenge for recurrent policies. During an interruption, the policy’s proposed actions are not executed, yet its recurrent state evolves with observations generated by externally selected manoeuvres. This altered context can make task-relevant information less accessible or distort how carried information influences subsequent decisions. Consequently, an interruption that resolves an immediate hazard does not necessarily ensure safe handback.

Table I summarises existing research relevant to interrupting recurrent navigation policies. Transportation research examines transitions between automated systems and human decision-makers, focusing on improving override timing and operator readiness [25, 26, 27]. In UTM and other safety-critical autonomous systems, DAA and RTA research instead addresses better hazard detection, safety monitoring, and recovery behaviour [3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 5]. Within RL, research primarily addresses the safety of learned behaviour and responsiveness to interruptions. Safe RL incorporates risk measures or safety constraints during training, whereas shielded RL masks or replaces actions that violate safety thresholds [29, 30, 31]. Corrigibility targets agents that accept or assist external corrections without manipulating the correcting authority [33, 34, 35]. Specifically, safely interruptible RL addresses how interruptions affect learning, developing algorithms that avoid seeking out or preventing future interruptions [32].

Action-modification research provides the closest formal abstraction of the interruptions considered in this paper. Langlois and Everitt [37] introduce the modified-action Markov decision process (MAMDP), which distinguishes the action selected by a policy from that ultimately executed following external modifications. Their analysis shows that some agents ignore modifications while others adapt their behaviour to avoid modifications that reduce reward. Human-in-the-loop RL also uses human overrides as demonstrations or feedback to improve policies during training [36].

Complementing these studies, recurrent RL has been applied to UAS navigation under partial observability [23, 28], while representation analysis examines which latent task variables are decodable from recurrent hidden states [24, 39]. Influence-aware memory restricts recurrent inputs to variables relevant to unobserved environmental states, reducing interference from irrelevant features [38]. Recurrent independent mechanisms similarly organise memory into sparsely interacting modules to improve robustness to environmental changes [40]. These approaches inform the analysis of recurrent representations and the design of structured memory architectures.

Existing literature highlights why interruptions are needed, when they should be initiated, and how they affect policy learning. However, a safe interruption does not guarantee safe handback. A research gap remains in understanding how interruptions affect recurrent representations, how they influence post-handback performance, and how they should be accommodated by recurrent policies. We address this gap through the following contributions:

Interruption of recurrent UAS navigation is formulated as a handback reliability problem and modelled as a partially observable MAMDP (PO-MAMDP).

Interruption of recurrent UAS navigation is formulated as a handback reliability problem and modelled as a partially observable MAMDP (PO-MAMDP).

A paired evaluation framework is developed to characterise the impact of interruptions across different trigger conditions, supervisor behaviours and override durations.

Interruptions are shown to reduce task-variable decodability from the recurrent hidden state, degrade agent performance and increase post-handback collision risk.

Three interruption-aware recurrent architectures are proposed that demonstrate increased robustness to interruptions without degrading interruption-free performance.

2. A paired evaluation framework is developed to characterise the impact of interruptions across different trigger conditions, supervisor behaviours and override durations.

3. Interruptions are shown to reduce task-variable decodability from the recurrent hidden state, degrade agent performance and increase post-handback collision risk.

4. Three interruption-aware recurrent architectures are proposed that demonstrate increased robustness to interruptions without degrading interruption-free performance.

title: RoboJudge: Multimodal Language Models as Judges for Embodied Video Generation
authors: Siyuan Ma,Yu Qi,Cheng Ye,Ruotian Peng,Xinyi Xu,Zitiantao Lin,Zedong Cai,Yijian Huang,Weiyang Liu,Siyuan Wang,Yandong Wen
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Video generation models are promising foundations for embodied world models,
but only if their generated rollouts are physically valid and faithful to task
instructions. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used
to judge these properties, yet their agreement with human judgments on
embodied videos has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap,
we introduce RoboJudge-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating
MLLMs as judges of embodied video generation. The benchmark measures two
fundamental dimensions, Physical Adherence and Instruction
Alignment, across 800 human-annotated videos from 8 source corpora and 10
video generators, spanning grippers, human hands, and dexterous hands.
Experiments reveal uneven alignment between existing judges and human ratings:
general-purpose MLLMs show lower agreement on physical adherence, while
specialized video judges designed for general-domain physical reasoning do not
consistently transfer to embodied scenarios. Motivated by these findings, we
construct RoboJudge-Train, comprising 12K videos annotated with 25K human-verified scores
and model-assisted rationales for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment. We fine-tune
a 9B MLLM on this dataset with supervised learning followed by reinforcement
learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B. Among the model judges
evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench, RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest
overall agreement, reaching a Pearson correlation of 0.7190.719 with a statistically
significant 0.089 gain over Gemini-3.7-Flash, the best-performing proprietary
baseline in our evaluation. Training on RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on external
benchmarks, including VideoPhy2 and Physion-Eval.
We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark
video generation models according to Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment.
introduction:
Recent advances in video generation have positioned generative models as a
promising foundation for embodied world models (Li et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2025; Shang et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b). Unlike general
video generators, embodied world models must predict how the physical world
evolves under robot actions or task instructions, providing imagined rollouts
for planning and policy learning. These rollouts therefore need to be not only
visually plausible, but also physically valid and instruction-consistent,
creating a pressing need for reliable evaluation.

Evaluating embodied generated videos is particularly challenging because they
require fine-grained assessment of physical interactions and task-level
correctness, while open-ended task execution makes reference-based similarity
intrinsically unreliable. Pixel, perceptual, and representation metrics capture
visual or semantic similarity to reference trajectories (Huynh-Thu and Ghanbari, 2008; Bakurov et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2018; Radford et al., 2021; Caron et al., 2021; Bardes et al., 2024), but cannot disentangle physical and task-level failures.
MLLM-based judges offer stronger multimodal reasoning (Zheng et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024), yet general-purpose MLLMs lack embodied-specific calibration (Qi et al., 2026b).
Meanwhile, specialized video judges target general-domain quality or physical
commonsense (He et al., 2024; He et al., 2025; Bansal et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026), rather than fine-grained manipulation dynamics, contact
relationships, and task completion.

To address this gap, we introduce RoboJudge-Bench, a
benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of embodied world model rollouts
along two critical axes: Physical Adherence (PA) and Instruction
Alignment (IA). Specifically, PA covers agent consistency,
scene consistency, and interaction realism; IA covers
agent match, object correctness, and goal
completion. The benchmark comprises 800 rollouts with instructions from
8 embodied source corpora and videos generated by 10 video generation models,
spanning parallel-jaw grippers, dexterous hands, and human hands across indoor
and outdoor activities. Each sample is annotated with 1–5 human ratings for
PA and IA, together with detailed rationales under a cross-review protocol.

Evaluation against 29 model-judge baselines and 8 non-MLLM metrics reveals
gaps between existing judges and human judgments. Frontier models show lower
agreement on physical adherence: GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026) reaches r=0.49r=0.49
on PA. Specialized video judges reach at most r=0.42r=0.42 on PA and 0.590.59 on IA,
while non-MLLM baselines show limited sensitivity to fine-grained physical
correctness. Failure analysis identifies cases in which existing judges overlook
interaction failures and physical hallucinations.

Motivated by these findings, we construct RoboJudge-Train,
a large-scale embodied-video judge-training dataset comprising 12K videos
annotated with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales for PA and IA. We
fine-tune a 9B MLLM from Qwen3.5-9B using supervised learning followed by
reinforcement learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B.
Among the model judges evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench, the resulting
RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest overall agreement, reaching a Pearson
rr of 0.719 compared with 0.401 for its base model. Training on
RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on VideoPhy2 (Bansal et al., 2026) and
Physion-Eval (Zhang et al., 2026).
We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark
video generation models using the same PA and IA criteria. These
capabilities also suggest broader downstream potential for online physical
rollout evaluation and agentic embodied video generation.
In summary, our contributions are three-fold:

1. RoboJudge-Bench. A benchmark designed for judges of embodied video
generation: 800 human-annotated rollouts from 8 corpora and 10 video generators,
spanning grippers, dexterous hands, and human hands in simulated and
real environments, rated on physical adherence and instruction alignment.

2. A systematic study of existing judges. We compare against 29 model-judge baselines and 8 non-MLLM
metrics and characterize gaps with human judgments, with failures
concentrated on fine-grained interaction errors and physical hallucinations.

3. RoboJudge-Train and RoboJudge-9B. We construct a
training dataset for embodied video judges, comprising 12K
embodied videos spanning 14 generators and real demonstrations, with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales,
together with a 9B judge fine-tuned from
Qwen3.5-9B via SFT and RL. It achieves the highest overall agreement among
the evaluated model judges and shows gains on OOD benchmarks.
As a downstream use case, we apply it to rank video generation models using
the same PA and IA criteria.
