title: Give the Model a Finger: Developmentally Aligned Evaluation of Counting in Vision-Language Models
authors: Yingxin Jia,Hui Geng,Wenxin Yang,Mohan Zhang
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Vision–language models (VLMs) are exact on small sets and drift into estimation on larger ones, a profile reminiscent of children before they master counting. Children cross the barrier with epistemic actions: pointing at each item while reciting number words, moving counted items aside, partitioning the array. We give VLMs the same actions as dumb image tools with no visual intelligence of their own (a numbered tag at a coordinate, a zoom, an eraser, a grid) in a training-free agent loop. Our central claim is about measurement, not intervention: a model that counts by marking leaves a normally hidden serial procedure on the image, and the developmental principles of counting (used as measurement theory, not as a claim that VLMs are children) turn those marks into an interpretable audit of serial visual reasoning: every tag is classified against point-level ground truth as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted (one-to-one correspondence), the answer is checked against the number of tags (cardinality), and order irrelevance is tested by forcing opposite traversal orders. Across 9 models, 682 images (a controlled dot-array battery; FSC-147, 8–80 objects; PixMo-Count, 2–10), and 7 harness conditions we find that (i) the exact-counting range is a model-specific signature spanning nearly two orders of magnitude (R80R_{80} from 3 to 150 dots); (ii) as an intervention the finger mostly fails: tags help 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs (CI-solid for one), hurt imprecise pointers, and rarely beat a verbal routine or a blind point list; what the loop buys is an auditable trace, not accuracy; (iii) as measurement it succeeds: a tag-perturbation probe shows that precise pointers read their answers off the tags, pointing precision tracks which models benefit, dense scenes fail by omission (consistent with children’s keeping-track errors), and models rarely revise after seeing their own tags; and (iv) the capacities dissociate: models follow an instructed traversal order yet often change their answer when it reverses, beyond repeat and rotation controls, and children’s regular-over-scattered advantage appears only under the routine and survives lattices that defeat a rows-times-columns shortcut.
introduction:
Ask a three-year-old how many crackers are on the table and, if there are two or three, the answer is immediate and exact. Ask about twelve and the child either guesses or starts to do something: touch each cracker in turn, say “one, two, three…”, slide the counted ones aside, and announce the last word as the total (Gelman and Gallistel, 1978; Fuson, 1988; Wynn, 1990). Two systems are at work: a fast, capacity-limited individuation of up to about four items (subitizing, Kaufman et al., 1949; Trick and Pylyshyn, 1994) and an approximate sense of magnitude (Feigenson et al., 2004; Xu and Spelke, 2000). Exact enumeration beyond that range is a learned procedure that recruits the hands and the space around the child: pointing keeps items and number words in one-to-one correspondence (Alibali and DiRusso, 1999; Saxe, 1977; Graham, 1999), moving items aside and scanning row by row prevent double counts and skips (Fuson, 1988; Potter and Levy, 1968; Beckwith and Restle, 1966), and partitioning turns one big count into several small ones (van Oeffelen and Vos, 1982): epistemic actions, performed not to change the world but to make a computation easier (Kirsh and Maglio, 1994; Kirsh, 1995).

Vision–language models (VLMs) look strikingly like the pre-procedural child: near-perfect on one to four objects, sharply worse after that, systematically under-counting dense sets, erring like noisy estimators rather than enumerators (Testolin et al., 2025; Tamarapalli et al., 2025; Che et al., 2026; Budny et al., 2025), with the count present in the visual features but mis-read at the output (Pang et al., 2026; El-Shangiti et al., 2026). VLMs have a number sense but no counting routine. The claim is not that a VLM is a child or models one, but that the developmental account of counting supplies testable hypotheses (which external scaffolds should help) and diagnostic variables (what to measure when they do not).

We therefore ask: if we give a VLM the epistemic actions that children use, does it count like a child who has learned to count, and does it fail like one? We build a training-free harness in which the model can draw a numbered tag at any image coordinate and see the tagged image, zoom into a region, grey out counted items, and overlay a coordinate grid. Every tool is a plain pixel operation with no detector, segmenter, or OCR behind it, so all perception and all decisions remain the model’s own; the harness only lends it a finger, a magnifier, and an eraser.

The deeper contribution is measurement. A model that counts by marking externalises, mark by mark, a serial procedure that is normally hidden in its activations; the developmental principles of counting give that trace a grammar, turning model-generated marks into an interpretable audit of serial visual reasoning. This is what developmentally aligned evaluation adds over a benchmark score: not whether a model counts, but which constituent capacities it has, pointing, one-to-one tracking, cardinal read-out, checking, order invariance, each measured on its own. Following the classic analyses of children’s counting (Gelman and Gallistel, 1978; Gelman and Meck, 1983; Fuson, 1988), we classify every tag as on-target, duplicate, or phantom and every object as counted or omitted against point-level ground truth, test cardinality against the tags and order irrelevance by forcing opposite traversal orders, and measure pointing precision, on a controlled dot-array battery and two photographic benchmarks, FSC-147 (Ranjan et al., 2021) (8–80 dot-annotated instances) and PixMo-Count (Deitke et al., 2025) (2–10).

(1) A developmentally aligned evaluation in which counting principles turn model-generated marks into an interpretable audit of serial visual reasoning: each principle becomes a measurable prediction (Table 3), and a wrong count decomposes into principle violations against point-level ground truth (Section 4). (2) A training-free harness of dumb epistemic tools for counting, each mapped to a child strategy and a counting principle (Section 3). (3) An empirical study over 9 models and 682 images with paired bootstrap uncertainty on every headline contrast (Section 5), showing that the constituent capacities dissociate across models rather than forming one “counting ability” (Table 2), and that the tools are diagnostic rather than therapeutic: a finger helps only models that can already point, and where it fails, the audit localises the missing prerequisite; the study costs under 153 US dollars, and all code, stimuli, and trajectories will be released.

title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines
authors: Yingxin Jia,Xuanyi Li
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because planners, prompts, and implementation quality vary together
across systems, and the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool
contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one
audited HighwayEnv testbed (kinematic observations, discrete meta-actions, 11 Hz,
gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We freeze the planner, encoder, and protocol, treat
the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools), and add token-matched
irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, scripted certificate policies,
caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port
(RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory TG-Mem with five variants, a retrieval-free
consolidated rulebook, and a flat KK-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a
property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of
ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test
p=0.011p\!=\!0.011) and have a negative pool-averaged effect, and even the rulebook’s apparent pool-immunity
(0.970.97 to 0.980.98 on five pools) collapsed to 0.030.03 to 0.980.98 on five fresh draws. (2) No
retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler, which sits significantly above both memories under
paired tests. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a scripted always-SLOWER policy and
by a single 1515-token caution instruction (both 0.980.98), and metrics that price caution erase the
rulebook’s lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. Neither
retrieved structure nor raw in-context history solves the oracle-solvable history-necessity diagnostic.
(4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool
comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We
release the testbed, diagnostics with certificates, the replay benchmark, audited ports, seeds, and caches.
introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as promising decision makers for autonomous driving that
reason over scenes in natural language. A recurring finding is that they improve substantially when given
an experience memory, a store of past situations and the actions that worked, retrieved and injected
as few-shot guidance at decision time (Wen et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024a; Mei et al., 2024). This paper asks the question those reports leave open. When does experience memory help,
and under which warmup experiences, prompt compositions, and decision cadences? Published comparisons
cannot answer this, because the memory varies together with the surrounding architecture and with
implementation quality, and the two factors we find to matter most, which experiences the warmup
pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them.

Our primary contribution is the controlled evaluation itself. We fix one planner, one encoder,
and one warm-up, freeze, and evaluate protocol, and we instrument it with controls this literature has
not used. The warmup pool becomes a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools with model-free
pool-level tests). Token-matched irrelevant-filler arms span content, dose, and a
disclaimer×\timesdomain factorial. Two constructed diagnostics are certified well-posed by scripted
oracles before any LLM run. Scripted non-LLM certificate policies bound what caution alone
achieves, metrics price caution rather than only collisions, and a quantified audit measures the
fidelity of the baseline ports. On this testbed we evaluate a probe suite that spans the memory
design space (§3 and §4). At the rich end sits TG-Mem (Temporal-Graph
Memory), our episodic design. Published driving memories retrieve flat text by embedding
cosine (Wen et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024a; Zhou et al., 2025; Mei et al., 2024) or a single-frame
grid (Chen et al., 2026), whereas TG-Mem stores episodes as small typed temporal graphs matched
by a combined structural and temporal score, a prompt-level driving instantiation of the temporal
knowledge-graph memory line (Rasmussen et al., 2025; Chhikara et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025), with five variants that toggle
curation, keys, and injection. At the distilled end sits a consolidated rulebook: the same
experience compressed once into at most eight rules (Zhao et al., 2024) and injected at every
decision with no retrieval. At the direct end sits a flat KK-step history baseline, and at the
content-free end a token-matched padding arm and a four-content filler suite. Each
probe is both a design under evaluation and a control for its neighbors.

The evaluation yields four findings (Figure 1). Each is a statement about this
testbed, HighwayEnv with kinematic observations, discrete meta-actions, a 11 Hz decision
cadence, and gpt-4o-mini for every decisive contrast, and each baseline statement concerns our
audited ports under this harness (§4), not the published systems. Table 1
maps each finding to the confirmatory evidence behind it.

(M1) The warmup pool acts as a lottery: the headline gains are knife-edges that resampling
reverses. Both headline gains, the diagnostic’s →0.950.45\!\to\!0.95 (p=0.001p{=}0.001) and the merge margin of
+0.15+0.15 (significant under pairing), are properties of a particular draw. Resampled, the diagnostic
effect spans 0.950.95 to 0.100.10, and on merge the reported pool is the best of ten disjoint pools: each
memory exceeds No-Memory in one pool of ten (exact sign test p=0.011p\!=\!0.011), sits significantly below it
in five, and has a pool-averaged effect near −0.20-0.20 (§5). A pool swap also flips the
flat memory’s entire disposition from aggressive to timid on the history-necessity diagnostic
(Figure 1c), and the rulebook’s “pool-immunity,” confirmed on five pools, reversed on
five fresh draws.
(M2) No retrieval design tested exceeds our token-matched fillers. Injecting content-free
tokens produces merge-safety changes comparable to the memories’. Fillers span 0.590.59 to 0.800.80 on merge against the memories’ 0.660.66 to 0.670.67, and the strongest
filler is significantly above both under paired tests. The designs that reach the collision-only
ceiling turn the caution dial hardest, and the dial needs no memory: a scripted always-SLOWER
policy and a single 1515-token caution instruction both score 0.980.98, and the rulebook’s best cells sit
at that operating point while metrics that price caution erase its lead (§5.1).
(M3) The operative ingredient dissociates (curation on merges, key precision on the
diagnostic), and representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. TG-Mem and its five
variants never robustly beat flat memory across splits. Its temporal edges, the design’s central
component, contribute at most marginally in a pool-conditional ablation. The key×\timesinjection
×22\!\times\!2 (Table S44) finds compact injection consistently harmful while the key-type attribution
flips with the pool, and even raw temporal context handed to the planner directly does not pass the
history-necessity diagnostic that memory was hypothesized to solve.
(M4) Baseline implementation quality silently inverts conclusions. A subtly crippled port
halved the flat baseline and manufactured a false win for our own method. We quantify the artifact and
release the audited ports.

(i) An evaluation framework for agent experience memory, with instruments this literature
lacks: the warmup pool as a resampled random factor with model-free pool-level tests, token-matched
filler and padding arms with a disclaimer×\timesdomain factorial (the nearest analog is exemplar
sensitivity in in-context learning (Lu et al., 2022)), oracle-certified diagnostics, scripted
certificate policies, caution-pricing metrics, and a quantified baseline audit.
(ii) A probe suite spanning the design space, all ours: TG-Mem, the first episodic
temporal-graph memory for closed-loop driving, with five variants, plus the consolidated rulebook, the
flat KK-step history baseline, and the filler instruments. (iii) Findings M1 to M4 from the first controlled closed-loop comparison of flat,
structured, temporal-graph, distilled, and history-based context (one protocol, three backbones), a
real-data-seeded replay benchmark (5454 highD cut-ins), and released ports, seeds, caches, and protocols.

title: PanoGraphGS: Unifying Panoptic Segmentation and Hierarchical 3D Scene Graphs with Gaussian Splatting
authors: Jinghan Gao,Siyu Wang,Dongyu Feng,Yiyuan Pan,Rong Xiong
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
3D scene graphs support language-guided navigation by organizing physical
entities and their containment and spatial relations into hierarchical maps.
Building such structured maps requires a scene representation that consistently
distinguishes semantic regions and object instances across viewpoints. To this
end, we present PanoGraphGS, a unified framework that integrates panoptic 3D
Gaussian representation learning with hierarchical 3D scene graph construction.
The framework learns semantic and instance features on shared Gaussian
geometry. Prototype-based semantic learning and association-based instance
learning produce consistent panoptic predictions across viewpoints. The learned
representation supports novel-view panoptic segmentation and direct
Gaussian-level panoptic decoding. A semantic-aware scene graph module further
recovers a floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy with containment and spatial
relations. We further release NaviGS, a real-world dataset for panoramic scene
understanding. The dataset provides 3DGS, mesh, RGB, semantic, and depth data. For 3D scene graph identification, PanoGraphGS
outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in object-node accuracy
by more than 50% points on average across Replica and
NaviGS.
PanoGraphGS also achieves
state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods in 2D
panoptic segmentation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of PanoGraphGS
in both hierarchical 3D scene
understanding and 2D panoptic segmentation. The project website is available at:
https://github.com/gaojh0333/PanoGraphGS.
introduction:
Panoptic 3D scene reconstruction is fundamental to language-guided robotic
navigation. Successful navigation requires embodied agents to recognize
semantic categories, maintain persistent instance identities, and reason about
spatial organization in a globally consistent map. Such
tasks require reasoning over nested containment and spatial relations. A 3D
scene graph formalizes this organization by representing physical entities as
nodes and their containment and spatial relations as
edges [1, 2].
3D Dynamic Scene
Graphs [3], Hydra [4], and
HOV-SG [5], have advanced structured spatial mapping.
However, these pipelines commonly rely on per-pixel RGB-D observations or
depth-derived geometry. Incomplete or noisy depth can degrade object-extent
estimation, cross-view association, room partitioning, and spatial-relation
inference. Moreover, existing methods typically construct scene graphs and
dense panoptic representations separately, requiring an additional stage to
associate panoptic predictions with graph entities.

These limitations motivate a unified 3D representation that preserves
geometry, semantic categories, and persistent instance identities while being
learned directly from multi-view RGB observations. 3D Gaussian Splatting
(3DGS) [7] provides such a representation through explicit,
spatially anchored Gaussian primitives and differentiable rendering.
Visibility-aware rendering lifts multi-view semantic and instance supervision
into a shared 3D field. The learned features can be rendered for novel-view
panoptic prediction or decoded directly from Gaussians for 3D entity
abstraction. Unified-Lift [8] learns Gaussian- and
object-level representations from multi-view segmentation cues. More recently,
GaussianGraph [9] extends 3DGS toward scene graph
generation by clustering Gaussian primitives and associating them with CLIP
features and spatial relations extracted from 2D foundation models. However,
its reasoning mainly focuses on object-level spatial relations and relies on
high-dimensional vision–language features for semantic association, while
clustering may discard fine-grained spatial information. Explicit
identification, matching, and hierarchical association across the
floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy remain unaddressed. Consequently, dense
panoptic prediction and hierarchical scene organization remain loosely
integrated. Establishing globally consistent panoptic predictions within a
Gaussian representation therefore presents two challenges. First,
viewpoint-dependent visibility and occlusion produce nonuniform multi-view
supervision. Second, the same physical object may receive different view-local
pseudo-instance identifiers across views, causing conflicting identity
supervision without cross-view association. Gaussian-level labels also do not
explicitly encode the floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy or its containment and
spatial relations. Recovering this structure requires joint reasoning over
Gaussian semantics, persistent instance identities, and reconstructed geometry.

To address these challenges, we propose PanoGraphGS, an end-to-end framework
that integrates panoptic 3D Gaussian representation learning with hierarchical
3D scene graph construction. PanoGraphGS jointly learns semantic and instance
features anchored to shared Gaussian geometry. The semantic branch combines
residual feature projection and category prototypes with confidence-weighted
supervision, while the instance branch associates view-local pseudo-labels with
persistent Gaussian instance identities to ensure consistent object
correspondence across views. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the
resulting panoptic Gaussian representation supports both panoptic segmentation
and direct Gaussian-level decoding. The
semantic-aware hierarchical reasoning module combines structural semantics with
Gaussian geometry to recover the floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy
and its containment and spatial relations, enabling structured spatial queries
such as locating the bed1 in the living room on floor1. CLIP [10] is further used to assign functional
categories to rooms. Our main contributions are:

We propose Prototype-Based Semantic Learning, which jointly optimizes 2D rendered and 3D Gaussian features in a unified semantic space, overcoming the limitation of optimizing features in only the 2D or 3D domain.

We propose Association-Based Instance Learning, which associates view-local instance masks with persistent identities for cross-frame consistent panoptic prediction, with confidence-aware supervision reducing the impact of unreliable labels.

We propose a semantic-aware hierarchical 3D scene graph construction method that organizes learned panoptic Gaussians into a floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy without additional training or RGB-D inputs.

We achieve state-of-the-art performance in both 2D panoptic segmentation and 3D scene graph construction.

2. We propose Association-Based Instance Learning, which associates view-local instance masks with persistent identities for cross-frame consistent panoptic prediction, with confidence-aware supervision reducing the impact of unreliable labels.

title: SynCalib: Breaking Dataset Shortcuts in LiDAR-Camera Calibration via Extrinsic-Controllable Synthesis
authors: Huihua Zhu,Shuyang Zhang,Dongqing Chen,Zhuo Yu,Jianhao Jiao,Yilong Zhu,Siyu Teng,Xiaopin Zhong,Zongze Wu
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Online LiDAR-camera calibration remains a fundamental yet challenging task in the
field of robotics.
Recently, deep learning-based data-driven approaches have emerged, offering high-precision,
targetless calibration capabilities.
However, existing methods often suffer from a critical dataset shortcut phenomenon
due to the lack of extrinsic diversity in their training data.
Networks tend to overfit to fixed nominal extrinsic configurations,
leading to severe performance degradation and poor generalization in real-world
deployments.
To address this limitation, we propose a highly generalizable data generation
framework tailored for training LiDAR-camera calibration networks.
Our framework leverages existing omnidirectional image datasets annotated with depth
ground truth to synthesize multi-modal calibration data under rigorous extrinsic
constraints.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that the data generated by our pipeline significantly
enhances the generalization and robustness of typical learning-based calibration
networks.
Furthermore, we conduct comprehensive real-world evaluations across various camera-LiDAR
configurations, validating the zero-shot transfer capability of models trained
exclusively on our synthetic data.
To facilitate future research and community use, the code for data generation, the
pre-trained models, and online benchmark datasets will be made publicly available.
introduction:
Multi-modal systems have become indispensable for modern robotics, with the combination
of cameras and LiDARs serving as the predominant
configuration [1, 2, 3].
Accurately estimating the extrinsic parameters between these sensors to achieve
precise spatial alignment is a critical prerequisite for downstream tasks such as
perception [4], navigation [5].

During manufacturing, robots typically undergo precise extrinsic calibration in
dedicated facilities using specialized fiducial markers (e.g., checkerboards).
While these target-based methods achieve exceptional accuracy by leveraging known
geometric priors, sensors deployed in the field inevitably experience extrinsic
drift due to mechanical vibrations and thermal stresses in harsh operational
environments [6].
Returning robots to the factory for re-calibration incurs prohibitive maintenance
costs and system downtime.
Consequently, targetless online calibration, which estimates extrinsics directly
from natural scenes without specialized facilities, has emerged as a practical
alternative.
Despite being marginally less accurate than target-based approaches, its operational
convenience and scalability make it highly desirable for mass-produced robotic systems.

Deep learning-based calibration methods have emerged as the dominant paradigm
in recent years, for its adaptability to various scenarios and excellent performance.
However, these methods suffer from a critical flaw of severe dataset bias [7, 8, 9].
Recent models are typically trained on several public datasets
(e.g., KITTI [10] and nuScenes [11]) with highly
restricted sensor setups.
This scarcity of diverse extrinsic configurations leads to severe representational
homogeneity in the training data (Fig. 1).
Consequently, instead of learning meaningful cross-modal associations, network
resorts to shortcut learning: It merely memorizes the spatial distribution
priors of LiDAR projections to minimize training loss.
Ultimately, this causes existing algorithms to overfit to the specific LiDAR distribution
and fail to provide reliable extrinsics in practice.

To tackle this challenge, our core insight is to systematically diversify the extrinsic
ground truths in the training data, thereby eliminating the conditions that foster
shortcut learning.
To this end, we propose SynCalib, a novel offline data synthesis framework
designed for arbitrary LiDAR-camera configurations.
By leveraging existing simulated environments equipped with omnidirectional cameras,
SynCalib synthesizes large-scale LiDAR-camera data pairs with fully controllable
extrinsic parameters.
This guarantees the richness of extrinsic configurations during network training,
fundamentally enhancing the model’s zero-shot generalization capabilities.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

A calibration data generation framework that enables model
training prior to physical sensor deployment.
Models trained with our synthesized data can be deployed in a zero-shot manner,
and effectively circumvent shortcut learning.

An extrinsics-controllable synthesis pipeline leveraging a simulated
omnidirectional visual system with dense depth ground truth.
This pipeline features fully controllable extrinsic sampling to ensure high-fidelity
data synthesis.

Comprehensive experiments demonstrating that our system successfully overcomes
the performance degradation caused by dataset bias in traditional training paradigms.

1. A calibration data generation framework that enables model
training prior to physical sensor deployment.
Models trained with our synthesized data can be deployed in a zero-shot manner,
and effectively circumvent shortcut learning.

2. An extrinsics-controllable synthesis pipeline leveraging a simulated
omnidirectional visual system with dense depth ground truth.
This pipeline features fully controllable extrinsic sampling to ensure high-fidelity
data synthesis.

3. Comprehensive experiments demonstrating that our system successfully overcomes
the performance degradation caused by dataset bias in traditional training paradigms.

title: OmniVLoc: Topo-metric Visual Localization for Omnidirectional Cameras
authors: Zhuo Yu,Shuyang Zhang,Huihua Zhu,Wenjia Ouyang,Zuo Zuo,Jianhao Jiao,Yilong Zhu,Xiaopin Zhong,Zongze Wu
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Omnidirectional cameras provide surround-view information, significantly overcoming
the field-of-view constraints for traditional visual localization systems.
However, existing localization systems fail to fully exploit the characteristics
of omnidirectional cameras, struggling to deliver accurate and robust localization
performance amidst scene content variations and illumination-induced appearance changes.
In this work, we propose OmniVLoc, a surround-view localization system based on
a topo-metric framework.
By integrating state-of-the-art global place recognition and monocular depth estimation methods,
we introduce a multi-constrained visual localization paradigm.
By solving a scale-aware pose graph and performing precise spherical bundle adjustment,
we accurately recover the metric-level pose for each query frame.
Furthermore, a hierarchical verification mechanism is designed to filter out erroneous
outputs across different stages, effectively bolstering the overall system robustness.
Extensive experiments on both public and our custom datasets validate the superior
accuracy and reliability of OmniVLoc.
To benefit the community, our source code and dataset will be made publicly available upon publication.
introduction:
Accurate metric visual localization is a fundamental prerequisite
for autonomous navigation in mobile robot systems [1, 2].
While traditional structure-based systems achieve high precision by establishing
2D-3D correspondences against pre-built 3D maps, they face significant scalability
bottlenecks.
Constructing and storing dense 3D points, local descriptors, and co-visibility graphs
incur prohibitive overhead in large-scale environments [3].
Furthermore, maintaining these 3D maps over extended periods is exceedingly difficult;
feature matching and triangulation are highly sensitive to viewpoint shifts and
illumination-induced appearance variations.
Consequently, dynamic environmental changes and map obsolescence drastically
degrade localization performance [4, 5], rendering
traditional 3D map-based paradigms inadequate for large-scale deployments and
lifelong autonomy [6] (as conceptually compared in Fig. 1).

In contrast, recent topo-metric localization paradigms [7, 8, 9]
replace dense point clouds with sparse topological image nodes,
significantly reducing storage and maintenance costs while performing local metric
recovery at these nodes.
However, existing topo-metric methods face two major limitations.
First, they typically rely on conventional cameras with a narrow field of view (FOV).
This necessitates redundant multi-view storage to capture the full scene during mapping,
and the limited visual context severely exacerbates perceptual aliasing during localization [10].
Second, local metric recovery in these systems is fragile in complex environments:
stereo-vision-based methods are bounded by physical baselines, while traditional
monocular approaches suffer from severe scale ambiguity and drift, compromising
absolute pose accuracy.

To address these challenges, we propose OmniVLoc, a surround-view localization system
based on a topo-metric framework.
By introducing this ultra-wide FOV camera, we effectively overcome the issues of
perceptual aliasing and map redundancy.
To achieve precise metric recovery without relying on pre-built 3D geometry or
stereo baselines, we introduce a multi-constrained visual localization paradigm.
Specifically, we leverage a visual foundation model (VFM) for monocular depth estimation
and formulate the query-to-map registration as geometric hypotheses regarding the
unknown depth scale.
By solving a scale-aware pose graph and performing precise spherical bundle adjustment,
OmniVLoc accurately recovers the metric-level pose for each query frame.
Additionally, a hierarchical verification mechanism is designed to filter out erroneous outputs,
effectively bolstering system robustness against illumination and scene variations.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

A continuous metric localization framework for surround-view topo-metric maps.
This framework obviates the need for pre-built 3D map points or depth maps,
providing a unified formulation for precise metric localization using
omnidirectional cameras.

A scale-aware factor graph optimization scheme.
It leverages VFM-derived monocular depth with scale uncertainty to construct
multi-hypothesis 3D-2D visual constraints, tightly coupled with temporal
motion priors to recover accurate absolute scales and poses.

A hierarchical verification mechanism based on multiple observation
and motion priors, ensuring system stability under severe perceptual aliasing
and feature degradation.

Extensive experiments on both public and our custom datasets, which validate
the superior accuracy and robustness of OmniVLoc compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

1. A continuous metric localization framework for surround-view topo-metric maps.
This framework obviates the need for pre-built 3D map points or depth maps,
providing a unified formulation for precise metric localization using
omnidirectional cameras.

2. A scale-aware factor graph optimization scheme.
It leverages VFM-derived monocular depth with scale uncertainty to construct
multi-hypothesis 3D-2D visual constraints, tightly coupled with temporal
motion priors to recover accurate absolute scales and poses.

3. A hierarchical verification mechanism based on multiple observation
and motion priors, ensuring system stability under severe perceptual aliasing
and feature degradation.

4. Extensive experiments on both public and our custom datasets, which validate
the superior accuracy and robustness of OmniVLoc compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
