title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
authors: Weinan Zhang,Chunhua Shen,Tianfan Xue,Bin Zhao,Bingqi Jiang,Zihan Guo,Zicai Cui,Yang Li,Ming Zhou,Xinyuan Chen,Lihe Ding,Xiao Chen,Yujin Wang,Shi Guo,Junting Dong,Tao Lu,Xing Shen,Haoyu Guo,Yao Mu,Haiyong Yu,Haoxiang Ma,Fuxian Huang,Qiaojun Yu,Yunsong Zhou,Kailin Li,Zirui Wang,Yufei Xue,Weishuai Zeng,Tao Huang,Zhigang Wang,Junli Liu,Pengyuan Wu,Pingrui Zhang,Haotian Wang,Dongzhan Zhou,Jiafei Cao,Feng Yuan,Xinyi Ye,Quanli Xuan,Mulin Yu,Shangding Gu,Kaiwen Song,Dong Wang,Jiarui Li,Kehui Liu,Zhongjie Jia,Dongjiang Li,Jiacheng Bao,Haoran Yang,Zhaoqing Chen,Yiming Sun,Bowen Zhou
abstract: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).
introduction:
For decades, artificial intelligence (AI) operated inside computers primarily, processing digital data and generating symbolic outputs without directly altering the physical world. Recent advances extend AI beyond this digital boundary by enabling it to perceive and understand physical environments, reason about them, and act within them. This emerging capability has given rise to physical AI, which studies how artificial systems shall interact with the physical world. Yet, what exactly is physical AI? What does its technical landscape look like, and what core challenges does it entail? And, what are typical application scenarios of physical AI? This chapter addresses these questions by tracing AI’s expansion from digital to physical space, defining physical AI and its boundaries with neighboring fields, and examining its core characteristics, system architectures, and application domains.

Artificial intelligence has developed through several complementary traditions, from symbolic reasoning and knowledge representation to statistical learning and deep neural networks. Deep learning substantially advances the ability of computational systems to extract useful representations from complex data, with major improvements in speech recognition, visual recognition, and related information-processing tasks. These achievements establish representation learning as a central methodological foundation of contemporary AI (lecun2015deep).

In this chapter, Digital AI refers to capabilities that operate directly on digital representations, such as text, images, software, and structured records. This definition emphasizes the system’s operational interface over the origin of its data. For example, while an image may depict a physical scene, recognizing its contents does not require the system to actually interact with that environment. Physical AI, in contrast, applies intelligence to perceive, influence, and adapt to physical processes through direct interaction. Definition 1.1 in Section 1.2 further clarifies this fundamental distinction.

The distinction becomes apparent when comparing the description of an action with its execution. An AI system may correctly explain how to pick up a glass while remaining unable to estimate its mass, establish a stable grasp, detect incipient slip, or adjust contact forces. Successful manipulation depends on relationships among geometry, material properties, sensing, and actuation that cannot be assessed solely through the linguistic plausibility of a response. The relevant criterion is whether the system produces the intended physical outcome under the conditions encountered.

This distinction is related to the symbol grounding problem of how symbols can acquire meaning through a system’s own capacities rather than solely through interpretation by an external observer. The formulation by harnad1990symbol identifies the limitations of defining symbols only through other symbols and motivates their connection to nonsymbolic representations. For physical AI, the corresponding engineering problem is to connect concepts such as support, contact, and stability to observations and action consequences.

Grounding should not, however, be reduced to a categorical claim that digital models possess no physical knowledge. Models trained on descriptions, images, videos, or simulated trajectories can acquire useful regularities concerning the physical world. The unresolved issue is whether these regularities support reliable intervention across changes in objects, environments, and operating conditions. Semantic competence, predictive accuracy, and physical competence are related but distinct properties.

Figure 1.1 summarizes this expansion from digital tools and simulated agents to real-world single-agent systems, multi-agent collaboration, and infrastructure-level physical AI. Across these physical deployments, the unit of analysis extends from an isolated model to the integrated system of computation, sensing, actuation, communication, and environment. This perspective has important historical precedents. brooks1991intelligence demonstrates an approach to robotics in which intelligent behavior arises through direct perception-action coupling, challenging the assumption that autonomous behavior must depend on a centralized symbolic description of the world. Contemporary physical AI extends this longstanding concern with situated action by incorporating learned representations, scalable training, and predictive models.

Physical AI operates under constraints that cannot be removed by increasing model capacity alone. Three characteristics are particularly important, namely, consequential interaction under uncertainty, perception of evolving physical states, and the integration of empirical learning with physical structure.

Physical systems are only partially observable. Object properties, external disturbances, and equipment conditions may be unknown or change during execution. Actions also affect the evidence available to the system. Moving a camera changes visibility, probing a surface reveals compliance, and applying force may alter an object’s configuration. Perception and action consequently form an interdependent process.

Physical interaction can incur recovery costs and irreversible consequences. A simulated episode can often be restarted from a saved state, whereas a spilled chemical, damaged component, or contaminated sample may require substantial intervention or may be impossible to restore. The operational distinction is that physical systems generally lack an exact, inexpensive reset mechanism. Planning must therefore consider the recoverability of future states as well as the likelihood of immediate task success.

Physical AI requires observations that are temporally and spatially meaningful. Vision can describe appearance and geometry, while force, touch, proprioception, temperature, pressure, and other measurements reveal complementary aspects of interaction. A manipulation system, for example, may need to distinguish visual contact from load-bearing contact and a completed motion from a successfully transferred object.

Although sensors typically produce sampled digital measurements, the processes they measure evolve in continuous time and may include discrete events such as impact, grasp release, or equipment switching. Reliable interpretation therefore depends on sampling rates, calibration, synchronization, coordinate frames, and measurement uncertainty. A correct estimate obtained too late may be unusable for control. More generally, computation and physical dynamics must be analyzed together because execution timing can affect system behavior (lee2008cyber).

Data provide evidence about real operating conditions, including effects that are difficult to model analytically. Physical knowledge provides structure that can restrict implausible predictions and reduce the burden of learning. Conservation relationships, symmetries, geometric constraints, and governing equations can be incorporated through model architectures, training objectives, simulation, or constrained decision procedures. Physics-informed machine learning formalizes several ways of combining observations with mathematical descriptions of physical processes (karniadakis2021physics).

The appropriate balance depends on the task. Explicit models may be effective when governing relationships are sufficiently understood, whereas learned components can represent uncertain interactions or compensate for model mismatch. Physical priors are themselves conditional on assumptions and operating regimes. For example, an inaccurate friction model or an inappropriate rigid-body approximation can produce systematic errors. Physical consistency therefore requires validation within the task’s operating regime, regardless of the model family.

Together, these characteristics shift evaluation toward closed-loop performance. Relevant measures include task completion, robustness to disturbance, response time, resource consumption, and recovery from failure. Prediction accuracy remains valuable, but its practical significance depends on how prediction errors propagate through decisions and physical execution.

Physical AI is motivated by tasks that require systems to act on the physical world. Flexible manufacturing requires adaptation to variations in parts and processes. Transportation and energy systems require coordinated responses to changing demand and operating conditions. Scientific experimentation requires procedures to be adjusted in response to measurements. Furthermore, extreme environments, such as deep space and the deep sea, drive the need for local autonomy, as communication constraints and physical hazards severely limit continuous human intervention.

These demands do not imply that established automation is inadequate in every setting. Carefully engineered automation remains effective where tasks and operating conditions can be specified in advance. The additional research challenge is to preserve useful performance when relevant conditions change and exhaustive preprogramming becomes impractical. Physical AI addresses this challenge by integrating interactive learning with perception, inference, prediction, and adaptation.

Several technical developments support this direction. Sensing and local computation provide the practical interfaces for observing and influencing physical processes. Simulation supplies controlled environments for training and evaluation, while methods for transfer from simulation to reality reduce dependence on collecting every training example on physical hardware. For example, tobin2017domain demonstrate that varying simulated visual conditions can support transfer of a vision model to real robotic tasks. Such results establish a useful transfer mechanism, while leaving its effectiveness dependent on the relationship between training variation and deployment conditions.

Learned physical models provide another foundation. Graph network simulators have demonstrated the ability to represent interacting particles and predict dynamics across fluids, rigid solids, and deformable materials within evaluated settings. These models illustrate how structured learning can support physical prediction beyond a single fixed configuration (sanchezgonzalez2020learning). For autonomous action, their potential value lies in evaluating candidate interventions before execution, provided that prediction errors and operating limits are understood.

Large pretrained models also offer reusable semantic knowledge. For example, RT-2 shows that vision-language pretraining can be combined with robot demonstrations to support robotic action and improve generalization in the reported experiments (brohan2023rt2). This provides evidence that capabilities developed through digital learning can contribute to physical interaction when connected to appropriate action data and interfaces.

These developments make it increasingly feasible to combine digital capabilities, physical models, and control mechanisms to study how systems acquire transferable physical skills while maintaining measurable performance within specified operating conditions.

At its most general, physical AI concerns the capacity of an artificial system to interact with the physical world. This monograph uses physical AI for this artificial-system scope. The term physical intelligence is retained for general capacities, bodily mechanisms, and source-specific usage. The following definition makes the notion precise.

Physical AI is the capacity of an artificial system to perceive physical environment states, maintain task-relevant representations of physical relationships and action consequences, and select and execute interventions through physical interfaces, using feedback to achieve objectives under physical, operational, and computational constraints.

This definition identifies a functional scope rather than a particular architecture. Representations may be explicit, implicit, or distributed across several components. They need not constitute a complete internal simulator, and action selection need not depend on symbolic reasoning. What matters is whether the integrated system can use information about physical conditions to guide and revise its behavior.

Four implications clarify the definition. First, physical grounding requires observations to be connected to relevant quantities, events, or conditions in the world. Second, the system must have a path for intervention, whether through direct actuation or commands to controlled equipment. Third, feedback must inform subsequent behavior, allowing discrepancies between expected and observed outcomes to affect execution. Fourth, claims of intelligent capability should be supported by evidence of task-relevant inference, prediction, planning, or adaptation, rather than inferred merely from the presence of sensors and actuators.

These criteria define a continuum of capability. A fixed feedback regulator and a system that adapts across changing tasks may share essential control principles, yet differ substantially in the breadth of conditions they can handle. The distinction between automation and Physical AI is therefore most useful when expressed through demonstrated capabilities and operating assumptions, rather than an absolute technological boundary.

Terminological care is also necessary because physical intelligence has an established, more specific usage in mechanics and robotics. sitti2021physical uses the term to describe functions such as sensing, actuation, memory, and computation physically encoded in an agent’s body. The broader definition of Physical AI adopted here includes such contributions while also encompassing computational and distributed systems that interact with physical processes. It should be understood as this chapter’s organizing framework, rather than a claim that the literature has converged on one definition.

Finally, key components should be distinguished from a complete system. A learned simulator, perception model, or action planner may provide an essential Physical AI capability. In isolation, however, it does not satisfy the system-level requirement for closed-loop physical intervention. This distinction allows purely digital modules to be recognized as enabling technologies without attributing autonomous physical competence to them prematurely.

Embodied AI posits that artificial intelligence requires a body to house the system and drive its active sensorimotor relationship with the environment (pfeifer2004embodied). The concept of embodiment focuses on how this morphology, along with sensing and action capabilities, directly shapes environmental interactions and guides behavior. Importantly, embodiment is by no means limited to humanoid or biologically inspired designs. For physically deployed agents, research further highlights how mechanical structures and material properties can intrinsically support adaptive behavior, thereby reducing the control burden on a centralized controller (pfeifer2007self).

Nor does embodied AI necessarily require a deployed physical robot. Simulated agents are widely used to study navigation, interaction, and learning under embodied constraints (shridhar2020alfworld). Habitat, for example, was introduced as a platform for training and evaluating virtual embodied agents in three-dimensional environments (savva2019habitat). Embodied AI therefore includes both simulated and physically deployed agents.

Within this chapter’s framework, physically deployed embodied AI constitutes a major realization of physical AI. Its characteristic analytical focus is the agent and its particular sensing and action capabilities. Physical AI adopts an additional system-level perspective, encompassing arrangements in which sensing, decision-making, and actuation are distributed across infrastructure. Figure 1.3 summarizes these distinctions and their overlap.

Consider an adaptive traffic-management system that estimates network conditions, changes signal timings, and evaluates the resulting traffic flows. Its interaction with the world is mediated by distributed detectors, communication links, and signal controllers rather than a single mobile body. Similar arrangements can be considered for factory coordination or power-system operation, provided that the system actually closes the loop between observations, decisions, and physical consequences. These are illustrative applications of the proposed definition, not claims that every traffic controller, factory scheduler, or grid-management platform possesses advanced intelligence.

Scientific equipment provides a concrete research example. Degrave and colleagues demonstrated deep reinforcement learning for magnetic control of plasma configurations in the TCV tokamak. The controller interacts with a physical process through the machine’s measurement and actuation infrastructure (degrave2022magnetic). Under the present framework, this qualifies as Physical AI even though the system lacks the conventional form of a mobile or manipulative robot.

Such systems are not independent of physical embodiment in the broadest sense, because sensors, actuators, and material processes remain indispensable. Their distinguishing feature is that the physical interface is distributed across an installation or network. Within this monograph’s framework, embodied AI emphasizes how an agent’s body shapes sensing and action, while physical AI emphasizes closed-loop intervention in real physical processes, including through distributed infrastructure. The two overlap in physically deployed embodied systems.

Physical AI intersects closely with cyber-physical systems (CPS), but the concepts describe different aspects of a system. CPS concerns the integration of computation with physical processes, including the consequences of timing, concurrency, and interaction between software and its physical environment (lee2008cyber). Physical AI concerns the capabilities exercised through that integration, including interpreting conditions, anticipating consequences, choosing interventions, and adapting behavior.

A CPS may operate effectively through fixed control logic without possessing broad inference or adaptation capabilities. Conversely, a physically intelligent system depends on the engineering properties of its computational and physical infrastructure, including dependable sensing, timely communication, and executable control. Physical AI can therefore be understood as a capability layer within many CPS architectures. Describing it as a possible development toward greater autonomy is useful, provided that this does not imply that CPS research excludes advanced cognition or that learning automatically improves an engineered system.

Digital twins occupy a different position. They provide digital representations associated with identifiable physical counterparts, with connections that support updating and comparison between physical and digital states. The literature identifies multiple characteristics and implementation choices, making it important to specify how a proposed twin is connected to its physical counterpart (jones2020characterising).

Within a Physical AI architecture, a predictive digital twin can support state estimation, diagnosis, and evaluation of alternative interventions. It may help estimate how a production line would respond to a schedule change or how equipment behavior would change under another operating condition. Such uses require more than a visually accurate replica. The representation must capture the variables and dynamics relevant to the decision.

A digital twin does not necessarily select or execute actions autonomously, and a Physical AI system need not maintain a comprehensive twin. A compact learned dynamics model may be sufficient for a particular control task. Likewise, a generic world model becomes a digital twin only when it is meaningfully associated with a specific physical counterpart and maintained through an appropriate update relationship. Counterfactual predictions remain conditional on the validity of the model and its assumptions.

These distinctions establish complementary roles. CPS describes the integration of computational and physical processes. Embodied AI examines intelligence through situated sensorimotor interaction. Digital twins provide representations tied to physical counterparts. Physical AI, in the framework developed here, identifies the capacity to combine perception, physical understanding, decision-making, and feedback into effective intervention. This system-level perspective provides the basis for the architectural elements discussed in the following sections.

Definition 1.1 characterizes Physical AI as the capacity to perceive physical states, maintain task-relevant representations, and execute interventions through feedback. In practice, this capacity takes the form of a persistent closed loop. Information processing and decision-making must be translated into physical actions, and subsequent behavior must be revised according to observed outcomes. Physical AI therefore operates through a cycle of perception, modeling, prediction, decision-making, execution, and feedback, rather than through a one-shot mapping from input to output.

As Section 1.2 emphasizes, Physical AI is not synonymous with robotic intelligence. Whether a system exhibits it depends on its ability to close the loop between perception and action, not on its morphology. The elements discussed in this section apply equally to autonomous vehicles, industrial equipment, automated experimentation platforms, intelligent buildings, and energy infrastructures. In such systems, perception, computation, decision-making, and execution are often distributed across devices, edge nodes, cloud platforms, and physical facilities rather than concentrated within a single device.

Operating in a continuously changing and uncertain world also means that actions are constrained by dynamics, geometry, time, energy, materials, and safety requirements, and that their consequences are not always reversible, as Section 1.1 discusses. A physically intelligent system must therefore answer not only “What should be done?” but also “Can it be done under the current conditions?”, “How can it be done safely?”, and “Does the execution produce the intended outcome?” Organized around these questions, Physical AI comprises four closely related elements, including physical state perception and estimation, physical world models, physical decision-making together with planning and control, and closed-loop feedback and multiscale adaptation. They correspond respectively to perception, representation, intervention, and feedback in the definition. The first three together constitute the physically intelligent agent, while the fourth connects the agent with the physical world into a continuously running loop. The relations among these elements, together with the data, hardware, and physical world on which they depend, are illustrated in Figure 1.4.

Physical AI begins with information about the environment, task-relevant objects, and the system itself. Vision conveys identity, pose, geometry, and motion. Force and tactile sensing reveal contact, friction, and material properties (dahiya2009tactile), while acoustic sensing detects collisions and vibrations. Proprioception measures the system’s own configuration and load, and industrial systems add process variables such as temperature, pressure, and current. Chapter 9 treats the sensors themselves. The concern here is turning their signals into an estimate of physical state.

Measurements are incomplete, noisy, delayed, and often misaligned across modalities, so calibration, multimodal fusion, and state estimation are needed to obtain a temporally consistent state with explicit uncertainty (Kalman1960; Baltrušaitis et al., 2019). Perception also supports active information acquisition. When observations are insufficient for a decision, the system can change its viewpoint, reposition sensors, or probe objects to estimate mass, stiffness, or friction, folding information acquisition into the decision loop (Bajcsy, 1988).

State estimates are organized into a world model, which describes the environment, the actions available to the system, and how physical states evolve over time (ha2018world; lecun2022path). It has two interdependent aspects. Representation captures what the model holds about the current world, and prediction anticipates what the world becomes after a given action.

Physical representations cover objects, poses, geometry, and spatial relations, together with velocities, masses, contacts, forces, material properties, affordances, and task constraints. A cup is at once a shape with a pose and an object that can be grasped, holds liquid, and spills when tilted. Representations may be explicit (maps, object lists, equations of motion, relational graphs), implicit (learned from data), or hybrid, combining physical priors with learning to retain interpretability while correcting for unmodeled effects. An effective world model is updated with each new observation and distinguishes directly observed, estimated, and unobserved states.

Prediction estimates the consequences of a particular action, covering trajectories, contact outcomes, equipment conditions, task success, and safety hazards over time scales from milliseconds to hours. Predictions may come from physical equations and simulators (raissi2019physics) or from transition patterns learned from data (sanchezgonzalez2020learning). Practical systems combine the two and revise predictions and their uncertainty online. In scenario simulation, the decision process submits candidate actions and the world model returns predicted outcomes with their uncertainty, enabling counterfactual comparison before anything is executed. This simulation runs online, unlike the physics engines and generative environments of Chapter 4, which are used offline to produce training data and test policies.

Physical decision-making selects actions from task objectives, the current state, predicted outcomes, and real-world constraints, usually through a hierarchy (kaelbling2011hierarchical; sutton1999options). At the top, the system sets goals and constraints and, when several physical agents share a task, allocates and coordinates subtasks among them. Foundation models for robot manipulation reason about the task and scene, decompose goals into executable steps, and produce action policies. Foundation models for whole-body motor control provide reusable feedback policies for executing movement goals and correcting deviations (zeng2025behavior; zeng2026scaling). The levels differ mainly in time scale, from minutes or hours for task allocation to seconds for policies and milliseconds for motor commands. The boundary separating task-level reasoning and action-policy generation from motor control and feedback correction varies across systems.

Execution takes many forms, from joints and end effectors to steering and braking, instrument scheduling, or valves, pumps, and switches. An action is thus best understood as an observable intervention that changes a physical object, environment, or process. Such interventions must be feasible, safe, and timely. A logically valid plan can still fail because of collisions, actuator limits, or latency, so safety checks precede execution, and monitoring and emergency stops stay active throughout.

Physical AI revises behavior according to the observed consequences of action. After each command, the system perceives again, checks whether the intended result is achieved, and updates its state estimate together with its world model and plan. When outcomes deviate from predictions, it identifies the cause and compensates, retries, replans, or terminates safely.

The loop resides in no single module but in the connections among the elements. Perception supplies the state, the world model answers action queries from the decision process, commands act on the world through actuators, and sensors return the consequences to perception (Figure 1.4). The loop thus closes through the physical world rather than inside the agent. Fast reactive control, such as tightening a grip when an object begins to slip, may bypass the world model and respond directly to the current state.

Feedback operates at three nested scales. The fastest loop connects motor control and feedback correction with the actuators and sensors, adjusting position, velocity, or force in real time. The task-level loop connects task-level reasoning and action-policy generation with the world model and revises plans as the task progresses. The slowest passes through the offline data and simulation infrastructure, where deployment data drive continual learning (parisi2019continual) and form a data flywheel. In multi-agent and infrastructure-scale systems these loops may be distributed across devices that coordinate toward a common objective, and humans may join them by providing goals, demonstrations, supervision, and intervention.

Physical AI therefore lies not in producing a plausible action or plan, but in sustaining this cycle of observation, prediction, action, verification, and revision under real physical constraints, whether the system is a single robot or distributed infrastructure.

Section 1.1 contrasts digital intelligence, whose objects of computation and evaluation are recorded content, with the Physical AI defined in Definition 1.1. This subsection develops three claims about what that contrast means for the trajectory of AI. Physical AI is the stage at which artificial intelligence moves from understanding and generating digital information to perceiving, predicting, and changing physical processes. It builds on digital intelligence rather than replacing it and provides one of the important paths toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).

The first extension concerns what the system perceives. Digital intelligence works on symbols and pixels that come from prior collection, curation, and encoding. Physical AI deals with physical states directly (Section 1.1), including the pose and velocity of objects, forces and friction at contact surfaces, pressure and temperature in fluids, and the composition and structure of materials. These states are continuous and evolve over time. They can only be partially observed through noisy sensors, and vision, touch, force, and other modalities must be fused within a common spatiotemporal frame. The object of perception thus shifts from previously recorded content to the current state of a world that keeps changing.

The second extension concerns what the system produces. Because physical systems lack an inexpensive reset (Section 1.1), a grasp, an injection, or a turn of the steering wheel changes the subsequent state of the system and often cannot be undone. Physical AI must therefore predict, before acting, how the world will evolve if a given action is taken. This prediction is interventional in nature and depends on causal relations and dynamics, not merely on statistical correlation (scholkopf2021causal).

These new capabilities do not make Physical AI a replacement for digital intelligence. The common-sense and domain knowledge accumulated in foundation models is the basis on which Physical AI understands and plans tasks (ichter2023saycan). In turn, Physical AI grounds that knowledge in measurable changes of state and tests it through real interaction. A large language model can search the literature, propose a hypothesis, and write an experimental protocol, but whether the protocol succeeds depends on accurate pipetting, stable temperature control, and correct sample handling. Only when digital reasoning is closed with physical execution can AI take part in the full process from posing a question and running an experiment to drawing a conclusion.

Section 1.1 explains that Physical AI enlarges the unit of analysis from the model to the system, and this enlargement has concrete consequences for how capability is attributed. The same policy may perform very differently on robot arms of different precision or in workshops with different lighting, and task success also depends on engineering conditions such as sensor calibration, fixture design, and safety interlocks. The shift also changes how general capability should be understood and measured, which leads to the third claim.

Benchmarks in digital environments are prone to overfitting, and it is hard to rule out memorization caused by contamination of the training data. The physical world is open, continuous, and impossible to enumerate in advance, and whether a task has been completed is decided directly by physical outcomes. Moravec’s paradox points in the same direction, highlighting that perceptual and motor skills that humans find effortless are among the hardest for machines to acquire (moravec1988mind). Physical AI therefore provides a demanding test of generality along four axes, including generalization to new objects and scenes as well as new task combinations, transfer across embodiments and tasks as well as from simulation to reality (tobin2017domain; openai2018dexterous), robustness to disturbances and sensor degradation as well as environmental drift, and long-term autonomy over days or months with little human intervention. Because mistakes in the physical world are often irreversible, evaluation cannot rest on task success rate alone. Real-time performance, sample efficiency, energy consumption, risk controllability, and recoverability after failure must be considered together, and they frequently trade off against one another. Physical AI is not the only such path, as mathematical reasoning, scientific discovery, and social interaction advance general capability from other directions, but it is the one in which capability is checked against physical reality.

Taking the degree of coupling between AI and the physical world as the axis, the position of Physical AI can be stated more concretely. At the loosely coupled end, AI acts as a digital tool that assists humans with design, analysis, and decision-making but leaves execution entirely to them. Next, simulated agents perceive and act in simulators or digital twins (jones2020characterising), where trial and error is cheap and safe but limited by the gap between simulation and reality. Physical AI proper begins when AI closes the loop in the real world. It starts with single-agent systems, such as a robot, vehicle, drone, or autonomous laboratory platform, where most current embodied intelligence research is concentrated. It then extends to multi-agent collaboration, in which groups of agents accomplish tasks that no single agent can, and finally to infrastructure-level Physical AI, in which distributed sensing, computing, and actuation resources embedded in cities, power grids, factories, and research facilities are scheduled and governed through common protocols. Section 1.5.6 returns to these three stages as the recurring physical compositions of deployed systems. In a network of autonomous laboratories spread across institutions, for example, the question is no longer only whether an experiment can be completed, but also how resources are allocated, how processes are audited, and how data ownership and reproducibility are established. These stages coexist and support one another rather than replacing each other. Digital tools and simulation continue to supply knowledge, data, and safety validation to physical systems. Physical AI thus occupies the tightly coupled end of this axis, where the value of AI is realized as a change in physical processes rather than only as the production of information. The application landscape in Section 1.5 makes this coupling concrete across industries, and Chapter 10 examines Physical AGI as a long-term research goal.

Physical AI connects the interpretation of physical state with decisions that change it, and its applications span individual robots, autonomous vehicles, instrument networks, factories, cities, and scientific facilities. These settings differ in scale by orders of magnitude, yet the questions that determine whether a system is useful remain largely the same, concerning what the task requires, what the environment allows, what resources are available, and which decisions may be taken without a human in the loop. Whether a particular configuration amounts to a deployable system is ultimately reflected in the cost of the valid work it produces. The subsections that follow first state the closed loop that every application instantiates, together with the four dimensions along which applications are described, namely task, environment, resources, and autonomy. They then survey four domains, from industrial operation through everyday services and public infrastructure to scientific inquiry, and finally extract the system archetypes that recur across those domains.

Every application of Physical AI instantiates one closed loop as shown in Figure 1.5. Physical perception acquires signals from the environment through sensors. State understanding assembles these signals into estimates of the objects, agents, and processes present, together with the representations and world models of how they evolve. Prediction and imagination extrapolate the estimated state forward and evaluate candidate actions, whether through learned dynamics or explicit physical simulation. Decision making and planning select and sequence actions under task and process constraints. Physical action executes the selected behavior through control and actuation, and the resulting environmental feedback becomes the input to the next cycle of perception. These stages give Definition 1.1 its operational form. Section 1.3 groups them into four elements comprising physical state perception and estimation, world modeling for representation and prediction, decision-making with planning and control, and closed-loop feedback with multiscale adaptation. The loop as a whole, rather than any single stage, defines an application. A system that perceives without acting merely observes its environment, and one that acts without state understanding merely executes a prescribed motion.

Conventional automation already incorporates feedback control, so the loop itself is not new (Åström and Murray, 2008). What distinguishes Physical AI is how the loop is sustained when conditions depart from those anticipated at design time, through adapting to changing conditions, interpreting unfamiliar tasks, and transferring knowledge across operations. Classical control holds a process near a setpoint under modeled disturbances. Physical AI re-estimates state, re-plans, and recovers when the task or the environment changes. The distinction is graded rather than binary. Applications occupy a spectrum from fixed procedures with local adaptation, such as an industrial manipulator re-grasping a shifted part, to open-ended task interpretation, in which a system must infer what is wanted from instruction, demonstration, or context (ichter2023saycan).

The position of an application on this spectrum is determined by the task rather than by the industry in which it appears. An application can be characterized along four dimensions, namely task, environment, resources, and autonomy. Resources include sensing, actuation, computation, energy, and human support. Autonomy specifies which decisions are delegated and when human participation is required (Parasuraman2000). These dimensions distinguish requirements that industry categories tend to merge. Within one factory, moving sealed containers and manipulating deformable materials impose different demands on contact control and recovery, and a laboratory may coordinate fixed instruments without a single mobile body. System composition and decision authority therefore require separate descriptions.

Industrial production, logistics, and agriculture involve transportation, manipulation, inspection, and process regulation. Physical AI offers value when variability makes fixed procedures costly to maintain. Parts arrive in unfamiliar configurations, crops vary in maturity, or equipment behavior changes with wear. The underlying pattern is common to these sectors. Fixed, engineered procedures are replaced by state estimation and adapted planning, while the process constraints within which the adaptation must operate remain fixed.

In an adaptive production system, visual and tactile observations update estimates of object and process state, while planning and control adjust operations within process constraints (lee2015; monostori2016). Variability enters as small batches, frequent product changeovers, and parts presented in unfixtured configurations, and the value is realized when changeover no longer requires re-engineering (vanbrussel1998). The benefit is measured by product quality, changeover time, resource consumption, and the effort of setting up a new task, while task variability and the resources required for changeover are the binding constraints. The limit of this development is the lights-out factory, in which no standing human presence remains on the floor. Lights-out operation does not eliminate human work. It moves that work to exception handling, supervision, and maintenance, and the cost of these activities becomes a primary economic variable rather than an overhead (Bainbridge, 1983).

Warehouses and distribution networks concentrate transportation and manipulation at high repetition rates, including automated storage and retrieval, mobile-robot fleets, sortation, palletizing and depalletizing, and parcel handling (wurman2008). The distinguishing problem is not the execution of any single motion but orchestration, which involves allocating physical work across many machines as demand fluctuates, replanning after disruption, and keeping physical flows consistent with the inventory records and delivery commitments carried by information systems (gerkey2004allocation). Local motion competence and network-level coordination are separate achievements. An operation can automate the former while the latter remains manual, and the gap between the two is closed in practice either by consistent state estimates or by buffer stock.

Agricultural settings concentrate the constraints of Physical AI, including biological variability, unstructured outdoor terrain, weather-dependent timing, and long deployment cycles. Operations under development span the production sequence, including inspection and patrol, seeding and planting, mechanical weeding, fertilization, plant protection, harvesting, and grading and sorting of produce (Bac et al., 2014), together with livestock monitoring and aquaculture operations (berckmans2017precision; fore2018precision). Value appears in two forms, namely precision, in which seed, chemical, and water inputs are reduced by acting at the resolution of individual plants or animals, and timeliness, in which operations are performed within short agronomic windows. The acceptance criteria are correspondingly biological and seasonal rather than volumetric, such as fruit harvested without bruising at the correct maturity, weeding achieved with a specified reduction in chemical use, or illness detected early enough for intervention.

Energy and mineral systems are high-risk and large-scale, including generation equipment, transmission corridors, pipelines, refineries, and open-pit and underground mines. Applications combine inspection of assets (such as turbine blades, transmission lines, and pipe corridors) (nguyen2018powerline), autonomous haulage and drilling (wang2017; marshall2008), and process regulation distributed across many devices. Equipment behavior changes with wear, which motivates continuously updated estimates of degradation in place of fixed maintenance schedules (jardine2006review). Limited access and the high consequence of failure shift the economics toward predictive operation and remote supervision. In these systems, safety cases rather than throughput determine which functions may be automated, and the allocation of authority between site automation and remote operation centers is itself a design decision.

Service applications place Physical AI in environments that are built for people rather than for machines. At one end are dedicated devices (single-purpose appliances that perform one task under human setup), and at the other are personalized embodied companions intended to share unstructured space with untrained users. Consumer-grade embodied products, from desktop companions to inexpensive legged and humanoid platforms, make this trajectory visible at retail prices, although the distance between demonstrations of interactive behavior and dependable household service remains substantial (srinivasa2012herb).

Human participation is an explicit design variable in these applications. Supervision, shared control, and selective delegation assign different responsibilities to users, operators, and machines. In human-facing services, decision authority and timely assistance matter alongside completion rates, so evaluation includes service quality, accessibility, and the burden placed on users and caregivers (hoffman2019fluency; nikolaidis2016mutual).

A household assistant must accommodate changing layouts and object locations, because neither residents nor their belongings remain arranged to suit a stored map (wisspeintner2009robocup). Cleaning, tidying, laundry, and meal preparation combine manipulation with continual re-estimation of where things are and what state they are in. Community services extend the same capabilities into semi-public space, including delivery to doors and lockers, patrol and monitoring, and check-ins on residents who live alone. In these settings, acceptance is determined not by peak capability but by the frequency and manner in which the system requests help. If a robot completes 90% of its tasks unaided but leaves the remaining 10% unfinished in mid-task, it shifts the burden to its users rather than removing it (forlizzi2006service).

A rehabilitation system must respect clinically established limits on force, range, and intensity while still challenging the patient enough for therapeutic effect. Applications include shared-control therapy devices that adjust assistance to measured performance, hospital logistics and delivery, continuous monitoring of activity, and assistance with activities of daily living (kyrarini2021survey). Clinical deployment adds requirements that are foreign to industrial settings. Interventions must demonstrate safety and efficacy under the conventions of clinical study (lo2010robot; esquenazi2012rewalk), responsibility for decisions must be traceable to accountable parties, and eldercare in particular must weigh privacy and dignity alongside capability (broadbent2009acceptance). In this domain, Physical AI cannot be separated from its regulatory and evidentiary context.

Retail, hospitality, professional cleaning, and food preparation occupy a middle ground, with spaces more structured than homes, because they are designed around service processes, yet occupied by the public and by staff whose cooperation cannot be assumed. Tasks include shelf monitoring and restocking, floor care, reception and guidance, and food handling to hygienic standards. Interaction with customers and employees is part of the task itself rather than a distraction from it, which places interface design and predictable, legible behavior on the critical path alongside manipulation competence. The economics are those of semi-structured spaces. Repetition is higher than in domestic service, while the tolerance for bespoke installation is lower than in industry.

Transportation, energy networks, and public infrastructure extend the concerns of the preceding sections across larger spatial and temporal scales. The unit of analysis shifts from one machine to populations of devices whose local actions must combine into system-level outcomes.

Vehicles and drones combine local perception and control with routing and coordination (yurtsever2020survey; murray2015). For road vehicles, the difficult problems are increasingly systemic rather than vehicular, including mixed traffic in which autonomous and human drivers share conventions, fleet scheduling together with charging and cleaning for shared robotaxi operation, and the interfaces between vehicle autonomy and traffic management (stern2018; varaiya2013). For low-altitude aircraft, coordination is the founding problem. Airspace organization, geofencing, and conflict resolution for large numbers of small vehicles must exist before individual autonomy is useful at scale (prevot2016utm). In both cases, the binding constraint is the coordination of many local planners toward network-level service quality.

Buildings, power systems, and water networks distribute sensing and actuation across many devices with no mobile body at all, an arrangement treated as a distinct system archetype in Section 1.5.6. Model predictive control of building climate, demand response across a power network, and leakage detection in a water distribution network illustrate the range (Afram and Janabi-Sharifi, 2014; siano2014demand; chan2018review). Communication capacity and consistent state estimates constrain coordination between local actions and system-wide outcomes. Value is measured by the reliability and continuity of service, energy and resource efficiency, and responsiveness to faults, observed over the scales of cities and seasons, which places a premium on sustained and validated operation rather than on peak performance.

Extreme environments impose additional restrictions. Disaster response combines difficult access, limited energy, and delayed or unavailable human intervention, making recovery mechanisms and bounded local autonomy particularly important. Search and rescue in collapsed structures, firefighting and hazardous-material intervention, and post-disaster inspection all require systems that decide and recover locally within a pre-authorized envelope and degrade safely when communication fails (murphy2014disaster; delmerico2019current; tranzatto2022cerberus). Public-safety applications sharpen the question of authority more than any other setting in this chapter. The conditions under which a machine may act, and the parties who are answerable for its actions, must be specified before capability is deployed rather than after.

Scientific applications use physical action to acquire evidence and guide inquiry. An autonomous laboratory selects experiments, operates instruments, measures outcomes, and revises subsequent choices (king2009; burger2020; macleod2020; dai2024). Scientific value depends on measurement validity, sample traceability, and reproducible interpretation, alongside experimental throughput.

The A-Lab illustrates this organization within a defined inorganic-materials synthesis workflow, integrating robotic operations, computational information, automated characterization, and active learning (szymanski2023alab). Its subsequent correction underscores the need to validate material identification and novelty claims separately from successful workflow execution (szymanski2026correction). Workflow autonomy (the reliable execution of planned operations) and epistemic autonomy (the production of claims that survive scrutiny) are different achievements, and evaluations in this field tend to measure the former while the value lies chiefly in the latter. Self-driven laboratory programs accordingly treat the validity chain from sample to published claim as part of the system to be engineered.

In scientific inquiry, simulation and digital twins, which Section 1.2.3 distinguishes from generic world models, serve as instruments for experiment design, parameter estimation, and controlled testing. Validation takes two forms. For policy training, it concerns whether simulated variation supports performance in reality. For an operational digital twin, it concerns the accuracy, timeliness, and uncertainty of the estimates used in decisions. The two uses impose different obligations. A training environment must cover the variations a policy will meet, while an operational twin must declare how far ahead, and with what confidence, its estimates may be trusted.

Autonomous laboratories change the division of cognitive labor in science rather than removing the scientist. In deployed systems, objective setting, prioritization among hypotheses, and the acceptance of evidence remain human responsibilities, while machines contribute breadth of search, uniformity of execution, and complete procedural memory. The interpretability of proposed experiments conditions trust. A suggestion whose rationale can be examined can also be disputed, and such dispute is one of the mechanisms by which science corrects itself. The productive design question, familiar from Section 1.5.1, is which parts of inquiry to delegate. Within a research program, the answer to this question is itself something to be established experimentally.

Space exploration combines scientific objectives with the most constrained communication, energy, and mass budgets in this chapter. Planetary rovers schedule a sol of activity within command latency (AutoNav), on-orbit systems service and assemble spacecraft, and in-situ instruments analyze samples that cannot be returned. Underwater operations share the pattern of difficult access, limited energy, and delayed or absent intervention (wynn2014autonomous). Both settings inherit bounded local autonomy as their organizing principle of deciding locally within a pre-authorized envelope, recording faithfully, and deferring the remainder to later analysis. This is the same principle identified for disaster response in Section 1.5.4, applied where the return of data is slower still.

Beneath the domain labels above, deployed systems assume a small number of recurring physical compositions, together with two modes that cut across them. Three compositions locate sensing and actuation together with computation in one body, in many bodies, or in the facility itself, while the two modes place either a human operator or a simulated world inside the loop. These compositions retrace the progression from single-agent systems through multi-agent collaboration to infrastructure-level Physical AI described in Section 1.4. Taken together, the five archetypes span the domains surveyed above, each of which can be read through the four dimensions of Section 1.5.1. Figure 1.5 shows both views together.

The first composition concentrates sensing, actuation, computation, and energy in a single mobile body, as in the household assistant (fu2025), the inspection quadruped (miki2022), the planetary rover, the delivery drone (loquercio2021). Its defining property is that resources and autonomy are co-located and bounded by one morphology, which in turn fixes the reachable task set. Most public attention attaches to this archetype, although the surveys above show it to be one composition among three.

The second composition distributes work across many cooperating bodies, as in warehouse fleets, agricultural machine teams, drone formations, cooperative transport (dorigo2021swarm). Capability emerges from task allocation, communication, and consensus rather than from any single member, and the fleet thereby acquires properties that its individual members lack, such as tolerance of the failure of one member (werfel2014collective; tolstaya2020decentralized; zhu2024self). Assessment correspondingly shifts to fleet-level quantities such as throughput, availability, and the reliability of the coordination mechanism itself.

The third composition embeds sensing and actuation in the facility itself, as in automated warehouses, lights-out factories, autonomous laboratories (gao2025unilabos), intelligent buildings, instrumented grids. No mobile body need exist. The laboratory described in Section 1.5.1, which coordinates fixed instruments without any mobile body, belongs to this composition. Engineering attention shifts from the agility of a body to the interfaces of a facility, including how materials, information, and people enter and leave, and the system boundary becomes an explicit design decision rather than the surface of a robot.

The first of the two cross-cutting modes extends a single person’s capabilities through intelligent hand tools, exoskeletons, augmented-reality task guidance, and collaborative robot cells (delooze2016exoskeletons; matheson2019human). The human retains decision making, while Physical AI supplies perception, guidance, and force at the point of work. Autonomy is deliberately low, and integration with the human is the design center rather than a constraint. Because responsibility remains with the operator, this archetype provides the economic baseline against which more autonomous alternatives are judged (iso10218_2025).

The other cross-cutting mode spans physical and simulated environments through sim-to-real policy training (tobin2017domain), operational digital twins, teleoperation with haptic and mixed-reality interfaces (hokayem2006bilateral), and hardware-in-the-loop test benches. The virtual channel may support development, remain part of operation, or serve both roles. Action may originate from a human operator, a learned policy, or a simulator, and its physical effect depends on how the resulting command is executed. The validation questions of Section 1.5.5, concerning whether simulated variation covers reality and how far estimates may be trusted, thereby become structural properties of the system rather than external checks.

The archetypes compose rather than compete with one another. An autonomous laboratory, for example, is an environment-scale installation that contains single agents, is trained through virtual-real interaction, is maintained by humans with augmenting tools, and is coordinated as a multi-agent system when replicated across sites. The physical composition fixes much of the resource profile of an application before any algorithm is selected, and the two modes then determine where authority resides and how much of the loop runs in simulation. For this reason, the four dimensions of Section 1.5.1 are best assessed per archetype rather than per industry.

This chapter introduces Physical AI as a system-level capacity to perceive physical states, maintain task-relevant representations of physical relationships and action consequences, and select and execute interventions through feedback under physical, operational, and computational constraints. It contrasts this capacity with digital intelligence, makes the contrast precise in Definition 1.1, and marks its boundaries against embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It then decomposes the capacity into four interdependent elements (Section 1.3), locates it on the axis of coupling between AI and the physical world (Section 1.4), and shows how deployed applications instantiate one closed loop under four assessment dimensions, across three physical compositions and two cross-cutting modes (Section 1.5). A single criterion runs through these perspectives. What a system can do is determined less by any individual model than by the integrated loop of perception, prediction, decision, action, and feedback, and by the physical and operational conditions under which the loop is sustained.

The remainder of this monograph develops that loop. Chapter 2 assembles the technical foundations shared by all four elements, including mathematical descriptions of the physical world, control theory and autonomous systems, embodied cognition, and learning and reasoning. The chapters that follow then take up the elements in order. Chapter 3 covers perception and state estimation. Chapters 4 and 5 cover physical data, simulation environments, and world models as resources that support prediction. Chapters 6 and 7 cover the foundation models and motor-control systems that realize decision-making and execution. Chapter 8 develops the definition, organization, task execution, and coordination of physical agents. Chapter 9 covers the hardware and systems that must sustain the loop reliably over long-term operation. The final chapters return to the questions left open here concerning how far the path toward general Physical AI extends (Chapter 10), how capabilities are evaluated and governed (Chapter 11), and what development strategies and longer-term outlook follow from them (Chapter 12).

The definitions and distinctions established in this chapter provide the vocabulary for all that follows. Whether a system amounts to Physical AI, where it sits between fixed automation and open-ended autonomy, and how much of the loop runs in simulation or under human authority are judged not by stated architecture but by demonstrated capability under specified conditions.

title: Latent Projection for Latent Planning
authors: Yoo Sung Jang,Michael Ryoo
comment: Accepted to the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Modeling Uncertainty in Robotic World Models
abstract:
Latent world models let an agent plan in latent space. The planner searches
for an action sequence that minimizes a cost, and that cost is often the
ℓ2\ell_{2} distance between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent.
The latent, however, is partly noise: the regularizer that prevents collapse
during world model training promotes variance in the directions carrying no
signal. We show that the
same regularizer also supplies the structure to prune that noise in the
latent. SIGReg drives the latent marginal to a standard Gaussian at every
step, and assuming further that the latent sequence is a Gauss–Markov process, the
transition is linear with its covariance
pinned by the map itself, z′|z∼𝒩⁡(A​z,I−A​A⊤)z^{\prime}\mid z\sim\mathcal{N}(Az,\,I-AA^{\top}).
Fitting the state dynamics AA therefore yields the covariance at no
additional cost, and in its eigenbasis each latent direction carries its own
uncertainty. Furthermore, constraining AA to be a normal matrix fixes that
basis across timesteps, so one eigenbasis measures the uncertainty over an
arbitrary number of steps and serves as a stable basis to compute the
planning cost on. We then restrict the ℓ2\ell_{2} cost to the kk-dimensional
subspace the state dynamics carry forward with the least uncertainty. The correction is
post hoc: the encoder, the predictor, the rollout, and the planner are all
left untouched, and only a single constrained matrix, AA, is fit. We
evaluate across six environments and show large gains on
the 2D navigation tasks, TwoRoom and PointMaze, raising success rate over
the plain ℓ2\ell_{2} cost by up to +54.7+54.7 points under a harder planning
setting.
Code is available at https://github.com/yjang43/lp2.
introduction:
Latent world models let an agent plan in representation space. An encoder
compresses an observation into a latent representation, a predictor advances that latent
under an action, and a planner searches for an action sequence that carries the
latent close to the goal. Every part of the loop involves the latent,
and learning this representation is a central design choice
that varies across latent world models
[34, 2, 57, 20, 19].

Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs)
[30], a recipe for general representation learning, are
widely chosen for their simplicity: a JEPA predicts the target’s representation
from the context’s representation, and that prediction objective is what shapes
the representation. Left unconstrained, the representation collapses to a constant,
so JEPAs rely on a regularizer to keep the
embedding informative. Recent instances of JEPA use regularizers that encourage
the embedding to lie in a structured distribution, most commonly an isotropic
Gaussian or a variant of it
[4, 50, 28].

LeWorldModel (LeWM) [34] builds a latent world model on this recipe,
training an encoder and predictor end to end from pixels with a two-term loss:
next-latent prediction and SIGReg [4], which pulls the
embedding toward an isotropic Gaussian. Similar to many other latent world models
[57, 2, 44],
LeWM plans by ranking candidate action sequences on the ℓ2\ell_{2} distance
between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent.

The simplicity of the cost, however, overlooks two sources of noise in the representation:
(i) the regularizer promotes variance in which noise fills the directions
carrying no signal; and (ii) the encoder, trained to represent observations,
retains content irrelevant to planning
[56, 49, 32]. The distance is then
measured partly along directions that carry no information about reaching the goal.

Ironically, the same regularizer that injects the noise also gives the
structure to repair it. The embedding is driven to be stationary under the
transition, and reading the latents as a Gaussian world model in the sense of
Klindt et al. [26], we find the noise is not free but pinned to
the transition itself: fit the state dynamics and the covariance comes with it.
By projecting onto a subspace determined by the covariance, we obtain a
representation restricted to the directions that are certain with respect to
the state dynamics. In general, the subspace moves under the transition,
but we show that it is fixed under a normality constraint on the state
dynamics. All of
this is post hoc: the only thing we fit is a constrained linear function; the
encoder, the predictor, and the planner are untouched.

Our main contributions are:

Uncertainty measure in a time-invariant basis.
Under SIGReg’s standard Gaussian marginal and a Gauss–Markov model,
the noise is pinned to the dynamics,
z′|z∼𝒩⁡(A​z,I−A​A⊤)z^{\prime}\mid z\sim\mathcal{N}(Az,\,I-AA^{\top}), where each eigenvector
carries its own uncertainty. Each step of the state dynamics generally
moves that basis. We show that when AA is a normal matrix, the retained subspace
is closed under the dynamics and the same basis serves every timestep.

A new planning cost. We measure the cost on the subspace
spanned by the kk eigenvectors of I−A​A⊤I-AA^{\top} with the smallest
eigenvalues: the directions the state dynamics carry forward with certainty.
Empirically, planning with this cost delivers large gains in success
rate on
the 2D navigation tasks, TwoRoom and PointMaze, of up to +54.7+54.7
points under a harder planning setting.

title: Steerable Pluralistic Policy Alignment from Anonymized Crowd Feedback
authors: Akansha Kalra,Ellen R. Novoseller,Vernon J. Lawhern,Daniel S. Brown
abstract:
Pluralistic alignment requires AI systems to learn from diverse populations whose preferences may reflect heterogeneous or even conflicting objectives, and to personalize their behavior to individual users.
Existing approaches in pluralistic alignment often assume access to annotator identities and rely on powerful pretrained representations to model individual preference variations.
We propose Preference-PCA Pluralistic Learning (P3L), a novel framework for pluralistic alignment that jointly learns trajectory embeddings and the shared basis of preference directions via PCA decomposition from heterogeneous crowd feedback without requiring annotator identities.
At test time, our approach enables rapid and accurate personalized reward learning and downstream policy optimization.
Experiments across multiple embodied control tasks demonstrate that P3L enables steerable personal alignment that generalizes beyond the offline dataset to out-of-distribution new users and attains competitive RL and test performance, while substantially reducing computational cost and supporting variable adaptation query budgets.
